name: Nebraska Examiner
title: At least 61 employees left Nebraska Department of Economic Development within 15 months
description: LINCOLN — After 26 years working in Nebraska’s Department of Economic Development, former director of field operations Sheryl Hiatt said she didn’t want to retire, but she felt she had no other option. According to Hiatt, changes made within the department — most of which came after Gov. Jim Pillen’s appointment of Maureen Larsen as […]
text:
Maureen Larsen, director of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development and former general counsel to the governor, at an inaugural public roundtable of Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen's cabinet. April 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — After 26 years working in Nebraska’s Department of Economic Development, former director of field operations Sheryl Hiatt said she didn’t want to retire, but she felt she had no other option.
According to Hiatt, changes made within the department — most of which came after Gov. Jim Pillen’s appointment of Maureen Larsen as interim director in July 2025 — made her time working there unpleasant enough that she chose to leave earlier than she previously planned.
She isn’t the first former DED employee to make such claims, as several have said the impacts of budget cuts and other new policies were designed to push employees out and shrink the department.
“They’re not doing anything right, and just tearing it down for the sake of tearing it down,” Hiatt said of the current DED leadership.
In less than a year-and-a-half, at least 61 employees have left DED, with only two of those involuntary terminations, according to department spokesman Justin Pinkerman. The department currently employs 69 full-time workers.
Data that Pinkerman shared with the Examiner shows that DED hit its peak of full-time employees in May 2025 at 115.25, which had dropped to 69.75 as of Aug. 26 this year. In that same time, Pinkerman said in an email, the department made 15 new hires, which factored in means that 61 employees left DED within that period.
The decimal points represent part-time employees in how the department measures its full-time equivalents.
Unprecedented attrition
Justin Hubly, executive director of state employees union Nebraska Association of Public Employees, said he’s never seen attrition numbers like this in any state agency, calling it “mind-boggling.”
“We ought to be doing everything we can right now to grow our state, considering the budget situation,” Hubly said. “And losing frontline staff at the Department of Economic Development is certainly not the way to do that.”
Pillen appointed Larsen interim director in July, replacing former director K.C. Belitz, and announced she would become the permanent director in November. Prior to her appointment, Larsen served as Pillen’s general counsel and deputy director of his Policy Research Office.
Pinkerman has said the department’s downsizing is part of a winding down of pandemic-era programs. He said because of this, the department’s spending dropped more than $185 million between fiscal years 2024-25 and 2025-26.
Hiatt said the economic recovery division — charged with managing DED’s allotment of American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds — at one point had more than 20 employees, and now DED’s website lists seven employees in the division.
A notable departure was the division’s former administrator, Javier Saldaña Jr., who left in June to take a job with the city of Omaha as its deputy chief of staff for economic development.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Hiatt said DED’s housing division also has been hit hard in the latest downsizing. She estimated the department had about 15 housing staff in early 2025, and now DED’s website displays six staff in the division.
That number may continue to shrink, as Pinkerman confirmed the department moved three housing positions — filled by employees based across Nebraska — to its central headquarters in Lincoln. Pinkerman said those employees were told they must work from the Lincoln office to continue in their positions.
Hiatt said one employee who lives in Omaha resigned shortly after receiving the order. Hubly confirmed this and said he believes the employee would have stayed at DED if he hadn’t been told to relocate. Hubly said he found it strange that the employee was asked to move, given that his supervisor in Omaha was not asked to relocate.
Of the two other affected employees, one based in the Panhandle chose to comply with the order, which took effect Aug. 24. Hubly said the other, based in Kearney, refused to move under their contract, which states that employees asked to transfer more than 50 miles can refuse, but the agency can terminate them in response.
Hubly confirmed that DED has initiated a layoff procedure for the Kearney employee. He said he found it frustrating because the employee could have been transferred to a DED vacancy near Kearney. Hubly said DED’s list of vacant positions is “dozens long,” and department officials didn’t give him a good reason why this employee couldn’t be transferred.
Pinkerman said there are currently 33 vacant positions at DED and the openings do not have assigned locations. He noted the department is currently hiring for an economist and a paralegal, and plans to add more job postings in other divisions in the future.
Pinkerman said the positions DED is seeking to fill were requisitioned before a hiring freeze Pillen enacted in a July memo. These positions, along with any new job postings, will be reviewed by the State Budget Division to ensure they align with the governor’s spending objectives.
Impact on rural communities
Hiatt said she knew of at least three vacant regional positions, including her own, that have not been filled, but couldn’t say if there were any close to Kearney. However, she noted that the placement of regional positions is not set in stone, and DED officials have the power to move them.
Pinkerman said the three impacted positions work on state housing programs that are being transferred to the Nebraska Investment Finance Authority under a bill the Legislature passed this year. DED has taken steps this year to transition the administration of some of its housing programs to the independent agency.
According to Hiatt, these regional positions have existed for decades and were added after the creation of the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, which has not yet been transferred to NIFA. She said the original purpose of the positions was to forge connections with local housing nonprofits to help generate applications, which later evolved into monitoring the projects awarded in their respective regions.
Hiatt said it’s difficult to find developers willing to work on housing projects in rural Nebraska right now, so losing that direct line of support will be challenging. She described the relocation order as a “big slap in the face to rural Nebraska.”
The reductions to regional DED positions, combined with limitations placed on field staff while she was there, made Hiatt feel that the department was intentionally reducing its footprint in rural Nebraska.
The number of DED employees who worked outside of Lincoln or Omaha fluctuated over the years, according to Hiatt. Prior to the latest downsizing, she said, it typically ranged between 15-20 employees, and now it’s down to about 10.
Leadership concerns
Hiatt listed several other changes implemented under Larsen’s leadership that she claimed were designed to push people out of the department. Following Pillen’s return-to-work order, Hiatt said, employees working from the Lincoln office were not allowed to leave before 4:30 p.m., and Larsen and other DED leadership routinely patrolled the office to make sure workers remained in their cubicles.
“It doesn’t matter what you’re doing as long as your butt is in the chair,” Hiatt said.
When asked about this, Pinkerman said, “Director Larsen has taken responsibility to ensure the agency’s compliance with the return-to-work order.” He did not answer whether these patrols were still in practice.
Under Larsen’s leadership, Hiatt said, communication across DED divisions also sharply declined. Before Larsen was appointed, Hiatt said, division leaders would hold regular meetings at least once a month; Larsen attended a couple and then canceled them.
Nebraska Legislature approves Maureen Larsen’s appointment as DED director

The cancellation drew concerns from division leaders, Hiatt said, as they were already seeing signs of degrading communication. In response, she said, division leaders opted to hold their own meetings without Larsen. Hiatt said she took the initiative to set the recurring calendar item.
This lasted until shortly after Stacey Parr was named deputy director of DED. Hiatt said Parr told division leaders that Larsen wanted to restructure the management meetings, so she canceled the calendar items.
The meetings Larsen scheduled had short agendas with little to no substance, Hiatt said. The last one she attended had two agenda items, one of which involved where employees should park outside the Lincoln office, she said.
Pinkerman said Larsen “changed the cadence of the agency’s regular management meetings to aid agency productivity and better prioritize strategic objectives.” He said DED leaders have scheduled daily meetings and hold monthly management meetings with division directors.
Overall, Hiatt said, DED’s new leadership showed a lack of care in managing the employees who work for them and didn’t put in effort to recognize their work.
Two weeks before her last day on June 2, Hiatt said, she sent an all-staff email announcing her departure, in which she included some leadership tips. She said she didn’t hear any response from Larsen, and on June 2 Parr sent a one-sentence email to DED staff acknowledging that it was Hiatt’s last day with the department.
After she cleaned out her desk at the Lincoln office, Hiatt said, another division director walked her out of the office. She said they reminisced about how former deputy director Dan Curran handled departing employees.
“Do you remember when Dan was here and somebody would leave … and we’d have cake and Dan would say really nice things about the person that was leaving?” Hiatt said the director asked her. “And I started laughing, and I said, ‘Yeah, this is not that.’”
Larsen and other DED leaders declined requests for in-person or phone interviews, instead answering questions via email through Pinkerman. Pinkerman said the agency does this for documentation and to ensure accuracy in their responses.
“Having this documentation allows DED to hold media outlets accountable for fairly and accurately reporting the agency’s statements,” Pinkerman said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Trump’s beef import plan: The trade off facing Missouri farmers and consumers
description: President Donald Trump has announced a temporary plan to suspend tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef over 90 days. The administration hopes the additional imports will increase supply and bring down record-high beef prices. For families facing record-high beef prices, any meaningful relief at the grocery store would be welcome. […]
text:
USDA Supervisory Agricultural Meat Graders at the annual national beef correlation event, Aug. 13, 2019. In 2019, the top four beef packers — Tyson Foods, JBS, Cargill Beef and National Beef — processed around three quarters of the nation’s beef in 27 facilities across the nation (Preston Keres/USDA).President Donald Trump has announced a temporary plan to suspend tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef over 90 days. The administration hopes the additional imports will increase supply and bring down record-high beef prices.
For families facing record-high beef prices, any meaningful relief at the grocery store would be welcome. But in Missouri, which ranks among the nation’s top three states for beef cows and has about 3.85 million cattle and calves, the plan raises a broader question: Can more imports ease beef prices without disrupting Missouri’s fragile cattle-herd recovery?
Today’s high beef prices reflect tight cattle supplies years in the making. Drought forced many ranchers to reduce their herds as pasture and forage became scarce, while the cost of raising cattle climbed sharply. Because cattle herds take years to rebuild, supplies remain tight while consumer demand remains strong.
Missouri has experienced the same contraction. USDA data show that the state had about 4.11 million cattle and calves in January 2023, including 1.95 million beef cows. By January 2026, the cattle inventory had fallen to 3.85 million head, including about 1.81 million beef cows. In just three years, Missouri’s total cattle inventory declined by about 260,000 head, or 6%, while its beef cow herd fell by roughly 139,000, or 7%.
Cattle producers worry that the import plan comes just as the industry is showing early signs of recovery. National USDA data show that the number of young female cattle kept for breeding increased 3% from a year ago, an important step toward rebuilding the herd. But expansion requires significant financial commitment. According to USDA data cited by the American Farm Bureau Federation, operating costs for cow-calf producers reached a record $1,762 per head in 2025, more than $400—or nearly 30%—higher than in 2020.
The timing adds to those concerns. The Farm Bureau estimates that roughly 70% of spring-born calves are sold between September and November, overlapping with the administration’s 90-day import window. Producers worry that a rapid increase in imports during this important selling period could put downward pressure on cattle prices and make herd expansion less attractive. If that slows rebuilding, tight domestic beef supplies could persist longer.
The concerns of cattle producers should not obscure the problem facing consumers. Ground beef prices have reached record highs, putting additional pressure on families already facing high grocery bills.
Imports offer one way to increase supply relatively quickly. The United States already imports lean beef that is mixed with fattier American beef to make ground beef, a common practice in the U.S. beef industry. Additional imports could therefore help ease some of the pressure on prices.
This leaves policymakers with competing concerns: providing consumers relief from high beef prices while maintaining the conditions needed for cattle producers to rebuild domestic herds.
The policy should make the additional imported beef cheaper. But how much will consumers actually save? Normally, beef imported beyond certain quotas can be subject to a 26.4% tariff, which the plan would temporarily suspend. Because the additional 300,000 metric tons represent only a small share of the overall U.S. beef market, the effect on grocery-store prices may be more limited.
The increase in imports has also raised questions about food safety and traceability. Earlier this month, nearly 30,000 pounds of Argentine beef were recalled after entering the country without the required import reinspection. No illnesses were reported, but the incident illustrates why maintaining strong inspection and oversight remains important as imports increase.
The administration is now looking beyond imports for ways to bring down beef prices, an increasingly visible affordability issue heading into the midterm elections. On Friday, Trump announced plans to make it easier for farmers and ranchers to process and sell their own beef, while criticizing the concentration of the meatpacking industry. The beef-processing industry is highly concentrated, with the four largest meatpackers handling about 85% of U.S. steer and heifer purchases. More competition and processing options could give producers additional ways to reach consumers, although the details of the proposal are still emerging.
Consumers need relief from high beef prices, while cattle producers face the costly, years-long process of rebuilding their herds. Imports can help meet demand when domestic supplies are tight, while greater processing competition and a stronger domestic herd could expand supply over the longer term. The challenge is finding the right balance during this period of transition.
That balance matters especially in Missouri, where cattle production supports not only farmers but feed suppliers, veterinarians, livestock markets, equipment dealers, and other rural businesses.
What happens over the next 90 days will therefore be watched closely at both the grocery store and on Missouri farms.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: From NJ to Louisiana and back: One Elizabeth woman’s path through ICE detention
description: Asylum seeker Lourdes Rosero believed her work permit would spare her from potential deportation. She was wrong.
text:
Protesters with Ice Out rally outside the Monmouth County Courthouse in Freehold on March 27, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The immigration agents stormed the Savino Del Bene warehouse from every angle: emergency doors, loading docks, the main entrance. 
By the time they reached Lourdes Rosero, the warehouse’s cafeteria had been converted into a processing station, with agents holding laptops, checking names against lists. Dogs and drones circled outside. Black cars parked along the front lot as far as Rosero could see. 
It was the brisk morning of Oct. 29, 2025, when Rosero got detained at a warehouse in the Avenel section of Woodbridge where she had worked daily for months. 
“It was like watching a movie,” she said in an interview in Spanish at her second-floor apartment in Elizabeth. “Like they were going after narcos. Not me. It was like they were looking for something very criminal.” 
Countless raids have happened in New Jersey since President Donald Trump launched a mass deportation and detention effort at the start of his second term. The raid that swept up Rosero and roughly 50 other workers was one of the largest here since the crackdown began. 
The New Jersey Monitor met with Rosero and her daughter, Diana, immigrants from Ecuador who have lived in New Jersey since 2021, over the course of several months. Rosero described her journey from the warehouse floor to her detainment at the Elizabeth Detention Center to the LaSalle ICE processing center in Louisiana to her uncertain future back in Elizabeth.
As a woman living in the U.S. without citizenship, she fears what’s next for her and for others who came to America seeking a better life under a new era of immigration enforcement. 
Lourdes Rosero of Elizabeth was arrested at the Savino Del Bene warehouse in the Avenel section of Woodbridge during an immigration raid on Oct. 29, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Rosero is one of roughly 11 million immigrants living in the U.S. without legal status. An estimated 500,000 live in New Jersey, with most coming from Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and Ecuador, according to the Migration Policy Institute. 
She and her daughter flew here in 2021 and overstayed their visa after seeing what they said was the “chance to have better days in our lives,” and the possibility to escape the domestic abuse she suffered for years from her former partner in Ecuador. 
Rosero believed she took a legal path. She filed for asylum, obtained an employment authorization document allowing her to legally work, and paid some taxes. She had no prior criminal charges or conviction. 
When agents approached her the morning of the warehouse raid, she handed over her work permit believing it would prove she could legally be there. They handcuffed her, and she still hasn’t gotten that work permit back. 
“I thought to myself, ‘I’m different because I have a work permit to be here, maybe the others don’t. I’m good, just stay calm. I have protection,’” she said. “Then I saw they didn’t care. They weren’t treating me any different. I said, ‘Why are you detaining me if I have a work permit? Look, I’m working here legally.’” 
The agent told her she had two options. She could sign a form for voluntary self deportation and receive $1,000 to restart her life in Ecuador, though she wasn’t sure where she’d end up because the Trump administration has not been deporting people to their native countries. Her other choice: She could be detained and fight her case through the judicial system.
It was a choice thousands of immigrants like her across New Jersey have faced in recent years — fight to stay, or take the money and go. 
She texted Diana, who continued to work so they could pay rent that month. 
“Fight, Ma,” her text said. 
With two migrant detention centers in New Jersey regularly cycling through thousands of people arrested in mass raids or individual targeted stops by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, immigration court hearings are a revolving door of people trying to find out what’s happening to them. 
Newark is home to one of the state’s two immigration courts. People largely appear virtually from jail — though not necessarily in New Jersey — and speak through an interpreter. Many appear in orange or tan jail uniforms, sitting in a metal chair for a hearing lasting mere minutes. Sometimes it takes longer to bring in the next detainee than to hold the hearing itself. 
On a December day, one judge saw a steady procession of cases, more than 20 people in one hour. Some were seen hours after being detained. Others had their cases rescheduled after months of detention. 
Among the detainees: A mother who sat with her son in her lap. A woman, 27 weeks pregnant, who left the hospital for the hearing. A Passaic County man who begged the judge to give him a work permit, to no avail. And a Toms River man who the judge decided to deport to Ecuador instead of the man’s home country of Colombia.
Other than a prosecutor representing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, lawyers aren’t typically present. The judge presents a few options: fight the case, accept voluntary departure to countries like Honduras and Ecuador, or explore options for relief with an attorney. 
Amy Torres, the executive director of New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice, said chaos is the only consistent hallmark of the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
The absence of lawyers is not incidental, said Amy Torres, executive director of the New Jersey Alliance for Immigrant Justice. Unlike U.S. citizens who get arrested, immigrants detained by ICE do not have the right to a lawyer provided by the government, leaving many scrambling hours after an arrest.
“It is on them to find the representation,” Torres said. “And when we know people are getting transferred within a day at times, sometimes put on the path to deportation within a day, you can imagine how difficult it is to find a pro bono attorney within that period of time. It’s just nearly impossible — but that’s exactly how it’s set up to be.”
Nationally, voluntary departures increased by 28-fold in 2025 compared to the prior year, according to the Deportation Data Project, a group that uses public records to track immigration enforcement, detention, and deportations. While ICE is supposed to publish numbers, the agency’s tracker is not updated regularly.
Before Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, ICE was carrying out roughly 300 arrests nationally per day. That number spiked to more than 1,500 per day by July 2026, the Deportation Data Project found. In New Jersey, the numbers were even higher: immigration agents arrested 2,080 people in July, the highest monthly total in four years and a nearly 150% increase from May to July. 
New Jersey now ranks eighth in the nation for immigration arrests. 
Some people ICE arrests have criminal convictions, but largely for petty offenses. An analysis by the Prison Policy Initiative found that 34% of people ICE arrested in New Jersey between May and October 2025 had pending criminal charges, with the most common charge being a traffic offense. The data did not break out what share of New Jersey detainees had no criminal record at all.
One of the defining features of Trump’s second term — distinct even from his first — is the widening of who ICE targets, Torres said.
“It actually doesn’t matter if you were undocumented or not,” she said. “We’re seeing even people with valid work visas, student visas — we’re even seeing green card holders — being detained and arrested by ICE. Things that used to be a safeguard, like a green card, that’s no longer the case.”
ICE officials did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
ICE Agents outside Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall during protests on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Department of Homeland Security officials have repeatedly defended their sweeping enforcement against visa holders, green card holders, and even people with pending applications, saying any status short of citizenship does not protect people from arrest. Trump has framed the crackdown as a fulfillment of a 2024 campaign promise, claiming ICE targets the “worst of the worst.” 
The White House’s website characterizes enforcement as “protecting U.S. sovereignty and safeguarding American communities.” 
“By prioritizing enforcement and accountability, the administration is restoring integrity to the immigration system and ensuring the law is applied consistently. These efforts protect American workers, reduce strain on local communities, and reinforce the nation’s right to control its borders and determine who enters the United States,” the website reads.  
ICE has grown its footprint in New Jersey since Trump’s second term began. Former Gov. Phil Murphy, a Democrat, signed a 2021 bill banning public and private entities from entering into contracts to house immigrant detainees, but a federal judge struck down the private entities provision as unconstitutional. That allowed private prison firm CoreCivic to retain its contract to detain immigrants at the 300-bed Elizabeth Detention Center and cleared the way for Geo Group to open Delaney Hall, a 1,100-bed immigrant jail in Newark, in May 2025. 
Federal officials plan to convert a vacant Roxbury warehouse into a mass processing center that could handle nearly 1,500 people. Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Attorney General Jen Davenport, both Democrats, and the township’s GOP leadership sued in March to block the project, arguing officials bypassed required environmental and procedural reviews before purchasing the $129 million site. The Trump administration in June said it was abandoning the Roxbury plan, then reversed course in July.
U.S. Rep. Rob Menendez, a Democrat whose district includes Delaney Hall, has visited the facility dozens of times since it opened. He regularly meets with detainees inside and checks on medical services and food options in the jail, which he says are both substandard. He maintains the detention center never should have opened. 
He noted that 2026 marks just the second year of Geo Group’s 15-year contract with the federal government to house detainees at Delaney Hall. 
“It makes me sad. Sad that this is the reality,” he said, speaking outside the jail while alarms blared, as they often do randomly when protesters and press gather. “I fear that not enough people are waking up or opening their eyes to what’s happening here, and that if more people don’t engage and see what’s happening, then they’re going to be silent while these things are happening in all of our communities.”
Menendez remains cautiously optimistic, though, and says he believes the injustices happening inside the immigration detention centers will end someday. 
“I hope it’s tomorrow. I hope it’s the day after. I wish it was January of last year, but I know it will end, and we just have to do our best to keep people safe and limit the damage until it is done, finally,” he said. 
That damage already is growing. Rosero’s arrest is part of a string of large-scale ICE operations that have hit New Jersey over the past year, uprooting families and workers from their Garden State homes. 
The raid that led to Rosero’s arrest saw 46 people detained by federal agents. In July 2025, agents arrested another 20 or so people at Alba Wine and Spirits in Edison. The following month, they took 29 people from an Edison warehouse. This past June, they detained 18 people at El Oaxaqueño, a family-owned restaurant and market in Lakewood, including six of its workers. 
Last November, agents raided a seafood market in Newark, the second at that location since Trump took office. Heavily armed agents in masks and bulletproof vests surrounded the business and shut down nearby streets. Alarmed neighbors shouted at them. 
Masked, armed agents stand outside Ocean Seafood Depot during an immigration raid in Newark on Nov. 19, 2025. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
That time, 13 workers were taken to Delaney Hall. But agents swiftly move people from facility to facility, meaning detainees don’t always remain in New Jersey for long. 
Sometimes, people are taken in one-off instances: a pastor stopped by agents in unmarked cars in March, a contractor pulled over near the Long Branch Home Depot and taken to Delaney Hall, an 18-year-old detained after visiting her friend at the Elizabeth Detention Center. Immigration groups like Eyes on ICE regularly post on social media when they spot agents detaining residents in places like North Plainfield, Freehold, and Dover. 
At a know-your-rights meeting held by local immigration group Make the Road, a landscaper named Victor said a homeowner threatened to call ICE on him after arguing with his boss over the cost. He feared returning to work, knowing co-workers had seen those threats carried out. Other attendees shared stories of the dictatorships they escaped in Latin America and parallels they see under the Trump administration. Even those who have become U.S. citizens said they were scared, asking about racial profiling. 
Immigrants’ fear and silence makes it difficult for local advocates to track the people ICE agents take. Torres described enforcement over the past 20 months not as a coordinated strategy but as deliberate disorder: mass raids at warehouses one week, arrests at immigration hearings the next, then targeted stakeouts, then nothing at all.
“The most consistent thing that we’ve seen is chaos,” Torres said. “Whenever we think we’re learning about a new emerging trend, things shift.”
Rosero considered voluntarily leaving. On one hand, it would allow her to return to her home country, where many of her relatives remain, with $1,000 in her pocket. But she had spent years seeking asylum and had obtained a work permit.
“I was between the sword and the wall,” she said. “I just knew I didn’t want to leave my daughter alone.”  
Rosero first was held at the Elizabeth Detention Center, two-and-a-half miles from her apartment. She spent eight days there, along with other women from the warehouse. Then an agent woke her at 3 a.m. ordering her to collect her things, and Rosero and other detainees were chained at the waist and handcuffed. They were loaded into a van, and when one woman who spoke English overheard agents talking about airports and airplanes, panic spread through the group. 



Quotation







That tranquility, the feeling of being able to go anywhere, knowing you’re not doing anything wrong, of feeling truly free, it’s totally gone.


– Lourdes Rosero


They were flown to a detention facility in LaSalle, about two miles northwest of Jena, Louisiana. She believes she arrived at 1 a.m., but she was losing track of time and days. Rosero had no lawyer confirmed to help her, and her daughter — in between work shifts at a daycare center — was piecing together contacts, drawing on a network of immigration organizations in New Jersey to find lawyers and navigating the mountain of paperwork she suddenly faced. 
In Louisiana, Rosero was handed an orange uniform. Detainees donned other colors if they were seen as “problems,” Rosero said, or if they were to be deported. She was depressed upon arriving at the dingy facility, and although she made friends, she struggled to see the path forward, she said. 
One night after barely eating the detention center food, she said — looking disgusted while recalling it — she sat on her hard mattress observing her uniform. She unfolded the pants in the dim light of the cell block and spotted writing along the leg: “I trust in my God, because for Him, nothing is impossible.” 
She cried as she recounted how she felt seeing that. It gave her the strength and courage she had sought throughout her journey. 
“I had complained so much about the uniform. That it was torn, used, dirty. And then I saw that, and I said, ‘Forgive me, Father. You’ve given me a message,’” she said. 
On Nov. 13, she had a hearing via Zoom inside the jail, where a judge set bail at $15,000. She doesn’t recall what was said, mostly because it unfolded entirely in English and she felt so emotional. But when the translator finally addressed her, she understood the payment requirement. Diana had been working with local organizations to help cover the bail, paid it by Nov. 18, and Rosero was released. 
“I felt peace. It felt like freedom,” she said.
A volunteer from a Louisiana-based immigration group picked her up, fed her dinner, housed her overnight, and helped her board a plane the next morning to Newark, where Diana met her. 
It’s been nearly a year since her arrest. Rosero remains unable to work without her permit. She measures her recovery in blocks walked outside her apartment. For the first few weeks, she didn’t step outside at all, staying inside her two-bedroom home. Then she started pacing the backyard. Then the front. 
Recently, she started walking to the bodega on the corner, and to Christ the King Church near Elizabeth. She’s still apprehensive when she has to walk to Broad Street, and remains cautious of black cars passing by her. 
“That tranquility, the feeling of being able to go anywhere, knowing you’re not doing anything wrong, of feeling truly free, it’s totally gone,” she said. “I don’t know when it will come back. I didn’t do anything wrong when I was arrested, so I fear it can happen again at any moment. I’m working my way to bravery.” 
In February, she appeared virtually before an immigration judge for the first hearing in her asylum case. She barely spoke — the hearing was in English and she didn’t understand most of it. The judge set an August deadline to present her evidence, including notarized documents and proof of when she entered the country. The cost of her legal battle has grown to an amount she can barely say out loud, more than $25,000. Most of it is funded through community organizations and her daughter’s hourly salary. They keep a tight budget for food and rent, although their landlord is understanding of Rosero’s situation. 
She’s studying for an insurance license now, looking for new ways to support herself and her daughter. She’s also in therapy to work through the nightmares and trauma of what she suffered. She keeps in touch with women she met at the jail through a WhatsApp group chat, “Las Gallinas,” or The Chickens.
She attends prayer groups, and constantly thanks God for helping her stay in America and keeping her from returning to Ecuador, where she says things have gotten worse as drugs run rampant and criminals take over towns.
Some days, Rosero says she’s fine, finding her way to the next day. But other days, she sees through her window a black car driving by slowly. 
Her next court date is later this month. She’s hoping she will have her work permit again by then, despite her confusion about how to get it reissued and her fear of visiting government offices. 
Still, she remains positive.
“God brought me here for a reason,” she said. “I still have many things to do.”
A car drives past Christ the King Church in Hillside on May 18, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Frustrated districts, ‘blindsided’ lawmakers: Inside the ending of an Oklahoma school supper program
description: A student picks out an apple in the school cafeteria at Thelma R. Parks Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 13, 2025. Oklahoma districts have complained of a recent decision by the state Department of Education to cancel a federally funded school supper program. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
text:
A student picks out an apple in the school cafeteria at Thelma R. Parks Elementary in Oklahoma City on Aug. 13, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — For eight years, Hartshorne Public Schools has designed its bus schedules, personnel contracts, lunch times and school hours around serving a late-afternoon supper to students. 
The southeast Oklahoma district stretched its school day to seven hours instead of the typical six, adding academic enrichment and homework help time after 2 p.m. to qualify for a federal program that pays for the third meal, Superintendent Jason Lindley said. 
Two weeks into Hartshorne’s school year, the Oklahoma State Department of Education shocked districts statewide when it announced it would discontinue the extended-day third meal option on Oct. 1, when the next federal fiscal year begins. The agency cited a lack of compliance with federal rules as the reason the program, known as Expanded Learning Time, must come to an end.
The timing of the Aug. 18 announcement — after the start of school and only weeks before the program’s cancellation — has prompted frustration from district leaders, state lawmakers and anti-hunger advocates. State records show 132 school sites, all in rural areas, were approved for the Expanded Learning Time option for the 2025-26 year.
Hundreds of pages of emails and documents Oklahoma Voice obtained through an open records request with the Education Department laid bare the confusion and disappointment directed at the state agency. The correspondence also details the agency’s ongoing dispute and legal concerns with a nonprofit involved in the supper initiative.
Multiple district leaders, including Lindley, emailed the head of the agency with complaints about the program’s cancellation, records show.
“To lose the program, especially in an email at the end of August, you basically have less than 45 days to end your program,” Lindley told Oklahoma Voice. “That’s a very short time frame in education. With schedules written, with contracts signed, with everything set up for the rest of the school year to have a third meal, we’re really going to have to work to find some solutions to this new problem.”
Hunger Free Oklahoma, which advocates for food access, publicly voiced its disappointment in the decision, which it said comes at a time when Oklahoma families are facing growing pressure on their grocery budgets and when other food assistance programs are experiencing cuts. 
Administrative complexity is not a good reason to end the program, the organization wrote in a public statement.
State Superintendent Lindel Fields encouraged districts to continue feeding students by switching to a similar federal program that provides snacks during after-school activities. 
State Superintendent Lindel Fields, center, speaks at an Oklahoma State Board of Education meeting June 8 at the Oklahoma State Department of Education building in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
He said his administration decided to discontinue the Expanded Learning Time option at the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s recommendation. USDA regulates school meal programs.
The question now shouldn’t be how to preserve the extended-day meal option, Education Department spokesperson Tara Thompson said.
“It should be how we work together to lawfully and sustainably meet the needs of the children and communities in Oklahoma,” she said. “That is why our work cannot end with identifying a compliance problem.”
Thirteen districts have begun the application process to transition from Expanded Learning Time to the after-school snack program, Thompson said. Meanwhile, school breakfasts and lunches remain unaffected.
The agency said it has no documents reflecting the total amount of federal funds the program encompassed.
Why is Oklahoma’s school supper program being canceled?
In an Aug. 20 video call with district leaders, which Oklahoma Voice has viewed, an Education Department official overseeing the program said state and federal authorities had discovered multiple cases of noncompliance with Expanded Learning Time rules.
“There was no identifiable academic or enrichment activity beyond the meal in many of those cases,” Kassi Reddell, the state director for the Child and Adult Care Food Program, said during the call. “If we were to remove that meal, effectively it would mean there was no program remaining.”
State officials had been warning since January that the program was in question and have been encouraging new applicants to pursue after-school snack funding instead, Reddell said.
That’s “just completely untrue,” Haworth Public Schools Superintendent Jerrod Lundry said during the call.
The state agency sent emails as recently as July 30 recommending districts sign up for the Expanded Learning Time option, he said. Lundry said there was no advance warning the program would be abruptly cut off.
Haworth, a district of 400 students in the far southeast corner of the state, doesn’t have the funds to set up an after-school program in the middle of the academic year, he said. Even if it did, that option likely would feed fewer students.
“We are a large geographical district,” Lundry told Oklahoma Voice. “We would not be able to run two different sets of buses. So even if we did run an after-school program, it would be for kids who have working parents who could come pick them up, and those are not necessarily the kids who need that third meal.”
Oklahoma lawmakers object to third meal discontinuation
The sudden cancellation has drawn bipartisan opposition from the state Legislature. Fifty Oklahoma lawmakers from both parties and chambers co-signed a scathing letter penned by Sen. David Bullard, R-Durant.
Bullard urged the state agency to suspend the changes until after the current school year. He questioned whether the Education Department had the authority to discontinue the program in the first place. 
“This policy appears to solve no demonstrated problem while creating a very real one,” Bullard wrote. “Schools that planned responsibly are being forced to change course after the school year has begun. Employees have already been hired. Food has already been purchased. Taxpayer dollars have already been committed. And at the end of all of it, children who were being fed may now go without a meal.”
He did not return a request for further comment.
The head of the Senate Education Committee, Sen. Adam Pugh, said he and other lawmakers were “blindsided” by the agency’s announcement.
Sen. Adam Pugh, R-Edmond, speaks at a Senate Education Committee meeting May 20, 2025, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Pugh, R-Edmond, said he directed a member of Senate staff to send an email to Fields to object to the lack of forewarning and consultation of lawmakers. 
The message, which the open records request revealed, warned the state Senate has developed a “​​growing frustration with (the Education Department) acting outside the scope of their authority.”
In an interview with Oklahoma Voice, Pugh said those frustrations started bubbling with the agency’s unexpected interpretation of a new law that doubled elementary recess time. 
Lawmakers and district leaders were caught off guard when the Education Department announced over the summer that it would no longer permit schools to count recess minutes toward instructional hours, causing a logistical headache with limited time to react, he said. 
Pugh said he believes the agency “acted rashly” with its latest decision. Although there is merit to scrutinizing the third meal program, he said the federal government did not require the state to cancel it immediately.
“Delayed implementation, it’s really that simple,” Pugh said. “Let’s give schools runways to implement these big things as opposed to pulling the rug from underneath them when school has already started.”
Feed the Kids denies fraud allegations in federal nutrition program
As concerns over the extended-day meals grew, a dispute has been brewing for several months between Fields’ administration and a nonprofit that many districts hired to help administer the program.
The conflict finally spilled into public view in May when Fields publicly called for an investigation into Feed the Kids, which oversaw Expanded Learning Time and after-school snack programs at more than 50 school sites. 
In exchange for a 15% fee, the nonprofit helped schools enroll more quickly in the programs and handle the administrative burden. 
The Education Department accused the organization of fraudulent practices, overinflating federal reimbursement claims and failing to address compliance issues in schools, according to a letter of “serious deficiency” sent in January.
The agency demanded nearly $345,000 in repayment and attempted to suspend the nonprofit from participating in federal child nutrition programs. Without recouping the funds and addressing noncompliance, the “USDA may take adverse action against (the state Education Department),” according to an internal state agency memo, which Oklahoma Voice obtained in its records request.
Feed the Kids executive director Dana Parker said she was “appalled” at the state’s accusations. 
“There was never, ever a meal served or a meal claimed that wasn’t served that we know of,” Parker told Oklahoma Voice.
A review officer from the Attorney General’s Office overturned the suspension in February, finding the Education Department uncovered concerning compliance issues with Feed the Kids but didn’t prove all its claims of fraud, according to records Oklahoma Voice reviewed.
The Oklahoma State Board of Education, though, voted in July to deny Feed the Kids’ application to continue working with districts’ child nutrition programs.
A legal battle over the $345,000 repayment is still ongoing.
The Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office is still reviewing the matter, a spokesperson said.
The USDA Office of Inspector General and the U.S. Attorney’s Office are going to investigate the organization, according to a June 11 email that Fields wrote to Gov. Kevin Stitt. 
The USDA’s investigative office didn’t return a request for comment, and the Oklahoma City-based U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. 
Parker and Feed the Kids co-founder David Lassiter said they’re unaware of any ongoing investigations.
Although Parker and Lassiter said they believe the Expanded Learning Time shutdown is a direct result of the dispute with their nonprofit, Education Department general counsel Jacki Phelps said the decision “was independent of any administrative action concerning Feed the Kids.”

name: WyoFile
title: Trump remains popular in Wyoming even as his beef, data center policies put him at odds
description:
Wyoming is one of a handful of states where the president’s approval rating is above 50%, though his numbers have slid considerably since 2025. 
The post Trump remains popular in Wyoming even as his beef, data center policies put him at odds appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
While polling shows Wyoming remains President Donald Trump’s strongest bastion of support amid low national approval ratings, his recent criticism of data center opponents and decisions on beef imports are putting him at odds with many of his local supporters, potentially risking his favorability in the Equality State. 
Last month, the Trump administration announced it would pause higher tariffs on ground beef imports, drawing swift criticism from conservative rural-state Republicans who say it will harm U.S. ranchers. Meanwhile, as concerns have grown in Wyoming over the proliferation of AI computing and data center development, Trump criticized communities recently for pushing back against such projects, warning that those who reject them risk becoming “backwards and poor.” 
Both moves precede Trump’s national approval rating sinking to 33%, its lowest point in his political career, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll. The polling also indicated widespread discontent over high levels of inflation and little appetite among Americans for the war with Iran. 
Meanwhile, a separate tracking poll of registered voters shows 54% of Wyoming approves of Trump. That’s considerably higher than the national average but an analysis by Newsweek indicates his popularity has fallen 25 points in Wyoming, one the biggest declines since Trump took office in January 2025. 
Whether Wyoming’s support of Trump wanes, however, isn’t likely to come down to a single policy, according to Jim King, a retired University of Wyoming political science professor. 
“The history of public opinion polling on presidents’ approval doesn’t show a single event will have an extreme, negative effect. It’s going to have to be more of an erosion effect over time, you know, one policy on top of another on top of another policy, where people feel they’re not being supported or represented,” King said. 
That’s where “real severe changes in approval ratings” happen, he said.  
Beef imports 
Trump announced a plan in late August to allow more than 660 million pounds of ground beef imports to enter the country, saying it was intended to lower prices for consumers since it would be sold at 25% below market rate. 
One of Wyoming’s longtime agricultural leaders told WyoFile he’s skeptical that’s how things will shake out. 
“How do you make sense of that? I mean, the marketplaces determine the price,” Jim Magagna, vice president of the Wyoming Stockgrowers, said. “I’d be surprised to see that the price of ground beef in grocery stores changes one penny because of it.” 
Jim Magagna strolls through the sagebrush after a morning of helping unload 750 sheep at his ranch on July 3, 2023. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Magagna said the policy is one thing. Trump’s rhetoric around it is another, he said, pointing to cattle futures falling in light of the announcement since traders expected a surge of cheaper foreign meat to compete with domestic supply. 
“That’s harmful,” Magagna said, since “markets react immediately in the short term.”
“In the long term, they tend to recover, and we get back to normal,” he said. “But short term, it’s negative impacts, and I think people are getting a little bit sick and tired of that.” 
Still, Trump has also done things to help producers, Magagna said. 
“We see it in the natural resource management arena, where we’ve seen very good things from this administration in terms of how we manage and are able to utilize federal lands for grazing,” he said. 
Republican Sen. Ogden Driskill, a Crook County rancher and businessman, shared a similar perspective, saying that his opposition to Trump’s beef import decision doesn’t mean he doesn’t support the president. 
“Trump Kool-aid drinkers have been coming after me,” Driskill said, because the state lawmaker challenged a decision “that cost people that are near and dear to me millions of dollars.” 
“All of a sudden, they’re like, ‘Well, you hate Trump.’ It’s like, ‘No, you don’t get it. I support him overall on a huge amount of issues,’” he said. 
While consumers deserve some relief from food prices, Driskill said, he questioned whether it’s “right to really penalize a sector of the economy that’s near and dear in Wyoming, so that you can buy some votes for consumers because you reduced the price of hamburger for 30 days.” 
Driskill’s not alone in his position, either. GOP lawmakers, including Wyoming’s U.S. Sen. John Barrasso criticized Trump’s plan from the get go. 
Data center development
Trump’s support for data center development isn’t an entirely new development, but the president has recently doubled down on his position that the U.S. must build more data centers to win the artificial intelligence race against China. His comments that communities that oppose data centers will become “backwards and poor” come amid a flood of proposals to build major facilities near cities such as Cheyenne, Casper, Wheatland and Evanston.
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., shakes the hand of President Donald Trump as Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., from left, and Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., look on at a campaign rally for Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., at the Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C., Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)
Meanwhile, recent Gallup polling shows seven out of 10 Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities. In Wyoming, that opposition has been split, while candidates aligned with the right-flank of the Republican party largely ran campaigns against data center development. 
The most prominent of those candidates included Secretary of State Chuck Gray, a longtime Trump loyalist who bested eight other candidates in the Republican primary race for Wyoming’s U.S. House seat. Gray campaigned on a strict pledge to stop the building of new data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. 
“In Congress, I’ll stop data centers,” he said in one ad. “No tax subsidies. No special treatment. No backroom deals for big tech billionaires.”
“If Silicon Valley wants to build their liberal empire,” he said, “they can do it somewhere else.”
Gray did not respond to WyoFile’s request for comment.

title: How does the Oklahoma House decide who’s in trouble? Your guess is as good as any.
description: It sure feels like Oklahoma leaders are in the business of cherrypicking which officials they want to make an example of these days. Because I don’t know how else to explain why House Republicans are suddenly so hellbent on citing a mysteriously elusive “precedent” as a reason to call an investigatory committee to hold state […]
text:
Lawmakers' desks on the Oklahoma House floor are pictured June 1, 2026 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)It sure feels like Oklahoma leaders are in the business of cherrypicking which officials they want to make an example of these days.
Because I don’t know how else to explain why House Republicans are suddenly so hellbent on citing a mysteriously elusive “precedent” as a reason to call an investigatory committee to hold state Rep. Danny Williams accountable.
They certainly didn’t exercise this precedent on at least two other occasions in the past year or so.
To be clear, we don’t know what the Seminole Republican is accused of having done beyond what Speaker Kyle Hilbert wrote in a very vague letter to his colleagues. Hilbert’s letter indicated that Williams is under investigation for “improper behavior” toward House chamber staff and “potential misuse of state resources.”
Hilbert, R-Bristow, wrote that his decision to refer the issue to the House Rules Committee follows chamber precedent set in 2017, a year that featured several, separate investigations into lawmakers.
But the so-called investigatory “precedent” seems a little subjective because it appears that Republicans pick and choose when to wield it. They didn’t call for anything similar when two other House colleagues were accused of behaving badly and didn’t immediately resign either.
Take state Rep. John Waldron, D-Tulsa, who was publicly accused in April of sexually harassing a subordinate by sending an inappropriate AI-generated image to her. In fact, rather than face legislative inquiry that could lead to an expulsion, he’s been allowed to continue to collect his paycheck until his resignation becomes effective Oct. 1.
In January, state Rep. Ajay Pittman, D-Oklahoma City, resigned after pleading guilty to forgery-related charges and receiving a seven year deferred sentence. There was no House investigation into her.
And don’t forget, state Rep. Ty Burns, R-Pawnee, pleaded guilty to three domestic-violence related crimes last August. When Burns finally felt it necessary to resign a day or so after entering his pleas, House leaders let him continue to serve for about a month longer without any investigation or calls for expulsion. His resignation was allowed to be effective Oct. 1, 2025.
And then, we’ve got Republican Secretary of State Benjamin Lepak, who was recently arrested on suspicion of public intoxication outside an Edmond McDonald’s. While he denies that allegation, the police body cam footage of Lepak’s arrest went national and is frankly an embarrassment to our state. His bizarre behavior tied up vital police resources in an Oklahoma municipality. Yet House leaders haven’t called on Gov. Kevin Stitt to fire Lepak, who is, coincidentally, the son of another Republican House lawmaker.
And why on earth are Democrats suddenly acting all high and mighty by demanding that Williams remove his name from the fall ballot where he’ll face an opponent in November? 
Democrats seem to have conveniently forgotten that they didn’t demand Waldron do any such thing when he put his name on the party primary ballot in June. In fact, Democrats circled the wagons and kept silent for months about Waldron’s alleged misconduct until a media outlet got wind of it.
In the past year, the public has unfortunately faced its share of legislators behaving badly. Yet after sitting idly on the sidelines for all of these, House Republicans are going after Williams with a vengeance?
Hilbert has OK’d spending a yet unknown amount of taxpayer dollars to hire an external law firm to conduct an investigation into Williams. We’ll use still more taxpayer resources to hold at least a daylong public hearing at the Capitol beginning Sept. 8. The committee has no real teeth, but could recommend Williams face sanctions or expulsion. The full chamber would need to OK booting Williams.
Even Williams said in an interview with Oklahoma television station KFOR that he’s not sure of what he supposedly did. He says the accusations aren’t sexual in nature and denied any wrongdoing.
That leaves one wondering what precedent exactly prompted this public committee hearing, because even allegations of sexual harassment or domestic violence in the past year haven’t prompted this level of scrutiny.
I would never wish ill on anyone, but in order to have this hearing, one would hope that allegations are very, very serious. Otherwise it’s going to look like House Republicans are persecuting each other based on who the cool kids are or which way the wind is blowing.
Cases considered by the House committee in 2017 involved accusations of several harassment by a male legislator to his female legislative assistant and an accusation of a grown man making an inappropriate comment to a high school page. That same year, a state senator resigned after being charged in a child prostitution case. Another senator was accused of embezzling campaign funds. And yet another was accused of sexual battery for inappropriate conduct with an Uber driver.
If House leaders want to resurrect investigative inquiries, that’s great, but they need to be applied equally and to anyone who behaves badly while elected, even if it’s outside the Capitol.
And that’s not what’s been happening, which sends a confusing and unfortunate message. Lawmakers have seemingly been allowed to police themselves, particularly when it comes to inappropriate behavior outside the confines of the Capitol.
And because of that, now it feels like lawmakers are picking and choosing winners and losers or burying their heads in the sand when certain accusations are uncomfortable, or once someone has resigned.
Because what happens outside the Capitol stays outside the Capitol, right?
Wrong. What our elected and appointed officials do affects us all regardless of whether it’s late at night outside a McDonald’s or in broad daylight in a Capitol office.
Our state has enough challenges to overcome already. We don’t need bad apples being allowed to continue serving, too.

title: Natural gas leads race to fuel Wyoming’s spiking data-center driven electrical demand
description:
Firm and conceptual plans would boost the state's electron output by 74% while coal-fueled power slips and plans for wind and solar are delayed.
The post Natural gas leads race to fuel Wyoming’s spiking data-center driven electrical demand appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
For 60 years, the Dave Johnston electrical power plant has stood over serpentine bends of the North Platte River in Converse County, its two towering smokestacks dominating the skyline as a symbol of Wyoming’s coal-fueled power might.
But the commanding presence of the carbon icon has been waning — first in 2009 when it was forced to share the skyline with a crop of wind turbines that began spinning nearby on reclaimed land that once was a coal mine that fed Dave Johnston’s burners. 
Now, not only is the coal plant on track to cede two of its coal-fired units to natural gas, an independent producer proposes to build a 430-megawatt natural gas-fueled power plant just to the north and, potentially, another gas power plant just to the west, rivalling Dave Johnston’s maximum capacity of about 745 megawatts.
One megawatt is enough electricity to power about 750 homes.
Fog rising from the North Platte River shrouds the Dave Johnston coal-fired power plant near Glenrock in January 2025. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“Economic growth requires a resilient power grid,” Rolling Cedar LLC says on its website. “A resilient power grid needs a mix of reliable production options, including dispatchable, firm power generation designed for the harsh conditions of Wyoming.”
The company — a partnership between North Carolina-based 8 Rivers and New Jersey-based Kindle Energy — is part of a growing trend that, at least on paper, promises to tap one of Wyoming’s other abundant fossil fuels to meet unprecedented electrical demand. There are about seven natural gas power generation projects in the works in Wyoming that, collectively, would add about 8,700 megawatts, according to WyoFile’s cursory survey of proposals in various stages of concept and development.
That equates to 74% of the state’s maximum existing electrical generation capacity of about 11,800 megawatts from all sources — coal, natural gas, wind, hydroelectric and solar.
“Wyoming has abundant resources to support a diverse generation portfolio,” Wyoming Energy Authority Executive Director Rob Creager told WyoFile via email. “The state remains among the nation’s top 10 producers of marketed natural gas, and increased use of Wyoming gas could generate additional investment, revenue and jobs.”
Most of the contemplated natural gas power projects are envisioned for “off-grid” use, to directly power AI computing data centers like Prometheus Hyperscale’s call for a combined 2,500 megawatts for its campus under contemplation in Natrona County and another one planned in Uinta County. Using natural gas-powered electricity to serve one or a handful of dedicated customers like those in the booming data center industry — the vast majority of the proposals — is part of the drive behind a multi-stakeholder push to allow “third-party” electrical generation in Wyoming, Creager noted.
Wildfire smoke turns the sun into a blood-orange disk between Douglas and Bill. (Alan Nash/@alannash59)
“Interest in third-party power generation continues to grow across Wyoming, largely driven by prospective large-load customers,” Creager said. “While some of this demand remains projected, other projects may require new generation in the near term.”
The Rolling Cedar project, however, envisions serving grid-connected customers, according to the company’s website, by cranking up generation intermittently to backfill the flow of electrons on the grid when the wind doesn’t blow and the sun doesn’t shine.
It’s the same type of electrical grid balancing strategy behind a controversial proposal to cycle water through hydroelectric turbines at Seminoe Reservoir.
Meanwhile, Wyoming’s legacy coal-fired power plants are producing electrons at an all-time low, while a surge in commercial wind and solar energy projects is sputtering.
For the past year, state officials have been fielding a wave of requests to push back construction start times for nearly 3,750 megawatts of planned wind and solar projects, according to state notices and a WyoFile analysis. The requested delays, which range from months to years, are primarily blamed on rising costs for materials and supply chain constraints.

name: WyoFile
title: What is the best way for Wyoming to address property taxes?
description:
Leaning more heavily on sales tax could shift control from local governments to Cheyenne. Marta Mossburg offers other paths to promote fairness, stability, transparency and fiscal restraint.
The post What is the best way for Wyoming to address property taxes? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
This November, Wyoming voters will consider Proposed Initiative Proposition 1. That proposal would exempt half of a property’s assessed value from taxes for those who reside at the property for at least six months per year. The homeowner would also have to have lived in Wyoming for a year to be eligible for the exemption. Land is excluded from the exemption. 

Opinion

Adoption of the statute would mean that second-home owners, those with rental property and those who spend less than six months in Wyoming each year would be treated differently than homeowners who spend the majority of their time in the state. The certified ballot language from Secretary of State Chuck Gray estimates government revenue reductions for the state of $92.6 million in fiscal year 2028 and $95.9 million in fiscal year 2029 if it passes. In June, the Wyoming Department of Revenue told a state legislative committee that its independent analysis showed revenue for state and local government entities could be reduced by as much as $124.7 million in fiscal year 2028 if it passed.
With reduced property tax revenue, local governments would have to either cut spending or find a replacement source of revenue to pay for schools, roads and other essential services. Many have talked about raising the sales tax as an alternative. Wyoming does not have an income tax, so raising it is not an option. 
Currently, Wyoming’s state sales tax is 4%. With the addition of local county rates, the average rate ranges between 5 and 6%throughout the state, with the highest rate of 9% found in two resort districts in Teton County. 
Tax Foundation research shows that substituting a higher sales tax for property taxes would require significantly higher state and county rates, would change taxpayer behavior in border areas, would hurt lower income people and erode local control of tax dollars. A recent Tax Foundation study of how eliminating the property tax in Florida would impact the state found that the Sunshine State would have to hike the sales tax to 15.34%to cover the loss, up from no more than the current 8% depending on the county.
Higher sales tax rates no doubt would change taxpayer behavior in Wyoming, especially of people in border regions who can cross state lines to find lower prices. This can not only hurt local restaurants, grocery stores and other retail businesses, but those on fixed incomes and lower-income individuals who spend a higher percentage of their money on purchases. It could also impact overall tax collected as people strive to save money wherever possible. 
Lastly, moving from a property tax to a sales tax would mean shifting control of local tax dollars from local elected officials to Cheyenne. 
Rising home values and assessments have justifiably concerned many taxpayers, especially the elderly on a fixed income or those of any age who struggle to make ends meet. 
While calls for scrapping the property tax are understandable, studies show the alternative — moving to a higher sales or income tax — would hurt the economy and job growth, provide inadequate funding and generate animosity between municipalities. 
An alternative property tax reform could instead focus on enacting levy limits to limit collections to the prior year’s plus inflation and population growth, while providing more transparency on the effect spending has on property taxes. This would shift the focus from assessments to the revenue needed to effectively run local government. To aid lower-income people of all ages, policymakers could also pass what are known as circuit breakers. Generally, there are two types. One offers relief when property taxes surpass a certain income percentage; the other basis discounts on a “sliding scale” of different income levels.
When paired with a reform known as Truth in Taxation, residents would be able to meaningfully constrain their property tax bills. These laws require local governments to advertise proposed property tax increases with detailed information and adequate time for public input and comment.
Property taxes supply 84% of local government revenue in Wyoming compared to 72% nationally. Reducing them in half as proposed by Initiative 1 could require a massive hike in the sales tax in order to fund core government services including roads, schools, libraries and other infrastructure. 
As an alternative, the Legislature could instead consider adopting levy limits, Truth in Taxation and circuit breakers to both provide transparency and consistency and help lower-income residents. Property taxes have been shown to be the most reliable funding source for local governments and the one that maintains local control over local resources. Rapidly increasing property tax bills are a real concern. The question is which property tax reforms offer the best path to foster fairness, stability, transparency and fiscal restraint.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho election officials worry about mail-in ballot changes proposed by Trump administration
description: Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect. In Idaho, like many other states, election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. […]
text:
A voter deposits a mail-in ballot at the drop box outside the Chester County Government Center in Pennsylvania on Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Across the country, state election officials are waiting to discover if federal courts will allow the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect.
In Idaho, like many other states, election officials are nervous the changes might come too close to the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two months away on Nov. 3. 
Why the rushed Postal Service plan for mail-in voting has states in a panic

The changes — proposed in a new U.S. Postal Service rule that implements an executive order by President Donald Trump — would require federal review of the design of absentee ballots and impose new rules on the design of envelopes containing absentee ballots, among other things. 
“In the moment, the biggest concern … is just we’re so close to the election,” Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official and an elected Republican, said in an interview last week.  “There’s the practical implications of getting absentee ballots out.”
McGrane said he isn’t sure that Idaho or other states would be able to fully comply with the USPS rule if it takes effect before this year’s election. He said county clerks across Idaho, who run the state’s elections, are busy finalizing ballots to print and mail out absentee ballots to military and overseas voters by Sept. 19.
In Idaho’s largest county, Ada — which is home to Boise — election officials have told the state they need to know about any changes to ballots by Wednesday in order to make changes before they print the ballots, said Trent Tripple, the Republican elected county clerk for Ada County. He said he also worries about making big changes months before the election.
“If you want the most secure election possible, do not put artificial timelines and make us change things at the last second,” he said in an interview. “If you’re doing that, I guarantee you there will be mistakes that are made — because we don’t have the time. We can’t back up an election.”
And that’s all on top of other potential ballot changes facing Idaho election officials as the Idaho Supreme Court weighs a lawsuit by the organizers of Proposition 1, an abortion legalization ballot initiative, that challenges state officials’ descriptions of the initiative.
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane discusses his presidential caucus experiences outside of his caucus site at Whittier Elementary in Boise on March 2, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)

 Absentee ballot restrictions are the latest attempt at federal intervention in elections

The Trump administration’s policies seek to regulate absentee voting, a type of voting that allows voters to vote early or by mail.
About 15% of Idaho voters use absentee voting primarily, ranging from seniors to people who use it for its ease of access, McGrane said. In Idaho’s primary election in May, more than 46,000 voters cast absentee ballots, according to the state’s tally. That was mostly Republicans, which made up nearly 32,000 of absentee voters, the state’s data shows. In the last general election, when winners are officially declared for public office, about 182,00 people voted by absentee ballots, according to state data from the 2024 election. 
In Idaho, voters can request absentee ballots without needing to state a reason. But state lawmakers in recent years have tried to change that through legislation.
‘Stop threatening your friends’: Idaho Attorney General’s Office lawyer blasts Justice Department

The attempted restrictions on absentee voting are one of several recent attempts by the Trump administration to clamp down on state voting processes. In one high-profile instance, a state government attorney representing McGrane sent the U.S. Department of Justice a stern letter warning the federal government to “stop threatening your friends” after the agency said it could prosecute local and state election officials who let noncitizens vote in federal elections. 
This spring, the Justice Department sued McGrane and dozens of other secretaries of state for not turning over sensitive information on their states’ registered voters, including partial Social Security data.
For now, the USPS rule is blocked by a federal court. But McGrane said his office is closely watching the legal developments.
McGrane said he was likely more prepared than most to brace for all the changes in elections recently. He said his career in elections started in Ada County just after the 2000 election, amid a contentious recount of the presidential election in Florida that brought concerns over partially hole punched “hanging chads.”
“Some of the narratives are the exact same,” McGrane said. “Election security was a major concern back in the 2000s.”
 What could the USPS rule change for Idaho?

Part of what the USPS rule would require is that absentee ballots all have trackable envelopes. McGrane said most counties already have tracking codes on envelopes of ballots that are headed to voters, but he said none have those trackers on the return to local election offices. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“We’re just trying to watch and trying to make sure too that we don’t have counties making massive changes that aren’t going to take effect, as well,” McGrane said. “There’s a cost component both in terms of time, but also dollars to the counties. That’s one of the things that we have to weigh through all this because we don’t want to be expending a huge amount of tax dollars for something that’s not taking place.”
Another change proposed in the USPS rule is to require that states upload data on which voters requested absentee ballots so the federal government can prove that they are registered voters. At a federal court hearing late last week, a Justice Department attorney couldn’t tell a judge whether a system to handle that data was operational yet, the Associated Press reported. 
Triple said Ada County, with a larger budget and staff than others, has more ability to handle changes than other smaller counties. He said the county was already planning to add the trackable codes to envelopes in the future, so the county already adopted that change for this election cycle. 
Trent Tripple serves as the Ada County clerk. Tripple previously served as the assistant chief deputy clerk and the chief deputy clerk inAda County. (Photo courtesy of Ada County)
But Triple, who serves as president of the Idaho Association of County Recorders and Clerks, said that many county officials are “not excited about having to change a bunch of stuff financially as well as time constraints for the upcoming November election.” 
He stressed that changing ballots isn’t a simple task. That’s because a resident’s specific address determines which taxing, legislative and congressional districts they live and vote in. 
“We have hundreds of variations of our ballots,” Triple said. “And so it’s not just changing one ballot and then printing 300,000 of them. It’s changing hundreds and hundreds of ballot styles and proofing all of those ballot styles to make sure we got them all right before we then can go out and print them.”
