title: Trump’s beef import plan draws criticism from Alabama organizations, politicians
description: President Donald Trump’s plan to import 300,000 metric tons of beef priced under market value drew rare rebukes from Alabama organizations generally supportive of him and provided an opening for an incumbent U.S. representative facing a difficult battle for re-election. Trump’s proposal, which he said aimed to address high beef prices, garnered backlash from[...]
text:
A cow rests at the Kentucky State Fair in Louisville, Kentucky on Aug. 27, 2026. President Donald Trump's plan to import 300,000 metric tons of beef has drawn rebukes from farmers and ranchers' organizations. (Chris Hughes for Kentucky Lantern)President Donald Trump’s plan to import 300,000 metric tons of beef priced under market value drew rare rebukes from Alabama organizations generally supportive of him and provided an opening for an incumbent U.S. representative facing a difficult battle for re-election.
Trump’s proposal, which he said aimed to address high beef prices, garnered backlash from farmers and politicians across Alabama for having a negative impact on domestic agriculture.
Alabama Cattlemen’s Association Chief Executive Officer Erin Beasley wrote in a statement on social media last month that “flooding the market with subsidized foreign beef only discourages cattlemen from making investments in their operations, ultimately slowing down herd rebuilding.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This administration needs to focus on policies that will encourage herd expansion and lower the input costs that have burdened the industry for some time,” the statement said. “Market manipulation will never be the answer, and (last month’s) announcement is another slap in the face for cattlemen everywhere, especially the more than 10,000 members in our organization.”
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, who is seeking re-election in a district the Republican-controlled Legislature redrew in May to favor Republicans, introduced legislation last week that would nullify the president’s proclamation and prevent the president or other elected officials from suspending, waiving or reducing any tariff, fee or duty on beef products unless Congress moves to do so first.  
“The initial reaction was somewhat surprised that he would be so disconnected from the struggle that cattle farmers are having right now, that the (agriculture) industry as a whole is having right now,” Figures said in an interview last week. “But on the other hand, we’ve seen several actions coming out of this administration that display a similar level of either a lack of understanding or just simply not caring about the impact of their policies on farmers.”
Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, the Republican nominee for Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, did not make a public comment on Trump’s proclamation last week. A message seeking comment was left with Marques Friday afternoon.
Amid the outcry, Trump Friday afternoon signed an executive order to make it easier for ranchers and farmers to process their own beef products and sell directly to consumers.
Certain organizations, such as the National Cattlemen’s Association, are opposed to allowing farmers and ranchers to sell products without the inspection citing food safety concerns.
The Alabama Cattlemen’s Association reported in January 2026 there were 1.2 million head of cattle and calves on Alabama farms. Alabama Cooperative Extension System reported that in 2022, there were 273,271 jobs in Alabama’s food, fiber, forestry, and green industries which accounted for 10% of the state’s workforce.
According to Federal Reserve Economic Data, ground beef prices first spiked in June 2020 costing $4.74 per pound before dropping to $3.96 per pound in December 2020. As of July 2026, ground beef prices are $6.86 per pound. 
Higher prices can likely be attributed to a smaller head of cattle. At the beginning of the year, the USDA reported 86.2 million head of cattle which was down from 86.5 million head in January 2025.
Rick Pate, the commissioner of Agriculture and Industries, said in a statement the proclamation is “unlikely to provide lasting relief” due to its temporary nature.
“Demand for beef remains strong during the recent higher prices. If prices rise too high, consumer demand will ease leading to price adjustments and producers retaining more heifers,” Pate said. “While I understand the intent behind federal actions, market forces will ultimately determine long-term outcomes.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Flock cameras divide Tennessee governments, residents over privacy as some end their contracts
description: Sullivan County, Tennessee Commissioner Joe Carr made headlines in August when he proclaimed at a public meeting that the CEO of security company Flock Safety “should be hanged” for treason, calling the company “one of the most hated” in America. His comments, though incendiary, come amid a reckoning over the security cameras monitoring traffic in […]
text:
The increasing use of Flock automated license plate readers, ALPR, is drawing scrutiny from East Tennessee elected officials and members of the public. (Photo: Getty Images)Sullivan County, Tennessee Commissioner Joe Carr made headlines in August when he proclaimed at a public meeting that the CEO of security company Flock Safety “should be hanged” for treason, calling the company “one of the most hated” in America.
His comments, though incendiary, come amid a reckoning over the security cameras monitoring traffic in many American communities over the past few years. The issue has sparked debate over the conflicting values of privacy and community safety.
With some communities sticking by Flock and others ending their contracts, there’s no clear consensus that has emerged on where communities will go from here.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Days after Carr’s comments, the Sullivan County Commission voted not to renew its Flock contract, which expires in January.  
Flock, a surveillance hardware manufacturer, is known for its automated license plate reader, ALPR, cameras, which have become controversial as local governments and law enforcement use them to help solve crimes. The cameras pick up images of vehicles and license plates on the road and feed into a nationwide network, allowing law enforcement to access cameras from anywhere in the country.
This has become contentious among the public, members of whom raise alarm over mass surveillance and privacy erosion concerns.
The Institute for Justice, a nonprofit public interest law firm, has catalogued more than 100 instances of law enforcement officers using the technology for non-law enforcement uses and stalking, including two in Tennessee. Some governments are rethinking using them, including in Knoxville, while Nashville has stalled implementation of the systems.
“The American people deserve better than to be used as a beta test for unproven technology that is turning local police departments into mini-CIAs,” said Carr in an email statement. 
Anderson County officials also have doubts:  the county will hold a town hall in September about its use of the cameras, and Anderson County Commissioner Chad McNabb said “around 75%” of residents had serious concerns about privacy relating to them. 
Still on board
Yet many east Tennessee municipalities swear by the utility of the cameras. Blount and Carter counties still partner with Flock.
In a letter to the Blount County Commissioners, Sheriff’s Office Chief Deputy Jeff French wrote that the department doesn’t track people using the cameras and doesn’t deploy AI tools to analyze the public. French writes that the department uses the cameras “as an investigative tool,” using it to find leads on crimes and look for vehicles already flagged as stolen or on national databases like missing persons.
Calling the benefits of the technology “real and significant,” French wrote that the cameras have “helped us locate missing and endangered persons, recover citizens’ stolen vehicles and property, monitor sex offenders near our schools, disrupt drug trafficking and apprehend violent offenders with arrest warrants.”
Much ado about cameras in Johnson City
Johnson City, which partnered with Flock for a 10-year contract in 2025, has 145 license plate readers and 145 pan/tilt/zoom cameras. The city also has gunshot detectors and two mobile security trailers.
At a city commission work session on Aug. 20, Johnson City Police Deputy Chief Mike Adams said the cameras were only used to take photos of cars and license plates — he said they do not track peoples’ movements and can’t take video. He added that the gunshot detectors can’t pick up human conversation.
He said the pan/tilt/zoom cameras were placed in public areas like parks or schools, and were used to monitor for crimes or suspicious individuals, including sex offenders.
Those who violate the use of the cameras would be fired, according to Adams, which he said happened in previous cases across the country. Adams said those firings proved the “system was working.”
“You’re not going to find someone who’d like to see [a bad cop] lose their job more than the cop trying to do the right thing,” he said.



Quotation







The truth is, there are civil liberties set up around cameras and surveillance, to catch abuses of those systems. The same arguments could be made about handcuffs, or interrogations – everything the police do has a civil liberty attached to it.


– Joe Wise, Johnson City Commission 


To Adams’ knowledge, no one in the Johnson City Police Department had misused the cameras yet, he told Tennessee Lookout.
Addressing privacy concerns, Adams said it was a “reasonable expectation” that people in public would be caught on some kind of camera somewhere.
He said Johnson City Police have been able to communicate easier with law enforcement in neighboring states to find people via license plates. 
“Before [the cameras], all you were doing was a report for the victim,” he said. “The suspect was out of Johnson City. We’d never see that stuff again.”
In one case, Adams said police were able to locate a child who had gone missing from a McDonalds. It turned out the boy had wandered off on his own with a friend, and was not in danger, but Adams said Flock had saved them a lot of time and helped ease the family’s worry.
“That wouldn’t have happened two years ago,” Adams said. “We wouldn’t have known where they were. We would’ve had to rely on Amber Alerts and community members to find them.” 
Johnson City Commissioner Joe Wise told the Lookout they have to “separate the technology from the misuse of technology.”
“The truth is, there are civil liberties set up around cameras and surveillance, to catch abuses of those systems,” he said. “The same arguments could be made about handcuffs, or interrogations – everything the police do has a civil liberty attached to it.”
“So the question is, really, are we going to use the tools responsibly, or are we going to turn our back on it, and leave our community less-adequately served on the public safety side?” he said.
Wise and Johnson City Mayor Greg Cox believe the public ultimately will appreciate the greater safety coming from the cameras.
“Most of the arguments out there are political arguments, and they have nothing to do with anything but creating a bunch of noise,” Cox said. “People are thankful there’s these tools out there for the police. Overwhelmingly, to me, there’s a positive conversation about it. We hear a lot more conversation than the things that get shared [online].”
Fired up
Despite government confidence, plenty of people are fired up and angry about the cameras. Some of them are angry enough to physically destroy them, including Adam Heimerman, an independent candidate for the 2nd Congressional District, who was arrested on four counts of vandalism after reportedly shooting four Flock cameras in his area.
Stockard on the Stump: Lee Administration walking tightrope on license plate readers

People have been arrested for vandalizing Flock cameras across the country. In Florida, police plant decoy Flock cameras to catch vandals.
After Flock CEO Garrett Langley told Fox News that focusing on privacy “prioritizes the wrong things,” the Flock critics leaked what they purported was his home address.
Flock officials didn’t respond to a request for comment by Tennessee Lookout.
The DeFlock movement
DeFlock.org has a map of where Flock cameras have been found across the country. The group’s goal is to “raise awareness about the threats [Flock] poses to personal privacy and civil liberties, and empower the public to take action.”
Local offshoot groups have sprung up. The man who runs the “DeFlock Johnson City, Tennessee” Facebook page is Johnson City resident Connor Beske.
He said he doesn’t have any particular qualifications except passion.
“I’m dumb and stubborn,” he said. “I’ll stick with something as long as I need to.”
In the three months since he started the page, he’s gotten more attention than he knows what to do with. 
“A lot of candidates” at the local and state level want to get involved, he said.
“There’s some lobbyists I’ve talked to working on this,” he said. “They’re like, can you drive to Knoxville and hang out with this and this lawmaker? I’m like, well I can’t because I have a job, and this is insane.”
Beske thinks the Flock cameras, and others like them, are a more serious problem than other privacy concerns such as Google tracking your phone or modern vehicles with smart features.
“If you don’t want them tracking you, removing a computer module from your truck isn’t a small feat, but you’re allowed to,” he said. “But if you drive that truck on the public road in a town with hundreds of cameras, you’re getting tracked anyway. You took all those steps, still the government circumvented all of it, and they still know where you’re going.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Democrats see rare signs of hope in solidly red Arkansas’ midterms
description: DARDANELLE — The annual Mount Nebo Chicken Fry, a mainstay of Arkansas politics for generations, saw a break from tradition this year. In election years, the Democratic and Republican parties usually rent two cabins as their headquarters for the day while they make their case to potential voters lured to the campground by carriage rides, […]
text:
Signs promote Democratic candidates on the November ballot outside a cabin at Mount Nebo State Park during the park's annual chicken fry on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)DARDANELLE — The annual Mount Nebo Chicken Fry, a mainstay of Arkansas politics for generations, saw a break from tradition this year.
In election years, the Democratic and Republican parties usually rent two cabins as their headquarters for the day while they make their case to potential voters lured to the campground by carriage rides, live music and chicken dinners. This year, the Libertarian party rented the Republican cabin.
The problem wasn’t a lack of Republican presence or interest but due to party members having previous commitments, said former Yell County GOP chairman Clay Hooten, who manned a tent the party used instead during the Aug. 29 event.


Election day is Nov. 3, and early voting begins Oct. 19. More information about voting locations and registration is available on the Arkansas secretary of state’s website. 


Even so, the two cabins were surrounded by signs promoting Democratic and Libertarian candidates on the November ballot. Democrat and Libertarian candidates, T-shirts and buttons outnumbered those of Republicans throughout the chicken fry, an unusual sight in the heart of a county where President Donald Trump won nearly 80% of the vote two years ago.
The scene was a small but hopeful sign for Democrats, whose efforts to break Republicans’ lock on Arkansas politics have fallen short for more than a decade. But Trump’s growing unpopularity, a recent poll and national attention surrounding races for the U.S. House and Senate are fueling Democrats’ belief that there’s an opening even in the reddest of states in November.
“I’m tired of people going to the polls to vote against something,” said Kelly Grappe, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state. “I want to give people something to vote for, and I have a vision for this state where the people truly do have a voice.”
The party still faces long odds in Arkansas, where top Republican candidates far outpace their Democratic rivals in fundraising. And at a time when national Democrats and political observers see Senate races in Republican-led states like Texas and Kansas as competitive, Arkansas isn’t viewed the same way. The Cook Political Report classifies the state’s races for governor, U.S. Senate and U.S. House as “solid Republican.”
But, with less than two months before Election Day, Democrats are trying to capitalize on what could be the most favorable political environment they’ve seen in years.



Quotation







We get people that call in that are Republicans that say, ‘I can’t vote for him. Tell me why I should vote for her.'


– Cindy Henry, a volunteer for Democrat Hallie Shoffner's U.S. Senate campaign



U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton addresses supporters at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock on March 3, 2026 after being declared the winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)

 US Senate race heats up

The biggest prize for Democrats would be the Senate seat held by Republican Tom Cotton, the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee who easily won his second term in 2020 with no Democratic opponent. 
He’s seeking a third term against Democrat Hallie Shoffner, a sixth-generation farmer who closed her family’s Jackson County soybean farm last year due to financial strain she attributes to the Trump administration’s tariffs.
An August poll from Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College showed Shoffner with a slim lead over Cotton, within the margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Shoffner has also made national headlines for her campaign’s focus on her rural background, the increasing cost of living and portraying Cotton’s policy priorities as against Arkansans’ best interests.
Republicans have pushed back on the poll. Another poll from Washington D.C.-based J.L. Partners showed Cotton with a sizable lead over Shoffner, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.

Cindy Henry organizes postcards for Hallie Shoffner’s U.S. Senate bid at the campaign’s Little Rock headquarters on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

But the Talk Business poll has ramped up enthusiasm for Shoffner, said Cindy Henry, a retiree from North Little Rock who volunteers for the campaign two days a week.
“We’ll get 40 to 50 calls a day [from] all kinds of people wanting to be heard, with all kinds of issues: personal, medical, jobs, farms, you name it,” Henry said.
Cotton’s campaign emphasizes that he “helped pass the biggest middle-class tax cut in American history, cut regulations to drive down energy production costs, secured the border with President Trump, and fights for a stronger military, bringing home billions of dollars to Arkansas communities in the process,” a spokesperson said in a Friday email.
Two super PACs, America One and Arkansans for Democracy and Justice, have spent more than $3 million combined on text messages and ads assisting Cotton’s bid. His campaign portrays Shoffner as too far left for Arkansas, criticizing her for remarks she made this year supporting defunding Immigration and Customs Enforcement “as it exists right now.”

Hallie Shoffner, running for a U.S. Senate seat, attends the Hope Watermelon Festival in Hope, Arkansas on Saturday, Aug. 8, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
 

Cotton’s campaign has also repeatedly highlighted Shoffner’s past donations to 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
Shoffner said in an interview that her campaign is “all about Arkansas,” accusing Cotton of trying to find a scapegoat for voters’ frustrations.
“I want to be the kind of public servant that looks to the future, a better future, and moves forward to that future,” she said.
Cotton has consistently allied himself with Trump, whose approval rating in Arkansas and nationwide has declined as the costs of necessities and groceries remain high.
Henry said she’s seen this firsthand as someone on Social Security and managing her family’s farm in Lonoke. Her farming income has plummeted while tariffs have raised the costs of insurance and utilities, she said.
The Arkansans that have contacted Shoffner’s campaign headquarters “want solutions, not rhetoric” and are becoming disillusioned with Cotton’s “same old song and dance,” Henry said.

From left: Libertarian lieutenant governor candidate Michael Kalagias, Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate Jeff Wadlin and Stand Up Arkansas co-founders Steve and Kelly Grappe chat at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry on Aug. 29, 2026. Kelly Grappe is the Democratic candidate for secretary of state. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

“We get people that call in that are Republicans that say, ‘I can’t vote for him. Tell me why I should vote for her,’” Henry said.
Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, who is garnering single-digit support in polls, is hoping that voter discontent with both parties could help him.
Wadlin’s candidacy is for “politically homeless” Arkansas voters who “feel like we should just be solving problems like neighbors, working together and not getting angry with each other over cultural issues,” he told the audience at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry’s pie auction.
 Central Arkansas House seat considered in play

All four of Arkansas’ Republican U.S. House members face challengers this year, but it’s the Little Rock area where Democrats are once again directing the most attention.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently added the 2nd District seat held by Rep. French Hill to its list of GOP seats it’s targeting. The Talk Business & Politics poll indicates that Chris Jones, the Democrat challenging Hill in central Arkansas’ 2nd District, has a slim lead over Hill within the margin of error.

U.S. House Financial Services Committee Chairman Rep. French Hill of Arkansas talks with Little Rock City Director Joan Adcock before a hearing on the Little Rock Housing Authority on March 13, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
 

This isn’t the first time national Democrats have touted the 2nd District as flippable. Past efforts by Democrats, including by state Sen. Clarke Tucker in 2018 and former state Sen. Joyce Elliott in 2020, have been unsuccessful. And a 2021 redistricting plan that moved some Pulaski County voters into other districts made it more favorable to Republicans.
In an Aug. 19 Fox News appearance, Hill said he’s confident he will win reelection because Arkansans “want to support the most conservative candidate in the race.” He denounced the Democratic Socialists of America in the same segment but did not attempt to tie them to Jones, the Democratic nominee for Arkansas governor in 2022.
But, like Shoffner, Jones has attracted national attention. He won Harris’ endorsement, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg headlined a rally for Jones.

Secretary Pete Buttigieg (right) joins Arkansas congressional candidate Chris Jones (left) on Friday, June 19, 2026 at the Dreamland Ballroom in Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)

Jones said the poll numbers and support from outside Arkansas make him “cautiously optimistic and determined.” He says he often reminds voters that Hill’s voting record has aligned with Trump’s priorities, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, which is expected to cut rural Medicaid spending by $15.5 billion per year over the next decade.
“A lot of independents and Republicans are saying, ‘Okay, this is a bridge too far, it’s too much, and it’s time for a new direction,’” Jones said.
Hill said in a Friday email that he’s heard some of the same frustrations from voters: “that the cost of living is out of control, houses are too expensive, filling up the gas tank isn’t affordable, and that Washington doesn’t care about what’s going on.”
He said he’s been “working tirelessly to address” the cost of living, mentioning his support for eliminating taxes on tips and overtime pay.
Hill also sponsored the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a bipartisan bill that became law in July without Trump’s signature, removing some of the regulations on housing manufacturing and bank loans for homebuyers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Colt Shelby (left) speaks to voters at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

 Libertarian spoilers?

A major question surrounding Arkansas’ midterm elections is the impact Libertarians could have.
The most prominent of the party’s candidates, gubernatorial hopeful Colt Shelby, had the stage to himself at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry’s pie auction.
Neither Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders nor her Democratic opponent, state Sen. Fred Love of Mabelvale, was present at the chicken fry. 
Shelby is from Franklin County, a typically Republican-voting area frustrated by the Sanders administration’s attempt to build a 3,000-bed prison in the county. He told the Mount Nebo audience that he takes “a common-sense approach” to running for office, which he’s never done before.
“You will not find anybody in this race that will work harder, smarter, better,” Shelby said.
Aaron Bratton, a physician from Russellville, said he’s voting for Shelby because “it’s time for an outsider” who isn’t “politically connected” to be governor because “neither major party represents people anymore.”
Sanders, whose campaign has more than $4.7 million in the bank, hasn’t engaged much with either Shelby or Love. She skipped a gubernatorial debate featuring the two at the Arkansas Press Association’s convention this year. Four years after launching her first campaign with a video prominently featuring Trump, her ads this year so far have focused on state issues like tax cuts and healthcare.

Stele James, a Democrat from western Yell County, showed support for Democratic secretary of state candidate Kelly Grappe and Libertarian gubernatorial candidate Colt Shelby at the Mount Nebo Chicken Fry on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Stele James, who has held leadership roles with the Yell County Democratic Party, said he believes Shelby has a real chance of winning as “that moderate candidate right there on the ground.”
“I see my Republican friends and people on my side that are flocking to his campaign because they’re tired of the divisive nature that the two-party system has produced,” said James, the president of the Two Rivers School District board.
James said he’s also excited about Grappe’s campaign for secretary of state.
Grappe’s GOP opponent is state Sen. Kim Hammer of Benton, who sponsored several 2025 laws placing restrictions on citizens’ ability to change laws and the state constitution via ballot measures. Some of those laws were blocked in federal court on First Amendment grounds last month.
The secretary of state’s duties include oversight of the ballot initiative process, which Grappe said is “absolutely rigged against the people.” She also said she’s met many voters who don’t know what the secretary of state does, and she sees this as a failure of the office’s civic education arm.
Meeting with voters at Mount Nebo, Grappe wore a hat emblazoned with the state’s motto: Regnat populus, Latin for “the people rule.”
Arkansas’ voter turnout has frequently been among the lowest nationwide. This might be due to a shortage of choices that invigorate voters rather than “voter apathy,” said Michael Pakko, chairman of the Libertarian Party of Arkansas and the party’s nominee for secretary of state.
The party is also fielding candidates for lieutenant governor, commissioner of state lands, a handful of state legislative seats and the 1st and 3rd U.S. Congressional Districts.
“I hope that we’ve given you enough choices this year,” Pakko told Mount Nebo attendees.

Signs promote Libertarian candidates on the November ballot outside a cabin at Mount Nebo State Park during the park’s annual chicken fry on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Q&A: South Dakota’s next attorney general aims to undo criminal justice reforms, just not right away
description: Lance Russell will be South Dakota’s next attorney general whether you vote for him or not.  At the Republican state convention in June, Russell earned the party’s nomination to seek the job of the state’s top law enforcement official, and its defense attorney when the state is sued. Attorney general is among the statewide offices […]
text:
Fall River and Oglala Lakota County State's Attorney Lance Russell addresses the South Dakota Republican Convention on June 27, 2026, at The Monument events center in Rapid City just prior to winning the party's nomination for attorney general. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Lance Russell will be South Dakota’s next attorney general whether you vote for him or not. 
At the Republican state convention in June, Russell earned the party’s nomination to seek the job of the state’s top law enforcement official, and its defense attorney when the state is sued.
Attorney general is among the statewide offices in South Dakota whose nominees are chosen by delegates at party conventions, not by voters in primary elections. The current attorney general, Republican Marty Jackley, is running for the U.S. House.
Russell is running unopposed to succeed Jackley in Nov. 3 general election. The South Dakota Democratic Party hasn’t nominated anyone to run for attorney general since 2018.
South Dakota attorney general urges beefed-up consumer protection after $53 million Meta settlement

Russell, a Hot Springs native and 1999 graduate of the University of South Dakota School of Law, has spent more than half his career as the Fall River County state’s attorney, beginning soon after he passed the bar exam. He’s also the state’s attorney for neighboring Oglala Lakota County, which is part of the Oglala Sioux Tribe’s Pine Ridge Reservation. Russell prosecutes the cases in that county that fall under state jurisdiction.
From 2009-2020, he stepped away from the prosecutor job to serve four terms in the state House of Representatives and two in the state Senate. He was elected state’s attorney for Fall River County again in 2020 and 2024, and will leave two years early to assume the role of attorney general. 
Russell bested Austin Hoffman and John Fitzgerald at the state convention with a campaign focused on undoing some of the reforms to criminal justice he opposed during his time in Pierre. 
Those reforms, to the adult system in 2013 and the juvenile one in 2015, ushered in drug courts, a presumption of probation for low-level felonies and a host of other policies meant to hold down the state’s prison population without hurting public safety. 
Russell argues the reforms haven’t worked for the adult system — South Dakota is building two new prisons in spite of them — and says institutions like the now-defunct boot camp for teens in Custer did a better job helping juveniles change their ways than the alternatives now used for kids who break the law.
The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
You’ll be the first attorney general since Gordon Mydland, who led the office from 1969 to 1973, to have served in the Legislature. How do you think your years in Pierre will color your approach to the job?
The nice thing is that I have the perspective of the legislator. I understand how they’re perceiving their job, so I can articulate to them in a manner that they hopefully will understand. 
The other thing is that I got a front row seat to watch the attorney general’s work in the Legislature. Legislators have a number of ideas. Marty did a really nice job of getting together with the legislators, having a relationship with them. He could talk to them and help them with their legislation and make sure that it wasn’t unconstitutional or illegal in some fashion.
That’s one of the big issues for the attorney general’s staff, to make sure that they have good communication with lawmakers so that we’re not passing legislation that gets us into federal court and gets us enjoined for doing something stupid.
As attorney general, you will have a Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liaison position. What do you see your office doing on the MMIP issue?
They have someone that has quite a bit of experience (in Marlys Big Eagle), so I’m excited about that. It’s my understanding that we do, in fact, have a robust office that is working with the tribes to a large degree and trying to implement something very close to the Amber Alert (for missing Native Americans). I’m thankful for that, and yes, I will be an advocate for it.
How would you approach tribal relations, and what have you learned by serving as a prosecutor adjacent to the Pine Ridge Reservation?
I feel like I have worked cooperatively over the last 25 years with the Oglala Lakota County commissioners and the tribe, and that we’ve had a pretty good working relationship. So I’m hoping to put that into effect statewide so we don’t get ourselves into trouble and get banned from the tribe.
$10 million settlement over online gaming child exploitation will fund safety, after-school efforts

I think that, unfortunately, a lot of what happened with (former Gov.) Kristi Noem getting banned from the Indian reservations just had to do with a lot of not understanding the different jurisdictions and what the state’s jurisdiction actually is. Because if you realize that you have limited jurisdiction on the Indian reservation and understand the contours of it, I think it helps you talk to people in a manner that is constructive, respectful and non-threatening. If you just understand your role as the state, I think that helps dramatically.
You opposed criminal justice reform as a lawmaker back in 2013 and 2015, arguing that leaning on community supervision would backfire. You campaigned on the premise that it has. What problems do you see?
The effectiveness of our juvenile justice system between when I started and now is like night and day. It’s just not working. If you talk to people at the schools, you will get a real good education in how destructive it’s been for the school systems to have these delinquents, who are adjudicated as such, essentially being sent right back to school. The schools have had a very difficult time dealing with it. 
The system no longer works. We just don’t have the resources we used to have. I remember when I would have kids come into the system that were absolutely defiant to the judges. Then they would spend 60 or 90 days at the boot camp up there in Custer. They would come back, they would stand in front of the judge, and they would stand up straight. They’d look the judge in the eye. They would respond appropriately. Then they’d go back to the high school here in Hot Springs or in Edgemont, and they would graduate. It would be a success story. 
But these days, it just seems like we eventually have these kids just dropping out of school. They’re not being given the resources they need. We no longer have the boot camp now. We have to send a lot of the children that need help out of state because we don’t have adequate resources here.
What would you want to see changed during your term as attorney general? Would you want to bring back a boot camp?
Over the next four years, it’s my intention to try and reform the system, but it is going to be an enormous job. It’s not going to happen overnight. I know that the attorney general’s office has been working on legislation, and my intention this first year is to try and implement a lot of the things that Marty’s been working on, not have an ambitious reform package for myself. Give me a year to work to explain the problems to the legislators and to the governor’s office, and to try and build some consensus to bring some legislation in subsequent sessions to try and fix some of the problems. 
Quite frankly, that’s the reason I ran for attorney general. My job has become so much more difficult to do since I came back from the Legislature than it was before, and I knew that I couldn’t fix it from Hot Springs. 
I’m going to do my best over the next four years to get some reforms that I think make some sense for the people, for the taxpayers and the victims, and quite frankly, for the people that are coming through the system, so they have the tools they need when they’re released to go back into the community and be successful.
Drug courts and other specialty courts are often cited as successful outgrowths of criminal justice reform. Do you see the value in those?
Here in Fall River and Oglala Lakota County, we don’t have any of those courts. My understanding of how they work is all third-hand. I tend to think I just need to be more educated on what they do, because I haven’t had a lot of experience with them.
Do I think that they’re as effective as they were envisioned to be? Probably not. But I need to not be too critical because I haven’t interfaced with it myself personally.
In a smaller jurisdiction that hasn’t gotten a lot of those resources, almost all of my experience has been that (the reforms) have made the work much more difficult for everybody involved in the process.
Is there anything else in particular you’d like people to know as we approach your first term?
Marty Jackley has done a great job as attorney general, as far as I can see. I want to continue a lot of his programs. I do want to tweak the system and make it work better for the locals, but what I will tell you is that at the state level, I think that the Division of Criminal Investigation, the State Crime Lab, the entities that are under the attorney general, have been working very well. Frankly, I don’t feel like I could have a better situation going in.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Free speech protection bill headed to North Dakota Legislature next year
description: A bill to protect people from getting dragged through court for exercising their free speech could go before North Dakota lawmakers in January. Sometimes people who speak out in the public interest are targeted by frivolous lawsuits intended to waste their time and money, and ultimately to silence them. This legal tactic is often referred […]
text:
The Burleigh County Courthouse is pictured on Thayer Avenue in Bismarck on March 13, 2024. A bill to be considered by North Dakota lawmakers next year aims to ensure the state doesn’t become a safe haven for frivolous lawsuits meant to curb free speech. (Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A bill to protect people from getting dragged through court for exercising their free speech could go before North Dakota lawmakers in January.
Sometimes people who speak out in the public interest are targeted by frivolous lawsuits intended to waste their time and money, and ultimately to silence them. This legal tactic is often referred to as a strategic lawsuit against public participation, or SLAPP.
Most states have passed laws designed to keep those kinds of cases out of the courts, though North Dakota is not one of them.
A group of state leaders has recommended that the Legislature change that.
Members of North Dakota’s delegation to the national Uniform Law Commission told the North Dakota Monitor they don’t feel SLAPP suits are an issue in North Dakota. But given most other states have already passed anti-SLAPP legislation, North Dakota may be at risk for attracting them, they said.
The issue has already come up in the ongoing legal battle between the developer of the Dakota Access Pipeline and the environmental group Greenpeace.
North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte asks a question during oral arguments on Dec. 18, 2023. (Photo by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)
A policy drafted by the commission could help ensure the state doesn’t become a safe haven for frivolous lawsuits meant to curb free speech, said North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte, who chairs the state delegation.
“I don’t know that we want to wait until we have a big problem,” he said.
The Uniform Law Commission looks for areas where it could be beneficial for states to work together on state policy, including by writing model legislation for states to adopt. It drafted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act in 2020 with the goal of making anti-SLAPP legislation stronger and more cohesive across the country.
“Many of these uniform acts have greater value when they are, in fact, uniform and adopted by most states,” Tufte said.
The North Dakota delegation of the commission this summer voted to recommend that state lawmakers adopt the act. If the 2027 Legislature passes the proposal, it would give state courts an official procedure for dealing with potential SLAPP cases.
Defendants who feel they are being sued in retaliation for their free speech would be able to formally request for the case to be dismissed at the outset of the lawsuit. The law would require that defendants provide evidence backing up their claim, and plaintiffs would have an opportunity to show that their suit is legitimate and legally viable.
If someone is found to have brought a frivolous lawsuit under the act, they have to pay the defendant’s legal expenses.
Rep. Larry Klemin, R-Bismarck, speaks on the House floor on Feb. 25, 2025. (Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“It all happens very fast, considering the way litigation usually goes,” said Republican state Rep. Lawrence Klemin, another member of North Dakota’s Uniform Law Commission. “It’s an expeditious way of getting that kind of lawsuit thrown out of court.”
Seventeen states have adopted the Uniform Law Commission’s act since 2020, according to the organization’s website, and more states have adopted similar legislation.
Those states have reported a “high degree of satisfaction” with the law, said Lane Shetterly, a former Oregon lawmaker who led the group that drafted the act. Shetterly said he’s not aware of any that have faced any major issues implementing it.
A range of organizations have expressed support for the policy, including the American Civil Liberties Union, National Right to Life Committee and a handful of First Amendment rights groups.
Greenpeace has alleged that the North Dakota lawsuit brought against it by the developer of the Dakota Access Pipeline is a SLAPP, though the court has not weighed in on this claim.
Energy Transfer claims Greenpeace is at fault for encouraging anti-pipeline protesters to damage its property near the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation in 2016 and 2017 and for orchestrating a campaign to defame the company to the public. Greenpeace alleges that Energy Transfer’s claims are baseless and that the suit is a ploy to harm the environmental movement. A Morton County jury in March 2025 sided with Energy Transfer in the case, a verdict Greenpeace has said it will appeal.
The judge in that lawsuit, Southwest Judicial District Judge James Gion, has ruled that he cannot evaluate whether the case is a SLAPP because North Dakota does not have legislation recognizing the legal tactic. Greenpeace’s global affiliate, Greenpeace International, has countersued Energy Transfer in the Netherlands under a European Union directive outlawing SLAPP lawsuits.
Jury finds Greenpeace at fault for protest damages, awards pipeline developer more than $660 million

Tufte said that members of North Dakota’s delegation to the Uniform Law Commission are aware that the state’s lack of anti-SLAPP legislation has been brought up in the Greenpeace case, though he said the commission has not discussed the lawsuit much.
Shetterly said while he isn’t familiar with the particulars of Energy Transfer’s case against Greenpeace, he said the group had organizations like Greenpeace in mind when it was drafting the legislation.
“We did talk generally about Greenpeace as an organization that is susceptible to SLAPP,” he said. “Lawful protest and speech are exactly the kinds of things that an anti-SLAPP statute is designed to protect and avoid years of litigation to resolve.”
Members of the media can also be vulnerable to these kinds of legal tactics, Shetterly said. He pointed to a 2017 West Virginia defamation case brought by mining executive Robert Murray against talk show host John Oliver over his coverage of Murray’s companies as one prominent example of a SLAPP. A judge dismissed the suit in 2018.
Klemin said the North Dakota Uniform Law Commission will sponsor the act during the 2027 legislative session. He said while he hasn’t yet heard feedback about the proposal from other North Dakota lawmakers, he doesn’t expect it to be controversial.
“It seems like an idea that protects your constitutional rights,” he said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Three North Carolina schools made big gains on chronic absenteeism. Here’s what they’re doing.
description: At Washington County High School, Principal Torrey Hines learned that some students were spending part of the school day at a barbershop instead of attending an intervention period, a designated time for additional academic support. So Hines went to the barbershop one morning to find out why. A student told him they skipped because intervention […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)At Washington County High School, Principal Torrey Hines learned that some students were spending part of the school day at a barbershop instead of attending an intervention period, a designated time for additional academic support.
Principal Torrey Hines, Washington County High School (Courtesy photo)
So Hines went to the barbershop one morning to find out why. A student told him they skipped because intervention was scheduled  first thing in the morning. Hines said the school responded by moving that intervention block to “smack dab in the middle of the day.”
The story was one of several examples shared by three principals at a recent State Board of Education meeting about how their schools have improved attendance.
North Carolina’s chronic absenteeism rate remains well above pre-pandemic levels. 
About 400,000 students were chronically absent during the 2024-25 school year, meaning they missed at least 10% of school days. That was about one in four students. 
The statewide chronic absenteesim rate has fallen from a peak of 31.2% in 2021-22 to 24.3% in 2024-25. Still, students who are chronically absent miss about 30 days of school on average, according to the state Department of Public Instruction.
DPI has identified more than 300 schools statewide as “Bright Spots” based on improvements in chronic absenteeism. The schools range from elementary to high school, and their approaches vary.
Principal Taimak Willis, Northwest Elementary, Pitt County (Courtesy photo)
At Northwest Elementary in Pitt County, Principal Taimak Willis said staff focus on understanding what is keeping students out of school.
“We believe that people matter. So yes, we’re talking about students, but what about the parents? Once we find out that there are attendance issues, we deal with the students, but we go and make sure that the parents have all of the resources and things that they need,” Willis said. 
Teachers are asked to alert school staff when a student misses two or three consecutive days. A social worker then contacts the family, and the school’s attendance team discusses next steps. 
In one case, the school connected a mother who was struggling with her mental health to resources and helped connect the family with transportation and other resources so the students could get to school.
Northwest also has a family resource center that has basic supplies such as toiletries and is equipped with a washer and dryer. Willis said the center can help students whose circumstances outside school are affecting their attendance.
The school also has an interpreter that works closely with families, including by making home visits. Willis said some students who had struggled with attendance now come to the front office to eat with the interpreter because of the relationship she has built with them.
Hertford County Middle School divides students into three groups based on attendance, said Principal Elenia Riddick. Those attending regularly, those trending toward chronic absenteeism, and those who are already chronically absent.
Principal Elenia Riddick, Hertford County Middle School (Courtesy photo)
The school assigns an adult to check in with students in the two higher-risk groups each morning. If a student is absent, that adult calls the family to find out what happened and whether the school can help. 
Building relationships with students and their families has been key to the school’s strategy, she told the board. 
“What we really focused on at Hertford County Middle School was those personal check-ins, making those connections with students,” said Principal Elenia Riddick, “and they’re excited about coming to school when they know somebody is there looking for them.”
Riddick said the school also tries to recognize students whose attendance improves by at least 5% after the first nine weeks. For some students who do not typically receive awards at school, it’s a big deal. 
Principal Hines also talked about efforts to make school more engaging. The school uses a house system modeled after the Ron Clark Academy, with students divided into teams that compete for points and recognition. The school plans to use attendance in the competition, with incentives for the house with the best attendance. 
Hines says his students have quickly embraced the house system.
“We’re noticing just within the first three weeks of school that kids are all in,” Hines said. “They want to come to school. They want to do well for their house.”
The school has also tried to make activities more relevant to students. During a week focused on hip-hop, students learned about the music, attended pep rallies and dressed as their favorite artists.
Parents are being held responsible for their kids’ crimes under new laws

Parents get daily calls showing whether their children attended school or arrived late. Social workers also make home visits. The school has partnered with outside providers to offer health and mental health services on campus.
Hines said some students miss school because they have responsibilities outside of it. Some care for younger siblings while their parents work. Others work to help support their families. Many parents work second- or third-shift jobs, making it harder for them to be involved with the school.
Shaun Kellogg, who leads DPI’s Office of Research and Promising Practices and the state’s AttendNC Counts initiative, said there was no single attendance program shared by the schools identified as “bright spots.”
The state has been studying those schools to understand what is behind their improvements. This summer, Kellogg and a colleague interviewed principals, counselors, social workers, data managers and other staff at seven bright spot schools.
“The numbers indicated that something special was happening,” Kellogg told the board, “but the numbers don’t tell us why.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Detroit district maintains growth in literacy and math on the 2026 M-STEP
authors: Hannah Dellinger - Chalkbeat Detroit, Micah Walker - BridgeDetroit
description: This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for Chalkbeat Detroit’s free newsletter to keep up with the city’s public school system and Michigan education policy. The Detroit school district made small year-over-year gains in reading, writing, and math in nearly every grade on state standardized tests last spring, results released Friday show.[...]
text:
The funding package President Donald Trump signed Feb. 3, 2026, includes $79 billion for the U.S. Education Department, representing a rejection by Congress of the president's plan to close the department. (Photo by kali9/Getty Images)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for Chalkbeat Detroit’s free newsletter to keep up with the city’s public school system and Michigan education policy.
The Detroit school district made small year-over-year gains in reading, writing, and math in nearly every grade on state standardized tests last spring, results released Friday show.
The district reached a 12-year high in the percentage of third graders scoring proficient or above in reading and writing, and it bucked a statewide trend of little to no improvement in early literacy.
Students in the Detroit Public Schools Community District still lag far behind statewide averages on the Michigan Student Test of Educational Progress, or M-STEP, however. For example, 14.1% of DPSCD third graders scored proficient or better on the 2025-26 exam compared to 38.2% of Michigan public school students.
Superintendent Nikolai Vitti said in a statement Friday that the results, many of which represented all-time highs for the district, reflect a broader trend of improvement.
“While students across the state (and country) continue to regress academically, our students are improving,” Vitti said.
The superintendent added the district needs to continue to “refine and scale” its success, particularly in literacy.
LaTrice McClendon, chair of the district’s board, said the results showed encouraging growth in math, adding “literacy still needs stronger gains.”
“We are not finished,” she said. “Detroit’s children deserve nothing less, and we will not rest until they get it.”
Researchers said long-term improvements in DPSCD on the exams, coupled with data showing fast student growth, indicate the district is making big strides to get students closer to where they should be academically.
Tara Kilbride, associate director of the independent research center Education Policy Innovation Collaborative at Michigan State University, said progress across all areas of the M-STEP over time suggests a systemic turnaround.
“That tells me that the improvements are likely not just an anomaly,” Kilbride added.
When evaluating test scores, an important factor to consider is that students in Detroit start out much further behind their peers in wealthier communities due an array of issues tied to poverty and systemic racism, said Jeremy Singer, assistant professor of educational leadership and policy at the University of Michigan-Flint.
“If a student is making a lot of progress every year and they are learning at an accelerated rate, they may still not cross proficiency,” said Singer, also a research affiliate at Wayne State University’s Detroit Partnership for Education Equity & Research.
Kilbride added, “That doesn’t mean the lower levels of proficiency aren’t something we should be concerned about.”
 DPSCD’s results show continued growth

Each spring, Michigan public school students in grades 3-7 take the M-STEP in English language arts and math. Fifth graders also take science and social studies M-STEP exams. Eighth graders take the PSAT in English and math. Eleventh graders take the SAT in the same subjects.
Exams were not given in the 2019-20 school year due to school closures during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2020-21, the tests were optional.
Compared to spring 2019 – the last year of testing before the pandemic upended learning – the improvements in DPSCD were noticeable in every subject and grade. For example, there was a 7.6 percentage point increase in eighth graders scoring proficient or better in English and a 6.8 percentage point increase in seventh grade math.
The year-over-year growth was smaller for the district in early literacy. A small dip in proficiency rates for sixth graders is attributed in part to unfinished learning when they were in kindergarten in 2019-20, Vitti said.
The district’s seventh grade cohort “continues to demonstrate large strides in their achievement,” and has consistently outperformed their peers, said Vitti.
On SAT results, also released Friday, 35.1% of students were at or above English benchmarks, as were 15.7% of students in math. Compared to spring 2019, those numbers increased by 6.6 and 4.3 percentage points respectively.
With smaller class sizes and more intervention for this year’s ninth graders as part of the DPSCD’s high school redesign, Vitti said the district anticipates more growth on the SAT.
Singer said the progress students make from the beginning to the end of the school year gives a clearer picture of district performance than the M-STEP, which is a snapshot of students’ performance on a single day.
A recent research analysis called The Education Scorecard suggests DPSCD is one of the best among similar districts across the country when it comes to the speed at which students are learning per school year.
 DPSCD attributes progress to better attendance, specialized support

Vitti told Chalkbeat in an email Friday that the district’s investments in recruiting and retaining certified teachers, using evidence-based curriculum, student interventions, as well as wraparound services for children and families, contributed to DPSCD’s academic improvements.
“We also have clear targets and stretch targets at the district and school level to hold one another accountable but to also problem solve and support when achievement is not improving,” he said.
Vitti said that might be what setDetroit apart from some statewide trends.
“I don’t see evidence of all of this with great consistency throughout Michigan and I believe nationally school districts have not completely shifted from the legitimate challenges of the pandemic.”
DPSCD has used a large portion of its $94.4 million “right to read” literacy lawsuit settlement to support students who are below grade level. The district has hired hundreds of additional academic interventionists and contracted more tutoring services.
As the district must spend the last of the settlement this school year, Vitti said it will likely have to make difficult budget decisions in order to keep the interventionists.
Imani Foster of 482Forward, a nonprofit focused on educational equity, said she believes the targeted support has helped students. She added more time is needed to see the full effect of the literacy funds.
“I think in five years we can look and see if the incremental change marked sustainable change,” she said.
In math, Vitti said teachers and students are becoming more familiar with curriculum based on the “why” behind math instead of only procedural skills.
“We have also been more targeted in our interventions to make sure that we are filling the gaps in pre-requisite skills at each grade level,” he said. “Younger students who were exposed to the math curriculum at earlier ages are higher performing than their older peers.”
Venessa Keesler, president and CEO of Launch Michigan, said DPSCD is “proof of concept” of what happens “if you get good curriculum, you train your educators, you stay the course, and you really are honest about what’s working and what’s not.”
Maria Montoya, a Detroit parent and education consultant, said consistency is key for the district to continue improvements.
Since pandemic-era school closures, DPSCD has significantly improved its rates of chronic absenteeism, defined as a student missing around 18 or more days in a typical 180-day school year. Missing too much school can make students fall behind and struggle to catch up for years.
While performance on the M-STEP has significantly improved for DPSCD since 2018-19, chronic absenteeism has only fallen back to a slightly lower rate, at 60.9%.
Singer said those data points could suggest DPSCD’s academic achievement is due to more than just better success in getting kids to school.
Both Singer and Kilbride said the data can’t definitively say which efforts have led to better performance on the M-STEP.
“My best hypothesis would be that it was a combination of coordinated support and strategies rather than one particular thing,” said Kilbride.
Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org.
Micah Walker is a reporter covering arts and culture and education for BridgeDetroit. You can reach her at mwalker@bridgedetroit.com.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Redside Foundation provides mental health assistance to the West’s outdoor guides
description: Considering Kami Bakken’s line of work, it’s difficult to imagine mental health being a major issue in her life. It’s more difficult to think there is a need for the Redside Foundation, an Idaho-based nonprofit that also provides mental health and other services to river, hunting and wilderness guides in Wyoming, Montana and Colorado. “We […]
text:
A guide leads horses and pack animals through a river crossing in Yellowstone National Park. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)Considering Kami Bakken’s line of work, it’s difficult to imagine mental health being a major issue in her life.
Kami Bakken is a river guide in the West. (Photo courtesy of Kami Bakken)
It’s more difficult to think there is a need for the Redside Foundation, an Idaho-based nonprofit that also provides mental health and other services to river, hunting and wilderness guides in Wyoming, Montana and Colorado.
“We have this romantic ideal about these rugged individuals from the West, and guides are perfect examples of that,” says Shannon Walton, executive director of Redside. “There’s a lot going on underneath that – the loneliness, depression, thoughts of suicide and high levels of substance abuse. In the regions we serve, we have the highest rates of suicide in the lower 48, among the highest rate of substance abuse in the lower 48 and the highest access to firearms in the lower 48. It’s a perfect storm regarding the need for support.”
Bakken, a river guide who lives in Jackson Hole and has a seasonal home in McCall, received the professional help she needed – after experiencing significant low points along the way.
The guiding itself is a pleasure. Her routine consists of spending a week, sometimes longer, guiding a group of 24 people downriver alongside a small team of guides.
“These trips are truly one-of-a-kind experiences, especially with the Middle Fork being a crown jewel of rivers in the United States,” she says. “The Salmon River is also one of the longest free-flowing rivers in the lower 48, and the river is constantly changing. So while the trips are somewhat innately life-changing, we also offer an experience that allows people to connect with this landscape and with each other.”
Bakken relishes every aspect of her job – educating folks about the history and the importance of the Salmon, the games played and even the cooking. She especially enjoys the close relationships with people who take the trips.
“From a guide’s perspective, you are on 24/7 and it’s that way non-stop for three months, or longer for guides that work year around,” she says. “And you are developing connections with people who are guiding with you, and they become your family. That sense of community and having people you can lean on is incredibly important to me.”
It’s an emotional let-down when the river runs end for the season and the wonderful people she met along the way are gone. It magnifies the stress of living in these pictures of paradise, financial and otherwise.
“There were times that I didn’t want to see the sun shine the next day,” she says.
Bakken is not alone, as Walton has seen as the Redside director. One immediate outlet is a helpline for those facing depression, or suicidal thoughts.
According to the foundation’s website, “Redside” is named for an infamous rapid on the Middle Fork of the Salmon River that “conjures up images of the majestic native sockeye salmon on its life-fulfilling journey to the heart of Central Idaho.”
 The foundation was formed in 2010 after the death of a popular Idaho guide, Telly Evans (1974-2010).
As stated on the website, “Sadly, behind his generous smile and unyielding passion, Telly hid a pain that would eventually steal him from the river and friendships he loved.”
With his death came the inspiration to provide a wide range of services for the guides – including healthcare access, financial planning and housing assistance. One of the toughest challenges for the guides, as Bakken will attest, is asking for help.
“There is no shame with seeking help,” she says. “Today, I’m good and I feel blessed. I don’t know if I would be here without Redside.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: In America’s most divisive era since the Civil War, Dolly Parton showed us a path forward
description: In a 1988 interview with Bill Moyers, Massachusetts Institute of Technology linguistics professor and intellectual Noam Chomsky discussed a common theme in his celebrated book “Manufacturing Consent.” Chomsky observed that it is extremely rare within America’s class-based, hierarchical power structures for an individual to rise up out of the ordinary; enter[...]
text:
Dolly Parton, pictured  in 2020, could have become a billionaire. Instead, she used her money to help others, including her native East Tennesseans and created a program to support childhood literacy. (Photo by Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)(Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images)In a 1988 interview with Bill Moyers, Massachusetts Institute of Technology linguistics professor and intellectual Noam Chomsky discussed a common theme in his celebrated book “Manufacturing Consent.”
Chomsky observed that it is extremely rare within America’s class-based, hierarchical power structures for an individual to rise up out of the ordinary; enter a position of immense wealth, power and influence and then turn around and use that position to improve the material conditions for “the folks back home.”
Examples are not difficult to find. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos started the company in his garage, but now his delivery drivers must labor under conditions even more dangerous than those faced by law enforcement officers. Sam Walton’s family built Walmart from nothing, but now their workers are the largest cohort of employed Americans so underpaid they must rely on public assistance. 
Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook when he was just 19 years old, but now his social media empire constructs algorithms that lead today’s 19-year-olds to internet addiction and even suicide. Elon Musk immigrated to the U.S. to pursue the American dream, but now he prevents others from that same pursuit by engaging in union-busting at Tesla, SpaceX and X.
Examine most American success stories, and we see Chomsky’s observation ring true again and again. 
And yet, every rule has its exception, and in this case, the exception boasted a towering blonde wig, an hourglass frame bedazzled with rhinestones and a smile like you wouldn’t believe.
Dolly Parton began helping others immediately 
There are many ways in which Dolly Parton broke the mold of the traditional capitalistic “rags to riches” success story. The first is how quickly she shifted her focus from advancing her career to helping others. Parton launched many charitable campaigns long before she became a centi-millionaire.
In 1988, when she was just 42, Parton created the Dollywood Foundation, which began as a local program to improve educational outcomes for children in Sevier County, where she grew up.
In 1990, Parton launched the Buddy Program, which paired seventh- and eighth-graders with an academic “buddy.” The program also pledged $500 to Sevier County students who graduated from high school. The combined measures led to dropout rates plunging from 35% to 6%. 
In 2000, Parton’s Dollywood Foundation expanded by awarding $15,000 scholarships to five Sevier County high school students from each year’s senior cohort.
And that was just the beginning.
The Imagination Library
One would be hard-pressed to find a greater act of such pure goodness as Parton’s Imagination Library. In 1995, Parton founded the Library with the modest goal of putting one free book per month into the hands of every young child from birth to age five in Sevier County, regardless of family income.
Dolly Parton sent a letter to each child, upon turning five, to congratulate them on their “graduation” from the Imagination Library. (Photo: Submitted)
Why focus on early childhood literacy? Because Parton connected the dots between illiteracy and poverty. Parton grew up in a modest cabin with her parents and 11 siblings, and her father was a poor sharecropper who could not read or write. Parton said that, despite his business savvy and work ethic, her father’s illiteracy prevented him from achieving his dreams.
In the early 2000s, Parton expanded the Library beyond Sevier County, taking it national. By 2003, the Library had distributed one million books. Twenty years later, it had gifted 200 million books. By the time of Parton’s death, the Library had sent out 332 million books to over 3 million children across the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Ireland.
“Dear Imagination Library Graduate,” Parton wrote in a letter sent to every child as they turned five, graduated from the Library, and entered school. “My how time flies. It seems it was only yesterday when your family and friends read you your first story. You were just a baby. Now you’re five years old and about to go to school. How exciting! I hope you have a great time in school. I bet your school will even have a library where you can check out books. You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go. Just remember the lessons my family taught me – dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things, and you can be anyone you want to be. You are terrific, and remember… I Will Always Love You.”
Breaking the mold
Parton cared more about you and me than she ever did about becoming exorbitantly wealthy. She could have become a billionaire, but instead she donated millions of dollars and thousands of hours of her time, first to helping the impoverished souls of the East Tennessee communities that raised her, then to helping those in need across the state, country and world.
In a nation where the wealthiest and most successful among us often turn around and pull up the ladder that helped them rise to the top, Parton spent her life reaching back down the ladder she had climbed, helping those the world had forgotten.
Parton broke every rule, both perceived and written, of American capitalism and success. And while her music might get us singing along and her colorful jokes might bring smiles to our faces, perhaps her best contribution was the road map she left for how we might all behave. 
As America faces its most divisive period since the Civil War, perhaps “I will always love you” can be more than just a song lyric. Perhaps it can be a North Star for how we treat each other.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota speed zone changes create shift in ticketing hot spots
description: North Dakota state troopers wrote fewer speeding tickets on stretches of interstate highway that went up to an 80 mph speed limit in 2025, but some areas where speed limits were reduced saw a spike in citations — especially at Dickinson.  North Dakota’s top highway speed went up to 80 mph on Aug. 1, 2025. […]
text:
Interstate 94 snakes through Valley City, North Dakota, an area that has a lower speed limit than most of the state's interstate highways, which went to an 80 mph speed limit on Aug. 1, 2025. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) North Dakota state troopers wrote fewer speeding tickets on stretches of interstate highway that went up to an 80 mph speed limit in 2025, but some areas where speed limits were reduced saw a spike in citations — especially at Dickinson. 
North Dakota’s top highway speed went up to 80 mph on Aug. 1, 2025. At the same time, stretches of interstate at Dickinson, Grand Forks, Jamestown and Valley City saw the speed limit reduced from 75 mph to 70 mph. 
State troopers wrote 223 tickets during the first year of Dickinson’s 70 mph zone, more than triple for the same area the previous year, according to data provided by the North Dakota Highway Patrol. 
Tickets in the Grand Forks reduced-speed area more than doubled from the previous year. Meanwhile, Jamestown’s 70 mph zone saw a slight increase in tickets, while Valley City saw fewer. 
Rep. Ben Koppelman, R-West Fargo. (Photo provided by the North Dakota Legislative Assembly)
Rep. Ben Koppelman, R-West Fargo, sponsored the bill authorizing the 80 mph speed limit. 
He said the feedback on the 80 mph limit has been “all positive,” but on the shift down to 70 around the four cities, “it’s all negative.” 
Koppelman said some people are blaming him because they think the new 70 mph zones were part of his bill for 80 mph as the top speed.
The decision to create those zones was made by the state Department of Transportation. 
“They created a speed trap,” Koppelman said of the Dickinson area.  
Koppelman said he has complained to Transportation Director Ron Henke, but got no indication the zones will change. 
Koppelman said he has talked with other legislators about addressing the situation in the 2027 session, but he said he is not aware of any bill drafts yet. 
Kirk Hoff, director of the Department of Transportation’s Design Division, said those four cities are large enough that additional traffic congestion at peak morning and evening commute times warrants the slower speed limit. 
He added that there are curves on I-94 in the Jamestown and Valley City areas where an 80 mph speed limit would not be safe. 
The Fargo-West Fargo and Bismarck-Mandan areas already had reduced speeds before last year’s changes.
The Department of Transportation also put in a 70 mph area near Medora, but Hoff said a further review of the curves in that Badlands area led to a decision to allow the 80 mph there. 
Hoff said he was not aware of any plans to alter the existing 70 mph zones. 
Rep. Ben Koppelman, R-West Fargo, the prime sponsor of a bill to raise North Dakota’s interstate speed limit to 80 mph, sits at his desk May 2, 2025. (Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Major Tom Iverson of the Highway Patrol said tickets in that area may go down as drivers remember to slow down. 
“If a roadway you’re just used to driving at 75 mph and it’s now 70, it may take a little bit of time to get used to,” Iverson said. 
Overall in the first year of those four 70 mph zones, troopers wrote 1,000 tickets, compared to 776 in the previous year. 
In the areas where the speed limit went up to 80, the number of speeding tickets fell to 4,742 in the 12 months starting Aug. 1, 2025, down from 8,361 the previous 12 months. 
The Highway Patrol also included data on the number of crashes on the interstates. 
Crashes went up in the new 80 mph areas — there were 505 crashes from Aug 1, 2025, to July 31, 2026, up from 469 the previous year.
Crashes also went up in the areas where the speed limit was reduced from 75 mph to 70 mph over the same time period, rising to 65 from 53 the previous year. 
Iverson said it is difficult to draw any conclusions on the effect of speed limit changes based on one year of crash data.
Speeding fines also increased as part of Koppelman’s bill. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com
