name: National
title: On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, States Newsroom editor remembers the heroes of Flight 93
description: On a rural stretch of land in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, an open meadow filled with bright wildflowers, a memorial grove of trees and a giant boulder marks the spot where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed on Sept. 11, 2001. States Newsroom’s Pennsylvania Capital-Star Editor-in-Chief Tim Lambert recently revisited the national memorial on this field — […]
text:
The crash of United Flight 93 is marked by a boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)On a rural stretch of land in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, an open meadow filled with bright wildflowers, a memorial grove of trees and a giant boulder marks the spot where United Airlines Flight 93 crashed on Sept. 11, 2001.
States Newsroom’s Pennsylvania Capital-Star Editor-in-Chief Tim Lambert recently revisited the national memorial on this field — where he happened to own a piece of land that was part of more than three dozen acres that made up the crash site.
“It’s always hard to come back here, but it’s always a chance to remember the sacrifices made by the passengers and crew of Flight 93 on that day,” Lambert said. “I think it’s important 25 years later to remember what they did and why they did it. They decided to act on a day that America was under attack.”
Debris at the Flight 93 crash site in Stonycreek Township, Pennsylvania, during cleanup operations in October 2001. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert)
On that day, al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four commercial planes. They slammed two into the World Trade Center towers in New York City and another into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. The fourth — Flight 93 — crashed in an open clearing near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
The 40 passengers and crew are remembered for sacrificing their lives when they tried to wrest control of the plane from the hijackers and stop them from hitting what was believed to be their intended target: the U.S. Capitol.
A Superman action figure left by a visitor at the base of Flight 93 passenger Louis “Joey” Nacke at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Pennsylvania, on Aug. 26, 2026. Nacke had a Superman tattoo, and is believed to have been one of the passengers who attempted to retake the hijacked jetliner. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Nearly 3,000 people were killed in what is the deadliest terror attack on U.S. soil. Forty-four people, including the four hijackers, died aboard Flight 93.
At the time, Lambert worked as a reporter for a public radio station in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.
“It was around 4:30 in the afternoon — among the chaos of the newsroom — and I looked up at this TV that was on a cabinet, and the reporter from one of the national outlets was standing at the corner of the Lambertsville (and) Shanksville Road,” Lambert recalled. “And it was at that moment, I stopped and thought, ‘Wait, we still own land near Shanksville, and it’s awfully close to that intersection.’”
The next morning, Lambert said, he listened to a voice message on his home answering machine from his dad, who recognized the crash site on television, realizing that it was their family property.
Lambert was in a unique situation. While reporters across the nation and around the world were covering the tragic event, he was the only journalist who had access to the Flight 93 crash site. He realized he had a huge responsibility.
“I was well aware that history was at the door, and I wanted to do things the right way,” he said.
Tim Lambert, center, interviews Somerset County Coroner Wallace Miller, left. Former WITF News Director Damon Boughamer on the right records the conversation at the Flight 93 crash site on Oct. 6, 2001. (Courtesy of Tim Lambert)
Lambert not only reported on the crash, but also assisted first responders and met with the families of the passengers and crew. He remembered what the land looked like that day. The plane had plowed into the ground at a high rate of speed, with the aircraft disintegrating into tiny bits and pieces, leaving a large crater.
Although the majority of the plane shattered and few bodies were recovered, authorities were able to identify the passengers and crew. More than 1,500 response members under the direction of the Federal Bureau of Investigation recovered fragments of the plane: twisted pieces of metal, tires, seat frames, luggage, clothing — most of which were no larger than a notebook.
The field was essentially a cemetery, and family members wanted to protect it. Only family members and some park rangers can visit the actual crash site. But the public can walk along the tall concrete walls of the nearby memorial, etched with the names of people who perished in the crash. Visitors can also go to a museum and walk through parts of the field to an overlook to view the crash site.
A boulder at the Flight 93 National Memorial marks the approximate spot where United Flight 93 crashed on Sept. 11, 2001, in Stonycreek Township, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Through the years, Lambert has visited the site to pay his respects.
“It’s been a while since I’ve been here, so it’s almost like a little homecoming to visit with old friends, even if it’s just looking out on the field and remembering those who gave their lives that day,” he said.
The museum features photos of family members of passengers and crew, with details about their lives and memorabilia, including photographs, jewelry and uniforms. For example, the husband of flight attendant Lorraine Bay donated her United Airlines ID and one of her uniforms, along with a wine bottle corkscrew she used for in-flight service.
“You know, with these exhibits, I want to take something that’s very large and abstract and offer different avenues for different people to come in and relate to it,” said Betsy Keene, curator for the National Parks for Western Pennsylvania, which includes the Flight 93 National Memorial.
“Families say they want their loved one to be remembered as an individual person, as more than just this one day.”



She said there are about 9,300 objects collected from the crash site and from families that are cataloged at the memorial, including 800 pieces of the aircraft curated over the years.
“We want to have these objects to help people relate and to pull them into the story and to help them understand who these people were, what happened here, and what it meant to the world at the time,” Keene said.
Memorial Superintendent Stephen Clark said more than 400,000 visitors annually come to the park, owned and operated by the federal government and managed by the National Park Service.
Visitors walk along the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County, on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“I think that this memorial, albeit 25 years, it’s still a glimpse. It’s still a blink of an eye in our nation’s history,” Clark said. “But I still think that even as the years roll on, this story will continue to be told.”
Through the years, Lambert said he’s had many chances to meet families whose loved ones died that day. As the 25th anniversary approaches, he said he plans to reflect on their stories.
“The memorial is beautiful. The memorial is very fitting. It’s a great tribute, and it’s a respectful tribute to the passengers and crew of Flight 93. But for me, I think about watching the land heal over the 25-year period,” Lambert said.
“To watch them sort of heal as the site heals through nature, and watch that sort of in tandem, is something that I will always think about anytime I look over that field.”
The American flag flies at the entry to the pathway that leads to the Wall of Names at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Stonycreek Township, Pennsylvania. The visitor center is in the background. (Photo courtesy of Tim Lambert)
Pennsylvania Capital-Star reporter Peter Hall contributed to this report. Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: On primary day, will New Hampshire Democrats and Republicans stick to playbooks?
description: In 2006, Carol Shea-Porter stunned the New Hampshire Democratic establishment, defeating a well-funded, party-backed opponent, Jim Craig, in the primary and then ousting Republican Jeb Bradley in the 1st Congressional District. And she did it with a progressive platform.  “There was a sense of: We don’t want Washington coming here and telling us what to […]
text:
Voters wait inside the Bow Community Center just before noon on Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)In 2006, Carol Shea-Porter stunned the New Hampshire Democratic establishment, defeating a well-funded, party-backed opponent, Jim Craig, in the primary and then ousting Republican Jeb Bradley in the 1st Congressional District. And she did it with a progressive platform. 
“There was a sense of: We don’t want Washington coming here and telling us what to do,” recalled Kathy Sullivan, the New Hampshire Democratic Party chairwoman at the time. 
Twenty years later, some progressive Democrats are hoping to replay that victory in New Hampshire’s state primary. And they can point to uncanny parallels. As in 2006, the president in 2026 is a second-term Republican president suffering low approval ratings driven by an unpopular war in the Middle East, and Democrats are vying to retake Congress.
But whether that environment can allow another left-leaning Democratic upset in the Granite State is less guaranteed. In the two decades since Shea-Porter’s upset win, Democrats have settled on a more predictable, less disruptive strategy to hold the 1st Congressional District, allowing Rep. Chris Pappas to hold the seat since 2018. 
“That’s sort of the pattern that has been out there for a while now,” Sullivan said. 
Now, as Pappas leaves the district to run for U.S. Senate, some left-leaning Democratic candidates are hoping they can interrupt the New Hampshire Democratic establishment playbook on Tuesday. 
For Republicans vying for their party’s nomination for U.S. Senate and Congress, another question looms Tuesday: How much does President Donald Trump matter in 2026?
The Bulletin spoke to Sullivan, Democratic strategist Jim Demers, Republican strategists Dave Carney and Jim Merrill, and three political professors. Here’s what’s at stake on primary day. 
What are the chances of a progressive upset?
The possibility of a surprise progressive victory in either the Democratic U.S. Senate or 1st Congressional District primaries appears unlikely, observers say. However, the restless mood within the Democratic Party in the past few months could make things interesting.
Left-leaning Democratic Socialists of America-supported candidates have pulled off surprise victories in a variety of primaries this year, from New York and Colorado House seats to Michigan and Florida Senate seats. 
In both of New Hampshire’s most competitive Democratic primaries, polling indicates that the progressive candidate is behind her more centrist opponents but has gained ground in recent months. Karishma Manzur, a scientist and first-time candidate competing against Pappas, has reduced Pappas’s percentage lead from 43 points in April to 13 points in August, according to a University of New Hampshire survey. And Carleigh Beriont, another left-leaning candidate, has increased her polling share of 1st Congressional District primary from 3% in June to 12% in August, according to St. Anselm College polling. 
“A progressive upset remains plausible,” said Dante Scala, political science professor at the University of New Hampshire. Plausible, but not expected.
Pappas has spent nearly $11.54 million since January 2025, according to Federal Election Commission filings from the Aug. 19 filing period, a staggering sum. Carney argued that aggressive spending is an indication of concern caused by a challenge from Manzur. 
Meanwhile, in the primary to fill the open seat in 1st Congressional District, mainstream Democrats Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen have dominated polls. But if the anti-establishment wave seen in other Democratic primaries arrives in New Hampshire, Beriont could benefit, Scala says. Though she is polling in third place, Beriont could win a plurality if Sullivan and Shaheen split the centrist or moderate vote. 
That would be a change of pace for New Hampshire Democratic congressional candidates over the past decade. Sullivan says she has heard demand among fellow Democrats in recent years. 
“People will say, ‘Why is it we always have to end up voting for the person who’s more centrist? When is it going to be our turn?’” she said.  
Carney, a former strategist for Rick Perry, argues a progressive win in the primary could energize Democrats, even if he would disagree with the choice. 
“We are not a crazy-ass state yet,” Carney said. “But nominating a bunch of socialists will give them energy. That will help in the general election because the left — the left of the left — is on fire. And the middle is not, and nor is our side on fire.”
Still, the progressives have major hurdles. Beriont and Manzur must overcome strong deficits in name recognition and campaign funding compared to their opponents. Sullivan and Pappas have run before, while Shaheen is the daughter of U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, giving all three natural political momentum, noted Wayne Lesperance, president of New England College and a former political science professor.
“The other piece is: Will they turn out?” Lesperance said of progressives. “Typically, people that are motivated to turn out have a connection to the party, which should favor a more establishment candidate.”
And New Hampshire Democrats might buck this year’s national left-leaning trend; the state has a long tradition of backing relatively moderate candidates. That’s often a strategic calculation — a concession by Democrats that independent voters are a major player in New Hampshire general elections. 
“The problem New Hampshire Democrats face is, you know, they might want in their heart of hearts to run more progressive campaigns or more aggressive campaigns, but I think they learned over the century that Republicans dominated the state that’s not what folks here necessarily are going to go for,” said Chris Galdieri, a politics professor at St. Anselm College. 
It’s also a function of the state primary electorate, which trends older in New Hampshire than in other states, he said. 
“This is a state that does not have a large minority population. It does not have a major urban center,” Galdieri said. “…You look at the surges of support for Abdul El-Sayed or Francesca Hong in the Upper Midwest and I don’t know that you have the same sort of potential base of support for those sorts of candidates (in New Hampshire).”
Will the ‘cautious centrist’ playbook continue to work for New Hampshire Democrats?
New Hampshire Democrats’ traditional approach to statewide and congressional campaigns can be traced to Jeanne Shaheen or former Gov. John Lynch.
The recipe may feel familiar: candidates who position themselves as pragmatic problem-solvers, not ideologues; who highlight federal funding victories, not bombastic floor speeches. It’s an approach geared more toward New Hampshire’s prevalence of college-educated, suburban voters, Galdieri says. 
“The model has been kind of a very traditional Democrat that kind of colors within the lines,” Merrill said. “None of them are from the DSA wing of the party, and they’re sober and serious, and they focus (on) constituent service.” 
To that template, Demers adds another characteristic: a focus on opposition to Donald Trump. 
“(Voters are) also looking at who is going to be the best voice to stand up and fight Trump in the next congressional session,” he said. “People have a lot of frustration, and a lot of people feel like they want change in this election, and that change is people who will stand up and take Trump on.” 
But while the playbook has worked successfully in the purple politics of New Hampshire, the primaries Tuesday could test that. Even if Pappas wins, for instance, a strong showing by Manzur could be an early indicator that the template needs to be updated, some argued. 
“It’s a very safe strategy when it works, until it doesn’t work anymore,” said Carney. “And the environment on their side has flipped. They don’t want polite. They want someone to go there to wreck the house, upset the apple cart, break the china.”
Will Trump affect the Republican primaries?
One major difference between 2006 and 2026 can be seen in the Republican primaries. Despite his low approval ratings among the general electorate, Trump continues to command high support within the Republican Party. And unlike Bush, Trump appears interested in continuing to wield that influence. 
“I really think that New Hampshire Republicans have finally and fully made their peace with Trump,” said Galdieri.
Merrill agreed, and pointed to Republican primaries in other states this year, in which Trump has helped defeat critics such as John Cornyn in Texas and Bill Cassidy in Louisiana.
“If you go back in the last 10 years and you look at the candidates who actively moved away from Donald Trump, it’s a very, very short list of successful ones,” he said.
That means the Republican fight for the 1st Congressional District nomination has not seen candidates waver on their support for Trump. Leading candidates Anthony DiLorenzo, Hollie Noveletsky, and Brian Cole have largely been supportive of the president’s positions on hot-button topics such as the Iran war and tariffs; the president endorsed DiLorenzo in July. 
And in the primary for U.S. Senate, the contest between former U.S. Sens. Scott Brown and John Sununu has to some extent been defined by Trump’s decision to endorse Sununu in February; an August University of New Hampshire survey found that Sununu led Brown by 40 points. 
“I think (Brown’s) air went out of his tent when Sununu got in the race, and then it was crushed when the president gave his endorsement,” Carney said. 
Lesperance said New Hampshire Republicans have managed to walk a daunting tightrope so far.
“They very much talk positively about the president, the president’s agenda, but at times you can hear them differ slightly,” he said. “In a way that’s subtle and that’s respectful and that has not earned them the ire of the president to this point.”
The lack of differentiation or interest in defying Trump suggests New Hampshire Republicans are wrestling less with their political identity than Democrats are, in part because of the relative stability that comes with being in leadership. But Merrill says the national dynamic for Democrats is also a reflection of the timing of this election, two years after Kamala Harris failed to stop Trump from his comeback win. 
“We went through what Democrats are going through now 10 years ago,” said Merrill, a former senior adviser to Mitt Romney in 2012, speaking on the Republican soul-searching caused after that election loss. 
Still, despite the relative ideological homogeneity in Tuesday’s Republican primaries, Merrill predicts the dynamic will only last so long. 
“Whatever the results of this fall are, I think you may start to see some people begin to look ahead as, ‘What does a Republican Party kind of post–Donald Trump look like?’… In 2027 you may start to see the outer contours of that.”
What will turnout tell us?
In addition to the winners, the voter turnout Tuesday could have effects on the November elections — especially when it comes to enthusiasm. 
On Sept. 3, Secretary of State Dave Scanlan predicted that 145,751 Republicans and 103,024 Democrats will vote Tuesday, based on an analysis of party registration and past elections. New Hampshire Republicans traditionally participate at higher rates than Democrats in state primaries, Scanlan told reporters. 
But some New Hampshire pundits say Trump’s low approval rating and the national push to flip the House and Senate could change that. “One of the things that would genuinely surprise me is if Republican turnout outweighs Democratic turnout,” Scala said, adding: “The excitement on the Democratic side seems to me to be a lot, a lot higher.”
Merrill agrees about the potential significance of Democratic turnout. “If it’s significantly above what it’s been, then that’s going to be a very promising leading indicator for them in November,” he said. 
Where should observers look for clues tonight?
There are a number of specific polling precincts that could give an indication of where things are heading Tuesday night, experts say.
Manchester Wards 1 and 2 traditionally command the highest Democratic turnout and report their results early, Sullivan noted; turnout in the Democratic primaries there will be an early sign of how high Democratic energy is generally, she said.
Demers will have an eye on Nashua, a city that “goes both ways” in general elections and could signal which party has momentum.
For those watching the Democratic 1st Congressional District primary, results in Dover, Portsmouth, and Somersworth could show the strength of the progressive vs. establishment candidates, while unusual Democratic turnout in Bedford, a Republican town that has become more purple recently, could also tell a story.
Finally, Scala says if Manzur’s progressive challenge to Pappas is to succeed, she must demonstrate gains beyond college towns like Durham, Keene, and Hanover, and give a strong showing in Concord and Manchester, Pappas’ hometown. 
Of course, the real analysis will begin after the results come in — both for pundits and for strategists, Merrill noted. “It’s good to win in November, but when you lose, those can be clarifying, transformational experiences,” Merrill said. 
Tuesday’s primary will be New Hampshire’s last in September, after legislators passed a law to move the state primary to June beginning in 2028. At least one observer is okay with that. 
“Can we have a worse day for an election than the day after Labor Day?” said Sullivan. “Like, oh my God.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: $68 billion is up for grabs in Medicaid. Who wants it?
description: What would you do with $68 billion? That is the size of the decision Indiana is about to make. The state recently launched a procurement so large it will determine who delivers health care to nearly 1.5 million Hoosiers. The companies that win will not be building highways or upgrading software systems. They will be […]
text:
In 2021, Medicaid accounted for about 15% of Indiana’s total budget. By 2023, that share had climbed to 18%. In the state’s most recent biennial budget, Medicaid now represents 22$ of total spending. (Getty Images)What would you do with $68 billion? That is the size of the decision Indiana is about to make.
The state recently launched a procurement so large it will determine who delivers health care to nearly 1.5 million Hoosiers. The companies that win will not be building highways or upgrading software systems. They will be responsible for caring for some of Indiana’s most vulnerable residents.
Earlier this year, Indiana Family and Social Services Administration Secretary Mitch Roob announced the $68 billion procurement for Indiana’s four Medicaid managed care programs.
Together, these programs account for roughly half of Indiana’s total Medicaid spending and serve very different populations:

Healthy Indiana Plan (HIP) covers adults 19 to 64 and functions as Indiana’s primary adult Medicaid program.
Hoosier Healthwise serves children and pregnant women with low incomes.
Hoosier Care Connect covers blind or disabled adults under 65 who are not eligible for Medicare.
Indiana PathWays for Aging serves Hoosiers age 60 and older who need long-term care, including nursing facility services.

There is a good chance you know someone who relies on one of these programs. This rebid is expected to affect nearly 1 out of 5 of our Hoosier neighbors.
So who gets to compete for a prize this large?
Today, Indiana contracts with five private Medicaid health plans to operate these programs. All are expected to be potential bidders.
Indiana has historically procured its major managed care programs separately. This time, the state intends to select one or more contractors to operate all four programs together. Roob has dubbed it the “Mother of All Procurements.”
That approach reflects a broader shift already underway across state government.
The Indiana Department of Administration, which oversees statewide purchasing, has begun using a strategy known as “category management.” In plain terms, the state has found that agencies often buy similar services from the same vendors at very different prices. By combining that purchasing power and negotiating as one customer, the state aims to reduce costs and eliminate inefficiencies.
Indiana to bid $68 billion in Medicaid contracts this summer

State officials say this approach is already showing promise. According to the Department of Administration, early and preliminary estimates indicate that applying category management across state purchasing could generate between $150 million and $200 million in savings within the first 12 months alone.
The $68 billion managed care rebid applies that same philosophy to Medicaid. Instead of negotiating four massive contracts independently, the state is attempting to use its full scale at once to improve value and better control long-term costs.
And that matters, because Medicaid is one of the fastest-growing areas of state spending.
In 2021, Medicaid accounted for about 15% of Indiana’s total budget. By 2023, that share had climbed to 18%. In the state’s most recent biennial budget, Medicaid now represents 22$ of total spending. Recent budget forecasts show Medicaid spending continues to grow faster than state revenue.
But placing $68 billion worth of care for Indiana’s most vulnerable residents into a single procurement does not come without risk. A system normally adjusted one program at a time could face disruptions, administrative challenges and potential gaps in care if the transition is not carefully managed. Those risks may affect health plans, state agencies and, most importantly, the Hoosiers who depend on these services.
Still, state leaders deserve credit for attempting something bold. If successful, the Mother of All Procurements could help slow a growth curve that threatens funding for other priorities such as K-12 education, public safety and higher education.
So, to the nation’s Medicaid health plans, sharpen your pencils. Indiana has launched the largest health care procurement in its history.
After all, it’s only $68 billion.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: What’s the Lincoln Party? Ballard’s secretary of state run could expand Indiana ballot access
description: Former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard touts his run for secretary of state under the new Lincoln Party banner as a way to burst open an easier path for independent-minded candidates to make the election ballot. ClaraMary Winebrenner, a Republican office holder-turned-independent candidate in DeKalb County, hopes the new party could break up what she sees […[...]
text:
Indiana secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard speaks at the Statehouse before delivering petition signatures needed to qualify for the November ballot on July 14, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard touts his run for secretary of state under the new Lincoln Party banner as a way to burst open an easier path for independent-minded candidates to make the election ballot.
ClaraMary Winebrenner, a Republican office holder-turned-independent candidate in DeKalb County, hopes the new party could break up what she sees as the current two-party monopoly.
But Max Engling, the Republican secretary of state candidate, has taken aim at the Lincoln Party push as lacking a defined ideology and transparency in how it would select future candidates.
Ballard’s success in the November election is key for the Lincoln Party initiative — if he receives at least 2% of the vote the party’s candidates will get their names on general election ballots for the next four years; if he tops 10% of the vote the new party would join Republicans and Democrats in nominating candidates through primaries.
How the Lincoln Party came about
Ballard, who won Indianapolis mayor races in 2007 and 2011 as a Republican, announced his independent bid for secretary of state in March.
But the following week he adopted the Lincoln Party identity, saying it was needed to “unlock ballot access” for other independents. Otherwise, they would need to clear Indiana’s requirement of obtaining certified petition signatures of registered voters totaling 2% of the most recent secretary of state’s vote in their district — nearly 37,000 for a statewide office.
Ballard is on the ballot against Engling, Democrat Beau Bayh and Libertarian Lauri Shillings. 
Ballard argues that Indiana’s signature requirement was set up by Republicans and Democrats to box out competitors from appearing on the ballot.
“The laws in the state have made it practically impossible to overcome that obstacle,” Ballard told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “It’s very purposeful, very punitive to make sure nobody will clear that hurdle.”
Ballard’s candidacy was spurred by the work of Nathan Gotsch, a 43-year-old former Fort Wayne high school video production teacher who ran a 2022 independent campaign for northeastern Indiana’s 3rd congressional district seat and got 5% of the vote.
Nathan Gotsch (Courtesy photo)
Gotsch started a nonprofit group in 2025 that formed Independent Indiana, with the stated aim of supporting independent candidates.
Gotsch approached Ballard late last year about the secretary of state’s race after the group’s polling found Ballard with support from nearly one-quarter of voters in a hypothetical matchup against current GOP Secretary of State Diego Morales and Bayh.
Despite Engling defeating Morales in the Republican state convention, Gotsch said Ballard remained competitive and the goal of achieving ballot access was achievable.
“If the General Assembly changes the rules on independents, which I think they still should, then we may not need this path,” Gotsch said in an interview. “We probably wouldn’t. But we’ve seen over and over that they have protected their monopoly on the political process. The way to break that is to create a party that allows other folks to compete with them on the same playing field.”
Picking future Lincoln Party candidates
The Libertarian Party has maintained automatic ballot access for its candidates since clearing the 2% mark in the 1994 election, with its secretary of state nominee gaining 5.7% of the 2022 vote.
Indiana law gives a “minor party,” such as the Libertarians, broad latitude to set rules for how delegates are selected for its state convention nominating candidates for the general election ballot.
Just how the Lincoln Party would organize itself under such a scenario isn’t clear.
Gotsch is listed as the Lincoln Party’s chairman under its organization statement filed with the Indiana Election Division in June. 
Indiana secretary of state hopefuls clash over voting rules, office audit

Gotsch said he has had discussions with people around Indiana who are interested in helping the party, but did not say who might join him in its statewide leadership.
“We’re trying to talk to smart people from different walks of life, people that have experience in politics, people that don’t,” he said. “Ultimately, it’s on us to be able to put something forth that the public can feel good about.”
Both Ballard and Gotsch indicated they would be involved in selecting the candidates who would gain the party’s support.
“The intent, in the future, is to run what we call practical problem-solving people that you’d be proud to have in office,” Ballard said. “Both parties have numerous purity tests. They have extreme ideology.”
Ballard said he’s in the secretary of state’s race to win the office but that it would take time to build out a party structure across Indiana.
“We’ll go little by little as we go,” he said. “We’re not going to flood the zone in the ’27, ’28 races. That’s not the intent. The intent is to find high-quality people who want to run. People who have a chance to win.”
The Lincoln Party logo.
State law calls for any party clearing 10% in the secretary of state race to select nominees for most federal, state and local offices through a primary.
Gotsch said the Lincoln Party could take advantage of the state law requiring a county party chair’s approval for any potential primary candidate who hasn’t cast their two most-recent primary ballots for that party.
“No one will have been able to say, ‘Well, I already voted in two of your primaries,’” he said. “That’s one of the things that the party, I think, will be able to use to make sure that we’re putting high-quality candidates up who can win. The size of the race, the size of the office, will determine kind of what the qualifications are.”
An independent candidate’s view
After previously winning four elections for DeKalb County prosecutor as a Republican, Winebrenner decided to run in 2024 as an independent for county commissioner.
ClaraMary Winebrenner. (Photo from campaign Facebook page)
A self-described “never Trumper” in a county where Donald Trump won nearly three-quarters of the presidential vote and no Democrats sought county offices, Winebrenner got 32% in her unsuccessful race.
Winebrenner said she spent about two weeks going door to door in collecting the roughly 250 petition signatures she needed to make the northeastern Indiana county’s ballot as an independent.
Independent candidates face many legal hurdles and “you’re on your own,” she said.
“Luckily, I’m an attorney and, luckily, I had run for office four times before this and worked on a number of campaigns,” she said in an interview. “But it is not easy to run as an independent because you have to figure out how and get the signatures. I would say that’s one thing that makes it easier at the local level. It’s doable, but it’s almost not doable at the state level because of the magnitude.”
Winebrenner said she intended to vote for Ballard in hopes that the Lincoln Party would give voters more choices and break up the control that Republicans and Democrats now hold.
“There’s not much of a platform for the Lincoln Party. It’s whoever wants to sign on, but maybe that’s OK,” she said. “People need to pay attention to who they’re voting for, and, frankly, the first step I think would be to get rid of straight-ticket voting. That should not be an option.”
Pushback on the new party
Engling — the Republican secretary of state nominee — has swiped at Ballard as insufficiently conservative on issues such as Indiana’s law banning transgender youth from girls sports and local tax increases during his time as Indianapolis mayor.
Engling extends that criticism to the Lincoln Party as presenting voters a blank slate of future support for what it regards as “high-quality candidates” without any stated ideology.
“To me, that says nothing about what they stand for,” Engling said in an interview.
Engling argues the Lincoln Party isn’t a serious political organization.
“You would think that they would have a party that has thought through what they want to do with that (ballot) access and what the point of the access is,” he said.
Former Indiana Democratic Chair Robin Winston speaks during the party’s 2026 state convention. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Former state Democratic Party Chair Robin Winston said Engling and Ballard have spent “an inordinate amount of time back and forth on each other” on matters unrelated to the secretary of state’s office.
Winston said he doesn’t understand the branding of the new party after Abraham Lincoln who not only was the first Republican elected president but has long been celebrated as the GOP’s historic leader.
“I don’t know that voters will necessarily see the name Lincoln Party as being an independent party,” Winston said. “It would be like us saying it’s the Kennedy Party, but it’s really not Democrats.”
The lack of information about how the Lincoln Party would select candidates also draws criticism from Engling.
“If they get over 2% then what will happen is that the chairman of the party, which is not Ballard, it’s Nathan Gotsch, could, by Indiana law, select a few of his friends to be the caucus, sit in a dark, smoke-filled room at a steakhouse basement in Indianapolis and pick who they want to run in races all around the state,” Engling said. “Not an open and transparent process.”



Ballard’s backers
Here are some prominent supporters of Greg Ballard’s Lincoln Party campaign:

Nathan Gotsch, Ballard’s campaign manager and Lincoln Party chair. He was a 2022 independent congressional candidate and started the group Independent Indiana.
John Lechleiter, former chairman and CEO of Eli Lilly and Co. Ballard’s campaign reported a $100,000 contribution from Lechleiter in July.
John Mutz, Indiana’s Republican lieutenant governor in 1981-89. Mutz has given at least $10,000 each to Ballard’s campaign and a political action committee supporting him.
Jason Dudich, state budget director under Republican Gov. Eric Holcomb and chief of staff in Ballard’s Indianapolis mayor’s office. Contributed $10,000 to Ballard’s campaign.
Kevin Kellems, an informal Ballard adviser who previously was a top aide to U.S. Sens. Richard Lugar and Dan Coats and Vice President Dick Cheney. Kellems has given $2,500 to Ballard’s campaign.
Former Republican state Rep. Rebecca Kubacki and her husband Michael Kubacki, the retired president of  Lake City Bank who served on the Indiana Economic Development Corp. board under Govs. Mike Pence and Eric Holcomb. They’ve each given $5,000 to Ballard’s campaign.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Local officials look to fill in gaps left by closure of birthing center in Cecil County
description: Cecil County leaders and community members are scrambling to piece together solutions to the loss this summer of the county's only birthing center, after the closure of the unit at ChristianaCare Union Hospital in Elkton.
text:
ChristianaCare Union Hospital in Elkton. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Cecil County leaders and community members are scrambling to piece together solutions to the loss this summer of the county’s only birthing center, after the closure of the unit at ChristianaCare Union Hospital in Elkton.
Talks have included recruiting new hospital systems to build a new maternity unit to relying on local emergency medical services to transport pregnant patients to other hospitals. Until a solution is found, problem pregnancies could be affected by the increased time it takes to get to another available hospital for care, Cecil County Executive Adam Streight said.
“Depending on where you’re at in the county, on a good day it’s a 45-minute trip,” Streight said. “Most places in the county, you’re talking an hour or more.”
Celia Karp, assistant professor with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said the closure of labor and delivery units leads to worse health outcomes and other logistical challenges, particularly for rural counties like Cecil.
“Closures of rural hospitals with obstetric care units have resulted in higher rates of preterm births,” Karp said. “Higher rates of births in hospitals that don’t have labor and delivery units, which aren’t equipped to deliver high-quality obstetric care … oftentimes result in added risk for pregnancies and deliveries by increasing the distance that people have to travel when they’re in labor.”
Rural hospital closures would mean long drives for pregnant women seeking care

The most recent March of Dimes report on maternity care deserts showed that the Eastern Shore had “moderate” access to maternal healthcare in 2024, when the Elkton labor and delivery unit was still open, whereas the rest of the state had “full” access. The data does not reflect how the closure of the Cecil County facility will affect other counties.
“It leaves a maternity care desert,” Karp said. “These closures are especially impactful for people who have pregnancy complications that might require immediate interventions.
“They disproportionately impact people who have less access to resources, as they’ll be forced to drive greater distances – oftentimes taking more time off of work, paying for childcare costs, just to reach the places where prenatal care is available,” she said.
Back in May, ChristianaCare executives announced that they would close the maternity ward this summer, leaving the county with little time to prepare for the absence of what can be life-saving obstetric care.
Streight said the county is in early talks with healthcare and hospital systems that may be interested in developing a new birthing center to Cecil County. But even if county officials find a good fit, construction of the unit could take 18 months to two years to complete, Streight said.
“You want to make sure that … you work with the right people and not just somebody who’s looking to take advantage of the situation or might have good intentions but doesn’t know what they’re doing,” he said.
He said that the closure is hurting the county and his biggest fear is that someone will die as a result of the loss in a birthing center.
“There’s this feeling of helplessness, not only for the community, but also because people elect us to solve problems, and this is something that we really didn’t have any control over,” he said, “but you’ve still got to find solutions.”
For the time being, ChristianaCare provides transportation services to patients who are inconvenienced by the labor and delivery unit closure. Those needing postpartum and prenatal care can receive those services in the outpatient facility in Elkton, while labor and delivery patient will be taken across the border to their Delaware obstetrics unit.
ChristianaCare Union Hospital in Elkton. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
But Streight says that it’s a temporary Band-Aid to help with the transition. Once those services are no longer available, he said the local Department of Emergency Services has offered to step up to ensure patients can quickly receive urgent pregnancy care.
“They’ve been rockstars in saying, ‘We’re going to make this work,’ but it’s going to put a lot of strain and stress on an already strained system,” Streight said. “They haven’t been inundated with a lot of these calls, partly because folks are going to ChristianaCare [which] is providing transportation for where they need to be.”
But distance will remain a major hurdle until a solution is found, Streight said. Distance is a particular concern for certain high-risk pregnancies that require urgent attention. In those situations, every minute counts, according to Karp.
“People who have pregnancy complications like gestational diabetes or hypertension, they’ll also be most affected by the closure of a local hospital that has a labor and delivery unit because those types of health complications can escalate really quickly,” Karp said.
“Having to drive an extra 20 minutes or an extra hour to reach the next closest hospital with an obstetric care unit can really make a huge difference in whether moms and babies get the care they need at a really critical time in their lives,” she said.
Karp said some of the care could theoretically be picked up by nearby health facilities through additional training.
“The biggest piece is for patients that are going into labor and having life-threatening obstetric emergencies,” she said. “This type of training can help providers who are not normally part of an LND [labor and delivery] unit at least stabilize patients that are coming in with these life-threatening obstetric emergencies.”
Karp says that it’s important for patients and healthcare providers to create “safe childbirth plans.”
“Including things like arranging transportation and potentially planning to stay a night in advance of potential delivery to a hospital further away and that may be in a different state,” she said. “Making those plans with the people in their lives and with their healthcare providers to ensure that they have a plan and it incorporates this additional time element needed had this hospital not closed.
“That’s unfortunately the reality of when health systems close,” she said. “It puts the onus on patients to do more of the mental gymnastics and the financial and time planning to make sure they’re able to get the care they need. It is a really unfortunate situation.”
Medical systems, health agencies get $80 million from feds to boost rural health

Karp also suggests that local health departments affected by the closure communicate with their constituents to ensure they are informed of the closure and what their options may be in the meantime.
Meanwhile, Cecil Health Officer Dr. Karyl Rattay has called for a taskforce on perinatal care to find short-term solutions for the absence of the hospital. She recently announced that Cecil County will receive more than $4.65 million from Maryland Rural Health Transformation Program, some of which will support the taskforce and boost maternal care in the county.
Streight adds that he’s been talking with the Moore administration, Maryland’s congressional delegation and state lawmakers, and is willing to “work with anyone” to ensure Cecil County residents are safe.
“Our community service folks are working together to try to find the best use of that money in terms of what we can do, at least short-term solutions, to try to mitigate the damage that this has caused,” he said. “This isn’t a political issue. It’s a human issue.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT towns are installing license plate reading cameras on school buses
description: More than half a dozen towns have contracted with BusPatrol to record any motorist passing a bus that’s displaying flashing red signal lights.
text:
City and town leaders across Connecticut have been fielding growing pushback from residents over automated license plate readers, which opponents say raise a range of concerns about privacy. 
But as many state and local leaders have called for a pause on the technology to weigh new policy guidance, several towns are installing AI-powered license plate readers on school buses.
More than half a dozen towns — including Vernon, Bridgeport, Danbury, Shelton, Stratford, North Haven and New Haven — have contracted with a company called BusPatrol, which installs the technology on the towns’ bus fleets, then uses it to gather footage of any motorist passing a bus that’s displaying flashing red signal lights. The company’s technicians log the events and provide the recordings to local law enforcement. 
Unlike some license plate reading cameras — such as those owned and operated by the company Flock Safety — BusPatrol’s aren’t continuously monitoring the roads. They are triggered “only when a school bus is stopped with its warning lights and stop arm engaged,” a spokesperson from BusPatrol said.

Since 2011, Connecticut has allowed digital video as evidence of a violation. A 2024 law change put more power in the hands of municipalities to establish video monitoring systems and issue fines.
And so far, they have caught quite a few. 
In New Haven, which installed the technology on more than 300 buses earlier this year, cameras have already recorded 12,000 incidents.
Marc Petruzzi, chief of police in Vernon — which announced its rollout last week — said the town installed the cameras to avoid future tragedies. 
“Passing a stopped school bus is one of the most dangerous things that a driver can do,” he said at a press conference announcing the initiative last week.
In the first three days of the program, BusPatrol cameras caught almost 100 motorists passing school buses, said David Owens, a spokesman for the town.
Still, some Connecticut residents are wary of the cameras — particularly when it comes to how the video they capture is stored and shared. 
“I think AI cameras on school buses should be banned, just as all AI cameras in the state and in the country should be,” said Dan Piper, an organizer for CT Civil Liberties Defense Committee and teacher in the Hartford area. 
Piper expressed concern over the possibility of video being shared with federal immigration enforcement agencies and connected to other databases that use AI for surveillance. 
“When someone tells me that we’re going to have more cameras that are connected to private databases that use AI to search for people, we know that those companies are sharing that information,” Piper said.  
A spokesperson for BusPatrol, said the company’s child safety systems are regulated by the state in which they’re installed. “BusPatrol retains information only for as long as it is needed for law enforcement review or required by law and is purged once the citation reaches its final disposition. By default, all data belongs to the school district,” he said in an emailed statement.
The school bus use case
It’s been illegal to pass a stopped school bus for decades in Connecticut, but state and local officials have struggled with enforcement. Each year, thousands of people drive past stopped school buses.
In the last six years, there have been 12 fatalities and 23 serious injuries in Connecticut involving school buses, said Josh Morgan, communications director at the Department of Transportation. It’s not clear how many of those incidents involved cars passing a bus with its lights flashing.
Teacher Ryan Dunia helps students get on a school bus for dismissal at Northeast School in Vernon on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Connecticut lawmakers have established penalties for passing a school bus at several hundred dollars per offense. In 2011, the state allowed local police and school districts to install cameras on buses to record incidents and to use that evidence against motorists accused of illegally passing a bus. It set the fine for a first-time violation — regardless of whether it was caught on camera — at $450.
In 2024, lawmakers updated the statute to give municipalities the power to authorize video monitoring system via ordinance, and it set the fine for first-time violations caught on camera at $250. The fine for violations caught by officers in-person is still $450.
But as cities and towns begin to deploy more bus cameras, residents in many communities in Connecticut are growing increasingly wary of any kind of automated license plate reading (ALPR) surveillance. 
That’s because Connecticut has rapidly become the state with the most ALPR cameras per capita in New England, according to DeFlock, which tracks ALPR installations. Municipalities and businesses across the state have installed nearly 800 ALPRs to date. 
Citizens’ concerns rose after reporting from CT Insider found that Connecticut ALPR cameras had been searched thousands of times by out-of-state agencies enforcing federal immigration and other states’ abortion laws. In recent months, residents have turned up at town meetings around Connecticut to register their opposition to technology that could be used for surveillance by other states or federal enforcement agencies.
Piper is one of those residents. 
“We have asked at town council meetings, do you have data that shows that the introduction of the cameras reduced crime? And they never can say that they do,” he said.
A Flock Safety spokesperson recently told Connecticut Public that at least half of the state’s police departments use some of the company’s services, including license plate readers and drones. A Flock Safety spokesperson declined to comment on the overall number of cameras in Connecticut in an email to The Connecticut Mirror.
Last month, Gov. Lamont called for a 30-day pause on municipalities installing new automated license plate readers while the Connecticut Police Officers Standards and Training Council develops guidance for data retention and data sharing. Lamont’s guidance addressed “school zone traffic enforcement safety devices, work zone speed control cameras, fixed ALPR devices, drones” but did not specifically call out school bus-mounted cameras.
Cathryn Vaulman, spokesperson for the governor, said in an email that the pause would allow “time to evaluate potential gaps in our existing legal protections and to give towns, police and the industry a chance to communicate the types of video technology and use cases more effectively.”
This reporting was made possible using AI-transcription of municipal meetings from YouTube.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: If you want to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month in Kansas, begin by speaking up for us
description: Hispanic Heritage Month is just around the corner. As a poet performing across Kansas and beyond, I traditionally find it the busiest month of the year. Organizations and institutions treat this time as most appropriate for paying Latino artists. I am not complaining about the added consideration afforded to me during this month of celebration. […]
text:
Former Kansas Poet Laureate Huascar Medina reads outside the Carnegie Center for the Arts in Dodge City International Festival in September 2019. (Topher Enneking)Hispanic Heritage Month is just around the corner. As a poet performing across Kansas and beyond, I traditionally find it the busiest month of the year.
Organizations and institutions treat this time as most appropriate for paying Latino artists. I am not complaining about the added consideration afforded to me during this month of celebration. Regardless of your heritage, any troubadour hawking books on the road to make a living knows you can’t spell “poverty” without the word “poetry.” 
This year has felt different.
I have not been contacted by as many organizations or institutions as in past years. I’m wondering if the volatile political climate, election season, or the current administration’s attacks on and punishments for Diversity, Equity and Inclusion is the culprit.  The threat of losing federal funding for diverse cultural programming has hamstrung well-to-do, progressive, forward-thinking entities.  
There is always the possibility that a poet may say something truthful that sounds political, causing an offended donor to invoke the ominous Hatch Act to cut federal funding. My work has been described as political, but in actuality it’s simply personal.  It’s an amalgamation of voices singing about the lived experiences of people like me, my friends, my family and people I will never meet. 
First- and second-generation immigrants live in the same place as people who do not want them there and, in some cases, loathe the fact that we live here at all, in the heartland.
When I consider the word heartland, I think of the heart as a container — a symbol of love, not one of hate. I still struggle with the hate present in this part of the country. The heartland feels more like a hateland, more like a hurtland, these days.  
Maybe the title of my latest book, “Protest as Love Poem,” is the concern. It sounds radical and political.
Yes, it is radical and political. It is radical to love in a world full of hate. It is radical to embrace empathy in the face of barbarism.
My love poems are civic poems, my civic poems are love poems. There is no difference. Advocating for the ones you love is romantic. Advocating for the safety of strangers is humane and endearing. 
This is why I believe collective survival is a love language. Collective survival is a group practice by those who care, share and work together to stay safe and meet basic needs during crises, difficult times, neglect or systemic oppression, rather than relying on self-reliance alone.
Some people’s love language preferences are giving gifts, words of affirmation and quality time. I prefer offering solidarity.
Spending that quality time in activism at a rally or march defending democracy or advocating for commonsense gun laws, indigenous rights, women’s rights, transgender rights or supporting pro-immigrant groups. So many human rights are being violated that we wouldn’t run out of date night activities. 
With all that said, I’m no longer interested in being the token Latino poet to check off an inclusion list. The time of being hired as a performer rather than a speaker is becoming less and less palatable to me.
Latinos are being targeted year-round by an increasingly secretive, militarized police force known as Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. Kansans are celebrating their brutality, and politicians are promoting hateful messages in political ads. Do you want to know what I think about that and how art functions as a mechanism of change?
Or do you just want me to entertain you with my trauma?
My questions to the organizations and institutions that want to hire me are straightforward: What have you done to bring awareness, mitigate or respond to the harmful attacks occurring to the communities I belong to, the communities you say you serve? Will you be OK with me reading protest poems about living and surviving in the middle of America?
Or do you just want a poem about love or nature that doesn’t quite address the nature of fascism, racism and xenophobia in the heartland? I can assure you, even the birds have changed their tune this season. You can’t escape the reality of the world around us. What’s happening is not normal.
I will give you this poem to share for free this Hispanic Heritage Month. I have others like it; some are more direct and loving. Read it. Share it if you’re really interested in discussing what’s happening right now to Hispanics in Kansas.
Backyard Cottonwood 
Apartment windows operate
as sanctuary exits. 
A clear view
of the American heartland
turned hurtland. 
The sky fell again today
and I’m unsure if we are
floating or drowning,
falling or flying.
In the new morning,
an American robin sings
the same song — an old
melody of survival: 
Breath is the nearest sky,
and it takes sky to sing,
and it takes sky to fly.
And the sky lives in most things,
so Heaven is in most things.
And the sky already knows,
not every song takes flight,
not every caged bird sings,
not everyone is free. 
Huascar Medina is a poet, writer, and performer who lives in Topeka. His latest book is Protest as Love Poem. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Health experts, lawmakers push for Pa. kratom regulation; proponents warn they’ll fight a ban
description: “Some people know that it can cause dependence and harm, and are intentionally using it that way ... But some people don’t. Then they get started on it and don’t realize they’re dependent until they stop.”
text:
A vape shop advertises kratom in Etters, York County. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Sarah Kawasaki first heard about kratom around five years ago. It wasn’t through her work — she’s an addiction medicine specialist at Penn State, and the medical director of their associated opioid treatment program — but through her personal life.
“People would say, ‘Hey, what do you know about kratom?,’” she told the Capital-Star. “And I’d be like, ‘What?’”
So Kawasaki began looking into it. Kratom, she found, is an herbal supplement with opioid-like effects. In low doses, it can act as a stimulant, and in higher doses it produces a more sedative-like effect. Along with being a recreational drug, many users have reported using it to manage chronic pain or opioid withdrawal symptoms.
As her interest grew, she began to notice advertisements at smoke shops and other stores around her neighborhood. Then there were a couple of patients who acknowledged using it.
Fast forward to the present and Kawasaki has 10 to 20 patients in central Pennsylvania she is treating exclusively for kratom use, most of whom (around 80%) had previously sought treatment for opioid addiction and managed to kick the habit.
“Some people know that it can cause dependence and harm, and are intentionally using it that way,” she said. “But some people don’t. Then they get started on it and don’t realize they’re dependent until they stop.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Kawasaki’s story is an increasingly common one in the world of addiction treatment. What, in America at least, was a little known substance, has become a growing source of concern for addiction specialists, ER doctors, and public health professionals — especially as potent extracts and synthetic kratom products become more widely available. 
Increasingly, treatment centers are advertising their ability to treat kratom addiction. And as its popularity has grown, kratom has caught the attention of journalists, lawmakers, drug policy researchers, regulators, law enforcement and parents concerned about what their children may be exposed to.
In Pennsylvania, kratom and more potent, related products remain legal. There are multiple bills moving through the statehouse that would ban or regulate them. But researchers warn there’s still a lot we don’t know.
“Is it orders of magnitude less dangerous than fentanyl? Probably,” Kawasaki said. “But we don’t really know the definitive answer to that. We don’t really have a grasp on how many people are using it, or how they’re using it.”
“That should be alarming to anyone,” she added. “I don’t want people to put something in their body that they really don’t know what it is, or what it’s doing, or what’s even in the bottle, and trusting that more than they would an actual FDA-approved, quality-controlled medication.”
What is kratom?
The plant kratom is made from is native to southeast Asia, where it’s been ingested for hundreds of years for medicinal, cultural, ritualistic and recreational reasons.
More recently, in America, kratom’s availability has boomed. Kratom and related products can be bought at gas stations, smoke shops and corner stores. That includes powdered forms of the leaf itself, highly potent extracts with stronger psychoactive effects, and lab-made synthetic products derived from its intoxicating compounds.
At the state and federal level, kratom and related products are hardly regulated.
Estimates for how many people in America have used kratom range from over one million to more than 20 million. But use is likely at an all-time high, and growing. 
7-OH products, a concentrated synthetic kratom derivative, are displayed at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 5, 2026, hours before a state ban took effect. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
A recent study from the University of Michigan found that more than half of reported users have struggled with substance use disorder. Roughly a quarter reported having major depression, and around 38% experience psychological distress.
“It takes up a very complex space in the substance use landscape,” says Laura Nettuno, a researcher at the think tank RAND Corporation’s drug policy research center. “On one hand, for some people, it’s harm reduction because it helps manage opioid cravings and symptoms of withdrawal. But on the other hand, it’s creating its own issue.”
Nettuno points to the proliferation of kratom extract products, which are made from the kratom leaf, but have larger amounts of its intoxicating compounds, and more potent synthetic products. In particular, there’s 7-hydroxymitraynine, or 7-OH.
Mmitragynine is the primary psychoactive ingredient in kratom leaf, and 7-OH is found in trace amounts as well. But lab-made products with higher 7-OH concentrations are far more potent and addictive. Those have become more widely advertised and available in stores and online. And because there is so little regulation, it’s not always clear which kratom products contain higher amounts of the compound.
While kratom-related overdose rates are much lower than other opioids, there’s little research available on its negative health effects. Kratom products can also contain a host of adulterants that are unreported. And its half-life is much shorter than opioids like fentanyl, meaning regular users can go into withdrawal in a matter of three to six hours after taking it.
According to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, there have been 17 overdose deaths where kratom was a contributing factor in the state this year. That includes overdoses where kratom was found in a victim’s system along with other substances. There were 33 in 2025, but data is preliminary.
The number of Pennsylvania Poison Control Center cases related to kratom has also grown in the last two years. Last year, there were 114, including 25 involving 7-OH. This year, through June 30, there have already been 106, including 41 involving 7-OH.
“More potent synthetic products are coming out of these labs, and they’re tweaking them faster than regulation can keep up with,” Nettuno said. “And they’re also putting them on the market faster than our surveillance systems can keep up with. “It’s very much an open question whether kratom and kratom-related products are really harm reductive or not, because we just don’t know anything.”
That makes deciding how to regulate kratom uniquely difficult.
“Any researcher who is doing their job well should tell you we really have no idea,” Nettuno said. “We don’t have good data systems to track use-prevalence over time, and certainly not at granular, geographic levels, like in the state of Pennsylvania.”
“It’s clearly a public health concern,” she added.
What’s less clear, Nettuno says, is how to regulate it.
“The regulation is evolving very quickly,” she said. “Products and producers are responding to that very, very quickly, and we don’t know what that means in terms of what products are going to be on the market six months from now that don’t currently exist today.”
Bills, bills, bills
In the last few years, Pennsylvania lawmakers have introduced a number of bills seeking to regulate kratom, though none have advanced to the governor’s desk.
Those with the most momentum would allow the sale of natural kratom leaf products to adults over 21, but would ban synthetic kratom products and some highly-potent extracts.
Rep. James Prokopiak (D-Bucks) is a co-sponsor on multiple bills. 
A shop in Salt Lake City advertises kratom for sale on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“They really have the same end goal, which is providing regulation of both natural and synthetic kratom,” he said. “[They’re about] putting real guidelines on it, greater transparency in what the actual product is, and providing safeguards against children getting ahold of them.”
Both bills Prokopiak is co-sponsoring would ban synthetic kratom products, create labelling and standards, and bar the sale of natural products to people under 21.
“From what we’ve heard, the synthetic [product] is really the one that can be made much more potent than a naturally occurring kratom,” he said. “We’re trying to balance sort of the health and safety of people, and also the ability of individuals to do what they want. But we want to make sure that people know what they are actually getting, and right now there are no packaging requirements. There are no safety warnings. There are no labelling requirements. It’s the wild west for kratom, really.”
Both bills Prokopiak is co-sponsoring would not make possession or use of kratom products illegal, instead putting liability on sellers. The bills, however, differ slightly in terms of who would be responsible for enforcing them.
One would give the Department of Health responsibility for testing and regulating kratom products. Another would create a new board.
Sen. Tracy Pennycuick (R-Montgomery) has been pushing for kratom regulation in the Republican-controlled upper chamber, where she’s sponsoring a bill that would ban the sale of synthetic kratom products, or kratom products with more than 2% concentration of 7-OH.
She became aware of kratom three or four years ago after talking to an emergency room doctor who asked what she knew about it. He had seen people come in after taking kratom products they said they purchased at local shops.
“Then I actually went to a gas station, and I was stunned you could actually buy it,” she said. “That put me on this path of: As an adult, I don’t care what you do. But I do want to make sure that if you’re buying a product, you know what you’re buying. And you’re not getting something that’s adulterated with any other chemical, and that you know what the efficiency of the dosage is.”
The growth in interest in regulating kratom among Pennsylvania legislators is coinciding with similar pushes at the federal level and in states across the country.
A 2025 report by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association found 24 states and Washington, D.C. had regulated kratom in some form. Five of those and the District of Columbia had made at least some kratom products a Schedule I controlled substance, along with drugs like heroin and LSD. Most had simply limited its sale, like what’s proposed in Pennsylvania.
In 2024 and 2025, 29 states, including Pennsylvania saw legislation proposed that would regulate kratom components or products.
A bag of kratom and a shake cup a pictured at Lora Romney’s home in Layton on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. Romney, 55, has atypical trigeminal neuralgia, which causes intense, burning, nerve pain in her face. Kratom, which the Utah legislature is considering banning, is the only non-opiate that she has found to alleviate the pain. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
More recently, the federal government has taken action to restrict some kratom products nationally.
The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has classified three synthetic compounds as Schedule I on an emergency basis, meaning the designation will last two years. That includes mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and MGM-16, potent compounds that produce opioid-like effects.
The DEA has also opened a public comment period on a proposed Schedule I classification for 7-OH.
Other states have recently taken action as well.
On Friday, North Dakota’s legislature passed a bill to ban synthetic kratom and regulate natural leaf products.
The governor of Iowa also called for a total ban on kratom last week after the state House passed a bill to do so earlier this year.
And in Montana, a panel of legislators just tabled a proposed bill to regulate kratom products on the grounds that it didn’t go far enough.
The lobbyist
Lawmakers who spoke with the Capital-Star all said they’ve spoken with lobbyists with a group called the American Kratom Association.
The group is ubiquitous when it comes to lobbying and advising on kratom regulation across the country, and has had a hand in crafting legislation in many states.
In 2024, the American Kratom Association reported $4.7 million in revenue, according to filings with the Internal Revenue Service. According to Mac Haddow, the group’s senior fellow on public policy, that’s primarily from businesses that manufacture and sell kratom products. He estimates there are around 250 in the country
Haddow says the association agrees with lawmakers that kratom needs to be regulated, but strongly opposes an all-out ban. They’ve advocated in Pennsylvania and other states to ban synthetic kratom products, as well as hyper-potent extracts, and to restrict its sale to people 21 and over.
“Back in 2018 when we saw, from a consumer perspective, that there were companies out there creating products that were dangerous, we started promoting our Kratom Consumer Protection Act,” he said. “That sets up specific criteria for product formulations, requires companies to label their products correctly, and makes sure they also have an age restriction.”
Haddow says he’s been a regular user of kratom for 10 years.
“When I was in college, I raced motorcycles and I banged myself up pretty good,” he said. “[Former U.S. Senator] Orrin Hatch recommended I start taking kratom, and I’ve been taking it for 10 years … He was a consumer of kratom.”
Haddow ran Hatch’s first Senate campaign in 1976, and then served as Hatch’s administrative assistant. Hatch retired in 2019 after serving for 42 years. He died in 2022.
Hatch was perhaps Congress’ strongest champion of the dietary supplement industry. He sponsored the landmark Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994. The law says vitamins and supplements do not have to meet the same strict safety standards as other drugs sold in the U.S. Instead they’re treated more like food. 
Since its passage, the sale and use of dietary supplements in America have boomed. 
That’s paved the way for the proliferation of kratom products, which are commonly sold and marketed as an herbal supplement.
“We’ve been working in Pennsylvania for three years,” Haddow said of the American Kratom Association. “We’ve been hard at work trying to educate members, and that’s been our effort so far.”
But as momentum builds for kratom regulation, Haddow says lobbying efforts will too.
“We’re going to step it up here now that we see there’s a pathway. So you’re going to see a lot of activity there.”
Filling the gaps
While there’s relatively little action at the state or federal level, local officials and law enforcement have been stepping up their calls for help.
Bucks County District Attorney Joe Khan co-signed a letter with a district attorney from Chester County asking the state Department of Health to use its emergency powers to make 7-OH and other kratom derivatives Schedule I controlled substances, a designation which would last for two years.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Unlike many of the bills being pushed by lawmakers in Pennsylvania, however, that would make possession of kratom a crime.
“At this time, DOH is reviewing the situation and considering all options to ensure any decisions support the health and safety of Pennsylvanians,” a spokesperson told the Capital-Star. “DOH is working to raise awareness and educate the general public …. These products are often sold in retail stores, which can make people assume they are regulated and safe when they are not.”
The spokesperson added that the department is performing additional outreach to health care providers and seeking feedback on what may be the best course of action.
“We have an emergency in Bucks County,” Khan said. “Over the summer, I became aware of this public health crisis in Bucks County, wherein we have these various smoke shops, gas stations, other retail establishments that are … luring children into stores and selling them all kinds of things. Some of those things are completely legal under Pennsylvania law. One of those things is kratom.”
Last week, Khan announced what is thought to be a somewhat historic action, getting an emergency preliminary injunction effectively shutting down a local smoke shop that he said was selling kratom to children.
Khan also wants lawmakers to act, but hesitated when asked exactly what they should do.
“I’m not in a position to really make recommendations about long-term solutions for people who are 21 or over,” he said. “What I am immediately concerned about is these substances falling in the hands of kids.”
