name: VTDigger
title: Vermonters will vote on constitutional amendment enshrining labor protections in November
description:
The measure, which has seen broad cross-party support in the Statehouse, would affirm workers’ right to organize and prevent lawmakers from easily reversing existing labor protections in the future.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermonters will vote on constitutional amendment enshrining labor protections in November.
text:
Members of the Teamsters local 597 union picket outside the Dairy Farmers of America plant in St. Albans on Tuesday, September 30, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Vermont voters will accept or toss an amendment to the state constitution in November that would affirm workers’ right to organize and collectively bargain, and prevent lawmakers from easily reversing labor protections in the future. 
The item, Proposal 3, will appear alongside Proposal 4, which would guarantee equal protections under the law regardless of a number of characteristics like race and gender identity. Changes to Vermont’s constitution can be introduced by the Senate every four years, and need to be approved by both legislative chambers in two consecutive bienniums. Proposal 3 was approved by the Legislature in both the 2024 and 2025 sessions, on either side of the 2024 election cycle, and can now be ratified or rejected by voters in the general election on Nov. 3.
Proposal 3, or PR.3, would prevent lawmakers from easily passing legislation in the future that “interferes with, negates, or diminishes the right of employees to collectively bargain” for conditions or terms of work. The language would also specifically protect labor agreements that make union membership a condition of employment at a particular company. 
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that such “union shop” agreements are illegal nationwide for public employees. Twenty-six states have adopted measures — commonly called “right-to-work” policies — that ban such agreements in the private sector too.
Constitutional protections like those in PR.3 are relatively unusual in the U.S. Vermont would be the seventh state to adopt an amendment enshrining the right to bargain. Among those six existing instances, only Illinois explicitly forbids “right-to-work” legislation, according to the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard Law School.
For Larry Moquin, who is president of Vermont’s AFL-CIO labor council and has been pushing for a version of PR.3 since 2022, Illinois has been a primary model. Recent fights surrounding public employees unions in Utah and “right-to-work”-style amendments to numerous state constitutions are part of a larger pattern of efforts to undermine organized labor across the country, he argued, illustrating the necessity of such robust long-term safeguards in Vermont.
“I think that the workers in the state deserve it,” Moquin said of the constitutional protections potentially afforded by PR.3. “People’s children and grandchildren deserve the same rights that we have.”
Rep. Conor Casey, an outgoing Montpelier Democrat who co-led the pro-labor Working Vermonters’ Caucus for the past several years, has mounted a campaign called “Yes on 3” to advocate for the amendment’s passage in November. The effort is a “one-man shop” at present, he said, and seeks to both convince the public of the measure’s necessity and fend off organized opposition to the change from national interests should it arise.
When Moquin approached him with the idea of a constitutional amendment years ago, Casey said, it struck him as the right step for Vermont. He too is worried about what he sees as a national push to restrict the power of U.S. labor movements in recent decades.
Collective bargaining in the workplace “is a form of democracy,” Casey said. “It certainly belongs in our constitution.”
Though PR.3 has seen cross-party support in both of Vermont’s legislative chambers — indeed, no senator voted against its passage last year — the proposal has met pushback from some think tanks and conservative lawmakers.
Clara Morrison, who leads the free-market economic policy think tank Right for Vermont Foundation, said she thought the proposal’s advocates had sometimes misrepresented its true ramifications, particularly given that federal policy already outlines many labor protections.
“What this amendment actually does is prevent workers’ from gaining the freedom to choose whether to join or fund a private union without risking their job,” Morrison said in an email Tuesday. 
The proposal’s broad language also essentially “blocks lawmakers from ever limiting what unions can demand,” Morrison added, which she argued could cause legal confusion with both federal and state law, and cost taxpayers in the long term if public employees’ union agreements could no longer easily be shaped through statute.
Rep. Lisa Hango, R-Berkshire, one of 15 House members who voted against the measure last year, expressed similar reservations to colleagues: “I simply do not support taking away a worker’s freedom to decide.”
Peter Teachout, a constitutional law professor at Vermont Law and Graduate School, told lawmakers in 2024 that he supported the language of PR.3, while noting that the measure would be “bounded in its operation” by federal law. He added in an interview that the amendment would likely provide organizing protections to a broader set of Vermont employees than is currently covered by statute — including farmworkers.
The federal National Labor Relations Act of 1935 guarantees organizing protections for many employees while exempting some groups, including agriculture workers. Such groups would not newly gain the ability to unionize in Vermont via the new amendment without judicial involvement or a statutory change, according to Rep. Emilie Krasnow, D-South Burlington, who has co-led the pro-labor caucus along with Casey.
For Moquin, PR.3 would also be a statement of intent to push back against wealth inequality. 
“Unions build generational wealth,” he said. Vermont taking the lead on labor protections, he added, would be “some good news in a time where mostly there’s been bad news for working Americans.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT tick populations are growing. Here’s what to know.
description: Some tick species are now active year round in Connecticut. Here’s what to know about the critters and how to stay safe.
text:
Ticks were once most active between March and October, but due to a consistent increase in warm weather spurred by climate change, varying tick species are now active year round in Connecticut. 
The state is home to around 15 species of ticks, and five of them impose significant public health risks as they can transmit several pathogens, like bacteria or viruses, that cause diseases, according to Dr. Goudarz Molaei, a research scientist at the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, who began studying ticks in 2015.
Black-legged “deer” ticks and American dog ticks are the most common species in the state, but there has been a recent prevalence of the invasive lone star tick, Gulf Coast ticks and longhorned ticks. 
Here’s what to know about the critters and how to stay safe.
What tick-trasmitted pathogens are common? 
Lyme disease, spread by deer ticks, is most common in the Northeast. Other transmittable illnesses spread by deer tick bites include babesiosis, a disease in which parasites infect red blood cells, and anaplasmosis, which is linked to a bacteria and has symptoms as varied as high fevers and headaches on one end of the spectrum and respiratory and organ failure on the other. Another transmittable illness, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which is a bacterial infection, can be spread by dog ticks. 
According to a Stamford Health article, the number of lone star ticks collected in the state jumped to 2,570 in 2025 from 72 the previous year. 
They are responsible for transmitting pathogens that cause ehrlichiosis, which induces high fever, severe headaches and chills, and alpha-gal syndrome, which induces a red meat and mammal-product allergy and is spread by lone star ticks through their saliva. Allergy symptoms can begin within three to six hours of consuming the product.
“Connecticut is probably the most northern state with an established population of lone star ticks,” Molaei said. “We suspect that other tick species are also involved [in the spread of alpha-gal.]” 
The number of longhorned ticks, which can also transmit pathogens for ehrlichiosis, are on the rise too. This species of tick is parthenogenetic, or capable of reproducing without relying on males. 
In 2021, researchers found established populations of this species in Bridgeport and Stratford. Since then, it has spread across Fairfield, New Haven and New London counties. 
How does a tick pick up transmittable diseases? 
Within a two to three year cycle, ticks lay eggs, which develop into larvae before becoming nymphs and then full-grown adult ticks.
They become infected with diseased agents based on the animals they feed on. However, its ability to transmit a pathogen depends on what type of tick it is. 
Deer ticks, for example, have to feed on various hosts to develop into the next stage of their life cycle. 
They’re usually born pathogen-free, but various feedings throughout their life cycle means it’s another opportunity to pick up a pathogen. 
“If they [larvae] bite rodents, pick up the disease agent, digest the blood, they would then develop into nymphs,” Molaei said. “If the blood that they have taken from rodents is infected, they are able to pass it onto nymphs.” 
According to Molaei, most adult deer ticks are probably infected. 
“If you go out and collect ticks, chances are, 50% of them could be infected,” he said. 
How can I stay safe? 
According to Molaei, prevention is key to steering clear of tick-transmitted pathogens. 
Ticks are surveyed in the state through both active surveillance, where researchers go outdoors and collect ticks from 40 sites on a daily basis, and passive surveillance, when the public submits ticks to their local health department or ACES for testing.
Researchers used to believe that ticks only frequented spaces with tall grass, but now they’re also found by beaches and sparsely vegetated areas. Molaei recommends wearing light colored clothing, tucking pants into socks, spraying clothing with chemicals like permethrin and conducting tick checks after outdoor excursions. 
“People have to be aware of their surroundings pretty much everywhere,” Molaei said. “Tick checks are not only important for humans but also important for their pet animals.”

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

The City of Ionia is scheduled to hold an informational meeting on data centers at 5:30 p.m. on Sept. 9 in the council chambers at Ionia City Hall. The city has not received any proposals from data center developers, WOOD TV’s Katie Rosendale reports, with city officials using the meeting as an opportunity to better understand the industry and what variables the city should consider if it is approached by a developer.

Updates

Ypsilanti City Council is one step closer to implementing a 60-day emergency moratorium on data center development. The city council gave its approval to the proposal on Tuesday, WEMU’s Caroline MacGregor reports, teeing up the moratorium for another reading before it can be passed in its final form.
Hyperscale Data, the owner of the Dowagiac data center at the center of a federal class-action lawsuit, announced that it has ceased Bitcoin mining at the facility as it prepares to provide data infrastructure for AI computing.
Following up on its previous report evaluating the policy controversies around data center development in Michigan, the Citizens Research Council of Michigan has released a second report focused on considerations local governments face regarding hyperscale data center developments. The report discusses the use of moratoriums, considerations around tax revenue, and community concerns, among other topics.

Legislative Action

State Senator and Michigan Republican Party Chair Jim Runestad announced plans to introduce legislation repealing a set of laws exempting data centers and their equipment from the state’s sales and use tax. “We shouldn’t be paying billion-dollar tech conglomerates to farm Michigan for its land, energy, and water. If they want to come here, they need to do it transparently and bring with them benefits for Michigan residents,” the White Lake lawmaker said in a statement.

News of Note

Michigan Advance’s Katherine Dailey examines U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) support for local control on data centers despite the Republican candidate for governor’s previous support of a version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that would have barred state and local governments from enforcing laws or regulations against artificial intelligence models, artificial intelligence systems or automated decision systems.
Beth LeBlanc of the Detroit News revisits the 2024 expansion of Michigan’s sales and use tax exemption for data centers, noting that the laws’ provisions bar the Michigan Economic Development Corporation from releasing any specific information about data centers applying for or making use of the exemption.
Writing for Michigan Advance, Elinor Epperson delves into the concerns around the plans to pursue classified research into nuclear weapons at the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory computing facility planned for construction in Ypsilanti Township.
A host of protestors greeted the more than 100 municipal leaders in attendance at a closed-door educational seminar focused on data centers, Abigail Taylor of News Channel 3 reports. Hosted by Professional Code Inspections, a company based in Allegan County, the event was intended to provide local leaders with “expert testimony explaining what to understand when it comes to planning for data centers, should the need arise.”
A statewide poll conducted by EPIC-MRA commissioned by the clean energy advocacy group Climate Power found that 73% of likely Michigan voters opposed federal tax breaks and other policies intended to speed data center development. It also found that 62% of voters opposed the development of data centers in Michigan.
The Investigators at Local 4 probed into public transparency concerns raised by residents of Lenox Township after a Freedom of Information Act request uncovered an email to Lenox Township Supervisor Anthony Reeder Jr. from a property owner stating “We have been approached by a large data center developer that would like to meet with you.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The state of labor in Minnesota in 7 charts
description: Minnesota’s labor market faced some turbulence over the past year, in part from the surge in immigration enforcement over the winter that left many immigrants afraid to leave their homes to work and shop. Unemployment in the state surpassed national rates in January for the first time since 2007, reaching its highest levels in five […]
text:
Dozens of concessions workers picket outside Target Field during a one-day strike on June 22, 2026. (Photo by Max Nesterak/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota’s labor market faced some turbulence over the past year, in part from the surge in immigration enforcement over the winter that left many immigrants afraid to leave their homes to work and shop.
Unemployment in the state surpassed national rates in January for the first time since 2007, reaching its highest levels in five years. Labor participation — the rate at which Minnesotans are working or looking for work — also declined sharply starting in January, though that trend is more in line with national numbers.
At the same time, Minnesota continues be a good place to work, with higher wages, job growth and union density than the nation as a whole, as well as worker protections such as the state’s new paid leave program.
Here are six charts on the state of labor in Minnesota.


Minnesota has had lower unemployment compared to the rest of the U.S. since at least the 1970s, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Population Survey.
There are two exceptions: in 2007, as the Great Recession was emerging; and in 2026, starting in January.
The January spike in unemployment coincided with Operation Metro Surge, during which people were afraid to leave their homes and encounter agents who shot three people, killing two, and detained citizens and legal immigrants. The last time unemployment was this high in Minnesota was five years ago, in 2021.
The Minnesota Department of Employment and Economic Development linked the state’s weak February jobs numbers with the federal law enforcement surge.
“February was a very challenging month for Minnesota communities due to the ICE presence, and that also contributed to it being a tough month for the state’s labor market,” said DEED Commissioner Matt Varilek in a statement.
Still, it’s not yet clear how much the dip in employment levels comes directly from the ICE surge. Unemployment in Minnesota has been steadily rising since a low in 2022.


Minnesota lost jobs, especially in construction and hospitality, during the winter’s ICE surge. Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show that Minnesota had 4,300 fewer construction jobs and 5,900 fewer hospitality jobs in February compared to the pre-surge November. The numbers are seasonally adjusted, meaning they take into account the expected annual dip in construction jobs in the winter.
Jobs numbers have bounced back since, growing 1.4% overall from June 2025 to June 2026. Mining and logging, construction, education and health services saw the biggest growth over the 12 months, while the finance and information sectors lost jobs.
An April report from progressive think tank North Star Policy Action said the steep declines over the winter in industries that employ significant numbers of immigrants, such as food service and construction, strengthen the case that Operation Metro Surge had a chilling effect on the state’s economy. The report found that Minnesota’s loss of construction jobs was the highest in the nation from December to February, the three months of the surge.


Minnesotans earn the highest average hourly wages in the Midwest — and the 6th highest in the nation — while enjoying a relatively low cost of living compared to the coasts.
The average hourly wage in Minnesota was $39 in 2025. According to the state Department of Employment and Economic Development’s 2025 cost of living calculator, a single person with no kids needed to earn around $18 an hour while a family of four with one working parent needed to earn around $35 per hour to afford the basics.
Hennepin County had by far the highest average wages in the state in the first quarter of 2026, followed by Ramsey County and Olmsted County, where Mayo Clinic is the largest employer.


Rates of union representation in Minnesota continued to go up in 2025, with nearly 16% of workers represented by a union. The state consistently has among the highest rates of union representation in the country owing to its pro-labor tradition and relatively favorable organizing laws. High union density helps bolster both union and non-union wages.
Union participation has been declining over the past half century, though, despite a resurgence in support in recent years. Union leaders blame the decline on federal laws hostile to organizing and a lack of meaningful enforcement against unfair labor practices.


Income inequality remains high across the country, including in Minnesota, where the top 10% of earners made 37% of all income in 2024.
Minnesota’s Gini coefficient — a metric of inequality that ranges from 0, representing exact equality, to 1, representing one person making all the money — stayed at .42 in 2024, slightly higher than Iowa’s and Michigan’s but still lower than the national average.

title: The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s address to the AFL-CIO fourth constitutional convention
description: Edtior’s note: The following are excerpts of King’s speech in Dec. 1961, when he sought to merge explain the shared interests of the Civil Right Movement and organized labor’s drive for economic justice. Courtesy of the Stanford University Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute.  Less than a century ago, the laborer had no […]
text:
King fought for economic justice, too. (Photo by Getty Images) Edtior’s note: The following are excerpts of King’s speech in Dec. 1961, when he sought to merge explain the shared interests of the Civil Right Movement and organized labor’s drive for economic justice. Courtesy of the Stanford University Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute. 
Less than a century ago, the laborer had no rights, little or no respect, and led a life which was socially submerged and barren. He was hired and fired by economic despots whose power over him decreed his life or death. The children of workers had no childhood and no future; they too worked for pennies an hour, and by the time they reached their teens, they were worn-out old men, devoid of spirit, devoid of hope, and devoid of self-respect. Jack London described the child worker in these words: “He did not walk like a man. He did not look like a man. He was a travesty of the human. It was a twisted and stunted and nameless piece of life that shambled like a sickly ape, arms loose-hanging, stoop-shouldered, narrow-chested, grotesque and terrible.” American industry organized misery into sweatshops and proclaimed the right of capital to act without restraints and without conscience. Victor Hugo, literary genius of that day, commented bitterly that there was always more misery in the lower classes than there was humanity in the upper classes.
The inspiring answer to this intolerable and dehumanizing existence was economic organization through trade unions. The worker became determined not to wait for charitable impulses to grow in his employer. He constructed the means by which a fairer sharing of the fruits of his toil had to be given to him, or the wheels of industry, which he alone turned, would halt and wealth for no one would be available. This revolution within industry was fought bitterly by those who blindly believed their right to uncontrolled profits was a law of the universe, and that without the maintenance of the old order, catastrophe faced the nation. But history is a great teacher. Now everyone knows that the labor movement did not diminish the strength of the nation but enlarged it by raising the living standards of millions. Labor miraculously created a market for industry and lifted the whole nation to undreamed-of levels of production. Those who today attack labor forget these simple truths, but history remembers them.
Labor’s next monumental struggle emerged in the thirties, when it wrote into federal law the right freely to organize and bargain collectively. It was now apparently emancipated. The days when workers were jailed for organizing and when in the English parliament, Lord Macaulay had to debate against a bill decreeing the death penalty for anyone engaging in a strike were grim but almost-forgotten memories. Yet the Wagner Act, like any other legislation, tended merely to declare rights but did not deliver them. Labor had to bring the law to life, by exercising in practice its rights over stubborn, tenacious opposition. It was warned to go slow, to be moderate, not to stir up trouble. But labor knew it was always the right time to do right, and it spread its organization over the nation and achieved equality, organizationally, with capital, and the day of economic democracy was born.
Negroes in the United States read this history of labor and find that it mirrors their own experience. We are confronted by powerful forces, telling us to rely on the goodwill and understanding of those who profit by exploiting us. They deplore our discontent, they resent our will to organize so that we may guarantee that humanity will prevail and equality will be exacted. They are shocked that action organizations, sit-ins, civil disobedience and protests are becoming our everyday tools, just as strikes, demonstrations and union organization became yours to ensure that bargaining power genuinely existed on both sides of the table. We want to rely upon the goodwill of those who would oppose us. Indeed, we have brought forward the method of nonviolence to give an example of unilateral goodwill in an effort to evoke it in those who have not yet felt it in their hearts. But we know that if we are not simultaneously organizing our strength, we will have no means to move forward. If we do not advance, and the crushing burden of centuries of neglect and economic deprivation will destroy our will, our spirits and our hopes. In this way, labor’s historic tradition of moving forward to create vital people as consumers and citizens has become our own tradition and for the same reasons.
This unity of purpose is not an historical coincident. Negroes are almost entirely a working people. There are pitifully few Negro millionaires and few Negro employers. Our needs are identical with labor’s needs: decent wages, fair working conditions, livable housing, old-age security, health and welfare measures, conditions in which families can grow, have education for their children, and respect in the community. That is why Negroes support labor’s demands and fight laws which curb labor. That is why the labor-hater and labor-baiter is virtually always a twin-headed creature, spewing anti-Negro epithets from one mouth and anti-labor propaganda from the other mouth.
The duality of interests of labor and Negroes makes any crisis which lacerates you a crisis from which we bleed. And as we stand on the threshold of the second half of the twentieth century, a crisis confronts us both. Those who in the second half of the 19th century could not tolerate organized labor have had a rebirth of power and seek to regain the despotism of that era, while retaining the wealth and privileges of the 20th century. Whether it be the ultra-white right wing in the form of Birch Societies the alliance which former President Dwight Eisenhower denounced, the alliance between big military and big business, or the coalition of southern Dixiecrats and northern reactionaries — whatever the form, these menaces now threaten everything decent and fair in American life. Their target is labor, liberals and Negro people, not scattered reds or even Justice (Earl)  Warren, former Presidents Eisenhower and Harry Truman, and President John F. Kennedy, who are in truth beyond the reach of their crude and vicious falsehoods.
Labor today faces a grave crisis, perhaps the most calamitous since it began its march from the shadows of want and insecurity. In the next 10 to 20 years, automation will grind jobs into dust as it grinds out unbelievable volumes of production. This period is made to order for those who would seek to drive labor into impotency by viciously attacking it at every point of weakness. Hard-core unemployment is now an ugly and unavoidable fact of life, and like malignant cancer, it has grown year by year and continues its spread. But automation can be used to generate an abundance of wealth for a people or an abundance of poverty for millions as its human-like machines turn out human scrap, along with machine scrap, as a by-product of production. And I am convinced that our society, with its ability to perform miracles with machinery, has the capacity to make some miracles for men, if it values men as highly as it values machines.
To find a great design to solve a great problem, labor will have to intervene in the political life of the nation, to chart a course which distributes the abundance to all instead of concentrating it among a few. The strength to carry through such a program requires that labor know its friends and collaborate as a friend. If all that I have said is sound, labor has no firmer friend than the 20 million Negroes whose lives will be deeply affected by the new patterns of production.
Now to say that we are friends would be an empty platitude if we fail to behave as friends and honestly look to weaknesses in our relationship. And unfortunately, there are weaknesses. Labor has not adequately used its great power, its vision and resources to advance Negro rights. Undeniably, it has done more than other forces in American society to this end. Aid from real friends in labor has often come when the flames of struggle heighten, but Negroes are a solid component within the labor movement and a reliable bulwark for labor’s whole program and should expect more from it, exactly as a member of a family expects more from his relatives than he expects from his neighbors. Labor, which made impatience for long-delayed justice for itself a vital motive force, cannot lack understanding of the Negro’s impatience. It cannot speak with the reactionary’s calm indifference of progress around some obscure corner, yet not yet possible even to see. That is a maximum in the law: justice too long delayed is justice denied.
How can labor rise to the heights of its potential statesmanship and cement its bonds with Negroes to their mutual advantage? First, labor should accept the logic of its special position with respect to Negroes and the struggle for equality. Although organized labor has taken actions to eliminate discrimination in its ranks, the standard expected of you is higher than the standard for the general community. Your conduct should and can set an example for others, as you have done in other crusades for social justice. You should root out vigorously every manifestation of discrimination so that some internationals, central labor bodies, or locals may not besmirch the positive accomplishments of labor. I am aware that this is not easy, nor popular, but the eight-hour day was not popular, nor easy to achieve, nor was a closed shop, nor was the right to strike, nor was outlawing anti-labor injunctions. But you accomplished all of these with a massive will and determination. And out of such struggle for democratic rights you won both economic gains and the respect of the country, and you will win both again if you will make Negro rights a great crusade.
Second, the political strength you are going to need to prevent automation from becoming a Moloch, consuming jobs and contract gains, can be multiplied if you tap the vast reservoir of Negro political power. Negroes, given the vote, will vote liberal and labor, because they need the same liberal legislation labor needs. To give just an example of the importance of the Negro vote to labor, I might cite the arresting fact that the only state in the South which repealed the right-to-work law is Louisiana. And this was achieved because the Negro vote in that state grew large enough to become a balance of power, and it went along with labor to wipe out anti-labor legislation.
The two most dynamic and cohesive liberal forces in the country are the labor movement and the Negro freedom movement. Together we can be architects of democracy. In a South now rapidly industrializing, together we can retool the political structure of the South, sending to Congress steadfast liberals who, joining with those from Northern industrial states, will extend the frontiers of democracy for the whole nation. Together, we can bring about the day when there will be no separate identification of Negroes and labor. There is no intrinsic difference, as I have tried to demonstrate. Differences have been contrived by outsiders who seek to impose disunity by dividing brothers because the color of their skin has a different shade.
I look forward confidently to the day when all who work for a living will be one, with no thought of their separateness as Negroes, Jews, Italians or any other distinctions. This will be the day when we shall bring into full realization the dream of American democracy, a dream yet unfulfilled. A dream of equality of opportunity, a privilege and property widely distributed. A dream of a land where men will not take necessities from the many to give luxuries to the few. A dream of a land where men will not argue that the color of a man’s skin determines the content of his character. A dream of a nation where all our gifts and resources are held not for ourselves alone, but as instruments of service, for the rest of humanity. The dream of a country where every man will respect the dignity and worth of human personality — that is the dream. And as we struggle to make racial and economic justice a reality, let us maintain faith in the future. At times we confront difficult and frustrating moments in the struggle to make justice a reality, but we must believe somehow that these problems can be solved.
There is a little song that we sing in the movement taking place in the South; it goes something like this: “We shall overcome / We shall overcome / Deep in my heart / I do believe / We shall overcome.” And somehow all over America, we must believe that we shall overcome and that these problems can be solved and they will be solved.
Before the victory’s won, some of us will have to get scarred up, but we shall overcome. Before the victory of justice is a reality, some may even face physical death, but if physical death is the price that some must pay to free their children and their brothers from a permanent life of psychological death, then nothing could be more moral. Before the victory’s won, some more will have to go to jail. We must be willing to go to jail and transform the jails from dungeons of shame to havens of freedom and human dignity. Yes before the victory’s won, before the victory’s won, some will be misunderstood; some will be dismissed as dangerous rabble rousers and agitators; some will be called reds and communists merely because they believe in economic justice and the brotherhood of man.
But we shall overcome, and I am convinced that we shall overcome because the arc of the moral universe is long but it bends toward justice. We shall overcome because Carlyle is right: “No lie can live forever.” We shall overcome because William Cullen Bryant is right: “Truth crushed to earth, will rise again.” We shall overcome because James Russell Lowell is right: “Truth forever on the scaffold / Wrong forever on the throne / Yet that scaffold sways the future.…”
And so if we will go out with this faith, and with this determination to solve these problems, we will bring into being that new day, and that new America. When that day comes, the fears of insecurity and the doubts clouding our future will be transformed into radiant confidence, into glowing excitement to reach creative goals, and into an abiding moral balance where the brotherhood of man will be undergirded by a secure, and expanded prosperity for all. Yes, this will be the day when all of God’s children — Black men and white men, Jews and Gentiles, Protestants and Catholics — will be able to join hands all over this nation and sing in the words of the old Negro spiritual, “Free at last, free at last / Thank God almighty, we are free at last.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Republicans created Missouri’s redistricting mess. Now they’re furious about it.
description: Attorney General Catherine Hanaway opened her response to Thursday’s Missouri Supreme Court decision with a quote from Benjamin Franklin “A republic, if you can keep it.” Things went downhill from there. Hanaway declared Missouri to be in a “full-fledged constitutional crisis,” accused the court of disenfranchising every voter in the state and promised an im[...]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins speaks to reporters following Missouri Supreme Court arguments Sept. 2 (Annelise Hanshaw/MissouriIndependent).Attorney General Catherine Hanaway opened her response to Thursday’s Missouri Supreme Court decision with a quote from Benjamin Franklin
“A republic, if you can keep it.”
Things went downhill from there.
Hanaway declared Missouri to be in a “full-fledged constitutional crisis,” accused the court of disenfranchising every voter in the state and promised an immediate appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Secretary of State Denny Hoskins joined in the revolutionary rhetoric (ironic for a guy whose trademark is a red coat), declaring: “We may have lost the battle today, but the war to preserve our constitutional republic is far from over.”
Constitutional crisis may be a little hyperbolic. But Missouri unquestionably has a mess on its hands.
We held a congressional primary last month using gerrymandered districts drawn by Republican lawmakers in 2025. The state Supreme Court now says those districts never legally took effect because enough signatures were gathered to hold a referendum. Come November, unless the U.S. Supreme Court intervenes, Missouri will return to the congressional map used in 2024.
Candidates who spent months campaigning in one set of districts will finish the election in another.
But before we start shopping for powdered wigs and declaring the republic lost, it is worth asking a simpler question: How did we get here?
The answer isn’t especially flattering to the GOP officials expressing the most alarm.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway at a press conference on March 31 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Hoskins declared the referendum insufficient on Aug. 4, arguing Missouri voters had no constitutional right to force a vote on congressional redistricting. He made the same argument in federal court in December.
Eight months earlier.
Opponents of the new map had already turned in more than 300,000 signatures in December. And a federal judge pointed directly at the problem now being described as a constitutional emergency: If the referendum qualified, the new congressional map could be frozen and the 2026 election disrupted.
Hoskins had authority to rule the petition insufficient once it was filed. If no number of signatures could make the referendum legal, there was nothing left to wait for. The constitutional argument was sitting right there. The same federal judge said as much, noting there was “no apparent reason” for Hoskins to incur the significant cost of signature verification given his stated belief that the petition was constitutionally deficient.
Hoskins waited.
In May, the Missouri Supreme Court again made clear that nobody could know which congressional map was actually in force until Hoskins made his decision and the courts reviewed it.
Hoskins waited some more.
His office sent hundreds of thousands of petition signatures to local election officials for verification. He asked them to check every one — rather than use the random sample state law allows — pushing the verification deadline from February to the end of July. The state proceeded toward the August primary using the new map.
Then, around 4 p.m. on Aug. 4, roughly an hour before his legal deadline expired and while voters were casting ballots in the primary, Hoskins finally declared the referendum unconstitutional.
Nothing had changed. Hoskins acted on the same legal theory the state had been advancing since December.
And on Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court called him on it.
The judges, all but two of whom were appointed by Republican governors, unanimously ruled that Missouri’s Constitution gives citizens the power to refer “any act of the General Assembly” to voters unless the constitution expressly says otherwise. Congressional redistricting is an act of the General Assembly. There is no exception for it.
And when Hoskins complained about the confusion, cost and logistical difficulty of changing maps after the primary, the court was notably unmoved.
Those arguments were “particularly misplaced,” Judge Ginger Gooch wrote, because “the secretary’s delay created the confusion, expense and practical difficulties of which he complains.”
For what it’s worth, Gooch was Hanaway’s law partner at Husch Blackwell before joining the bench in 2022.
It boils down to this: Missouri officials knew in December that the legality of this referendum could determine which congressional map would govern the 2026 election.
Hoskins had eight months to make his call. The state had eight months to press the legal argument it had already chosen. They waited. Now they are complaining about the consequences of their own delay.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: Remembering 9/11, scoring a debate, eluding truth
description: Three thoughts … Hundreds of thousands of Nebraskans will join millions of Americans this week to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the horrible shorthand for violence and death that came to our shores. Much as JFK’s assassination or Pearl Harbor became seminal moments for earlier generations, 9/11 did for Gen Y and Gen Z. […]
text:
Smoke rises from the site of the World Trade Center attack on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001. (Photo by Paul Morse/U.S. National Archives)Three thoughts …
Hundreds of thousands of Nebraskans will join millions of Americans this week to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the horrible shorthand for violence and death that came to our shores. Much as JFK’s assassination or Pearl Harbor became seminal moments for earlier generations, 9/11 did for Gen Y and Gen Z.
Twenty-five years ago this week, I gathered around a television in the newsroom of the Grand Island Independent with reporters, editors, ad reps and pressmen to watch the world as it was irretrievably altered. I had been called back from an assignment just in time to see the North Tower of the World Trade Center collapse.
We, as a nation, would never be the same.
The Independent staff then set about publishing an “extra,” a special edition of a newspaper that would hit doorsteps later that afternoon. The extra we produced and ran on Sept. 11, 2001, was one of only a handful ever printed in the 141 years of the newspaper’s history.
I wrote one story for the extra, an interview with the cousin of a graphic artist in our advertising department. She gave me his number on the off chance he might answer amid the terror of that morning. I was shocked when he did. Out of breath and hurrying to get out of Manhattan, he told me he had seen the second plane making its way toward the World Trade Center, flying above the Hudson River, murderers mixed among the hundreds of innocents onboard. He was essentially running for his life.
The evil and fear that unfolded that morning altered our national psyche. How we see each other. How we see the rest of the world. How we choose to navigate the increasing antipathy among humans towards each other.
We must never forget how the events of 9/11 made us feel, frightened us, steeled our resolve. We might also do well to remember the sense of unity and community we felt with one another and even among those around the globe who had proclaimed, “Today we are all Americans.” Granted, its staying power waned, but for several months we saw through and over the many divisive walls we had erected. Too bad it took trauma and tragedy to do that.
Meanwhile, we remember.
* * *
My score card for the Nebraska State Fair’s Osborn/Ricketts debate worked out to be par for the course. As expected, neither said anything particularly new, GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts touting his experience, what an incumbent usually does, and iIndependent Dan Osborn his plan for change, the bailiwick of the challenger.
The hour was spent with the pair agreeing on more than either might cop to, but having a non-partisan in the race lent itself to the sadly quaint notion of common ground.
The panel’s questions covered a good range of topics in an hour, although I wanted to hear more about why anyone would want membership in a club with the reputation for abdicating its federal government co-equalness to the president. Or the ongoing push by the current administration to disenfranchise voters. And whatever happened to that whole Epstein law all of Nebraska’s cCongressional representatives voted for but which seems now to have been buried beneath war, sketchy food and measles?
Still, even if we already knew most of the substance, the debate gave a side-by-side measure of style and demeanor, in which I found Ricketts’s rapid-fire and Osborn’s measured responses instructive. One suggestion: Please leave time for the candidates to question each other.
The evening did have a low point. Ricketts’ continued an annoying use of the term “Democrat Dan” for Osborn (37 times in the hour and at least once in every answer). The indecorous name-calling grew old quickly, and by the time debate moderator Dave Griek turned out the lights, it had taken on the vibe of one of those petulant, doom-mongering political ads on TV.
The high point: that both candidates showed up for a debate.
* * *
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recently accused the Pennsylvania Health Department of lying about two measles deaths, touting the federal government’s “commitment to transparency and telling the American people the truth — a foundational principle of the Trump administration.”
Wait … what? Transparency? The truth?
In a word, no. From why we’re at war to reflecting-pool fiction to election-fraud fairy tales to every “greatest,” “most” or “nobody has seen anything like it,” the truth from this administration is extraordinarily elusive. Nor is it only the president. His commerce secretary recently said data centers don’t use water. His vice president once insisted immigrants were eating their neighbors’ pets. We could go on … for a long time.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Union healthcare workers protect NJ patients when laws and regulators cannot
description: Healthcare workers and patients alike face a growing threat that cannot be addressed through collective bargaining alone, nurse and union leader Debbie White writes.
text:
Healthcare workers and patients alike face a growing threat that cannot be addressed through collective bargaining alone, nurse and union leader Debbie White writes. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)This Labor Day, New Jerseyans should take a moment to appreciate the nurses, healthcare professionals, and support staff who care for our communities every day. When healthcare workers have the protection of a union, patients benefit too. Union members can speak up about unsafe conditions, advocate for their patients, and fight for quality healthcare without fear of retaliation. 
Over the past three years, Health Professionals and Allied Employees healthcare workers have negotiated stronger staffing protections and safer working conditions in hospitals across New Jersey. These improvements did not come easily, but they have made a real difference for patients and caregivers because we knew the improvements were grounded in science.
Today, however, healthcare workers and patients alike face a growing threat that cannot be addressed through collective bargaining alone. Increasingly, hospital operators are making decisions that endanger access to care, while government regulators lack the authority and enforcement needed to stop them.
Over the last year, New Jersey has witnessed two alarming examples of hospital systems disregarding state requirements and reducing critical healthcare services, even closing hospitals, before receiving the necessary approval from the New Jersey Department of Health.
Last year, Hudson Regional Health abruptly cut inpatient services at Christ Hospital in Jersey City despite assurances that it had the money and resources to sustain and improve the facility.  Hudson Regional acquired the system in bankruptcy only months earlier.  First, the hospital cut services dramatically, then, over the next few months, closed its doors entirely, leaving a community without a neighborhood hospital and healthcare workers without jobs.
Hospitals are not shopping centers or office buildings. They are essential community institutions that provide lifesaving care. When a hospital closes or services disappear, patients suffer the consequences and neighboring hospitals are forced to deal with the displaced patient population. 
After the Christ Hospital closure, the patient wait times in Jersey City Medical Center shot up dramatically because it remained as the only acute care hospital in one of New Jersey’s largest cities. Patients continued to come to Christ Hospital, unaware it had closed.
Unfortunately, despite a clear violation of the law and without the required approval of the Department of Health, Hudson Regional Health had closed a hospital and opened the door for other hospital operators to recklessly flout state Department of Health regulations.
The closure of Christ Hospital exposed a troubling reality: New Jersey’s healthcare oversight system lacks the enforcement tools needed to hold bad actors accountable before irreversible harm is done and it seems other health systems may be learning this as well.
Heights University Hospital, formerly known as Christ Hospital, in Jersey City closed its doors earlier this year, leaving the state’s second-largest city with just one hospital emergency room. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Earlier this year, Inspira Health applied to eliminate inpatient critical care services at its hospitals in Elmer and Mannington, which would leave Salem County residents without local ICU care. Salem County is a largely rural area where many residents rely on these hospitals as their nearest source of critical care, and questions remain about whether alternative transportation and EMS capacity are sufficient to reliably reach other Inspira facilities. Even though the Department of Health has not approved the closures, most of the affected critical care nurses have already accepted alternate positions and are no longer working in the ICUs — underscoring that Inspira is proceeding with the transition before regulatory approval is final.
Healthcare workers depend on the Department of Health to inspect facilities, enforce regulations, and protect patient safety. Workers are often the first to identify unsafe conditions and report them. Union contracts help protect those who speak out, but healthcare workers cannot enforce state law. That responsibility belongs to government regulators.
Recognizing these shortcomings, legislation introduced earlier this year, S4395/A5185, would strengthen the Department of Health’s enforcement powers. The proposal would greatly increase financial penalties for violations and allow the state to appoint a receiver to manage hospitals whose operators repeatedly disregard critical requirements and violate laws.
Those changes are badly needed. Current penalties are often treated as just another cost of doing business. Meaningful consequences are necessary if we expect healthcare operators to meet their obligations to patients and communities.
The closure of Christ Hospital by Hudson Regional and the loss of Inspira ICU beds in Salem County should be viewed as urgent warning signs. Health Professionals and Allied Employees unionized workers were instrumental in sounding the alarm in both cases. The nurses in Jersey City and in Salem County are, first and foremost, patient advocates and recognized and reported these illegal actions.
When hospitals lose inpatient services, emergency departments, or critical-care capacity, the effects ripple throughout entire regions. Patients wait longer for care. Ambulances travel farther. Neighboring hospitals face greater strain. Families without reliable transportation encounter even more barriers to treatment.
Healthcare workers also pay a steep price. Dedicated professionals lose jobs, careers are disrupted, and remaining staff face heavier workloads under increasingly difficult conditions. Communities lose experienced caregivers whose knowledge and commitment cannot easily be replaced.
Operating a hospital is a privilege that carries profound responsibility. Healthcare systems exist to serve the public, not simply to maximize financial returns. When owners choose to operate these essential institutions, they must be held accountable for maintaining safe, reliable access to care.
New Jersey cannot become a healthcare desert and a place where rules are optional, and enforcement comes too late to prevent harm. Patients deserve better. Healthcare workers deserve better. Our communities deserve better.
This Labor Day, let us recognize the union healthcare workers who continue to fight not only for fair treatment on the job, but for stronger protections for patients, stronger hospitals, and a healthcare system that places community needs above corporate convenience.
Debbie White, RN, is president of the Health Professionals and Allied Employees, the largest union of registered nurses and healthcare professionals in New Jersey. It represents more than 15,000 nurses, social workers, therapists, technicians, medical researchers, and other healthcare professionals in hospitals, nursing homes, home care agencies, blood banks, and university research facilities, and is affiliated with the American Federation of Teachers, AFL-CIO.

name: Daily Montanan
title: The opportunity too many Americans have never heard of
description: Will I ever be able to retire? It’s a question millions of hard-working Americans are asking themselves right now. I read that the median retirement savings for working-age Americans is just $955. That’s not a typo. Rising costs, shrinking savings, and economic uncertainty have made retirement feel farther away than ever. While there isn’t a […]
text:
Eva Villasana (Photo courtesy of Pacific Steel and Recycling)Will I ever be able to retire?
It’s a question millions of hard-working Americans are asking themselves right now. I read that the median retirement savings for working-age Americans is just $955. That’s not a typo. Rising costs, shrinking savings, and economic uncertainty have made retirement feel farther away than ever. While there isn’t a simple or singular answer to this question, I’ve come to believe there is one opportunity that too many people have never even heard about.
Just a few years ago, I was one of them.
For nearly 20 years, I worked in retail management. I loved developing people, helping teams succeed, and exceeding customer expectations. The companies I worked for had competitive benefits, medical insurance, 401(k) matching programs, and even stock purchasing options. Still, I couldn’t shake the feeling that something was missing. I worked hard every day, yet retirement still felt like something I was chasing on my own. A big part of me also wanted my work to mean more than earning my next paycheck.
Then, while visiting friends and family in Montana, a conversation with a close friend changed my entire life. She worked at Pacific Steel & Recycling. There was an exciting new position they created in training and development.
She smiled and said, “When I read the job description, it was as if they were describing you.”
After some further conversation, I forwarded my resume. Before the interview, my friend’s advice was simple: “Eva, Pacific is an ESOP so do your research.” An ESOP? What’s that?
That’s where I did what most people would do: I Googled ESOP (Employee Stock Ownership Plan). There were links, articles, definitions. Facts like ESOPs are six times less likely to lay off employees, and ESOPs improve retirement security. I also noticed some of my favorite brands like Bob’s Red Mill and Litehouse Foods are employee owned and I never knew it. By the time I closed my laptop, I felt like this had to be too good to be true.
If you’ve never heard the term ESOP, you’re not alone. An ESOP is an Employee Stock Ownership Plan, and it’s a retirement benefit that gives employees an ownership stake in the company. This ownership stake does not have to be purchased. It’s gifted. Google gave me the technical definition, but it couldn’t even begin to define how being an employee-owner feels.
A few weeks later, I was offered the position at Pacific Steel & Recycling and began my transition from employee to employee-owner.
I expected my first few months to be very similar to every other job I’ve ever had. They weren’t. Every day, I saw people who genuinely cared. They cared about doing the job well and constantly improving. There was a sense of ownership that was impossible to miss. This ownership culture showed up in the ways people treated each other, the way they solved problems, and the pride they took in their work.
At Pacific, we call it “ownership in action.” Every employee owner has a voice, the opportunity to improve the company, and the responsibility to help us succeed together. One example is a company-wide program we borrowed from Hypertherm, a longstanding New Hampshire-based ESOP company. They shared a best practice that gives employee-owners opportunities to identify improvements, solve problems, and strengthen business. One of our employee owners took that idea, made it Pacific, and implemented our Continuous Improvement Activity (CIA) program. We have implemented more than 2,200 ideas since the program started.
Employee ownership also shows up at Pacific in how we interact with the communities we serve. I’ve seen firsthand the incredible efforts our people pour into volunteering and investing in a wide variety of charitable causes.
Today, there are still far too many Americans who have never heard of employee ownership or ESOPs. There are fewer than 6,500 ESOPs in America and only 34 in Montana. Employee ownership isn’t something people should discover by accident. It deserves to be mainstream, which is why I’m glad to add my voice to Expanding ESOPs, a coalition of nearly 100 organizations working to grow employee ownership here in Montana and beyond.
This Labor Day, I hope we celebrate more than hard work. I hope we create more opportunities for Americans to become employee owners. More Americans should know how it feels to have a voice, a shared purpose, and a real stake in their companies.
Eva Villasana is a training and development specialist at Pacific Steel & Recycling, based in Great Falls.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska awarded over $5 million in federal grants to expedite transportation projects
description: OMAHA — Overlooking Interstate 480 from downtown Omaha Friday, state officials celebrated Nebraska’s receiving $5.15 million in a collection of federal grants aimed at speeding up ongoing transportation projects. The awards allocated to the Nebraska Department of Transportation include a $1.15 million Regional Infrastructure Accelerator (RIA) Grant to fund t[...]
text:
Sean McMaster, administrator of the Federal Highway Administration, speaks to Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and Nebraska Department of Transportation Director Vicki Kramer at a press conference on Sept. 4, 2026. (Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Overlooking Interstate 480 from downtown Omaha Friday, state officials celebrated Nebraska’s receiving $5.15 million in a collection of federal grants aimed at speeding up ongoing transportation projects.
The awards allocated to the Nebraska Department of Transportation include a $1.15 million Regional Infrastructure Accelerator (RIA) Grant to fund the Accelerating Critical Connections for Elevating Livability in Nebraska (ACCEL-NE) Program, $2 million through the Innovative Finance and Asset Concession (IFAC) Program and $2 million awarded with the Omaha-Council Bluffs Metropolitan Area Planning Agency under the Prioritization Process Pilot Program, according to department spokesperson Samantha Bernt.
Sean McMaster, administrator for the Federal Highway Administration, said the goal of the grants is to expedite several major transportation projects in the state, some of which have been ongoing for years and others that have yet to get started. These include development of the Lincoln East Beltway and easing congestion along the bottleneck of Interstate 80 corridor connecting to Interstate 680 and Interstate 480, which McMaster listed as a priority recognized by the U.S. Department of Transportation.
“We are moving quick,” McMaster said. “This unprecedented execution is the fastest and most massive competitive grant delivery in the agency’s modern history, and exceeds the last four years of the last administration.”
McMaster said on the federal side, officials are open to moving at the speeds each state prefers. Later, Pillen said he wants to “put the pedal to the metal,” noting that the longer infrastructure projects take to complete, the more expensive they become.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
U.S. Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., was not one of the official speakers at Friday’s conference, but he attended and spoke in support of the grants. He agreed with Pillen’s point that time adds cost to infrastructure projects. He noted that the Pentagon was built in just over a year and said the U.S. should strive to return to similar construction speeds.
“We’ve lost what’s made us great,” Bacon said.
Pillen has repeatedly said he wants to ensure Nebraska gets its fair share of federal aid, and on Friday he touted that during his first term, federal funding to Nebraska rose to $3.5 billion.
Pillen said he wants to change the narrative about Nebraska so that it’s no longer considered a flyover state but a “fly-to state.” He said the grants announced on Friday will be a big piece of accomplishing that.
“It’s a great sign that we are open for business,” Pillen said. “Nobody can compete with us. There’s no better place in the world to live.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama union membership declines amid aging workforce, outsourcing
description: Alabama’s union membership declined last year amid a broader decline of the workforce, the aging of union members and outsourcing.  According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Alabama’s total employment dropped from 2.110 million in 2024 to 2.090 million in 2025. Labor union representation fell from 140,000 in 2024 to 131,000, or from 6.6% […]
text:
A youngster holds up a pro-union sign at Laborfest in Milwaukee on Labor Day, Sept. 2, 2024. The percentage of unionized workers in Alabama has declined amid an aging population, outsourcing and technology changes. (Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Alabama’s union membership declined last year amid a broader decline of the workforce, the aging of union members and outsourcing. 
According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Alabama’s total employment dropped from 2.110 million in 2024 to 2.090 million in 2025. Labor union representation fell from 140,000 in 2024 to 131,000, or from 6.6% of the workforce to 6.3%. The number of workers represented by unions also fell, from 165,000 in 2024 (7.8% of the workforce) to 150,000 (7.2%) in 2025. Nationwide, the unionization rate is 10%. 
Alabama was historically one of the most unionized states in the South, due to the number of manufacturing jobs available during the 1940s. As late as 2015, about 10% of the state workforce belonged to unions, though the numbers have been declining since. 
A study by the Illinois Economic Policy Institute and the Project for Middle Class Renewal at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign released last week estimated that nationwide, unions added over 400,000 members last year.
Labor unions are growing, but where depends on state politics

Bren Riley, president of the Alabama AFL-CIO, said in an interview Thursday the decrease can be attributed to the closing of factories, such as Goodyear’s plant in Gadsden.
The plant once employed up to 4,000 people, but when it closed in 2020, it had about 400 after Goodyear shifted production to North Carolina and Mexico. The Associated Press reported that April that the plant “reached a deal with labor to shutter its plant at Gadsden for good.” A message seeking comment on the closure was left with Goodyear Friday morning.
“It took until 1943 to get a to get a union (at Goodyear’s Gadsden plant) and get a collective bargaining agreement, and the sad thing about it is, we’ve lost a lot of good union jobs in Alabama and the South, and it’s because sometimes greedy corporations care more about profits than they do paying a decent wage,” Riley said.
The aging of the state population is another factor. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in 2025, 19% of Alabama’s population was 65 or older. Riley said AFL-CIO is working to engage the younger population as well.
“We’ve got committees, we’ve got programs set up to reach out. We call it our next gen program, the next generation of union leaders,” he said.
Riley also said campaigns against unions played a role. Workers at Mercedes-Benz in Vance in 2024 launched a campaign to organize under United Auto Workers, but ultimately lost the vote after a sustained campaign against the union by state and business leaders. 
“It scares them to death because in these organizing campaigns, they’ll take a guy like me that’s out in front of this organizing campaign, like working at Mercedes, they’ll fire me for being involved in that kind of stuff,” Riley said. “And then the union, on behalf of that fired person, they’ll get them several thousand dollars down the road, but what value is that to that plant floor? They (say) ‘hey, I ain’t gonna fool that union.’”
Riley said building community is important when trying to encourage others to unionize.
“If you had to go to church with them, you go to church … If you had to drink beer, you (drink beer). You gotta build a relationship with these folks,” he said.
Riley also said he was concerned for the direction of the workforce because of how rapidly technology is advancing.
“These data centers are going somewhere. You know, if they don’t come to Alabama, they’re gonna build them in Georgia,” Riley said. “What we want to do as labor is to make sure when they do come, by God, union folks build them and maintain them. There’s a lot of jobs building them, but after they’re built, how many jobs will it take to maintain them?”
Despite all of the challenges facing unions, Riley said AFL-CIO is “proud of what we do.”
“We’re proud of the work our folks do, and hopefully, and maybe we can get the message across to them (corporations) that we’re not the damn enemy. We want a partner,” he said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Labor Day 2026: North Carolina ranks best for business economy, dead last for workers
description: North Carolina is consistently ranked among America’s top states for business. But a new ranking by Oxfam lists the state dead last in this year’s 2026 Best States to Work Index. Oxfam, a global nonprofit focused on poverty and inequality, examined 37 policies including wages, worker protections, and the right to organize to determine which […]
text:
Housing costs, rising fuel and grocery prices have working North Carolinians feeling stretched this Labor Day. A new ranking by Oxfam lists the state dead last in this year’s 2026 Best States to Work Index.(Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) North Carolina is consistently ranked among America’s top states for business. But a new ranking by Oxfam lists the state dead last in this year’s 2026 Best States to Work Index.
Oxfam, a global nonprofit focused on poverty and inequality, examined 37 policies including wages, worker protections, and the right to organize to determine which states do the best job of supporting workers in all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.
“This year, while workers are facing extraordinary economic hardship, we looked at how far wages go toward the cost of living for a family of four,” said Patricia Stottlemyer, Oxfam America’s policy director. “In North Carolina, the minimum wage of $7.25 only meets 19% of the cost of living.”
Because women and workers of color are overrepresented in low-wage jobs, raising the minimum wage would help millions of workers, according to Oxfam.
NC Budget and Tax Center Policy Analyst Alex Campbell(File photo)
Stottlemyer notes that North Carolina has not raised its minimum wage since 2009, while neighboring Virginia raised its hourly minimum wage to $12.77 per hour this year and passed legislation to increase the minimum wage to $13.75 per hour January 1, 2027.
Republican state lawmakers have resisted raising the state’s minimum wage because they say very few people actually work for minimum wage anymore. They say the current demand for labor has driven pay higher. But advocates say that’s not true for every job market, especially in rural areas with few job opportunities.
Alex Campbell, a policy analyst with the North Carolina Budget & Tax Center, said raising the minimum wage substantially could boost average annual pay for over 1.5 million working North Carolinians.
“If we increased the minimum wage to two-thirds of the national median wage, that would provide an average annual pay increase of $6,100 for North Carolinians, and it would benefit a third of our workforce,” Campbell told NC Newsline.
Stottlemyer said North Carolina also comes up short when it comes to policies like requiring paid family and medical leave, paid sick leave, protections for domestic workers, and caregiver discrimination protections. The Oxfam index says North Carolina’s “right-to-work” laws prevent employees from forming unions to negotiate higher wages and better benefits.
Affordability crisis for workers
On Wednesday, the N.C Budget & Tax Center co-hosted an online public hearing to discuss the affordability crisis and how it’s affecting low- and middle-income workers.
Caroline Hakel (BTC livestream)
Caroline Hakel is a public school educator who moved to Henderson County after earning her teaching degree in Ohio. Hakel said unlike the Buckeye State, teachers here cannot collectively bargain for better wages and working conditions.
“I’m a single teacher and I’ve struggled to find affordable housing. Rental prices continue to rise and buying a house feels like a pipe dream,” said Hakel.
Fair-market rent for a one-bedroom apartment in Henderson County is $1,429 per month, leaving her cost-burdened on her teacher’s salary.
Hakel said she’d like to see state lawmakers restore master’s pay and consider funding childcare for teachers. She said while the raise that came in July’s state budget was welcome, veteran teachers were left behind.
“This should be embarrassing that this is what is considered significant,” said Hakel.
In neighboring Transylvania County, KC Collins, a member of the Worker & Living Wage Coalition, is working two jobs to make ends meet. The county’s economy is largely dependent on tourism centered around nearby state and national forests.
“The focus on tourism as the key to our local economy has led to incredibly seasonal income and financial uncertainty for workers, especially after Hurricane Helene,” said Collins.
Collins said living in a state that is number one for businesses means nothing if it is also last in conditions for workers.
She also said affordable housing is a chief concern.Like many of her peers, she lives with roommates to make rent more affordable.
In Durham, Ieisha Francis works as a Certified Nursing Assistant in an assisted living facility. Over the past decade she’s noticed more apartments and houses being built, but fewer workers can afford them.
“There are people in Durham that are homeless, that sleep in their cars, that have to pay for hotels to stay in or have to stay with family members,” Francis said. “How is this even possible when they are working?”
The average annual pay for a CNA in Durham County is just under $38,000 annually, according to ZipRecruiter. But Francis said she’s increasingly juggling soaring utility costs  and rising grocery prices.
Hunger crisis widens in North Carolina as food banks face more demand, federal cuts

“It’s not just me that I’m feeding. I have four grandchildren. So I have to also make sure that they’re fed as well,” said Francis. “It’s a real struggle.”
The struggle to make ends meet is beginning to affect the state’s business ratings, too.
In July’s CNBC ranking of “America’s Top States for Business” North Carolina’s rating for quality-of-life, based on key metrics like affordability, childcare, and safeguards against discrimination,was substantially lower than in 2025.
Stottlemyer is urging North Carolina policymakers to look at the places that top this year’s Oxfam index — California, the District of Columbia, New York, Illinois, and Oregon.
“These labor policies we track are key levers in addressing the affordability crisis,” said Stottlemyer.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s wildfires: The risk doesn’t end where insurance does for our small businesses
description: Wildfires continue to burn across Idaho, consuming hundreds of thousands of acres, forcing evacuations, and disrupting entire communities. The wildfires have forced a reckoning and reminder of the ongoing and evolving risk that countless Idahoans face each year. Homeowners are often the central focus of media and news cycles following natural disasters. Howe[...]
text:
Wildland firefighters perform backfiring operations in July 2026 on the Tartar Fire near Weiser, Idaho. (Photo courtesy of the National Interagency Fire Center)Wildfires continue to burn across Idaho, consuming hundreds of thousands of acres, forcing evacuations, and disrupting entire communities. The wildfires have forced a reckoning and reminder of the ongoing and evolving risk that countless Idahoans face each year.
Homeowners are often the central focus of media and news cycles following natural disasters. However, small businesses are often the ones facing the quieter crises: catastrophic losses that traditional insurers either limit from coverage or exclude altogether.
Northwest late summer days marred by historic drought, exacerbating wildfires

We saw a similar fact pattern play out on a large scale following the Palisades Fire in Southern California. Risks became too large for traditional insurers to cover, so they increased premiums while decreasing coverage, leaving thousands of small business owners uninsured and vulnerable to significant risk and losses.
For many companies, particularly those with specialized operations, traditional insurers are failing to keep pace with the needs we are seeing from our local businesses.
By nature, insurance is a reactive industry. Insurers collect data, organize coverage offerings, and roll out plans once they assess the risks – all while reviewing data by looking in the rearview mirror.
In today’s volatile landscape, a reactive approach no longer works, and it’s the primary reason why we are seeing a crisis in the insurance market.
Congress also recognized this shortcoming in insurance and risk planning, which is why it created Section 831(b) of the Internal Revenue Code. This provision allows small businesses to self-insure against fortuitous risk through the creation of captive insurance plans, providing them the ability to tailor their policies to match their unique needs and otherwise difficult-to-cover risks.
We see these plans successfully implemented across a variety of industries. Notably, industries that have seen significant growth of micro-captive insurance are the ranching and agriculture industries.
Pointedly, as the Tartar Fire burned, Idaho’s ranchers were some of the most affected, being hit with devastating losses and inadequate coverage. This fire, which has now burned more than 158,000 acres, caused damages that will take years to repair.
Going through the process of rebuilding is challenging enough; coupled with inadequate insurance, it becomes even more of a daunting task.
Risks will continue to rise and as communities across Idaho, the West, and the rest of the country continue to navigate these challenges, our policymakers should recognize and support our small business owners proactively.
By leveraging a forward-focused approach to risk management and supporting existing tools like 831(b) plans, we can ensure that resilience is built long before the next disaster strikes.
Small businesses need access to practical risk management tools to help them prepare – not simply respond. That is the crux of an effective risk management strategy. As crises and risks continue to evolve, it is critical that our policies and approaches evolve alongside them.
By clarifying the rules surrounding Section 831(b), our lawmakers can help ensure that America’s small businesses are ready the next time disaster strikes, because it will, guaranteed.
