name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas students learn about 9/11 attacks through oral histories
description: Army veteran Wesley Jackson remembers his confusion when co-workers told him two planes struck the World Trade Center on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001.  After processing the news of the terrorist attacks, Jackson realized his days as a peacetime soldier were over, and it was only a matter of time before he was deployed […]
text:
Debbie Miller, a journalism instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College in Bentonville, discusses a 9/11 assignment with her students on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Army veteran Wesley Jackson remembers his confusion when co-workers told him two planes struck the World Trade Center on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001. 
After processing the news of the terrorist attacks, Jackson realized his days as a peacetime soldier were over, and it was only a matter of time before he was deployed to the Middle East. 
“My whole life changed in an instant,” he said. 
Twenty-five years later, Jackson is teaching Arkansas State University students about the impact of that day as an assistant professor of history. 
Friday marks the anniversary of the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people when hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a rural field in Pennsylvania. Arkansas history, journalism and political science teachers with vivid memories of that day are using oral histories to better explain its significance to students who weren’t alive in 2001. 
Learning history for students isn’t about dates and people, Jackson said.
“It’s the skills they’re learning about — critical thinking, decision making and being good stewards of the future,” he said. 
‘The uncertainty of it all’
Marie Totten, a visiting assistant professor in the University of Central Arkansas’ history department, said her students often hear about 9/11 in the context of conspiracies, and want to learn how to sift through false information. 
“They recognize that they’re addicted to their phones and their phones are created to make them addicted, that the algorithm is created to show them information that may not be true, and they want to learn the skills to combat that,” she said. 
 


Let us know what you think...


 



Some misinformation is dispelled through an oral history assignment that involves Totten’s students interviewing someone, often a grandparent, about their memories of Sept. 11. Talking to a trusted source can help push back against conspiracy theories students see online, she said.
“They’re a very curious generation, they just don’t know who to ask or what questions to ask,” Totten said. 
Jackson said conspiracy websites often use cherrypicked or misleading information, which is why he teaches students the importance of looking at all available evidence. 
Although he can share his personal experiences as a soldier sent to Afghanistan and Iraq because of the Sept. 11 attack, Jackson said like any primary source, he’s just one piece of the puzzle and it’s important to look at multiple sources to see the broader story. 
Jackson also teaches students that the narrative around historical events continuously changes as more information is uncovered. 
TSA shares passengers’ personal information with immigration enforcement, documents show

“That’s why I tell them it’s important to understand that history is an ever-evolving thing,” he said. “It’s a living creature. It’s not set in stone.”
Aneyda Reynaga, a journalism student at NorthWest Arkansas Community College, was born three years after the attacks and said she grew up learning about it at school through sometimes “graphic documentaries” that could make you feel “queasy.”
Education about the attacks typically focuses on the event itself, but it’s also important to discuss what happened after, Reynaga said.
“Growing up, I didn’t even know TSA was because of 9/11, I thought it was always a thing,” she said, referring to the Transportation Security Administration established after the attacks. 
Reynaga recently learned more about the event while interviewing her dad and aunt for a class assignment, and said she was most surprised to hear that their lives went on as usual, with her aunt still expected to go to work that day.  
The assignment also helped Reynaga understand how the attacks affected the entire country. 
“It made me see the uncertainty of it all because Arkansas is so far from New York, and the fact that people felt scared or they felt uncertain of what was going to happen all the way over here, I think it really gave me a new perspective on everything,” she said. 
‘How history transpires’
Debbie Miller, a veteran journalist and instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College, said she’s had students like Reynaga write about Sept. 11 over the years, but it felt particularly relevant to discuss this semester in light of the 25th anniversary. 
Interviewing family allows novice journalists, who may prefer communicating via text or email, to have a comfortable space to practice talking and interacting in person, Miller said. The assignment also allows students to connect with family in a way they might not have, she said.
Debbie Miller, a journalism instructor at NorthWest Arkansas Community College in Bentonville, watches as a student shares a video during a 9/11 discussion on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)
The attack on Pearl Harbor during World War II was a significant moment for Miller’s parents’ generation, but Miller said she doesn’t recall ever thinking to ask her parents about their experiences. Looking back, Miller said she wishes she had listened more when they were sharing stories. 
“I want to encourage curiosity in a safe space and encourage them to make more connections with their family members that they haven’t really thought about,” she said. 
At John Brown University, political science professor Daniel Bennett has students read a Politico Magazine oral history that describes what it was like aboard Air Force One for the eight hours it was in the air following the attacks. 
Something that resonates with students today is how technologically different the world was 25 years ago, Bennett said. The lack of social media or smart phones and the inability to communicate as easily is “pretty striking for what today’s students are typically familiar with,” he said. 
“We’ll also raise it in the context of how did this affect future conversations about civil liberties in the scope of protecting national security versus individual freedoms, as well as maybe this being the last unifying moment in American politics,” Bennett said. 
For many of today’s students, 9/11 is becoming just another major moment in American history, the same way Pearl Harbor or President John Kennedy’s assassination was remembered by older generations, he said. 
“I think for future generations, it’ll lose the magnitude of how important of a moment it was for myriad reasons,” Bennett said. “I don’t think that’s something to be happy about or even lamentable, it’s just kind of how history transpires.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Concierges, adjuncts, potato chip tasters: US employers relying more on ‘disposable’ workers
description: When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a […]
text:
There’s no way to climb a ladder without rungs.
(Photo: John Lund/Photodisc via Getty Images)
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.
When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.
These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.
I am a labor economist. In my new book, “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment,” I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.
3 different varieties
To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.
I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.
1. Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce.
2. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees.
3. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.
Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.
Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.
Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.
In 1970 people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Part-time marginal workers
Another example of marginal work is part-timers.
Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.
A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.
When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.
“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”
Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.
The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.
Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.
Forces behind this trend
Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable?
A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.
Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.
An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”
This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.
Outsourcing cleaning services might seem like a good way to cut costs, but in hospitals it can undercut safety. (Photo: Jupiterimages/BananaStock via Getty Images Plus)
Less pay and job satisfaction
My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.
In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.
The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.
Paul Osterman is professor emeritus at MIT’s Sloan School.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: How many South Carolina college grads stay in state for work?
description: Over the past decade and a half, about 60% of SC college grads went to work in the Palmetto State in the year after receiving their diploma.
text:
Students walk on the grounds of the University of South Carolina campus in Columbia, S.C. , on Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — Over the past decade and a half, more than 60% of South Carolina college graduates went to work in the Palmetto State in the year after receiving their diploma.
But by year three, that drops 10 percentage points, and by year five less than half of those same graduates are still working in the state, according to a new study by the state’s employment agency.
On a national basis, South Carolina lands in the middle third of states when it comes to retaining its graduates.
Economists from the state Department of Employment and Workforce tracked technical and four-year college graduates from the class of 2010 through the class of 2023, who are now three years out of school — to see how many stayed in South Carolina to work and how many left to pursue a job or further their education elsewhere.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The study, which relied on unemployment insurance wage records, did not count federal government workers, the self-employed or military members. Researchers also adjusted for students who went on to further their education in South Carolina rather than joining the workforce after graduation.
The study also measured how many students go to work within their field of study.
“Are nursing students becoming nurses or are they working as (medical) office receptionists?” said Erica Von Nessen, one of the researchers.
Lawyers, architects and health care students are the most likely to have careers in South Carolina that most closely match their degrees, the researchers found.
But they also took the data a step further to see how some degree-holders’ skillsets might still translate into jobs not directly related to their studies.
“One of the things we found was there are a substantial number of people with an English major who become paralegals,” researcher Bryan Grady said. “When you think about the skills that you acquire as an English major and the skills that are required to be a paralegal, there’s clearly an overlap there.”
Speaking to manufacturers and business people in Columbia last week at an annual workforce conference put on by the state’s largest industry group, Von Nessen and Grady highlighted findings on some of the state’s most in-demand fields — education, nursing and engineering.
Here’s how many are graduating from SC colleges with in-demand degrees. It’s not enough.

Engineering graduates, for example, tend to take a few years to find work in their field. In the first year after graduation, fewer than 62% of students found work as engineers at South Carolina companies. By year four, that rose to nearly 71%.
Those that didn’t get an engineering job right away still tended to be designers, construction managers, financial analysts or office clerks in the state.
And while the state often talks about struggling to keep teachers in the classroom, Von Nessen said nearly 70% of graduates were still working in education 15 years later.
“That’s very encouraging to me because I was thinking, ‘Oh, are we going to see something like 30% retention,’” she said.
Of nursing graduates, most got jobs in South Carolina right away — 98% — and stayed in them for a long time — 80% remained in the field 15 years later.
On the other hand, Grady said, business graduates were less likely to work in the state. But downtown Charlotte, the country’s second largest banking center, is just 10 miles north of the South Carolina border.
“It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to figure out that they’re going to want some some business majors up there,” he said.
Von Nessen and Grady’s study was part of larger legislative efforts to reshuffle oversight of the state’s workforce development efforts.
A 2023 law put all state-funded workforce development programs under the employment department’s microscope, making sure programs run by various agencies are all delivering on their goals.
Other tenets of the law included an annual analysis of job openings versus college graduates available to fill them.
“I think a lot of the discussion has been around career pathways and pipelines of we just need to plug people into these holes,” Grady said. “But the fact is, there are a lot of factors that determine what kind of job somebody ends up with. How do we make sure that the workforce of South Carolina as a whole has a wide variety of skills that employers are interested in, so that we don’t have to scramble?”
In the future, Von Nessen said they hope to work with colleges to measure how well their efforts to keep graduates in state are working.
More SC colleges want to help pay students who land summer internships

For example, the University of South Carolina offers $3,000 to students who participate in internships in high-demand industries in the state, such as aerospace, automotive, energy, financial services, healthcare, insurance and manufacturing.
More than 2,862 students across the USC college system, 74% of them in-state, have participated. They’ve gone to work for 891 companies across 43 South Carolina counties, according to a statement from the university. The school has awarded more than $8.6 million in stipends since the program started three years ago
Clemson University, too, operates a similar program but the school did not provide updated numbers in time for deadline.
The internship programs are taxpayer funded, with $4 million going to Clemson annually and $3 million now going to the USC system.
Coastal Carolina University had asked state legislators to spend $390,000 annually to start its own Teal Works Program, but the funding didn’t make it into the final budget.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Increasing SNAP error rates could be good news for Florida (really)
description: Florida’s anticipated error rate in the federal food security program called SNAP appears to be on the rise — a move that could wind up helping the state avoid costly penalties in the short run. After dipping to 12.97% for federal fiscal year (FFY) 2025, the unofficial payment error rate for FFY 2026 is an […]
text:
Florida's SNAP error rates are back on the rise. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Florida’s anticipated error rate in the federal food security program called SNAP appears to be on the rise — a move that could wind up helping the state avoid costly penalties in the short run.
After dipping to 12.97% for federal fiscal year (FFY) 2025, the unofficial payment error rate for FFY 2026 is an average 14.49%. (Federal fiscal years open each Oct. 1.)
That’s higher than the anticipated national error rate of 10.62%, also based on data through March, a Department of Children and Families, the Sept. 1, 2026, report shows.
The report does not contain error rates by county. But it does highlight error rates by region.  Northeast Florida had the highest error rates (19.3%), followed by southern Florida (18.81%) and southeast Florida (16.47%).
Payment error rates measure the accuracy of each state’s eligibility and benefit determinations in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Errors are unintentional mistakes and are not considered fraud.
High error rates don’t bode well for people who rely on the food security program, or for the federal government that until now has footed the entire costs of the program.
But it could be good financial news for Florida, which may avoid having to pay a $1 billion penalty if it wants to continue to participate.  
Enrollment in SNAP has dipped by double digits over the last year — 2,285,099 residents enrolled in the program in June, down from 2,970,283 in June 2025, data maintained by the DCF shows.
That’s about a 23% reduction.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
SNAP provides nutritional support for low-income seniors, people with disabilities living on fixed incomes, and other individuals and families with low incomes. Although funded by the federal government, SNAP in Florida is administered by DCF’s Office of Economic Self-Sufficiency, which is responsible for determining eligibility.
Before the One Big Beautiful Bill Act became law, SNAP benefits were funded entirely by the federal government. The new law slashes $186 billion in funding and for the first time puts cost-sharing requirements on states beginning in FFY 2028.
States with payment error rates of 6% or higher are required to contribute to the costs of food as follows:

5% of the cost of benefits for error rates above 6%.
10% of the cost of benefits for payment rates between 8% and 10%.
15%, of the costs of benefits for error rates above 10%.

On the other hand …
But the federal law delays the cost-sharing requirements for states with comparatively high payment error rates compared to the rest of the nation.
For instance, states with payment errors of 13.33% or more in FFY 2025 aren’t required to contribute to the costs of the program until FFY 2029.
Florida’s payment error rate had been 12.97% and the state didn’t qualify for that one-year delay. Based on the cost-sharing calculations, Florida faced a $1 billion tab beginning Oct. 1, 2027.
However, the law gives states a second chance to delay the cost-sharing requirements by allowing them to use either their FFY 2025 or FFY 2026 error rates.
Florida economists agree that the unofficial  2026 error through March rate is high enough, according to the report, to push cost sharing requirements back another three years.
“If Florida’s final FFY 2026 (payment error rate)  is at least 13.33 percent, implementation of the state cost-sharing requirement would be delayed until FFY 2030,” the Long Term Financial Outlook notes.
Economists annually prepare a  snapshot of the state’s budget situation for the next three years. The outlook, required by the Florida Constitution, is meant to put legislators and other state officials on notice about whether a budget surplus or deficit looms.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: So many election surveys. So few voters willing to pick up the phone.
description: The missed call log in Dr. Eric Bai’s iPhone has a sea of phone numbers with unfamiliar area codes. Some of them are likely from pollsters wanting to ask him about the upcoming Rhode Island primary elections.  A few times, he’s answered only to end up staying on the line to complete a survey. “I […]
text:
A phone displays a text message from Dynata inviting the recipient to participate in a 'short survey' on Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) The missed call log in Dr. Eric Bai’s iPhone has a sea of phone numbers with unfamiliar area codes. Some of them are likely from pollsters wanting to ask him about the upcoming Rhode Island primary elections. 
A few times, he’s answered only to end up staying on the line to complete a survey.
“I felt bad,” Bai, 32, of Providence, explained.
But he’s busy, juggling part-time jobs as an internal medicine doctor at Thundermist Health Center in West Warwick and a product designer for health technology company ITO Health. 
Mostly, he lets the calls go to voicemail.
Response rates in public opinion polls plunged after cell phones replaced landlines. Researchers turned to new recruitment methods, survey platforms and statistical sampling techniques as alternative solutions.
Gov. Dan McKee’s campaign insists the new methods are inaccurate. 
Hours after an Aug. 27 University of New Hampshire survey came out, showing McKee 38 points behind his Democratic primary challenger, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, the governor’s campaign team slammed the results as “bogus,” calling the research institution “an unreliable pollster.”
Previous polls, including by UNH and WPRI-TV 12 in partnership with Emerson College Polling, showed McKee trailing Foulkes by a smaller margin of 15 to 20 points.
Andrew Smith, director of the UNH Survey Center, shrugged off the criticism.
“It’s the oldest play in the book: The first thing you do if you don’t like a poll is attack the methodology,” Smith said. 
He would know. After four decades in academic survey research, Smith, 65, is no stranger to candidates criticizing his work. Human nature has stayed consistent in an ever-changing world of public polling.
But even Smith acknowledges that skewed participation in public polling persists.
“We’re still trying to figure out ways to diminish that,” he said.



How pollsters work

Assemble the group

How respondents are gathered falls into two main categories: probability and non-probability methods. In the former, they are chosen completely at random, with phone numbers arbitrarily dialed or texted. Alternatively, participants are contacted based on specific traits, like where they live, how old they are, and their voter activity. 
In either method, a new set of respondents can be recruited for every survey, known as a sample. Or, pollsters can turn to a pre-subscribed set of participants contacted weeks, or months ahead of time who have agreed to take the survey, known as a panel. 
Polls often combine multiple techniques.

Make contact

Phone calls and text messages are the predominant forms by which pollsters contact their selected group of participants. But in non-probability polls, targeted ads on Instagram, Facebook, and other social media platforms are also an option. A few polling groups have returned to postcard invitations, too.

Survey time

Surveys are predominantly conducted online through third-party platforms like SurveyMonkey, making it easier and more convenient for participants to complete the questionnaire on their own time frame. It also makes data collection faster for pollsters.

Calibrate 

Researchers use the demographic information provided by respondents to weight the answers to best reflect the broader group they are trying to represent. Census data, registered voter breakdowns and turnout in past elections are often measurements against which pollsters consider sample information in election surveys. This is how margins of error are determined.



The missing middle 
The 2016 and 2020 presidential elections put the problem with polling front and center. Blue-collar Republicans didn’t participate in public surveys, leading to polls that overstated voters’ support for the Democratic candidate in each cycle.
More recently, in August, progressive candidates in the Democratic primaries for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan and governor of Wisconsin fared worse than polls indicated, suggesting moderate Democratic voters may also be the latest casualty of the “non-response bias” problem in polling.
“There’s no doubt that right now in Democratic primaries, the well-educated progressive voter is much more likely to answer these polls than the more mainstream, less well-educated, working class voter,” said Adam Myers, an associate professor of political science at Providence College. “No one in the polling world has figured out the right formula.”
McKee’s campaign is counting on it.
“If this same issue exists in Rhode Island primary polling, it would indicate that polls overestimate support for Helena Foulkes and underestimate support for Dan McKee, assuming that pollsters overindex on the discontented subset of Democrats who oppose incumbent politicians,” Sophie Mestas, a McKee campaign spokesperson, said in an emailed response.
Foulkes’ campaign did not respond to requests for comment. 
Divergence between polls and election results is why Matt Foster tries to answer as many of the text invitations for local surveys as he can.



Quotation







There’s no doubt that right now in Democratic primaries, the well-educated progressive voter is much more likely to answer these polls than the more mainstream, less well-educated, working class voter.


– Adam Myers, an associate professor of political science at Providence College.


The 45-year-old Providence resident and bank risk manager and registered independent says he’s taken at least a half-dozen online surveys gauging his opinion on candidates, elected officeholders, and state issues within the last few months.
“I’ve never done it before, so I figured this election cycle, I would see what it was like,” Foster explained. “I was just curious.”
Some are more arduous than others. If it takes more than five minutes to complete, Foster sometimes stops midway, he said.
But he likes the idea that his participation as a self-described moderate — a group underrepresented in other Democratic primary surveys —  might help researchers tweak their recruitment methods and statistical calculations.
Cue the poll parade 
Salve Regina University’s The Pell Center Aug. 18 poll put Foulkes 20 points ahead of McKee among the 394 likely primary voters surveyed from Aug. 3 to 11.
The WPRI-Emerson poll released one week later showed McKee narrowing the gap to  15 points behind Foulkes among 522 likely primary voters who took the Aug. 21-22 survey. Two days later, UNH’s poll put Foulkes 38 points ahead among the 451 likely Democratic primary voters in the Aug. 20-23 survey.
A fourth survey by the University of Rhode Island’s Rhode Island Survey Initiative published Tuesday asked about the gubernatorial candidates in a general election matchup. But the poll, conducted July 29 to Aug. 13, did not ask the 500 respondents about the primary race between Foulkes and McKee because survey researchers didn’t know if the results would be ready to publish before the Sept. 9 primary.
“I didn’t want to waste a question on something that would be old anyway,” said Julie Keller, an associate professor of sociology at URI and lead researcher of the survey initiative.
During the three-week span of surveys, there were three live debates between McKee and Foulkes, a highly-anticipated Supreme Court nomination, and a Washington Bridge update.



How they compare
The University of New Hampshire Survey Center draws from a probability panel of pre-recruited 2,300 Rhode Island voters, supplemented with new, randomly recruited, voters at the time of a new survey. 
Emerson College Polling uses a probability sample in its polling for WPRI-TV 12, randomly texting numbers from a purchased list of registered voters supplied by a third-party vendor.
Embold Research, which conducts polls on behalf of The Pell Center, uses a nonprobability sample of respondents recruited through targeted ads on Facebook and Instagram, along with text messages. The dynamic online sampling allows pollsters to adjust their ads as responses come in to find the demographic groups they are missing.
YouGov, which conducts polls for the University of Rhode Island, uses a non-probability panel of participants recruited through online ads, referrals, random phone number dialing, and sponsored solicitation. Participants receive incentives through a points-based loyalty program that can be exchanged for cash.



“Polling is truly a snapshot in time,” said Katie Sonder, associate director of The Pell Center.
As Spencer Kimball, director of Emerson College Polling, sees it, the problem isn’t with the poll but how people interpret it.  
“What the public expects out of a poll is to pick the winner,” Kimball said. “Polls need to be read as a range of scores at a specific point in time.”



Quotation







What the public expects out of a poll is to pick the winner. Polls need to be read as a range of scores at a specific point in time. 


– Spencer Kimball, director of Emerson College Polling


Methodology matters. Are respondents chosen entirely at random, or are they recruited because they represent target demographics, including a history of voting? Are they contacted by phone or by text? Can they complete the survey online? And how is the raw data from their responses statistically weighted to better reflect the broader electorate?
Particularly in primary elections, traditionally plagued by low turnout, researchers don’t actually know who the group they’re trying to represent is. 
Gov. Dan McKee addresses supporters during an event to mark the opening of his campaign headquarters on West Exchange Street in Providence on Saturday, April 25, 2026. (Courtesy of McKee’s reelection campaign)
They can look at past primary turnout as a guide, but that’s not always accurate. A young, enthusiastic candidate like New York Mayor Zohran Mandani can bring out groups of voters who haven’t participated in the past. The 2025 city mayoral election drew the most voters of any city race since 1969, with a surge in ballots cast by voters under age 40. 
Could that happen in Rhode Island?
“You can’t say for sure,” Smith said. “We have a great tendency in general to overestimate our desire and intentions in voting.”
Bad for democracy? 
Perhaps democracy would be better served without any public election polling at all? 
“The obsession with electoral polls and campaigning is bad because so much of coverage of campaigns is about the horse race,” Myers said. “It would be a lot better if the focus of campaigns, and media coverage of campaigns, was about the issues.”
Bai said he had not paid any attention to the results of recent polls in preparation for voting in Democratic primaries.
“I think I should vote based on what I think, not what other people are voting for,” he said. 
He continued, “When I think about the value of polling, I wonder who it’s really for? It’s not for me as a voter.”
But it’s important to researchers like Smith, offering a rare opportunity to test survey methodology against concrete Election Day results.
Polls can also help inform campaigns on which demographic groups they need to target, while alerting voters to the fact that there’s an election happening at all, Kimball said. 
Roughly 1 in 5 Democratic voters were still undecided in the gubernatorial primary race in all three surveys; in the primaries for lieutenant governor and attorney general, nearly half of likely primary voters hadn’t made up their minds yet.
McKee campaign spokesperson Mestas emphasized the importance of public outreach in the campaign: TV ads, door-knocking, and phone banking among them. 
“While public polling is often used by pundits to pontificate on the state of the race, it is not a helpful tool to inform campaign strategy — in part because of methodological issues that have been rife in polls of the Democratic primary electorate this cycle [sic] but largely because polls are only one part of a much bigger picture,” she wrote in an email. 
At least some of McKee’s messaging against Foulkes appears to have broken through to Bai, who referred to Foulkes as “that CVS lady.” But, he also didn’t know that McKee was running again, admitting he had only a “vague sense” of the candidates.
“That’s on my to-do list for this upcoming weekend,” Bai said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A song of perseverance from Eastern Kentucky echoes across the state
description: The small, solitary, scrawny, pine tree grew out of an abandoned, rotting wooden train trestle tie in Whitesburg.  But what it produced helped many people devastated by the floods that killed 45 people as the raging waters swept through portions of Eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia and southern West Virginia between July 25 and Aug. 1, […]
text:
A small but strong pine tree grew out of a railroad trestle in Whitesburg, Ky. Two composers wrote a song about it that continues to reverberate. (Photo provided)The small, solitary, scrawny, pine tree grew out of an abandoned, rotting wooden train trestle tie in Whitesburg. 
But what it produced helped many people devastated by the floods that killed 45 people as the raging waters swept through portions of Eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia and southern West Virginia between July 25 and Aug. 1, 2022. 
Many homes and parts of some communities were swept away by the deluge.
It was said to be the deadliest natural disaster to hit Eastern Kentucky in more than 80 years – and an unlikely pine tree in downtown Whitesburg played a role in easing the hurt.
Roy Crawford, a local engineer and musician, noticed the four-foot-tall pine tree on a walk in late 2021.
He admired its persistence in living in a hostile environment.
So taken was Crawford that he adorned the tree with a few Christmas balls. He shared a photo of the decorated tree on Facebook with delighted friends. “People saw it as perseverance over adversity,” he said.
Roy Crawford is the co-author of “The Trestle Tree,” a song about perseverance in Eastern Kentucky. (Photo provided)
Crawford  even told then-Whitesburg High School band conductor Jason Griffith that he thought the tree was worthy of a song.  He asked Griffith to write one for it. Griffith declined and told Crawford he should do it.
Crawford did with help from Donald Sorah, a professor of music at the nearby University of Virginia’s College at Wise.  
“Donald did 95 percent of the composition,” said Crawford.
The two produced the composition “The Trestle Tree.” 
Cane River Music, a boutique prints music distributor in McKinney, Texas, says the song is replete with “uplifting, primary melodic ideas, reflecting the quiet strength and improbable life of the tree.”
It notes that the song “shifts into a minor key played distinctively by the brass and woodwinds, musically representing the heavy trials, struggles and everyday challenges faced by the community,” but “returns triumphantly to the main theme, symbolizing survival, recovery and enduring hope.”
Donald Sorah (Photo provided)
The song’s world premiere was in Whitesburg on Memorial Day 2022 by KYVA Summer Winds, a professional wind and percussion orchestra. Based in southeast Kentucky, it features around 75 musicians—including public school music teachers, college professors, and advanced students—from Kentucky, Virginia, Tennessee, and Ohio. Griffith, the founder of the band, directed it that spring day.
The concert was held just a few yards away from the Trestle Tree.
Later, the local tourism commission cut down the weeds and other growth at the trestle site.  The pine tree was no more.
A deluge hits Whitesburg
Then the floods came. Whitesburg was hit hard. 
This is what the National Weather Service said happened:
“Between July 25th and July 30th, 2022, several complexes of training thunderstorms developed south of I-64 and brought heavy rain, deadly flash flooding, and devastating river flooding to eastern Kentucky and central Appalachia. These thunderstorms, at times, caused rainfall rates in excess of 4″/hr. across complex terrain that led to widespread devastating impacts.”
The NWS said resultant flooding led to deaths and “widespread catastrophic damage. Entire homes and parts of some communities were swept away by flood waters, leading to costly damage to infrastructure in the region. Over 600 helicopter rescues and countless swift water rescues by boat were needed to evacuate people who were trapped by the quickly rising flood waters.”
Crawford suggested to Sorah that they use the song to raise money for the flood victims.
They decided to sell sheet music  of the song with band and orchestra versions for $50 and a fee for performance.  They raised more than $5,000.
Area high school bands and several orchestras played the song.
The University of Louisville Symphonic Band performed it in September 2022 in Louisville, followed by concerts at The Dordt University in Sioux City, Iowa, in May 2023, and with Symphony of the Mountains in Pennington Gap, Va., in June 2023.
However, the crowning moment for the composition came when Louisville Orchestra director Teddy Abrams accepted Crawford’s request for the Louisville Orchestra to play it. 
Abrams added it to the orchestra’s “In Harmony Tour of the Commonwealth” program.
Launched in 2022, the tour has grown into one of the most ambitious and sustained orchestral touring initiatives in the state. It is supported by $2.1 million annually from the Kentucky General Assembly, It has reached more than 52,000 people across 49 counties in Kentucky through concerts, schools, libraries, and community partnerships.
Bringing the song to life
On the night of Feb. 26 this year, hundreds of people packed the gym of Western Hills High School in Frankfort to hear the prestigious Louisville Orchestra in one of its free “In Harmony Tour” performances.
The program included works by classical composers like Beethoven and Tchaikovsky.
And halfway through the program was the work by Sorah and Crawford.
Sorah was in attendance that night.
“A world-class orchestra brought it alive,” said Sorah. “I was enthralled from the first note and it just got better and better.
“I later told Teddy that I thanked him and the orchestra for treating it with so much respect, as they do with works by the classical composers. I already had a high opinion of him but it increased tremendously that night.”
After the concert, one of Sorah’s friends jokingly told him, “I saw your name and others on the Louisville Orchestra program. I know Sorah but who is that Tchaikovsky guy?”
In a recent email, Teddy Abrams said “The Trestle Tree” is “a beautiful example of how music can carry the story of a place and its people. Created by my friend from Whitesburg, Roy Crawford, and his collaborator Donald Sorah, the work is rooted in a very real Kentucky story. 
“What began with this small tree growing against the odds in Whitesburg became a powerful symbol of resilience for a community that has endured so much. ‘The Trestle Tree’ is exactly the kind of work we want to celebrate through the Louisville Orchestra’s In Harmony Tour.”
Abrams said the point of In Harmony to make sure the music played reflects the region.  
“That means creating space for Kentucky composers, artists, traditions, and stories to be part of the program,” he said. “The Trestle Tree carries a story of resilience and community and gives us the opportunity to share something that is authentically Kentucky with audiences across the state.”
The song that keeps giving
Kyle McQueen painted a water color of the Trestle Tree that now hangs in Whitesburg’s City Hall. (Photo provided)
About half of the proceeds from “The Trestle Tree” song bought school musical instruments to replace those lost in the flood.  
The rest went to a Letcher County flood recovery group. Member Jeffery Justice of Whitesburg said the money helped flood victims whose homes were destroyed or damaged buy items like washers, dryers and shingles for roofs.
Kyle McQueen of Richmond saw a photo of the original “trestle tree,” heard the story and painted an image of it. 
His watercolor painting hangs today outside the office of Mayor Tiffany Craft in Whitesburg’s city hall. “I had it framed,” said Craft. “I think it is wonderful that these two men shared the character of this community in music.
“I hope a lot of people get to see the painting and hear about that tree.”
Crawford agreed. “It reminds people that we can get through hard times.”
Visit YouTube’s “The Trestle Tree (Sorah/Crawford) performed by Teddy Abrams and the Louisville Orchestra” in concert in Frankfort on Feb. 26, 2026, at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3_D4Xo9kvto to enjoy the song.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Wendell Berry’s death should be his revival in our culture
description: Throughout his life, Kentucky writer Wendell Berry described death not as an end, but as a stage in a cycle of renewal. Those who die return in body to the earth and endure in the memory of those who loved them. In “Three Elegaic Poems,” dedicated to his dying grandfather, Berry says the old man […]
text:
Wendell Berry with Nip and Jed, Lane's Landing Farm, Henry County, KY 2012. (Photo by Guy Mendes)Throughout his life, Kentucky writer Wendell Berry described death not as an end, but as a stage in a cycle of renewal. Those who die return in body to the earth and endure in the memory of those who loved them. In “Three Elegaic Poems,” dedicated to his dying grandfather, Berry says the old man is “set free in our remembering.” “Grown brighter than vision. . . he’s hidden among all that is, and cannot be lost.”
Berry’s death at age 92 comes while his ideas are as relevant as ever. The tired labels of “liberal” and “conservative” are blurring, just as Berry himself always defied easy categorization. He held prescient and timely fears that rootless people would snap in the face of rapid change and ruthless power.
In a time of division, and with the hope of reconciliation, it’s worth examining how Berry’s ideas might apply to Kentucky today.
Hard work is a central value in Berry’s writings and at the forefront of what Kentuckians hold dear. And from debates about welfare cuts to the need for jobs that can pay rising bills, it is at the core of our major political debates.
For Berry, work was not just about sacrifice and drudgery. He was in favor of labor as a vocation; work as a calling with purpose. He advocated for more small farms not just because he was an agrarian. He had a Jeffersonian vision of widespread ownership where work is a source of pride and a nourishing contribution to self and community. It’s a far cry from the many jobs of today that are stripped of ownership and meaning, and that leave workers alienated and vulnerable.
Wendell’s Berry’s writings were also about place. In a world of “anywheres,” Berry encouraged becoming a “somewhere.” Knowing a physical place and its people intimately and over time instilled an ethic all on its own. “What I stand for,” said Berry, “is what I stand on.”
That principle is on display in the current debate over data centers in rural Kentucky. Republicans, Democrats and Independents are defending the character of their communities, an integrity they see as threatened by power- and water-thirsty data centers.
Opposition to data centers also comes from growing concerns about artificial intelligence, especially among young people. Berry, who never owned a computer and farmed with horses, was a lifelong critic of unbridled technology. 
At his angriest, Berry railed against the power of unaccountable corporations that ravaged communities to bolster profits. These concerns are also spreading, as with a Mercer County man who spoke out against a local data center proposal and told Kentucky Public Radio, “Conservatism is dead, and that’s unfortunate. And a corporatocracy has taken over.”
Berry’s criticism of the economic system focused most on agriculture, as in his 1977 book “The Unsettling of America.” There he took on the agribusiness model that ever more rapidly consolidates food production in the hands of a powerful few. Now dwindling beef farmers, for example, are caught in a globalized system and captive to the wishes of four massive corporations that control the market. They struggle under the Trump tariffs and are speaking out about new efforts to undercut prices with imported beef.
Berry praised the alternative of the New Deal-era tobacco program, which his grandfather inspired and his father helped create. The program was designed around farmer-led cooperation and resulted in fair prices from modest patches. Here was a government that created a framework that empowered local people and communities. That’s much different than one that takes control away and distributes wealth upward.
In “The Hidden Wound,” Berry described racism as something that doesn’t just harm Black people but corrupts whites as well. In a time of backlash against talking about race, he reminds us of the loss we all experience from a broken whole.
Berry was a small-r republican and a small-d democrat. He expected people to live with virtue and devotion. And he hammered the powerful that exploit and extract. His alter ego, the “Mad Farmer,” called on people to “denounce the government and embrace the flag.” 
Wendell Berry sought an economy that linked the soul and the household to the land, community and everything beyond. If we want to avoid “The World-Ending Fire,” the title of another Berry book, we might well listen to his words “lest the dead die a second and more final death.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Amtrak to suspend Virginia-to-D.C. service for critical track upgrades Oct. 16–26
description: Rail passengers traveling through Virginia’s Northeast Corridor should expect cancellations, route changes and may need to rely on bus connections beginning Oct. 16, due to major track upgrades. This is part of Amtrak’s “Pause for Progress,” a critical infrastructure upgrade to replace aging track components at the A-interlocking control point in Washington[...]
text:
An Amtrak train parked at the Richmond Staples Mills Station. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Rail passengers traveling through Virginia’s Northeast Corridor should expect cancellations, route changes and may need to rely on bus connections beginning Oct. 16, due to major track upgrades.
This is part of Amtrak’s “Pause for Progress,” a critical infrastructure upgrade to replace aging track components at the A-interlocking control point in Washington D.C., temporarily suspending service from Oct. 16 to Oct. 26.
Amtrak said the A-Interlocking in the First Street Tunnel is responsible for routing Amtrak and Virginia Railway Express services between Virginia stations and Washington D.C.
Amtrak said the existing switches and crossovers are “beyond their service life,” which requires a 10 mph speed restriction that affects operations. 
“Customers traveling to or from Washington, D.C. from the south should expect significant service reductions and train cancellations,” Amtrak said in a statement.
Due to the suspension, trains traveling through Virginia will effectively end at Alexandria, with only a limited number continuing north. Most trips to Richmond, Charlottesville, Lynchburg and Hampton Roads will be served by express buses.
Once travelers are north of Washington, the Northeast Corridor trains continue normally on the Washington–New York–Boston segment. 
Amtrak said the work will improve safety and reliability, reduce delays and meet future demand by replacing outdated switches, installing modern electric switch systems and repairing and strengthening the tunnel’s foundation.
Representatives from Virginia Railway Express and Virginia Passenger Rail Authority, in statements to the Mercury, acknowledged the disruption while underscoring the project’s importance to Virginia’s passenger rail network.
“VRE supports Amtrak’s work to upgrade A-Interlocking in the First Street Tunnel, and we applaud investments that keep our rail corridor in a state of good repair,” said Katie Choe, VRE CEO. “While some VRE passengers will need to adjust their travel plans during the week of October 19-23, these upgrades will ultimately allow us to run more reliable service and improve the passenger experience at Union Station.”
Mike McLaughlin, chief operating officer for the Virginia Passenger Railway Authority, said the agency has worked with Amtrak, CSX, Norfolk Southern, VRE and the North Carolina DOT to minimize the impact of the “Pause for Progress” construction on passengers.
“We understand that these infrastructure projects are a disruption to our passengers,” McLaughlin said. 
Amtrak Virginia will offer some service to Alexandria, VRE will operate service to L’Enfant in Washington during the construction period, and the agency is coordinating additional connections with Amtrak, VRE and WMATA to help passengers affected by the disruption.
McLaughlin said replacing A-Interlocking is critical to Virginia’s passenger rail service because just over 40% of Amtrak Virginia passengers connect to Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor via the route.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The energy Virginia needs is the energy we can build now
description: Virginia’s energy needs are changing quickly, and to address them we must respond even quicker. Data centers, new manufacturing, population growth and other economic development are driving electricity demand higher, putting additional pressure on an already strained grid.  At the same time, Virginia imports more power than any other state in the nation, and[...]
text:
Solar panels in Cumberland County, Va. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia’s energy needs are changing quickly, and to address them we must respond even quicker. Data centers, new manufacturing, population growth and other economic development are driving electricity demand higher, putting additional pressure on an already strained grid. 
At the same time, Virginia imports more power than any other state in the nation, and Dominion Energy anticipates 23% of our electricity supply to come from out of state in 2027. Relying on other states’ wholesale electricity prices, instead of allowing Virginia utilities and regulators to set rates by Virginians for Virginians, is costing ratepayers.
If we want to keep our economy growing, attract new investment and maintain reliable electricity for families and businesses, we need to produce more of the energy we use here at home, and we need to do it quickly.
This is becoming more than an energy policy question, but rather an economic development question. 
Companies considering Virginia for business need confidence that the electricity will be available and affordable when they need it. Communities need reliable power to support existing businesses and attract new ones, and families need an electric grid that can keep pace with growing demand without placing unnecessary upward pressure on their bills. 
If Virginia cannot provide enough electricity to support growth, we risk limiting the very economic opportunities that have made the commonwealth an attractive place to live and do business.
Ensuring reliability statewide is one reason we are seeing more rapid solar development. 
A recent “Speed-to-Deploy” fact sheet from the Solar Energy Industries Association illustrates how quickly different energy resources can move from early-stage development to operation. Utility-scale solar takes an average of about 1.4 years to reach operation, while battery storage takes about 1.7 years. 
By comparison, a natural gas combustion turbine takes a little over two and a half years, a natural gas combined-cycle plant requires about four years and nuclear projects can take more than 15 years. 
Natural gas timelines, however, could be much longer due to various parts backlogs, with some manufacturers claiming it could take five to seven years to manufacture a gas-powered turbine. 
Those timelines matter. Virginia is not planning for an energy challenge that might arrive decades from now. Demand is increasing, and we need new generation that can come online within a reasonable timeframe, and frankly, we needed more energy yesterday. 
Solar and battery storage give Virginia tools that can be deployed relatively quickly to help meet that growing demand. They can also be developed across a range of communities and project sizes, allowing localities to reap the economic benefits of new energy infrastructure. 
That does not mean these resources should replace longer-term investments in baseload generation. It means Virginia should use the resources available to us based on what they can contribute, and when they can realistically come online.
Those aforementioned benefits extend beyond the electricity itself. Solar projects can provide new tax revenue for counties and local governments, create construction and maintenance jobs, support local businesses and provide landowners with a new source of income. 
For rural communities in particular, responsible solar development can bring private investment to areas that may otherwise have limited opportunities for large-scale economic development, without adding strain to public services. When projects are properly sited and developed with community input, they can become another piece of a locality’s economic development strategy.
Solar can provide another avenue for private investment, while giving willing landowners an opportunity to generate income from their property and giving local governments a new source of tax revenue.
None of this means solar is the only answer to Virginia’s energy needs. We need a diverse energy portfolio that includes nuclear, solar, natural gas, battery storage and other resources, along with continued investment in transmission and the broader electric grid. Different technologies have different strengths, and reliability requires us to lean into all of them.
However, diversification of our grid should not mean overlooking the resources that can be deployed the quickest. If Virginia is serious about meeting rising electricity demand, strengthening our energy security and reducing our reliance on power imported from other states, we should use every responsible tool available to us. 
The challenge before us is not simply finding more energy. It is creating enough energy, in the right places, and getting it online in time to meet the demand that is already here. On that front, solar and storage have a clear and important advantage.
We should be planning for the energy system we will need decades from now while also deploying resources that can help address demand in the next several years. The commonwealth should not have to choose between planning for 2040 and meeting the energy needs of 2028. We can and should do both.
