name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The 2nd Congressional District: As Goodlander seeks reelection, three say she hasn’t earned it
description: In New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, there are three leading candidates who want to take Rep. Maggie Goodlander’s place in the U.S. House of Representatives: Paige Beauchemin, Lily Tang Williams, and Victor Orlando. Voters living in the western half of the state from both parties will go to the polls Tuesday and make their primary […]
text:
Clockwise from top left, Maggie Goodlander, Lily Tang Williams, Paige Beauchemin, and Victor Orlando are vying to represent New Hampshire in the 2nd Congressional District. (Screenshots)In New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, there are three leading candidates who want to take Rep. Maggie Goodlander’s place in the U.S. House of Representatives: Paige Beauchemin, Lily Tang Williams, and Victor Orlando.
Voters living in the western half of the state from both parties will go to the polls Tuesday and make their primary picks.
Democratic voters will decide whether to keep Goodlander as their nominee or go with a new nominee in Beauchemin, a progressive state representative.
On the Republican side, Williams and Orlando lead the polls, but voters will also see Michael Callis and Dan Nicolson on their ballots, who have not campaigned as actively.
A freshman rep seeking a second term
Goodlander has represented the 2nd District since winning election for the first time in 2024.
Before returning to her home state and running for Congress, Goodlander worked at the Department of Justice under President Joe Biden. Before that, she was a foreign policy adviser for the late U.S. Sens. John McCain and Joe Lieberman; served as an attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during President Donald Trump’s first impeachment hearings; and as a clerk to former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Stephen Breyer.
While she was born in Nashua, Goodlander’s work took her away from New Hampshire. In her first bid for Congress, she faced “carpetbagger” allegations for running for office immediately after moving back to her home state.
U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander speaks to reporters in the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s Office on June 12, 2026. The congresswoman had filed for reelection prior, but came to the State House during the filing period to meet with supporters, journalists, and the secretary of state ceremoniously. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“Two years ago the people in the 2nd District put their trust in me,” Goodlander said, “which has meant that every day since, I’ve woken up and tried to really listen and understand what their challenges are and what their opportunities are, and how I can deliver on both.”
As a freshman representative, Goodlander has been a centrist voter serving on the Armed Services Committee and the Committee on Small Business. In an interview with the Bulletin, she touted her involvement in the lawsuit that overturned some of Trump’s tariffs, her public opposition to rate hikes at local utility companies, and her vote for the bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act.
“It’s a bill that is going to help us build more homes, which is exactly what we need right now to bring down costs,” she said of the housing legislation. “And it’s a bill that’s going to help us take on predatory corporate practices. It’s a first step that I want to build on. I think we’ve got a lot of follow-on work to do.”
Goodlander also emphasized the “unprecedented moment in our country’s history” she argues Trump has created.
“We have the most dangerous president in American history, who is responsible for a full-blown affordability crisis that has very clear culprits,” she said. “He’s waged wars: the war in Iran and these trade wars that have absolutely crushed people at every corner of this state.”
She characterized herself as someone fighting against Trump’s agenda.
“We’ve got an administration that’s trying to dismantle government from within,” she said. “And making it (government) work has been my singular focus because that’s how you deliver for people.”
An August UNH poll showed Goodlander handily beating Beauchemin, 59%-19%.
A progressive challenger
Beauchemin has represented Nashua’s Ward 4 in the state House of Representatives since winning a special election in 2023. She’s a registered nurse and a mother of three who has tried to characterize herself as the working-class, everyday person in the race.
In the State House, she’s supported maternal health-related legislation and mostly progressive causes. She also faced a formal reprimand from her House colleagues earlier this year for brandishing her middle finger at Gov. Kelly Ayotte during her State of the State address.
Paige Beauchemin
Beauchemin told the Bulletin that Goodlander’s 2025 vote in favor of the Laken Riley Act, which Beauchemin opposed, was one of the top reasons she got into the race. Goodlander was one of 46 House Democrats who voted in favor of the legislation, an immigration and law enforcement bill pushed by Republicans following the death of a Georgia nursing student at the hands of an immigrant. The bill was criticized by progressives and immigration advocates who argued it disregards immigrants’ due process rights, gives too much power to state attorneys general, and strengthened ICE ahead of a series of aggressive crackdowns in Minneapolis, Chicago, and elsewhere. Opponents also argue crimes by immigrants are rare and that Riley’s tragic death was an outlier.
“She really courted the Latino vote and told them she would be there for them,” Beauchemin said. “And then her first vote, she betrayed them. So that for me really showed where she is on integrity.”
Goodlander told the Bulletin she disagrees with the notion that the vote lifted guardrails off of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She said she voted for it because “we are a nation of immigrants, and … we’re a nation of laws too, and I believe that in this country, if you’ve come here unlawfully and you commit a crime, there should be immigration consequences for that.”
According to the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, the Laken Riley Act requires ICE to detain immigrants charged but not convicted of certain crimes with no provision allowing for the person’s release if the criminal charges are later dropped. Notably, the law applies to immigrants with legal status in the country.
Beauchemin has also taken aim at campaign funding Goodlander received from pro-Israel groups. Beauchemin said as congresswoman, she would vote to end aid to Israel.
U.S. military aid to Israel has become a flashpoint in Democratic politics as public opinion sours on Israel amid its multi-front wars, and as more and more independent experts conclude the Middle Eastern country is committing genocide against the Palestinian people.
“She will not recognize the genocide that is happening in Gaza,” Beauchemin said of her primary rival. “She takes AIPAC and other Israel-aligned lobby money, and that is another deal breaker.”
Goodlander has recently curtailed her support for Israel. In July, she voted in favor of an unsuccessful effort to cut $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel
“I’ve said that we need a reset in the relationship,” Goodlander said. “And that reset, at bottom, really comes down to a reset in how American taxpayer dollars have been used over the past two years.”
Beauchemin said if elected, she’ll push for a single-payer Medicare for All system, an end to the Citizens United v. FEC (a 2010 court decision that opened the door to “dark money” in politics), and pro-immigrant policies. She emphasized the differences between her and Goodlander.
“You’ve got a situation here where you could not have two people who are more different,” Beauchemin said. “Our backgrounds, our personalities, our philosophies, our priorities, our values. You take one look, you listen to each of us for two minutes, and it’s very, very clear how different we are.”
Seeking a rematch
Williams, who lives in Weare, is a perennial name on the ballot in the 2nd Congressional District. This is her third time running for the seat. On Tuesday, she’s hoping to earn a rematch with Goodlander, who defeated her in a close 2024 general election. Williams earned 47% of the vote that year in a left-leaning district that includes Keene, Concord, and West Lebanon. Williams also ran in 2020, but did not win the primary.
Williams is a libertarian who moved to New Hampshire from Colorado — where she also ran unsuccessfully for Congress — as part of the Free State Project. She was born in China and has made her upbringing there and opposition to the Communist regime central to her political persona.
Lily Tang Williams files paperwork to run for the U.S. House of Representatives in New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District on June 4, 2026 in the secretary of state’s office. This is her third time running for the seat and it could be a rematch against incumbent Rep. Maggie Goodlander. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Williams believes the dynamics would be different in a general election rematch with Goodlander this cycle.
“She’s an incumbent,” Williams said. “She has to come out, explain her vote, and defend her voting record. And I’m focused on kitchen table issues for Granite Staters who are struggling, and I’m in touch with regular people who don’t have resources.”
Williams has been seen as a far-right candidate for much of her career. Last election cycle, she faced criticisms of antisemitism for sharing memes online alleging the Holocaust was spurred by Jews who “gave up their firearms to Hitler.” During a 2024 debate, she wouldn’t say that Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election.
However, she’s sought to portray herself as more moderate this time around. Williams has released what she’s calling her “10-point good government plan.” The plan includes term limits for members of Congress, banning individual stock trading by members of Congress, and a requirement that the federal government always have a balanced budget.
Williams said that in the 2024 election she struggled because Goodlander had such a large fundraising advantage. Since that election, Williams has garnered a large social media following after a video clip from a debate went viral, and she’s said she wants to leverage that to increase out-of-state donations to close the gap. This cycle, she’s raised a little over $1 million, according to the Federal Election Commission. In the 2024 election cycle, she raised just over $700,000 in contributions. Goodlander, with her strong Washington connections, has raised over $3.2 million in contributions this cycle, per the FEC.
“We are still (the) underdog,” Williams said. “Like she has four times more money, but we have more resources now than last (cycle) to get my campaign messages out. And because lots of people still don’t know who I am, and they know more about her because she’s incumbent, so we still have a very big uphill battle to fight.”
Williams said she’s less concerned about her primary rival, Orlando, because he doesn’t have as many resources behind him.
“I feel pretty comfortable about the primary,” Williams said. “It’s not as intense as last cycle because I had 12 Republicans in the primary with me, and some had more money and more establishment PAC endorsement. So this time I just have one person who is actively campaigning, but he doesn’t have any resources.”
A pro-labor Republican
In order to face Goodlander in the general election, Williams has to first defeat Orlando, a pro-labor Republican who has partially self-funded his campaign. The polling shows she’s likely to do so. In the UNH poll, 58% of surveyed voters chose Williams compared to 2% who chose Orlando, with 38% undecided. 
Orlando, who owns a roofing company and lives in Hollis, has sought to portray himself as the candidate who can tackle affordability challenges.
Victor Orlando
“I’m running for office because every single person in this state is feeling it right now when it comes to affordability,” he said in an interview. “Every single one of us.”
Orlando wants to implement small practical fixes that he believes will stem inflation and help Americans’ wallets.
“I’m not going into this going, ‘Hey, I’m going to change the world and wave a magic wand and fix everything,” Orlando said. “No, I realize I’m one of over 400 people, and I have to get half of them to agree with me to do anything. I know it’s going to be small little victories over and over again, but that’s exactly what we need someone to advocate for in New Hampshire.”
Some of his proposals include eliminating patents on certain seeds to allow for competition in the market to bring down food costs; giving tax breaks to municipalities that adopt regulations that promote more homebuilding; and enacting a federal version of a bill proposed in the New Hampshire state Legislature — House Bill 396 — that sought to allow farmers to slaughter animals on their own farms instead of offsite slaughterhouses.
Orlando said he’s more focused on the issues that matter to New Hampshire than his competitor Williams. He specifically cited her vocal opposition to the policies of the Chinese Communist Party.
“She is very big on anti-China,” he said. “That’s her main thing. That’s her platform. That’s who she is. And I don’t disagree with her that China is a threat. China is a problem, and we need to be very careful with China, but I look at this as, China didn’t mess up the cost of our food. China didn’t mess up our immigration. China didn’t mess up our healthcare. China definitely didn’t spend all our money and put us in a deficit and all this debt. We did that to ourselves.”
Orlando also argues that New Hampshire’s congressional delegation didn’t do enough to secure funding for the state in the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. He said he would’ve worked harder to negotiate with colleagues and get some New Hampshire specific-funding included in the bill. Similarly, he supported the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but believes New Hampshire delegates should’ve pushed for funding.
“I would have voted for it,” he said of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, “but I also would have got in there and negotiated some more stuff for New Hampshire. Like I love no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, that type of stuff. But I would have gone in there and said, ‘Hey, New Hampshire needs some new roads up north. We need some damn help.’ And guess what? That bill I think passed by one vote in the House. I could have been that one vote and been like, ‘Hey, give me $100 million in road grants for the state of New Hampshire.’ And guess what? They would have done it because they were desperate to get it passed. That type of negotiation is how you get things done.”
Getting to the polls and voting
The polls will open at varying times on Tuesday morning depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot. New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. To register to vote on Election Day, voters will need to provide proof of their identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), age (also driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport, naturalization papers, or other proof), and domicile (government-issued ID or documentation with an address on it).

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Labor votes: Discontent will accompany blue‑collar voters to the polls in the midterms
description: When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline. For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is […]
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump greets retired UAW auto worker Brian Pannebecker while speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?”

All workers – unionized or not – are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline.
For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is bleak. Threats from AI and robotics abound. Pledges by U.S. and international corporations to invest in new plants remain largely pledges. The roughly 400,000 federal job cuts during President Donald Trump’s second term have disrupted lives. Many of these jobs were previously represented by labor unions.
As a labor studies scholar, I believe weariness and wariness will accompany blue-collar voters to the polls in November. As such, the candidates who have practical ideas for turning the economy around and exhibit empathy for Americans worried about how to pay their bills could receive the bulk of the union vote.
The union vote
Over generations, the majority of union members have sided with Democratic candidates, even if that support has wavered since the 1970s.
The 2024 presidential campaign was no exception. The majority of union members voted for Democratic candidates, but at a far lower rate than in the 1960s.
Why does this matter in 2026?
Union voters play a bigger role in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Nevada, three swing states where the share of voters who belong to unions is above the national average of 10%. In closely contested House and Senate races, even a small shift in union votes could influence the outcome.
What’s in store for November?
How large is the union vote?
The latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show that the percentage of U.S. unionized workers has fallen over the past four decades.
In 1983, 20.1% of U.S. workers were represented by a union. In 2025, the rate was 10.0%, or 14.7 million people. Union membership among public sector workers (32.9%) is more than five times higher than that of private sector workers (5.9%). In close elections, the volatility of these voting blocs matters.
During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to reduce consumer prices, bring back manufacturing jobs and respect workers’ rights.
As the midterm elections approach, I believe the president’s performance on these issues in the eyes of union voters will determine which party controls the House and Senate. And the signs are not promising for Trump, with recent polls indicating the president’s support among union households is eroding.
Manufacturing and inflation
The U.S. economy has lost 75,000 manufacturing jobs since January 2025, a 0.6% decline. These jobs have steadily declined since the 1980s, so Trump’s policies are not solely to blame.
Furthermore, Trump’s off-again, on-again tariffs may help some U.S. manufacturers. That’s because tariffs can erase the advantages of low-cost overseas labor. As economist Laura Veldkamp noted in July 2026, Trump’s tariffs “made it more profitable for American manufacturers to set up and produce here.”

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

The bigger problem, though, is that even if some manufacturing returns to the U.S., the work will likely be done with the latest manufacturing technologies, which tend to reduce the need for workers. That does not bode well for significant job creation.
In July 2026, Moody’s financial analyst Mark Zandi told Marketplace that more manufacturing output “doesn’t translate into jobs.” He explained that there has been more activity in the tech sector and in the defense-aerospace industries, but “these factories just don’t employ a lot of people.”
Additionally, Trump has not established a clear plan to lower inflation. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that food prices in July 2026 were up 3.0% from July 2025. This increase is slightly above the historical average.
There’s one more factor to consider. Many older blue-collar workers – many of them former union members – across New England, the Great Lakes, Ohio and western Pennsylvania remain angry about the epic industrial collapse of the 1970s and 1980s.
This kind of generational suffering can show up in the voting booth in a big way. And I don’t think voter surveys and polls are able to measure the depths of this rage.
Union representation
The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 allowed government workers to unionize. But a March 2025 White House announcement said the legislation had enabled “hostile Federal unions to obstruct agency management.”
Through an executive order and mass layoffs across the federal workforce in 2025, Trump has presided over a dramatic change in public sector collective bargaining in Washington, D.C.
Offering guidance on the 2025 executive order, the U.S. Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to end their collective bargaining agreement.
In response, the American Federation of Government Employees condemned the action in an email to its members, saying the Trump administration was “illegally strip(ping) collective bargaining rights from hundreds of thousands of federal workers.”
Federal unions have challenged the White House’s March 2025 executive order. In 2026, independent arbitrators have also ruled against the administration’s efforts to circumvent labor agreements with some federal workers. And in June 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts struck down an effort by the Trump administration to exercise control over union elections at federal agencies.
Whether unionized industrial workers support their public sector counterparts remains to be seen.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island Elections Project aims to make elections more accessible to voters in the state
description: On paper, Rhode Island does not share many characteristics with the ruby-red states of the South. Yet when it comes to one important measure of electoral democracy, Rhode Island feels very similar: Too many elections offer voters little or no meaningful choice. After the primary on Wednesday, Sept. 9, many Rhode Islanders will already know […]
text:
The Rhode Island Elections Project website aims to help the state's voters better understand the candidates for the General Assembly and the issues facing the state. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)On paper, Rhode Island does not share many characteristics with the ruby-red states of the South. Yet when it comes to one important measure of electoral democracy, Rhode Island feels very similar: Too many elections offer voters little or no meaningful choice.
Two University of Rhode Island graduate students have launched a nonpartisan website to help voters learn more about General Assembly elections.
After the primary on Wednesday, Sept. 9, many Rhode Islanders will already know who their next state representative or senator will be, two months before the general election. In some districts, the decisive election will have been the primary. In others, there will have been no contest at all.
Competitive elections are not simply about whether Democrats or Republicans win. They give voters choices, force candidates to make their case to the public, and give elected officials a reason to remain responsive to their constituents. A healthy democracy should not routinely be decided at the filing deadline.
The numbers paint a striking picture. In 2024, more than half of the seats in the Rhode Island Senate were uncontested in the general election, as were nearly two-thirds of the seats in the House of Representatives. Of the 38 Senate seats up for election, only two were competitive using a margin of 10 percentage points or less as the threshold. Among the contested Senate races, the average margin was around 22 percentage points. The long-term trend is also concerning: The number of competitive races has been declining since 2016. In 2014, around 16% of House races were competitive by our measure, whereas by 2024, this figure had fallen to around 10%.
At the same time, elections have become increasingly expensive, while running an effective campaign has become more difficult. In the second quarter alone, more than half a million dollars was spent on Rhode Island House and Senate races, with almost $1.5 million dollars raised. Rhode Island is on track for its most expensive state election season yet, even though its legislative elections are less competitive than they were a decade ago. Despite these trends, many Rhode Islanders remain unaware of just how uncompetitive their elections now are.
One of the reasons we created the Rhode Island Elections Project was to address this problem. The project is independent and is designed to make Rhode Island’s elections easier for everyday voters to understand. 
This nonpartisan initiative brings together information on elections, candidates, voting, and elected officials in one place, with the goal of helping Rhode Islanders better understand the issues, make informed decisions, and participate in the electoral process. 



Quotation







The project is independent and is designed to make Rhode Island's elections easier for everyday voters to understand. 


Rather than requiring voters to navigate multiple government websites, spreadsheets, and campaign finance filings, the project compiles election information and presents it visually. It is our mission to make the political landscape more visible and accessible. You can search for candidates, view their policy priorities and see who has endorsed them. Want to know how many times a lawmaker running for reelection has been absent while the General Assembly was in session? Want to see how many bills they introduced? The site gives you the answers. You can track legislators’ performance, explore their districts, and examine electoral competitiveness, turnout, and election results over time. 
We have also started to make Rhode Island’s notoriously difficult-to-navigate campaign finance information more accessible. Voters can see how much candidates have raised and spent, how much cash they have on hand, the composition of their funding and the types of Political Action Committees and interest groups contributing to campaigns. 
None of this tells voters whom they should support. That is deliberately not our role. The purpose is to give Rhode Islanders the information they need to make that decision themselves.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The 1st Congressional District: Eastern NH voters have plenty of options Tuesday
description: With four-term U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas relinquishing his seat in order to run for Senate, there is a wide open race for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. And it’s a crowded one. Three main candidates lead the pack in the GOP primary for the 1st District. Hollie Noveletsky, a businesswoman from Newfields, is leading in […]
text:
Several candidates, in both parties, are battling it out to represent the 1st Congressional District. Here, the U.S. Capitol is shown on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)With four-term U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas relinquishing his seat in order to run for Senate, there is a wide open race for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District.
And it’s a crowded one.
A group of CD1 Republicans struggling to differentiate themselves
Three main candidates lead the pack in the GOP primary for the 1st District.
Hollie Noveletsky
Hollie Noveletsky, a businesswoman from Newfields, is leading in the most recent poll. An August UNH poll showed 28% of surveyed voters preferred her. She’s the CEO of Novel Iron Works, and she’s run for this seat before. In 2024, she was runner up in the Republican primary. This year, she’s tried to pitch herself as the pro-Donald Trump candidate in the race.
However, it was Anthony DiLorenzo, a Portsmouth businessman, who earned Trump’s endorsement. The UNH poll had him as a close second with 25% of the vote.
In a more distant third place is Manchester State Rep. Brian Cole, who has sought to leverage his experience in the state Legislature to prove to voters that he’s the one who can get things done in Washington, D.C. In the UNH poll, 7% of surveyed voters said they’d vote for him.
Lindsey Anderson, of Moultonborough, is polling at 1%, and Melissa Bailey dropped out of the race before endorsing DiLorenzo. Bailey’s name will still be on the ballot.
Noveletsky said she stands with the Trump administration on issues such as trade, a topic that has elicited criticism from small-business owners impacted by his steep tariffs.
“We all believe in free trade,” she said during a WMUR debate last week. “It is a global economy, but we need to have fair trade, and since NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Agreement) we have hollowed out our manufacturing in exchange for cheap goods, and so we need to bring back our trade partners to the table to renegotiate our trade agreements. And we use the tariffs as a carrot or a stick.”
She has also applauded the Trump administration for shutting down immigration at the southern border, supported Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency elimination of USAID and the firing of federal employees, and opposes “red flag” laws that would allow courts to temporarily take guns away from people who pose a danger to themselves or others.
Anthony DiLorenzo
DiLorenzo has been criticized by his primary opponents for not being sufficiently conservative. During the WMUR debate,  Noveletsky and Cole attacked DiLorenzo for saying that he has no issue with a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who lack permanent legal status but pay taxes and have not been convicted of a felony.
“I’ve already answered the question several times,” he said. “I’ve been very, very clear about this. I believe in enforcing the immigration laws, and I would prioritize dangerous people first over people that are working and paying taxes. But the bottom line is, our laws call for deportation if you’re here illegally, and I support our laws.”
DiLorenzo supports some bread and butter fiscal conservative policies such as a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution. He also says he fully supports Social Security and Medicare, and that he wants to keep transgender girls and women off female sports teams and out of locker rooms.
Cole boasts that he’s the only leading GOP candidate in elected office.
“I’m the only person in the race that actually has legislative experience,” he said in an interview with the Bulletin. “… That’s the difference between me and the other candidates. Day one, when I get into Washington, I’m gonna be able to hit the ground running. I know what I’m going to be doing. It’s not going to be a learning curve for me.”
Brian Cole
His signature achievement as a legislator came when Gov. Kelly Ayotte signed legislation he sponsored, House Bill 1735, which expanded the state’s Right to Try Act. The bill offers experimental treatments to those with “chronic and debilitating” conditions even if they aren’t dying from the illness.
“That’s going to change lives,” he said. “… Besides the health benefits and people having access to it and everything like that. You’re talking about creating big-time paying jobs for people in New Hampshire, the biotech industry. This is a trillion-dollar industry.”
He also touted his time on the House Ways and Means Committee, where he opposed legislation that would’ve increased taxes on second homes in New Hampshire.
Before Pappas was elected in 2018, Republicans and Democrats traded off in the 1st District. From 2006 until 2018, it switched hands four times between Republican Frank Guinta and Democrat Carol Shea-Porter, with Republican Jeb Bradley holding it before that. Political observers are now wondering whether that means voters in the district, which includes Manchester, Portsmouth, and Laconia, have moved to the left or whether Pappas was a uniquely strong candidate. November may provide insight.
Two moderates and a cluster of progressives on the Democratic side
The Democratic side of the race is even more crowded.
Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen, two center-left Democrats, lead the polls, while Carleigh Beriont, the third-place candidate, has been consolidating progressive support in the race’s homestretch. Two other progressives, Christian Urrutia and Sarah Chadzynski, have trailed in polls, and Urrutia dropped out of the race on Sunday and endorsed Shaheen. Matthew Emerson, Sarah Bella Spinoza, and Bill Conlin will also be on the ballot
Maura Sullivan
Sullivan, of New Castle, is a Marine Corps veteran. She worked in the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense under former President Barack Obama. This is her second time running for the seat. In 2017, she was the runner-up to Pappas among 11 candidates in the primary. The August UNH poll showed 24% of surveyed voters preferred her.
Shaheen garnered 19% of voters in the same poll. She is a former Portsmouth city councilor and works in the biotech industry at a Manchester firm called ARMI, which is run by Dean Kamen. She’s also the daughter of former governor and current U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is retiring from Congress after November’s elections.
Beriont, a Hampton Select Board member, has tried to position herself as the progressive choice in the race and has built momentum in the final weeks of the primary. At 11% in the UNH poll, she’s still well behind Sullivan and Shaheen. State Rep. Heath Howard, another progressive candidate, dropped out of the race last month and endorsed Beriont (his name will remain on the ballot) after that poll was conducted. Howard had garnered 10% of voters in that poll.
Chadzynski, another progressive, earned 1% of voters in the poll.
All of the Democratic candidates in the 1st District support some form of Medicare for All. Sullivan has proposed “Medicare for All who want it,” which would expand Medicare to everyone but allow them to opt out if they’d prefer to keep a private insurer. The rest of the candidates support a single-payer system where Medicare replaces private insurers. However, Shaheen and Beriont said they’d accept a system like Sullivan’s proposal if they thought it was the only way to make Medicare for All happen. While Chadzynski supports single-payer Medicare for All, she says she doesn’t think it’s feasible in a divided Congress and said she would focus on more piecemeal measures.
Stefany Shaheen
There have also been fights over campaign finance. Sullivan and Shaheen have raised $3.6 and $2.4 million, respectively. The race could become the most expensive congressional primary in state history, at somewhere around $12 million when all the numbers come in. 
During a televised debate on WMUR Thursday, Shaheen attacked Sullivan over her campaign funding, saying that 90% of her money comes from out of state — a claim Sullivan denied before lobbing thinly veiled nepotism charges at the daughter of New Hampshire’s senior senator. 
Sullivan also accepted nearly $300,000 from donors who also donated to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (commonly known by its acronym AIPAC), leading to attacks from Shaheen and the progressives. Amid worsening public opinion of Israel and as a growing number of independent experts conclude the Middle Eastern country is committing genocide, AIPAC has become a flashpoint in Democractic politics, particularly among those arguing that accepting the money will make candidates beholden to the country’s demands for military aid. 
Carleigh Beriont
After the New Hampshire Union Leader reported that Beriont received $500 from a New Jersey donor who had also donated $25,000 to AIPAC, the candidate publicly announced she was returning the donation.
Still, like the GOP candidates, the leading candidates have often struggled to differentiate themselves from one another. They all oppose the federal government’s aggressive immigration crackdown. They all support reopening impeachment hearings against Trump. They all want to protect access to abortion.
On Tuesday, voters will determine whose message was most effective.
Getting to the polls and voting
The polls will open at varying times on Tuesday morning depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot. New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. To register to vote on Election Day, voters will need to provide proof of their identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), age (also driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport, naturalization papers, or other proof), and domicile (government-issued ID or documentation with an address on it).

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: U.S. Senate: Here’s what separates Manzur and Pappas, Brown and Sununu
description: After U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement early last year, the race for a New Hampshire U.S. Senate seat became wide open. On the Democratic side, U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas and Karishma Manzur are vying for the nomination in Tuesday’s primary elections. Pappas, who has led in the polls throughout the race, represents the […]
text:
While John Sununu is facing off against Scott Brown in the U.S. Senate Republican primary and Chris Pappas faces Karishma Manzur on the Democratic side, Sununu and Pappas have sought to make the race about each other. (Screenshots from the four campaign sites)After U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced her retirement early last year, the race for a New Hampshire U.S. Senate seat became wide open.
On the Democratic side, U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas and Karishma Manzur are vying for the nomination in Tuesday’s primary elections.
Pappas, who has led in the polls throughout the race, represents the more moderate establishment choice while Manzur has attempted to offer a progressive alternative.
When they arrive at the polls Tuesday, voters will also find David Jarvis, Maxwell Saal, and John Vail on their ballots, but Pappas and Manzur have led the most active campaigns by far.
On the GOP side, two former U.S. senators are trying to convince voters to send them back to Washington, D.C.
John Sununu served in the U.S. Senate from 2002 until 2008 when Shaheen defeated him in his first reelection bid. Now that Shaheen is retiring almost two decades later, he’s asking Granite Staters to give him back the seat.
Scott Brown was first elected to the U.S. Senate in a special election in Massachusetts. After he lost reelection in 2012, he moved to New Hampshire and unsuccessfully ran for U.S. Senate in 2014. President Donald Trump appointed Brown ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa in his first term. Now, Brown is running for U.S. Senate again.
Rounding out the Republican ballot are Tom Alciere, Sky Danley, Andy Martin, Mary Maxwell, Richard A. McMenamon II, and Sabrina Ann Smith.
On the Democratic side, a centrist vs. a progressive
Pappas, a Manchester Democrat who has represented the eastern half of New Hampshire in the House since 2019, was the first to jump into the race. A center-left Democrat, Pappas was named the most bipartisan Democrat in Congress by the Lugar Center in 2023.
Indeed, some of his most significant votes have been ones in which he crossed the aisle.
Chris Pappas
Last year, he voted for the Laken Riley Act, an immigration and law enforcement bill pushed by Republicans in the wake of the death of a Georgia nursing student at the hands of an immigrant. That bill was widely criticized by progressives and immigration advocates who argued it disregards due process, gives too much power to state attorneys general, and strengthened ICE ahead of a series of aggressive crackdowns in Minneapolis, Chicago, and other cities. Opponents also argue crimes by immigrants who lack permanent legal status are rare and that Riley’s tragic death was an outlier.
In 2020, he was one of just six Democrats voting against the Marijuana Opportunity Reinvestment and Expungement Act — which sought to legalize cannabis federally — over his concern about a provision that would’ve expunged federal convictions.
He’s recently been touting his support for the DISCLOSE Act, which aims to curb “dark money” in politics. The legislation, which he sponsored this year, would require groups like super PACs to disclose political donors who give over $10,000. It also seeks to prevent money transfers between organizations meant to hide the identity of the original contributor and expand disclosure requirements for the funders of political ads, among other things.
In a purple state like New Hampshire, Pappas argued that he’s “shown through four tough campaigns for the House that I can attract Republicans and independents” and “truly build a coalition.”
Pappas faces a progressive challenge on Tuesday in the form of Karishma Manzur. An activist and a scientist from Exeter, Manzur counters Pappas’ campaign finance push by pointing to her own campaign finances.
“I’m not taking a single cent from corporate PACs, super PACs, AIPAC, foreign-aligned lobbies,” she said. “Nothing. I’m only taking money from regular folks here in New Hampshire and across the country. That is it. Therefore, nobody owns my vote.”
If elected, she wants to attempt to overturn Citizens United v. FEC, a 2010 Supreme Court decision that opened the door to dark money in politics. To do that, Congress would need 67 senators and two-thirds of the House to vote in favor of a constitutional amendment.
She’s made Pappas’ support for Israel and the financial backing he’s received from pro-Israel groups a cornerstone of her campaign.
Pappas’ campaigns since 2018 have received over $600,000 in direct and earmarked contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, as well as more money from other pro-Israel funders.
Pappas has long supported U.S. aid to Israel. In February, at AIPAC’s 2026 Congressional Summit, he called himself “a strong supporter of the bipartisan U.S.-Israel relationship, which is a cornerstone of our national security policy.”
Recently though, bipartisan U.S. support for Israel has eroded among Democrats, and public opinion is souring on Israel. This comes as its multi-front wars drag on and more and more independent experts are concluding the country’s military is committing genocide against the Palestinian people.
In recent months, Pappas has moderated his stance. In July, he voted “present” — neither in favor nor against — on a measure to restrict weapons sales to Israel. He called that a “tough vote” when asked about it at the Manchester event last month, explaining that “what (Israeli President Benjamin) Netanyahu has done over the last few years is indefensible and unsupportable, and I think this is an important moment for a reset with respect to the U.S. policy toward Israel.” He said that Israeli security is “important to our national security and so is the plight of the Palestinian people.” He said he hopes Palestinians receive aid soon, that Hamas lays down its arms, and that Netanyahu loses reelection in October.
She supports a single-payer Medicare for All system.
“A single-payer universal healthcare system will be cheaper than the current system and cover all Americans,” Manzur said. “In addition to that, if anyone wanted to have some supplemental private health insurance, that’s fine. But every single person should be covered. Healthcare should not be a for-profit enterprise that it has become.”
Karishma Manzur
Manzur also supported the Road to Housing Act, bipartisan legislation that was just enacted in an effort to address skyrocketing housing costs nationwide. Pappas voted for that bill as a representative.
In an August poll from St. Anselm College, Pappas held a strong lead over Manzur at 59% to 28%; 13% of respondents were unsure. The most recent UNH Granite State Poll, also from August, pointed to a slightly closer race: a 47%-34% advantage for Pappas, with 18% undecided.
Manzur has never held public office before. Asked why voters believe she could be effective in the Senate without any experience, she said: “I’m the only one who actually has a vision. When I launched, Pappas and Sununu, they didn’t even have a policy platform on their website. They were just going to run on their millions of dollars because it didn’t matter. All they need is money. What I’m bringing to the people is, as a scientist, I’m very evidence-based. I’m showing them how we can bring the money back home from being wasted on endless wars, how we can bring the money home by making sure we have a fair tax code, where … all these billionaires or the mega corporations are paying, paying their fair share of taxes, we can bring those trillions of dollars right here in New Hampshire and across this country.”
Pappas’ message to potential Manzur supporters: “I’m proud of the support I have, which comes from organized labor across the board in New Hampshire, which comes from small-dollar donors, and … but again, this is a campaign of ideas that’s really focused on how we beat John Sununu and MAGA Republicans and flip the majority in the U.S. Senate.”
Two former U.S. senators trying to make their comeback
Sununu did not respond to the Bulletin’s requests for an interview for this story. He held a commanding 54%-24% lead over Brown in the St. Anselm Poll and 60%-20% in the UNH poll.
Similar to Pappas’ positioning toward Manzur, Sununu has sought to shift attention away from Brown and toward the general election. He skipped a televised WMUR debate with Brown last week and has focused his television ads and campaign statements on Pappas.
Sununu comes from a politically connected family in New Hampshire politics. His father is a former governor who also served as White House chief of staff under President George H.W. Bush, and his brother was governor until early last year.
John Sununu
Elected at age 38 in 2002, he was the youngest person in the Senate. He was a supporter of the war in Iraq and of ending the 1984 Federal Assault Weapons Ban, which expired during his term. Some notable actions included voting against a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage and filibustering the PATRIOT Act, which expanded the government’s surveillance abilities and has been criticized by privacy advocates. He was also sponsor of legislation to privatize Social Security, which he’s been attacked for by Democrats during this campaign. An analysis from The Washington Post found Sununu voted with the Republican Party’s position 84% of the time.
Brown, meanwhile, was a centrist Republican during his brief tenure in the Senate. For example, in 2011, Brown voted with President Barack Obama’s legislative positions 69.6% of the time, according to Congressional Quarterly. He sponsored the STOCK Act, which was signed into law by Obama and required members of Congress to disclose stock transactions and sought to ban insider trading. However, he was a strong opponent of Obama’s signature legislative feat, the Affordable Care Act.
Asked during a phone interview if he would vote to repeal the ACA and what he envisioned  to replace it should he be elected, Brown said: “I can’t fix health care in a 30-second phone call, nor would I even do it. But what I would say is that I will absolutely volunteer to be on the task force to find solutions because I am a problem solver.”
Scott Brown
In 2026, Brown has sought to position himself in the minds of primary voters as more right wing and as the pro-Trump candidate.
For example, he’s touting Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, an omnibus bill that touched nearly every segment of the federal government. He has been vocal about his support for the provisions in that bill that eliminated some taxes on tips and overtime. Asked what he would say to voters’ concerns about the Medicaid and SNAP cuts included in that bill, Brown said SNAP shouldn’t be run by the federal government anyway (the program is currently jointly run by states and the federal government). He wishes the federal government gave states block grant funding to run it by themselves.
“We can do it better than the federal government,” Brown said. “I believe in block granting the SNAP money to us directly, and the same with education funds. I believe we should take those education funds and block grant them to our states because we can do it better.”
Asked about his level of concern over the massive increase to the federal government’s debt that the One Big Beautiful Bill brought via tax cuts, Brown said: “The hope was that we would actually create jobs and actually add to the job base and the tax base that would offset that.”
Still, Trump has endorsed his opponent Sununu in the race, likely a calculation by a president paying attention to polling numbers.
Like Sununu, Brown has been trying to focus on criticizing Pappas.
“Chris Pappas, all he does is complain,” Brown said. “You know, blame, blame, blame, and he doesn’t actually come up with solutions.”
Getting to the polls and voting
The polls will open at varying times on Tuesday morning depending on the municipality. Voters can find out where their polling location is and which races will be on their ballot on the Secretary of State’s website at https://app.sos.nh.gov/pollingplacesampleballot. New Hampshire allows same-day voter registration. To register to vote on Election Day, voters will need to provide proof of their identity (driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), age (also driver’s license, government-issued photo ID, or passport), U.S. citizenship (birth certificate, passport, naturalization papers, or other proof), and domicile (government-issued ID or documentation with an address on it).

title: Concierges, adjunct professors, potato chip tasters: US employers rely on ‘disposable’ workers
description: When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a […]
text:
U.S. employers are leaning more and more heavily on adjunct, part-time and contract workers with lower pay and fewer rights. (Getty Images)
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.
When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.
These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.
I am a labor economist. In my new book, “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment,” I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.
 3 different varieties

To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.
I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.
1. Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce.
2. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees.
3. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.
Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.
 Who are marginal workers?

Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.
Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.
In 1970 people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.
 Part-time marginal workers

Another example of marginal work is part-timers.
Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.
A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.
When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.
“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”

Paul Osterman’s book, ‘Disposable Workers,’ explains how ties between employers and their employees are fraying. Harvard University Press
Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.
The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.
Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.
 Forces behind this trend

Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable?
A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.
Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.
An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”
This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.
 Less pay and job satisfaction

My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.
In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.
The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The entirety of humanity sweeps me along as I drive across the capacious expanse of Kansas
description: Driving across the toasted green plains of Kansas toward an event in Lindsborg on Sunday, I found myself overwhelmed with gratitude. Not gratitude toward a particular person or institution, although goodness knows I’ve been beyond lucky in my associations with both. No, I found myself grateful on a much deeper level — grateful for the […]
text:
A deeply blue sky stretches across the Kansas plains, as witnessed from a rest stop off Interstate 70. (Photo by Clay Wirestone/Kansas Reflector)Driving across the toasted green plains of Kansas toward an event in Lindsborg on Sunday, I found myself overwhelmed with gratitude.
Not gratitude toward a particular person or institution, although goodness knows I’ve been beyond lucky in my associations with both. No, I found myself grateful on a much deeper level — grateful for the ability to live and work and exist at this moment in 2026, in this place — the state of Kansas. 


Roving with Clay Wirestone
Opinion editor travels Kansas and beyond for stories off the beaten path. Read them all here.


I understand if you don’t share that feeling. There’s a lot awry in the world around us. Political ads for this fall’s election already pollute the airwaves, and the threat of technological upheaval lurks around every corner.
Yet I am nonetheless lucky. And I suspect that you are too.
This past week, I found myself returning to a deceptively simple webpage called Any Human Ever. I would recommend you click on the link and go try it yourself, but in essence the site allows you to simulate, at random, the life of any human being who has ever lived. Ever.
More than 100 billion people have lived on Earth, from the beginning of our species until now. That’s a lot of folks. Many of those people lived and died before the advent of modern medicine and commercial agriculture. Many of them died in infancy or had their lives cut short by diseases like cholera. 
Those who are lucky enough to make it into their 40s or beyond seldom traveled more than a day or two away from their home villages. Most weren’t literate. And because of the mortality rates mentioned earlier, these survivors witnessed their parents and children die around them at alarming rates.
We talk a lot about trauma these days. We talk about trauma created by our upbringings, neighborhoods or other challenges in life.
Imagine the collective trauma experienced by billions of human beings who lived through our planet’s past. Their lives were, as British philosopher Thomas Hobbes suggested, “nasty, brutish, and short.” Many experienced their allotted span of years as little more than a unyielding agony of loss and privation.
They were not rich. They were not even middle class. They were dirt poor, malnourished and without the access to resources or entertainment we take for granted today.
Here are just three of the randomly generated people produced for me Sunday. We start with an unnamed girl.
In 45,665 BCE, a girl was born on the Ganges Plain, near present-day Varanasi. Her name went unrecorded. She lived in a mobile band of about 40 people. Her dwelling was a brush or grass windbreak. She was the second of six children. She mostly ate foraged roots, river fish, wild boar, and wild greens and roots, with wild berries in season. She was about 143 cm in height (4 ft 8 in).
Of the three children she had, two boys survived past childhood. The farthest she ever travelled from home was 3 days’ walk, to the far edge of the band’s seasonal range. She spoke an unrecorded prehistoric language, and her faith was animism and shamanism. She spent her working life as a gatherer of wild plants and small game. Death came at 19, in an accident.
Next, meet Urraca.


Urraca was born on the Iberian Peninsula, near present-day Toledo, in 659 CE. She grew up in a hamlet of about 40 people. Her home was a whitewashed stone house. She was the third of four children. Her father died when she was 42, her mother when she was 47. Urraca’s table was mostly wheat bread, chickpeas and broad beans, pork and cured ham, and cabbage and onions, with grapes, figs, and olives in season. She stood about 157 cm tall (5 ft 2 in).
Urraca married at the age of 27. She had six children; four boys survived past childhood. Her farthest journey was half a day’s walk, to a neighbouring village. She spoke Late Latin, and practised Christianity. Urraca’s work was that of a farmer working the family land.
At 23, she lived through a cold, sunless year caused by the far-off eruption of an unidentified volcano in the tropics. At 25 she watched Halley’s Comet pass. The Umayyad conquest of Hispania broke out when she was 52.
She died of typhoid fever at 52. Her line came to a single grandchild. Her body was buried in consecrated ground beside the church, in a shroud, and later in a coffin.
Finally, we have Kotys.
Kotys was born in 89 CE, in the countryside near Belgrade. His village was home to about 350 people. Kotys’s dwelling was a timber and wattle-and-daub house. Among five children, he was the fourth. He ate largely wheat and millet bread, beans and sheep cheese, pork and lamb, and cabbage, onions, and leeks, with plums and apples in season. He followed Thracian polytheism and spoke a Palaeo-Balkan language. He died still a child, in an accident.
Lindsborg painter Mike Hartung (right) explains his latest exhibit at the Smoky Valley Arts & Folklife Center on Sunday. (Photo by Clay Wirestone/Kansas Reflector)
Yes, we are lucky.
I believe that most of us understand this, deep down. We don’t have to look many generations back in our families to find subsistence farmers or voyagers who traversed continents in search of better lives. We understand that our predecessors struggled because we are not so many generations removed from them.


Yet our minds become accustomed to our circumstances. We have all become accustomed to living in a world with transport and nutrition and entertainment, and socialization all at the ready. We may face fiscal stress, but for many of us that stress mostly affects the size of the bounty we enjoy.
I do not mean to cast aspersions on anyone’s efforts to better themselves or set an individual court. After all, the reason I was driving across the state to Lindsborg was to sign copies of my new book and hobnob with Kansas Reflector fans.
I wrote the book. I’ve worked five years at the Reflector. I created the circumstances that made my trip possible.
But the opportunity to live here in this moment, and in these circumstances, was entirely luck. I could have been born or raised in an entirely different time — with an entirely different outcome.
We don’t like to dwell on these topics. So much about our lives remains outside of our control. We are so many grains of sand, tossed in the air and coming to rest wherever we may. Even those of us with religious faith must acknowledge that the God has, at the very least, smiled upon us.
So for a moment this morning, during this Labor Day vacation, remember the question posed by Dr. Seuss: “Did I ever tell you how lucky you are?” Spare a moment for gratitude at the cosmic chance that deposited us here and aware.

title: Discontent will accompany blue‑collar voters to the polls in the midterms
description: When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?” All workers — unionized or not — are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline. For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is […]
text:
Former Senate President Troy Jackson joined local postal worker unions, which rallied to save the U.S. Postal Service outside the Bangor Post Office on March 20, 2025. (Photo: Nathan Bernard/ Maine Morning Star)
When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?”
All workers — unionized or not — are dealing with higher prices for food and gasoline.
For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is bleak. Threats from AI and robotics abound. Pledges by U.S. and international corporations to invest in new plants remain largely pledges. The roughly 400,000 federal job cuts during President Donald Trump’s second term have disrupted lives. Many of these jobs were previously represented by labor unions.
As a labor studies scholar, I believe weariness and wariness will accompany blue-collar voters to the polls in November. As such, the candidates who have practical ideas for turning the economy around and exhibit empathy for Americans worried about how to pay their bills could receive the bulk of the union vote.
The union vote
Over generations, the majority of union members have sided with Democratic candidates, even if that support has wavered since the 1970s.
The 2024 presidential campaign was no exception. The majority of union members voted for Democratic candidates, but at a far lower rate than in the 1960s.
Why does this matter in 2026?
Union voters play a bigger role in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Nevada, three swing states where the share of voters who belong to unions is above the national average of 10%. In closely contested House and Senate races, even a small shift in union votes could influence the outcome.
What’s in store this November?
How large is the union vote?
The latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show that the percentage of U.S. unionized workers has fallen over the past four decades.
In 1983, 20.1% of U.S. workers were represented by a union. In 2025, the rate was 10.0%, or 14.7 million people. Union membership among public sector workers (32.9%) is more than five times higher than that of private sector workers (5.9%). In close elections, the volatility of these voting blocs matters.
During the 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised to reduce consumer prices, bring back manufacturing jobs and respect workers’ rights.
As the midterm elections approach, I believe the president’s performance on these issues in the eyes of union voters will determine which party controls the House and Senate. And the signs are not promising for Trump, with recent polls indicating the president’s support among union households is eroding.
Manufacturing jobs and inflation
The U.S. economy has lost 75,000 manufacturing jobs since January 2025, a 0.6% decline. These jobs have steadily declined since the 1980s, so Trump’s policies are not solely to blame.
Furthermore, Trump’s off-again, on-again tariffs may help some U.S. manufacturers. That’s because tariffs can erase the advantages of low-cost overseas labor. As economist Laura Veldkamp noted in July 2026, Trump’s tariffs “made it more profitable for American manufacturers to set up and produce here.”
The bigger problem, though, is that even if some manufacturing returns to the U.S., the work will likely be done with the latest manufacturing technologies, which tend to reduce the need for workers. That does not bode well for significant job creation.
In July 2026, Moody’s financial analyst Mark Zandi told Marketplace that more manufacturing output “doesn’t translate into jobs.” He explained that there has been more activity in the tech sector and in the defense-aerospace industries, but “these factories just don’t employ a lot of people.”
Additionally, Trump has not established a clear plan to lower inflation. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reports that food prices in July 2026 were up 3.0% from July 2025. This increase is slightly above the historical average.
There’s one more factor to consider. Many older blue-collar workers — many of them former union members — across New England, the Great Lakes, Ohio and western Pennsylvania remain angry about the epic industrial collapse of the 1970s and 1980s.
This kind of generational suffering can show up in the voting booth in a big way. And I don’t think voter surveys and polls are able to measure the depths of this rage.
Union representation
The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 allowed government workers to unionize. But a March 2025 White House announcement said the legislation had enabled “hostile Federal unions to obstruct agency management.”
Through an executive order and mass layoffs across the federal workforce in 2025, Trump has presided over a dramatic change in public sector collective bargaining in Washington, D.C.
Offering guidance on the 2025 executive order, the U.S. Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to end their collective bargaining agreement.
In response, the American Federation of Government Employees condemned the action in an email to its members, saying the Trump administration was “illegally strip(ping) collective bargaining rights from hundreds of thousands of federal workers.”
Federal unions have challenged the White House’s March 2025 executive order. In 2026, independent arbitrators have also ruled against the administration’s efforts to circumvent labor agreements with some federal workers. And in June 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts struck down an effort by the Trump administration to exercise control over union elections at federal agencies.
Whether unionized industrial workers support their public sector counterparts remains to be seen.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Policy experts ask Michigan to strengthen workers rights as state grapples with economic challenges
description: As the nation takes a beat in recognition of the American labor movement on Monday, the Michigan League for Public Policy is calling on the state to do more for its workers. In a report released on Labor Day, Patrick Schaefer, an economic security policy analyst for the organization, analyzed recent trends in Michigan’s labor […]
text:
A construction worker listens as a labor leader speaks at a rally for a sustainable road funding solution in the coming fiscal year budget. Sept. 3, 2025 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan AdvanceAs the nation takes a beat in recognition of the American labor movement on Monday, the Michigan League for Public Policy is calling on the state to do more for its workers.
In a report released on Labor Day, Patrick Schaefer, an economic security policy analyst for the organization, analyzed recent trends in Michigan’s labor economy. The result is a series of recommendations on policies Michigan lawmakers could adopt to support its workforce.
At the time of the report’s publication, Michigan’s unemployment rate was at 5%, remaining largely stable over the last year. The nation’s average unemployment rate is 4.2%, with Michigan holding the eighth highest rate in the nation.
The state’s rate of labor underutilization — which includes unemployed workers, individuals who are working part time and would like to work full time, and people who are available and willing to work, but have not looked for a job because they don’t believe there are jobs available to them — is sitting at rates comparable to the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, the report said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, the state’s labor underutilization rate averaged 9.1%, sitting above the national average of 7.9%.
“While Michigan’s labor underutilization rate is still fairly low compared to its historic rates, the rate at which it is increasing compared to the national average paints an uneasy picture of Michigan’s labor market,” the report notes.
The Michigan League for Public Policy also noted a 1.7% decrease in labor force participation, marking the largest decrease the state has seen since the pandemic.
The decrease was due to a number of factors, the report explained, including retirements, people staying in education longer, job-seeking fatigue, and the increased cost of child and elder care.
“The most recent data indicates there are 1.2 job seekers per job opening in Michigan, indicating there are simply not enough jobs for everyone,” the report states. “Finally, in 2025, the average cost of full-time center-based infant childcare is $14,064 per year in Michigan, leaving some to choose to exit the workforce rather than pay the exorbitant cost.”
The report also addresses the continued decline of manufacturing jobs in Michigan and whether artificial intelligence and the tech industry can provide meaningful economic development in the state.
“It is clear we are looking for a new industry to rebuild a strong working class. However, the truth is that AI, data centers and the tech industry do not seem to be the answer,” the report states. “We cannot bank on the chance of capturing a booming industry. It would be far more prudent to invest funds in removing barriers to employment in the state, not in corporate incentives.”
The report said that large scale data centers deliver significantly fewer permanent jobs than manufacturing facilities, comparing the Open AI data center under development in Saline Township, which is expected to create 450 permanent jobs, with Ford’s Michigan Assembly Plant, which employs more than 6,000 residents.
Instead of spending money in an attempt to bring data centers and tech companies into Michigan, the League of Public Policy argued state funds would be better spent on investments into K-12 and higher education, public infrastructure, and affordable childcare to help bring young families into the state.



Quotation







It is clear we are looking for a new industry to rebuild a strong working class. However, the truth is that AI, data centers and the tech industry do not seem to be the answer.


– Michigan League for Public Policy


Although the median wage in the state has grown 8 cents between 2024 and 2025, the Michigan League for Public Policy said that the median Michigan worker is only making 19 cents more per hour than they did pre-pandemic.
Additionally, not all workers have seen wage increases, the organization said, with the median hourly wage of Black residents falling by 43 cents over the last year, when accounting for inflation.
“That worsens a widening gulf between Black and white hourly wages in the state, with the median white worker now taking home 23.4% more than the median Black worker,” the report states.
The median female worker also saw their wages dip by 16 cents between 2024 and 2025, with women now earning 20.3% less per hour than the median male worker across the state.
In its recommendations, the Michigan League for Public Policy called on lawmakers to increase the state’s $13.73 minimum wage to a rate that ensures full-time workers can afford necessities like housing, food, utilities and medicine.
It also called for the state to eliminate the minimum wage for tipped workers, which allows employees to pay their workers $5.49 per hour if they received at least $8.24 in tips.
The league notes that women, particularly Black women, are more likely to work in tipped positions or other low-paying jobs. The tipped wage is set to increase, but those wages can be inconsistent, making financial planning more difficult, the report states.
The report also called for lawmakers to move forward with a policy to ban employers from requesting salary or credit history during the hiring process, noting that incorporating that information into hiring decisions can perpetuate wage discrimination and have a long-term compounding effect on a worker’s salary.
On labor rights in Michigan, the report noted that the loss of manufacturing jobs often means the loss of union jobs, as the industries that come in to fill vacancies in the job market are often non-union, or jobs that include high barriers to entry.
“Michigan must push for stronger worker rights and better benefits to strengthen both Michigan families and the overall economy,” the report states. “The solution is not to just regrow Michigan manufacturing, though that can be a vital component. What is important is that workers are allowed to organize and negotiate for better wages and benefits.”
On those grounds, the Michigan League for Public Policy advocated for the repeal of state laws barring local governments from having their own minimum wage. It further called for the establishment of prevailing wages, the mandating of paid leave for workers, or otherwise adopting and enforcing employment discrimination or policies that go beyond the benefits and protections guaranteed by the state.
The Michigan League for Public Policy also called for a ban on captive audience meetings, employer-mandated meetings held during organizing efforts where employers advocate against unionization. While the National Labor Relations Board banned the practice in 2024, the ban has since been appealed, and the board’s general counsel has asked for the ban to be reversed.
