title: Then Again: Armed with a spirit of discovery and a gun, the first lady road-trips through Vermont
description:
Eleanor Roosevelt had planned a getaway. But the trip also helped reshape expectations of what a first lady could do — and helped cement her role as a partner in her husband’s presidency. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Then Again: Armed with a spirit of discovery and a gun, the first lady road-trips through Vermont.
text:
Eleanor Roosevelt takes target practice with the revolver issued to her by the Secret Service. Photo credit Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library
The gun was the compromise Eleanor Roosevelt grudgingly accepted. The first lady would carry one on her upcoming tour of New England and Quebec in July 1933. 
Secret Service officials weren’t pleased with this scant security. They had insisted that agents accompany her on the trip, but Roosevelt was having none of it. In that case, they said, she needed a police escort, or at least a chauffeur. Still no. Roosevelt rejected any kind of security detail. She would drive herself; she loved driving. 
Her husband, Franklin Delano Roosevelt, had been president for barely 100 days, but she was already eager to temporarily escape the scrutiny she endured as the president’s wife. “(S)ince I could still drive without having people recognize me,” she wrote in her autobiography, “I had been looking forward with a great deal of pleasure to this holiday.”
The Secret Service had reason to worry about her safety. Just months earlier, in February 1933, when FDR was president-elect, he had survived an assassination attempt in Miami. But carrying a revolver, provided by the Secret Service, was the most protection the fiercely independent first lady would accept. She unloaded the gun and stored it in the glove compartment of her bright blue Buick convertible. 
On her road trip, she would be entering hostile territory, politically speaking. FDR had become president by thrashing his Republican opponent, then-President Herbert Hoover, in the election of 1932. FDR had won all but six states, and his wife would be visiting three of them: Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine. Vermont was by far the most anti-FDR state in the country; voters here preferred Hoover by more than 16 percentage points.   

First lady Eleanor Roosevelt, seen here posing at the White House, loved driving and the freedom it gave her. Photo credit Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library

Eleanor Roosevelt had a strong interest in understanding and bolstering the lives of rural Americans and was deeply committed to the administration’s efforts to lift the country out of the Great Depression. She had already passed through Vermont earlier that summer. That first visit was only for a day, June 23, as she drove from Massena, New York, to the coast of Maine, where she was meeting her husband. With her were Nancy Cook and Marion Dickerman, a lesbian couple who were old friends of hers. In fact, the three had started a furniture company together in 1926, with Cook, a skilled woodworker, creating the designs and overseeing the factory, Dickerman investing money, and Roosevelt promoting the business. The company provided jobs for immigrants, as well as local farmers during their off-season.
Newspapers the next day told the stories of Vermonters who had been stunned to suddenly encounter the first lady, whose visit was unannounced. Roosevelt was trying to keep a low profile so that, as much as possible, this could be a relaxing trip, not a visit by a dignitary. A group of women told the Burlington Free Press they had been driving together toward St. Albans when they noticed several people, who turned out to be Roosevelt and her two friends, gathering daisies and clover blossoms by the roadside. When the driver honked a greeting, the first lady smiled and waved. 
Roosevelt and her companions were next spotted in Richmond, where they ate lunch under a large elm on the terrace of a restaurant and hotel named The Richmond. A local pharmacist grabbed his camera and snapped a couple of photos of the women, which are perhaps the pictures that appeared in the next day’s Free Press. The newspaper’s four-sentence report offered few details other than the saccharine comment that Roosevelt “was enjoying to the utmost the superb scenery and weather” and that she was wearing a simple blue dress, a powder blue sweater and a white band to hold back her hair.  

The June 24, 1933 edition of the Burlington Free Press brought news that the president’s wife had been in Vermont the previous day. Eleanor Roosevelt was photographed with traveling companions Marion Dickerman and Nancy Cook when they stopped for lunch at The Richmond hotel in Richmond, Vermont.

Before leaving Vermont, Roosevelt was spotted again at 4 p.m. in St. Johnsbury, where she purchased maple candy at the Maple Grove Inn before buying more maple products at the Cary Maple Cabin. “She made her purchases so quickly that she was out and away almost before it was realized there who the distinguished customer had been,” wrote the Caledonian-Record. “…(Then) she skillfully piloted her trappy sports roadster on its way.” 
“Now that Mrs. Roosevelt has learned the way to St. Johnsbury, it is hoped that she will come often,” the local newspaper gushed, despite the fact that Vermont voters weren’t particularly enthused about FDR, “and if she can persuade the President of the United States to come with her some time all the better. The latchstring is out.” 
Two for the road
She did return, just two weeks later, but she didn’t bring her husband. Instead, her traveling companion for this three-week road trip was Lorena Hickok. Like her earlier whirlwind tour through the region, this trip would give Roosevelt a break from the constant attention she received as first lady, a role she hadn’t been eager to adopt. It would also let her tick a couple items off her bucket list, including driving on the Gaspé Peninsula and to the top of Vermont’s Mount Mansfield.
The trip gave her time away with Hickok, or “Hick,” as she was known to friends. Hickok was a prominent newspaper reporter who had covered FDR’s 1932 presidential campaign, but she feared her closeness to Eleanor would jeopardize her objectivity if she covered his administration. Instead, she soon joined it, becoming the chief investigator for the Federal Emergency Relief Administration. During the road trip, newspapers referred to her as Eleanor Roosevelt’s secretary. Early Roosevelt historians described the two women as merely close friends, but now the consensus among scholars is that their relationship was romantic. 
The pair began their road trip in early July, visiting sites in upstate New York, including Ausable Chasm and the grave of abolitionist John Brown. After driving through Burlington on July 9, they reached their hotel, The Richmond (where Roosevelt had lunched on her previous visit), at 7:30 p.m. Roosevelt planned to drive up Mount Mansfield the following day. 
Although Roosevelt had declined Secret Service protection during this trip, an officer for the Vermont Motor Vehicle Highway Patrol, the precursor of the Vermont State Police, stood guard outside the hotel. The next morning, highway patrol officers escorted Roosevelt and Hickok to Waterbury, where they planned to visit the new Civilian Conservation Corps camp. “The officers then left her,” the Montpelier Evening Argus reported, “as she did not desire an escort through the state, preferring to travel simply and unostentatiously.” 
As they drove to the camp, they were met by journalist Harry C. Whitehill, who invited Roosevelt to speak live on air at WDEV, the local radio station he had co-founded two years earlier. The first lady agreed to stop by the station after her visit to the CCC camp.

Eleanor Roosevelt, center, and Lorena Hickok, back to camera, were overnight guests at The Richmond, a hotel in Richmond, Vermont, in 1933.Photo credit Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library

The Civilian Conservation Corps, which provided public works jobs for young men, was a major part of FDR’s New Deal program. Workers at the Waterbury camp would be tasked with building a large earth-filled dam on the Little River, a waterway that had contributed to the disastrous flooding that ravaged Vermont in 1927. When the first lady visited, the camp had been under construction for only a month. During her tour, she spoke with some of the young men working there and investigated whether the meals served to them would be nutritious.
Roosevelt kept her promise to stop by WDEV but never spoke on air. It was Sunday, and the station manager didn’t want to interrupt the religious service being broadcast at the time. 
To the top of Vermont
For a visit by a first lady, the trip’s itinerary was rather loose. Roosevelt decided against driving up Mount Mansfield on the planned day, due to poor visibility. Instead, they drove east on Route 2 (Interstate 89 was nearly three decades in the future). A passing motorist recognized the first lady and raced ahead to Montpelier to spread the news of her imminent arrival.
On her June trip through Vermont, Roosevelt’s car had borne Washington, D.C., plates. For this trip, she switched to New York plates. The change provided a measure of anonymity, but traffic in Montpelier was moving slowly that morning. Some people had time to recognize and wave at the famous motorist passing by, particularly when Roosevelt had to wait at the traffic light at the corner of State and Main. 
Roosevelt continued east, passing through St. Johnsbury, where in true tourist style she stopped to buy more maple candies. These were perhaps a treat for her youngest child, 17-year-old John, whom she and Hickok visited at the polo camp he was attending in Whitefield, New Hampshire. After spending the afternoon with John, the pair drove back through St. Johnsbury at 8 p.m. 
By about 9:30 p.m., Roosevelt had reached Montpelier, where several passersby noticed her sitting alone in her car, parked on State Street. Hickok was on an errand. A woman named Ruth McGovern approached the car and chatted with the first lady for about seven minutes, she told a reporter. During the conversation, Roosevelt mentioned that she was rather tired.
Despite her fatigue, Roosevelt was committed to experiencing the Green Mountains. Shortly before 10 o’clock, she phoned someone in Waterbury (press reports don’t say who) to report that she was headed to Mount Mansfield. A police officer had told her it was too dangerous to drive up Mansfield at night, and she was offered a driver to take her to the top, but she was determined. A Waterbury selectman and the president of the local Chamber of Commerce, driving separately from Roosevelt, escorted her up the Toll Road to the Summit House. The party arrived at around 11:15 p.m.
“(W)hen told that Mrs. Roosevelt would soon reach the Summit House the management was alive to the honor of entertaining the most distinguished guest on Mount Mansfield in recent years,” the Waterbury Record reported. “There was so much stir about the hotel that over night guests who had retired early to get up early, to observe the sunrise, were awaked, dressed and were ready to receive Mrs. Roosevelt. Every light in and around the Summit House was turned on and when Mrs. Roosevelt came within seeing distance of the Summit House she was assured, even in the middle of the night, that she was very, very welcome.”
The following morning, the newspaper stated, the mountain was socked in by clouds, but Roosevelt and Hickok hiked to the Chin. They returned to the mountaintop hotel to find a delegation of seven young women from Stowe, who presented the first lady with a bouquet and invited her to visit the town. 
Roosevelt and Hickok climbed back into the roadster at about 11 a.m. and drove down the Toll Road. At the bottom, they were met by yet another local delegation. The first lady shook hands with everyone and was presented with another bouquet, this one of red clover, the state flower. While posing for a group photo, Roosevelt commented, “It must take a great deal of courage to be a Democrat in Vermont.”  

Eleanor Roosevelt and Lorena Hickok taking in a view during the Quebec leg of their 1933 trip. Photo credit Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library

When Hayley Lever, a well-known New York City artist, learned that the first lady was staying overnight at the Summit House, he left a phone message that he hoped she would visit the Art Students League exhibit he had organized at the Lodge in Smugglers Notch. Roosevelt accepted the invitation. After showing her and Hickok the exhibit, he presented the first lady an etching of a schooner, which she said her husband would appreciate; he loved boats. By this point, Roosevelt must have wondered how many more gifts she was going to have to find room for in her convertible.
She received one more before she left Vermont. At Smugglers Notch, she met 83-year-old “Bronco” Charlie Miller, said to be the last living Pony Express rider. Miller, dressed in “full regalia” (presumably a fringed buckskin riding outfit), presented Roosevelt with a hand-carved walking stick fashioned from Vermont wood.
Roosevelt and Hickok then headed north through Smugglers Notch — Lever warned them to “mind the curves” — and after a couple of brief errands in Newport, crossed into Canada at Derby Line.
The pair took full advantage of the two weeks they had left before they were expected back in Washington. They visited Quebec City and explored the Gaspé Peninsula. While touring Maine, Hickok was stunned to witness Roosevelt knowledgeably discussing potato prices and that year’s crop with a farmer “as easily and confidently as though she had spent her whole life raising potatoes in Aroostoock County!” Hickok later wrote. In reality, Roosevelt had remembered the details from an article she read in that morning’s paper. She was a quick study.  
Bringing the world to FDR
Once back in Washington, the Roosevelts and Hickok had dinner together, and the first lady shared what she had learned from conversations with ordinary Americans during the trip. Hickok was struck by how the first lady served as the president’s eyes and ears, how enthralled he was by the details of the outside world that she brought back to the White House. It was a role the first lady would play for the rest of FDR’s 12 years in office.  
The road trip served as an inflection point. Although it had been planned as a getaway with Hickok, not a fact-finding mission, the trip helped redefine what a first lady could do. Previously, the role of the president’s wife was almost entirely ceremonial. Going forward, first ladies could take an active role in helping shape and communicate policy. Eleanor Roosevelt began writing a newspaper column and annually traveled 40,000 miles or more in representing the administration. 
Throughout her time as first lady, Roosevelt refused Secret Service protection. Agency officials no doubt worried about her safety. Her friend and a former FDR bodyguard, Earl Miller, intervened. If a pistol was going to be her sole defense, she should at least know how to shoot one. Miller gave Roosevelt a firearms lesson on Oct. 11, 1933, her 49th birthday.
In retelling the incident, Roosevelt wrote: “I finally learned to hit a target. I would never have used it on a human being, but I thought I ought to know how to handle a revolver if I had to have one in my possession.”
Still, she later admitted, she sometimes left it behind.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa should treat AI savings as matching funds for mentorship
description: Iowa is spending public money to expand apprenticeship because employers need a reliable way to turn beginners into skilled workers. Companies adopting artificial intelligence should apply the same logic to the time the technology saves. In April, Iowa Workforce Development announced more than $3.25 million in apprenticeship grants to advance career pathways[...]
text:
When employers automate routine tasks that junior employees used to do, they may lose a valuable training opportunity. (Stock photo by David Espejo/Getty Images)Iowa is spending public money to expand apprenticeship because employers need a reliable way to turn beginners into skilled workers. Companies adopting artificial intelligence should apply the same logic to the time the technology saves.
In April, Iowa Workforce Development announced more than $3.25 million in apprenticeship grants to advance career pathways. The state describes registered apprenticeship for employers as structured training that combines paid work with instruction and learning under experienced mentors.
That mentor relationship becomes more important when AI removes routine early-career tasks.
The Stanford Digital Economy Lab’s August 2026 Canaries update found that the employment shortfall for workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations widened from 15% in the July 2025 data vintage to 19% by June 2026.
Employers do not need to preserve every repetitive task. They should automate routine preparation where AI performs well. But they should stop treating every saved junior hour as a labor cost that can simply disappear.
Those hours once carried learning value.
A junior employee building a report saw how inputs connected to outputs. A new insurance worker reviewing ordinary files learned which facts made a case unusual. An entry-level finance employee preparing analyses learned which assumptions senior colleagues challenged. Repetition supplied the examples from which judgment grew.
AI can replace much of the preparation while making the learning more deliberate.
Iowa employers should create a mentor-match rule. When AI saves experienced employees time on drafting, research, scheduling, reporting, or administrative work, reserve part of those savings for coaching newer employees. The company contributes the technology dividend; the mentor contributes the judgment.
Then redesign junior work around verification. Let AI produce the first pass. Ask the newer employee to check whether claims match source material, reconcile numbers, identify missing context, investigate exceptions, test assumptions, and explain what still requires a human decision.
The best review sessions should focus on mistakes and edge cases. Why did the AI output look plausible but fail? Which exception changed the answer? What information should have triggered escalation? These conversations turn automation into a teaching tool.
Employers should measure the result through time to independent competence. How long before a new hire can recognize a weak output, handle ordinary exceptions, communicate uncertainty, and complete routine decisions with limited supervision?
That metric matters because AI can create two very different futures. One company can automate routine work, hire fewer beginners, and discover later that it has too few experienced people. Another can automate the same preparation while accelerating how quickly the remaining beginners become capable.
Iowa’s apprenticeship investments already recognize that employers benefit when learning happens inside real work. AI should strengthen that principle rather than undermine it.
Treat saved time as matching funds for mentorship. Then judge the technology partly by whether it helps Iowa workers climb the career ladder faster.

title: 38 new affordable apartments open in downtown Burlington
description:
The site of a former veterans’ hall and homeless shelter has transformed into a five-story affordable housing complex.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  38 new affordable apartments open in downtown Burlington.
text:
The Post Apartments in downtown Burlington on Sept. 4, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
The site of a former veterans’ hall and homeless shelter in downtown Burlington has transformed into a five-story affordable housing complex. 
The Post Apartments, developed by the nonprofits Champlain Housing Trust and Evernorth, has 38 units that will remain subsidized in perpetuity.
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders helped earmark $1 million in federal money for the $24 million project. At a ribbon cutting event on Friday, he said the project should serve as a model locally and beyond.
“In the city of Burlington, in the state of Vermont, in the United States of America, we have a massive, massive housing crisis,” Sanders said. “Maybe instead of spending hundreds of billions of dollars fighting a war that we never should have gotten in, we might want to be investing in low-income and affordable housing.”
Sanders supported the creation of a precursor to Champlain Housing Trust when he served as Burlington mayor in the 1980s.

U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., speaks at a ribbon-cutting event for the Post Apartments in downtown Burlington on Sept. 4, 2026. Photo by Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

The new apartment complex has eight efficiency-sized units, 26 one-bedrooms and four two-bedrooms. Nine units are set aside for people exiting homelessness, and ten have Section 8 vouchers attached to them, meaning tenants generally won’t pay more than a third of their income toward rent. Monthly rents start at $1,160.
The developers wrapped up construction earlier this year, and the building is currently fully occupied.
The ground floor hosts a new veterans’ center as well as office space for the Chittenden County Community Justice Center. The building is fully electric and has a solar array on the roof.
Constructing “infill” projects like this in downtowns can prove tricky, as builders contend with dirty soils and tight lots. 
This location, near the intersection of Main St. and S. Winooski Avenue, was particularly challenging: the apartment complex sits next to a gas station and near a decommissioned sewer in a ravine that once ran through the neighborhood. That led the developers to seek about $1.6 million in what are known as Brownfields remediation funds from the state to clean up the soil.
Like most affordable housing projects, this one brought in funding from a wide array of sources: 20 different budget lines, in this case. Major money came from federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, as well as COVID-era federal stimulus funds allocated by the City of Burlington and the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board.
“Today we get to celebrate this result, a place for our community, for our veterans, for people who are experiencing homelessness, a place where our neighbors can live with dignity, safety, and affordability,” said Champlain Housing Trust CEO Michael Monte. “It’s a good thing.”

title: Joe Lombardo and the largest tax increase in Nevada history
description: A Joe Lombardo campaign ad that says Aaron Ford is horrible because Ford has supported tax breaks for data centers (a policy Lombardo continues to support) also flashes on your screen the words “FORD VOTED FOR THE LARGEST TAX INCREASE IN NEVADA HISTORY.” The largest tax increase in Nevada history was enacted in 2015. Valued […]
text:
The crew Gov. Joe Lombardo is riding with now had a lot more to do with enacting the largest tax increase in Nevada history than Aaron Ford did. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)
A Joe Lombardo campaign ad that says Aaron Ford is horrible because Ford has supported tax breaks for data centers (a policy Lombardo continues to support) also flashes on your screen the words “FORD VOTED FOR THE LARGEST TAX INCREASE IN NEVADA HISTORY.”


The largest tax increase in Nevada history was enacted in 2015. Valued at $1.3 billion at the time, it consisted of a package of tax measures, including: the creation of a gross receipts tax on business; an increase in the modified business (aka payroll) tax; extensions of taxes that had been scheduled to expire; and an increase to the cigarette tax.


The tax package had been spearheaded by Republican Gov. Brian Sandoval in cooperation with the gambling and resort industry, which (if memory serves) was willing to accept a small increase in the payroll tax in exchange for making Nevada’s non-gaming businesses finally pay a business tax — thus minimizing any imperative to raise the gaming tax.


Republicans controlled both the Senate and the Assembly at the time, and bipartisan support for Sandoval’s tax package in both chambers was large enough to easily clear the state constitutional requirement that new or increased taxes must be approved by two-thirds majorities in both houses.


The vote in the Senate was 18 to 3. Ford was one of the 18. Among the eight Republican state senators also voting for the largest tax increase in Nevada history was Ben Kieckhefer, who would later become Gov. Lombardo’s chief of staff during Lombardo’s first legislative session, and James Settelmeyer, who Lombardo as governor would appoint Director of the state Dept. of Conservation and Natural Resources. Settelmeyer also unsuccessfully sought the Republican primary nomination for Nevada’s 2nd congressional district this year, and was backed by Lombardo.


Another anti-Ford ad, being aired by the Lombardo-aligned Better Nevada PAC, says Ford as a state senator voted to raise taxes 15 times, taxes which, according to the ad, would total $3 billion. 


At least two of those votes, and about half the $3 billion, are accounted for by the 2015 Sandoval tax package. Presumably.


I say presumably because it’s not clear what votes on which taxes the Better Nevada PAC is referring to in its ad. This week I repeatedly asked the political consulting firm November, Inc., whose Jeremy Hughes, according to the firm’s website, “is once again leading Better Nevada PAC,” for citations identifying each of Ford’s 15 votes and their dollar amounts. The firm failed to respond. 


November Inc. is a highly regarded political consulting firm, and not just in Nevada. It’s hard to believe the firm would create an ad for a client without having facts to back up the charges in the ad. November Inc.’s failure to provide citations in an ad placed by the PAC that November Inc. leads, however, makes it difficult for the public to know for sure to what degree the statements in the PAC’s ad are true.


But, to reiterate, presumably the Sandoval tax package is the cornerstone of the ad’s claims.


According to November Inc.’s website, Hughes also managed Sandoval’s reelection (over only token opposition, by the way) in 2014, and also consulted on Republican Mark Hutchison’s successful campaign for lieutenant governor that year. Hutchison, who would become a Better Nevada PAC fixture,  was not only a gushing supporter of Sandoval and his agenda in 2015. Hutchison had come to the lieutenant governor’s job straight from serving as a Republican state senator, and was no doubt helpful in whipping up support among his former Senate Republican colleagues for the largest tax increase in Nevada history.


The crew Lombardo is riding with now had a hell of a lot more to do with enacting the largest tax increase in Nevada history than Aaron Ford did. If Lombardo sincerely feels Ford’s vote for something another Republican governor accomplished that Lombardo hasn’t — a major legislative achievement — disqualifies Ford to be governor, how nauseating it must be for Lombardo to have all those people who did so much to pass the largest tax increase in Nevada history working right under Lombardo’s nose.


The more likely scenario, of course, is Lombardo himself doesn’t take the ads aired on his behalf seriously.


Which raises the question: Why should anybody else?
This column was originally published in the Nevada Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘An unprecedented day’: How Vermonters learned of 9/11 — and who remembers 25 years later
description:
“The biggest thing for me was how much America came together,” an eyewitness with state ties recalled of the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. “There wasn’t the nonsense that’s in the news now.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘An unprecedented day’: How Vermonters learned of 9/11 — and who remembers 25 years later.
text:
Smoke billows over the Manhattan skyline on Sept. 11, 2001. Photo by Daniel Hulshizer/AP

Driving to work on the bluebird morning of Sept. 11, 2001, I turned on the car radio to hear that hijacked planes had struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, set the Pentagon afire outside Washington, D.C., and slammed into a seemingly random field in rural Pennsylvania.
My first response: What kind of shock jock is trying to re-create the 1938 Martian-invasion broadcast drama “The War of the Worlds”?
A quarter-century later, I’m one of many Vermonters who can recall the rest of the story. Then again, about 100 million Americans — nearly one-third of today’s population, the U.S. census reports — weren’t born yet in 2001 or were too young to remember.
“The current generation lives in a world that was created by 9/11,” Burlington historian Garrett Graff says in the new Netflix documentary “Turning Point: Generation 9/11.” “If you start to scratch at almost any aspect of our daily lives in the United States today, I can show you how 9/11 changed that part of our country.”
Scholars point to the combined attacks’ death toll of nearly 3,000 people — at least 15 with ties to the Green Mountain State, according to online records — and the resulting birth of the “war on terror,” the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and increased surveillance, partisanship and polarization.
Vermonters, for their part, talk of things more personal.

Flames shoot from the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C., on Sept. 11, 2001. Photo by Will Morris/AP

Vermonters woke on Sept. 11, 2001, to headlines reporting the aftershocks of then-Gov. Howard Dean’s announcement that he wouldn’t seek a sixth term the next year.
“Many were still reeling from the news,” noted one of three front-page Rutland Herald stories on the subject.
On television, morning shows were minutes from signing off when American Airlines Flight 11, traveling from Boston to Los Angeles, flew into the World Trade Center’s north tower at 8:46 a.m.
“We just got a report in that there’s been some sort of explosion,” said “Good Morning America” co-anchor Diane Sawyer amid footage of the 110-floor skyscraper belching smoke.
A block and a half away from the crash, Michael Rosen — a 1974 Rutland High School graduate turned financial software developer — had seen the fluorescent lights flicker, heard a sharp scratch in his phone line, felt the floor shake. He was still speculating on the cause when United Airlines Flight 175, on its way from Boston to Los Angeles, smashed into the south tower at 9:03 a.m.
“The people in our corner office shrieked and groaned,” Rosen went on to write in “What Else But Home,” a 2009 memoir I reported on for the 10th anniversary of 9/11 in 2011.
Rosen had phoned his family and was preparing to flee when the south tower fell at 9:59 a.m., followed by the north tower at 10:28 a.m.
“The sky was gray cloud rushing toward us,” Rosen wrote of the first collapse. “Palms flat against the glass, I waited as the plume came but realized the windows might burst and I shouldn’t be there. I stepped halfway back. The room went dark.”
Across the East River in Brooklyn, Norma Hardy — who retired this past March as Vermont’s first Black female police chief — was home preparing for her afternoon shift as an officer for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, owner of the World Trade Center.
Hardy had yet to see or hear the news when her mother called. Did she know about the twin towers? The American Flight 77 from Washington, D.C., to Los Angeles that had crashed into the Pentagon at 9:37 a.m.? The United Flight 93 from Newark, New Jersey, to San Francisco that had plowed into a Pennsylvania field at 10:02 a.m.?
Skip work and stay home, Hardy’s mother said. But the officer wasn’t deterred. She had received a medal of valor for helping commuters and children trapped after the first World Trade Center bombing in 1993. Driving through a dark highway tunnel to Manhattan on 9/11, she emerged to an instantly changed world.
“It was just complete chaos — people running, people bleeding, people trying to wash their eyes out, people hurt and looking for help,” Hardy told me for a 20th anniversary story. “We didn’t know if other planes were coming, if someone was going to start shooting at us, if things would start to explode. It was like a scene from ‘The Twilight Zone,’ I usually tell people, because I can’t think of what else would describe it.”

Workers check the United Airlines Flight 93 crash site near Shanksville, Pa., on Sept. 11, 2001. Photo by Keith Srakocic/AP

As a Rutland Herald reporter on 9/11, I arrived at the newsroom to see colleagues watching it all live on television.
“It is completely impossible to understand why this is happening,” “Today” show co-anchor Katie Couric told viewers before the steely twin towers, each a quarter-mile high, crumbled into clouds of ash.
Professionally, we raced to print an early afternoon “extra” edition — the first for the morning publication since Vermont Gov. Richard Snelling died of cardiac arrest in August 1991 and the second since President John F. Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963.
“This is the most devastating attack on the United States of America since Pearl Harbor,” Bernie Sanders, then Vermont’s congressman, told the paper. “We have to acknowledge that this is an unprecedented day.”
Personally, everyone reeled with questions. Had our co-workers heard from their grown children living in New York and the nation’s capital or leaving on morning flights? Or the family and friends unaccounted for coast-to-coast amid groundings of all aircraft and evacuations of everything from the Statue of Liberty to Seattle’s Space Needle?
All struggled to make landline calls, as the iPhone wasn’t introduced until 2007.
“Within minutes of the terrorist attacks, telephone lines, wireless relays and internet news sites were jammed by users trying to find out what was going on,” a colleague wrote in a story. “Communication company officials said their networks couldn’t handle the overload.”
Our family and friends were accounted for by the time the “extra” edition rolled off the presses at 1:23 p.m. Not that anyone could exhale. The Herald’s regular deadline just hours away, we turned our attention to the ripple effects.
The Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant, then operating in Vernon, went to its highest state of alert.
“Yankee stands in super-high profile,” a Nuclear Regulatory Commission member told the paper. “There’s nothing else in Vermont that would do that damage.”
Vermont Catholic Bishop Kenneth Angell led a special Mass in Burlington, not knowing that his younger brother, David, an Emmy Award-winning writer and producer of such television comedies as “Cheers” and “Frasier,” had been killed on the first plane to hit the World Trade Center.
ABC News anchor Barbara Walters and CNN host Larry King doggedly sought an interview once news of the death was reported later that day. The bishop declined. But as Christmas approached, he agreed to speak with a state-based reporter. I arrived at the church’s Chittenden County office that December to find Angell surrounded by more than 1,000 cards and letters.
“I’m sorry your brother went to heaven,” one child wrote in a crayoned condolence.
That sparked a bittersweet smile in a man who believed in eternal salvation.
“Personally, it’s a day that will affect me very deeply,” said Angell, who died in 2016. “But we’ve got to go on. We have to forgive, as difficult as it might be.”

Barre Rock of Ages workers Evan Ladd (left) and Andy Hebert cut granite in 2019 for New York’s National September 11 Memorial & Museum. Photo by Lisa Rathke/AP

Television networks aired round-the-clock 9/11 coverage for five days, surpassing the record of more than 70 consecutive hours after Kennedy’s assassination. The Herald printed special front pages and stories for a week, offering such headlines as “Officials watch, wait in Vermont” and “Local crews standing ready to help.”
For the first anniversary in 2002, I wrote about dozens of state observances, including outgoing Gov. Dean sharing a moment of silence at Windsor High School and Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel speaking at Middlebury College. 
“The question everyone is asking is how does one remember Sept. 11?” Wiesel told a crowd that filled all 1,000 seats in the campus chapel. “I wish I knew the answer. One thing is clear. If I’m here it’s because I believe in your right to have a better future.”
For the 10th anniversary in 2011, I wrote about Rosen’s view from his office window.
“I watched so many people die, but I wasn’t dead,” Rosen told me. “When you look at how delicate things really are … If you’re lucky enough to live, respect those who died — but keep living.”
For the 20th anniversary in 2021, I wrote about Hardy seeing clouds of smoke dissipate into a silver lining.
“The biggest thing for me was how much America came together and showed resilience,” she told me. “That stays in my mind, especially now when everybody seemingly hates everybody. Then, there wasn’t the nonsense that’s in the news now. Everyone remembered they were all Americans, even if it was only for a little bit of time.”
Today, much has changed. Take Rosen, whom I email annually this time of year. He’s now living and working in Vietnam as founder of that country’s first independent whisky distillery.
“I feel mostly betrayed by Sept. 11,” Rosen most recently messaged, speaking not only of that day’s losses but also its lingering health effects on survivors. “Aside from that, life is magic. Truly.”
Hardy, now traveling in her retirement, will mark the anniversary with an annual video call with others who were present at what history calls ground zero.
“My thoughts, as usual, are on those that were lost on that day and the many people affected by illness,” she most recently emailed. “It is important that we never forget.”
But how does one remember if they weren’t alive or old enough to comprehend back then? Perhaps by learning now. A quarter-century ago, I thought my grandparents’ stories of Pearl Harbor were irrelevant tales of a time gone by. Today, recalling images of a fall day morphing into something that looked like a nuclear winter, I see things differently.
Disclosure: Garrett Graff is a member of the board of trustees for the Vermont Journalism Trust, which owns VTDigger.

name: Washington State Standard
title: US employers are relying more and more on ‘disposable’ workers
description: When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a […]
text:
(Photo via Getty Images)
When I leave my Boston condo every day, I say good morning to the concierge, who works for a contracting company providing staff to residential buildings. When I conduct an interview in a nearby building, the people who clean that office at night are contractors. The person who serves me my lunch sandwich is a part-timer with no career prospects in that job.
When my best intentions to eat well are for naught and I gorge on Doritos, I remember that the tasters PepsiCo hires to test the chips’ addictiveness are contractors.
These are all examples of what I call “disposable jobs.” People who have them work at an employer’s site, but their employer makes no commitment to them regarding career prospects or job security. My research shows that employers treat more than 1 in 3 U.S. workers as disposable. That comes to just under 57 million full- or part-time workers out of the nation’s workforce of 162 million.
I am a labor economist. In my new book, “Disposable Workers: The Transformation of Employment,” I explain why this is happening, what forms it takes, how common it is, what the consequences are for people and for society, and what can be done about it.
 3 different varieties

To learn more, I commissioned a nationally representative survey of over 6,000 people in late 2022. I also interviewed nearly 100 workers, employers and policymakers.
I found that there are three categories of disposable workers.
1. Contractors who are employed by a staffing firm but work at a client’s site. Examples include temporary office workers, building cleaners and security guards. Many of these people are poorly paid, but some, such as travel nurses, are highly compensated. My survey shows that these contractors account for 13% of the workforce.
2. Freelancers who work for companies, organizations or agencies without being employees. Examples include Uber and Lyft drivers, food delivery drivers, computer programmers and freelance journalists. In my survey, organizational freelancers represent 5% of the workforce. I don’t include in this category freelancers who work for individual people, such as most dog-walkers and handymen, because my focus is on how employers treat their employees.
3. Marginal workers who are employed by companies, organizations or agencies. They lack career opportunities, and their jobs have high turnover built in. Marginal workers account for 17% of the workforce in my survey.
Marginal work is important due to its magnitude and because although those jobs look standard, they are designed to be disposable.
 Who are marginal workers?

Staff attorneys are quintessential marginal employees. They’re hired by law firms as employees, but the central feature of their jobs is that they are not on the promotion ladder to partner. Unlike their career-track counterparts, they have no job security. They are often hired to do the grunt work on a specific case, with the understanding that there is no commitment to keep them on if business lags or the project ends.
Adjunct professors are another good example. This group includes part-timers who teach a small number of courses and full-time contract faculty, but in both cases they lack job security and aren’t on track to obtain permanent, tenured, academic jobs.
In 1970 people with tenure or tenure-track jobs constituted 73% of those teaching at colleges and universities. By 2021 only 32% had that status, and the rest were adjunct instructors or contract faculty.
 Part-time marginal workers

Another example of marginal work is part-timers.
Employing part-time workers costs less than having full-timers on the payroll. Part-time jobs pay an hourly wage that is nearly 20% below what workers with full-time jobs earn after age, education, occupation and industry are taken into account. When benefits are considered, the gap rises by another 5%.
A second advantage of part-timers from the employer’s perspective is higher turnover, which provides an easy path to be able to adjust the size of the workforce and which enables them to avoid investing in career development.
When a team of researchers led by professor Susan Lambert interviewed 88 employers that pay low wages, they found that many use part-time work to make their workforces more “flexible.” One manager explained that high churn of part-timers gave the company so much flexibility that they didn’t need temp workers.
“Temp workers: We don’t need them,” he said. “Wait a day for turnover.”
Evidence that employers try to maximize the number of people working for them part time instead of full time and with benefits arose after the Affordable Care Act fully took effect in 2014.
The ACA requires that employers with 50 or more employees either provide them with health insurance or pay for them to buy it, but only for people who work 30 or more hours a week. Otherwise they pay, as of 2026, a penalty of US$3,340 per uninsured employee.
Another team of researchers compared trends in part-time work in three low-wage industries – retail, hotels and restaurants, before and after the ACA rolled out. They found that the use of part-timers increased by 500,000 in the years after the Affordable Care Act was implemented. This suggests that companies add to their part-time ranks to save on the health insurance costs of standard employment.
 Forces behind this trend

Why do employers want many of their workers to be disposable?
A primary motive is to save money. Employing freelancers and contractors means they can avoid mandatory benefits such as Social Security contributions and, for larger employers, contributing to the cost of health insurance.
Marginal workers, to be sure, do receive these benefits. But the high turnover built into their jobs means that their employers can invest less in their training and avoid the management costs otherwise associated with layoff severance and fair treatment on the job.
An additional motive for many employers is a lack of respect for what front-line employees can contribute. A 2023 report from the McKinsey consulting firm illustrated this tendency when it asserted that 5% of employees deliver 95% of “an organization’s value.”
This claim, which I believe is inaccurate, still speaks volumes about the attitude of McKinsey and the firms they interviewed regarding the other 95% of workers. They see those employees as disposable.
 Less pay and job satisfaction

My survey showed that contractors, freelancers who work for employers and marginal employees all earn less than regular workers do.
In addition, the survey found that contractors and marginal workers are notably less satisfied with their jobs compared with regular workers, whereas freelancers, due to their ability to choose where and when to work, are more satisfied.
The public also pays a price for the use of disposable workers. As examples, researchers have found that hospital infection rates rise when cleaners are contract workers and that the use of contractors leads to a higher rate of industrial accidents.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Legislators deserve a pay increase — if they do the job
description: According to a recent South Dakota Searchlight story, legislators could get a 4% raise when they gather in Pierre this January. Legislator pay is set at 20% of the state’s household median income as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. The median household income is expected to go up this year, bumping annual legislative salaries […]
text:
Legislators listen to Gov. Kristi Noem present her annual budget address in the South Dakota House of Representatives on Dec. 5, 2023. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)According to a recent South Dakota Searchlight story, legislators could get a 4% raise when they gather in Pierre this January. Legislator pay is set at 20% of the state’s household median income as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. The median household income is expected to go up this year, bumping annual legislative salaries from $15,970 to $16,608.
Tying legislator pay to the median household income was a smart move on the part of the Legislature. It was always awkward for lawmakers to propose, justify and vote on raises for themselves. That’s particularly true for lawmakers who specifically campaign on going to the Capitol to cut spending and government waste.
In years like this, the state budget’s “Big Three”— state employees, education and health care — probably wish they had a deal just like lawmakers. A 4% raise looks pretty good to them, after initially getting no raise in the governor’s proposed budget. At the end of the last session, they did get a 1.4% raise. However, there is a catch in the Legislature’s deal that may give the Big Three pause about asking for similar treatment. One of the selling points for lawmakers, one of the ways they justified making themselves eligible for a raise every year, was the notion that their pay could go down if the state’s median household income dropped.
Lawmaker salaries could top $16,000 during next year’s South Dakota legislative session

More than 16 grand seems like a generous paycheck for spending nine weeks in Pierre. The legislative session, however, is far from the only responsibility of our elected officials.
They serve on a wide variety of standing committees that can meet throughout the rest of the year. There are summer study committees exploring special topics. Sometimes that exploration can take lawmakers on the road as they seek testimony across the state from stakeholders and taxpayers.
Another call on their time includes the opportunity to attend conferences and seminars. It’s easy to scoff at these as taxpayer-funded junkets, but they often provide the best chance for citizen-legislators to get the training that they need.
Any effort to boost the pay for lawmakers serves to open the door to a more diversified Legislature. For too long the Legislature was largely the domain of lawyers, farmers and the retired — the only people who could afford to spend the winter in Pierre. Paying better wages opens up the possibility of seeing more younger people, more businesspeople and more women elected to office.
South Dakotans can’t afford to cheap out on legislator pay if they want to expect adequate, professional representation in Pierre. By the same standard, lawmakers have to earn that pay. In the recent past, thanks to the shenanigans of some lawmakers, the ship of state has sometimes resembled a showboat.
Lawmaking should be serious business, but some legislators take a less than serious approach. Examples include:

An adopted resolution to “seek the Lord most high,” admonishing South Dakotans to pray and fast every July.
Failed legislation seeking to place the 10 Commandments in every public school classroom.
One legislator pulling a vanishing act before a critical vote on economic development incentives for data centers.
Risking millions in federal highway funding for a bill that would have allowed drivers and passengers the personal freedom to not wear a seat belt.
Seeking, unsuccessfully, to deny funding for the Huron School District over its bathroom policy.
Proposing, until cooler heads prevailed, to return $87 million in federal funds earmarked for high-speed internet access over worries about the national debt.
Attempting to relitigate the COVID-19 pandemic by seeking legitimacy for drugs that have a less than legitimate background.
Threatening to put librarians in handcuffs if they allowed obscene material to fall into the hands of minors.

Serving as a legislator takes an odd combination of political ambition, policy expertise and winter driving skills. It should also take a level of professionalism and seriousness that won’t cause taxpayers to raise their eyebrows when they hear that lawmakers are getting a raise in pay. As the pay for legislators increases, we can only hope that the level of their competence increases as well.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi’s last competitive US House races occurred in 2010. Will 2026 change the trend?
description: Rep. Gene Taylor, D-Miss., left, and President George W. Bush watch a Mexican Marine clean up Hurricane Katrina debris at the 28th Street Elementary School in Gulfport, Miss., on Monday, Sept. 12, 2005.
text:
For a brief two-year period from 2008 until 2010, Democrats, despite not having won a presidential election in Mississippi since 1976, held three of the state’s four U.S. House seats.
But Mississippi’s 2026 U.S. House races are happening in November against the backdrop that since 2010 Republicans have held three of the four seats.
In 2010, Democrats Travis Childers, who held the 1st District seat in north Mississippi for one two-year term, and Gene Taylor, who held the 4th District seat in south Mississippi from 1989 until 2010, were defeated.
Both Taylor and Childers first won their congressional seats in special elections. Taylor won in 1989 when newly elected Republican U.S. Rep. Larkin Smith died in a plane crash. 
In office, Taylor often was a thorn in the side for both parties. The Republicans could not defeat him. But Taylor often voted against the national Democrats. He voted to impeach Democratic President Bill Clinton, and he often did not vote for the Democrats’ choice for speaker. There were countless other examples where Taylor voted against the Democratic side.
While Taylor held the 4th District seat for more than a decade after winning the special election, Childers served only one term before being defeated by state Sen. Alan Nunnelee of Tupelo.
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Travis Childers  Credit: U.S. House of Representatives
Childers won a special election after incumbent 1st District U.S. Rep. Roger Wicker was appointed to the U.S. Senate by then-Gov. Haley Barbour when incumbent Trent Lott unexpectedly resigned.
Childers, who was a former chancery clerk in Prentiss County in northeast Mississippi, initially won the seat in part because of the geography of the district. The district included both populous DeSoto County in northwest Mississippi just south of Memphis and rural northeast Mississippi anchored by Tupelo.
Northeast Mississippi voters, by and large, put party preference aside and voted for Childers, a fellow northeast Mississippian, over Republican Southaven Mayor Greg Davis from DeSoto County.
But in 2010, the Republicans nominated Nunnelee, another northeast Mississippian, removing Childers’ geographic advantage.
It could be argued the 2010 elections were the last competitive Mississippi House races. Republican state Rep. Steven Palazzo defeated Taylor 52% to 47% while Nunnelee upended Childers 55% to 41% in the November 2010 general election. Since Taylor’s and Childers’ losses, no Democratic candidate in any of the three majority-white districts has garnered as much as 35% of the vote.
Significant focus has been given to this November’s U.S. Senate race where Democratic District Attorney Scott Colom of Columbus is attempting to upend Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Much less attention has been given to the four U.S. House seats, where all four incumbents have opposition.
In Mississippi’s only majority-Black district, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson has been nearly as dominant electorally as his Republican colleagues in the three majority-white districts.
The bottom line is that the challengers in all four U.S. House races face long odds this November.
Various metrics have long identified Mississippi’s U.S. House districts as being non-competitive. Through the years, the respected Cook Political Report, based on its analysis of data, has ranked all four Mississippi House districts as high on its partisan voting index. In other words, the three majority-white districts have a strong Republican lean while the majority-Black district has a significant Democratic tilt.
Earlier this decade when the Mississippi Legislature was redrawing lines for the four U.S. House districts to ensure equal populations in each district based on the 2020 U.S. Census, the Democrats, led by Rep. Thompson, tried to make the districts less partisan. Thompson offered to take in more Republican-leaning areas to make his 2nd District more compact and in the process more competitive.
But Republicans, fearing that Thompson’s offer also would make the 3rd District represented by Michael Guest of Rankin County more competitive, rejected that offer.
The Legislature is expected to take another stab at congressional redistricting in the coming months in light of this year’s U.S. Supreme Court landmark ruling that allows minority voting strength to be diluted. Republican Gov. Tate Reeves and others have cited the ruling as an opportunity to defeat Thompson, only the second Black Mississippian to serve in the U.S. House since the 1800s.
It will be interesting to see which – if any – of the four U.S. House districts become more competitive as a result of that Supreme Court ruling and the anticipated redrawing of districts by the Mississippi Legislature at Reeves’ behest. Redrawn districts would first be used in the 2028 election.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Looming ballot deadline complicates GOP appeal of Missouri redistricting decision
description: The U.S. Supreme Court appeal filed late Friday by Missouri Republicans could be the surprise plot twist that results in a GOP triumph or an epilogue to a saga of a goal that stayed tantalizingly out of reach. In the filing, Republicans surrendered on the question of whether Missourians will see a referendum on the […]
text:
Missouri Republicans want the U.S. Supreme Court to overrule a decision of the Missouri Supreme Court ordering a congressional election in the districts used in 2024 (Jane Norman/States Newsroom).The U.S. Supreme Court appeal filed late Friday by Missouri Republicans could be the surprise plot twist that results in a GOP triumph or an epilogue to a saga of a goal that stayed tantalizingly out of reach.
In the filing, Republicans surrendered on the question of whether Missourians will see a referendum on the gerrymandered congressional map muscled through a 2025 special session. The filing from Republican Attorney General Catherine Hanaway in the name of Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins asks just that the revised map, used to nominate candidates in eight districts on Aug. 4, be the controlling boundaries for the Nov. 3 general election.
“On the one hand, Richard von Glahn — the referendum petition’s proponent — will get his referendum vote on Missouri’s congressional map regardless of what this court does,” wrote Lou Capozzi, the state solicitor general, in the application for an emergency stay. “The only question is whether he (joined by a small minority of the state’s voters) can void a congressional map before he gets his vote. On the other hand, Missouri cannot run a timely, lawful federal election absent a stay.”
This is the congressional district map passed in 2025 and used in the Aug. 4 primary. (Screenshot from Missouri House website).
The court is being asked to stay the effect of Thursday’s Missouri Supreme Court decision that found People Not Politicians, the political action committee that sponsored the referendum petition, had submitted enough signatures for a constitutional use of the referendum power. 
As a result, Judge Ginger Gooch wrote, the new congressional map passed by the General Assembly had not taken effect and the court ordered Hoskins to conduct the general election in the boundaries used for elections in 2022 and 2024.
The redistricting plan passed in 2025 “is not the law and has never been the law,” Gooch wrote in a footnote to the unanimous opinion. “There is only one valid congressional redistricting in effect — the congressional redistricting the General Assembly established in 2022.”
If the Supreme Court does not intervene, the election is expected to result in six Republicans and two Democrats winning. An order to use the 2025 map is expected to give the GOP seven seats because the boundaries of six districts were rearranged.
While the referendum may prevent the map from being used in future elections, the prize is the extra GOP seat in a year where Republicans worry about losing their slim majority.
The application went to Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who is the Supreme Court justice assigned to the Eighth Judicial Circuit. Kavanaugh gave People Not Politicians a deadline of noon Monday to file a response.
Mike Wolff, a former Missouri Supreme Court chief justice and dean emeritus of St. Louis University School of Law, said he expects Kavanaugh to deny the stay. 
“There is no authority given to the federal courts to tell a state how to conduct its elections, except the Voting Rights Act, which is pretty much dead, or another constitutional principle,” Wolff said. “Other than that, the federal courts don’t have any business telling the states how to run their elections.”
The Missouri congressional district map passed by lawmakers in 2022 and used for the 2022 and 2024 elections. The Missouri Supreme Court ordered this map to be used for the Nov. 3 election (Missouri Secretary of State’s Office).
Michael Smith, an associate professor of law at the University of Oklahoma, said he expects Kavanaugh to consider carefully whether the procedures and deadlines in Missouri’s state election laws have been met.
Smith is the author of a research paper, “Missouri’s Law of Constitutional Interpretation” and he sees the Missouri Supreme Court decision as being firmly supported in the text of the Missouri Constitution and precedent.
“What the Supreme Court is going to do, I would like to hope, is uphold the Missouri Supreme Court ruling, given its compliance with state law,” Smith said. 
People Not Politicians issued a statement saying it expects the Supreme Court to rule against Hoskins and Hanaway.
“Anyone with a basic understanding of civics knows the legislature, which in Missouri includes the people via the referendum, is who makes law, not the judiciary,” von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians, said in a news release Saturday. “The Attorney General is asking the Supreme Court of the United States to create a law that has never been the law in Missouri.”
In the application for an emergency stay, Capozzi argued that reverting to the districts used in 2022 and 2024 is impossible and violates the rights of voters who participated in the primary.
Behind the drama in Washington, actions are occurring while a state law deadline looms.
U.S. Rep. Bob Onder of Lake St. Louis, who represents the 2nd District, and state Sen. Rick Brattin of Harrisonville, GOP nominee in the 5th District, and two voters, sued Hoskins in federal court for the Eastern District of Missouri asking for an order blocking the Missouri Supreme Court ruling from being implemented.
“The entire state of Missouri has now been plunged into legal and electoral uncertainty over which congressional maps govern Missouri’s 2026 general election and which candidates represent whom,” Republican Party attorney Marc Ellinger wrote in the filing. “This court should issue all appropriate relief without haste to ensure free and fair elections in November.” 
Ellinger asked for an expedited consideration. 
On Saturday afternoon, Hanaway’s office, instead of defending the Missouri Supreme Court action, said in a filing on behalf of Hoskins that it agreed with Onder and Brattin.
“The Missouri Supreme Court’s order patently violates federal law in several respects,” Capozzi wrote.
Chuck Hatfield, attorney for People Not Politicians, said he believes Kavanaugh will refuse to issue the stay because the only reason the decision is being made now is because of choices Hoskins made to delay.
“A person who has done wrong cannot ask for relief to solve an injury they caused,” Hatfield said.
And he said the Eastern District lawsuit violated basic principles that a true dispute must exist between the parties for the courts to intervene. Hatfield filed a motion to intervene in the case Saturday afternoon, writing there are “serious doubts that a genuine adversarial proceeding exists in this action.”
“Cheech agrees with Chong that pot is groovy,” Hatfield said in an email. “Its what’s known in the law as a collusive lawsuit.”
After Hatfield filed the motion to intervene, Chief District Judge Stephen Clark issued an order giving the parties until noon Monday to file additional arguments on “whether federal abstention doctrines” mean the case should be dismissed as well as the impact of the pending U.S. Supreme Court appeal.
The decisions that delayed legal action on the basic questions surrounding the referendum were discretionary actions by Hoskins.
People Not Politicians submitted more than 300,000 signatures on Dec. 9, two days before the redistricting law was set to take effect. At that point, Hoskins had the option of using a random sample of the lot to determine if it had the required 5% of voters in six districts, or sending pages out for line-by-line verification.
A random sampling procedure would have required Hoskins to deliver his decision on the sufficiency of the petition by early February, weeks before candidate filing began. Instead, by using line-by-line verification, the deadline was pushed to Aug. 4, the date of the primary, and Hoskins won an interim decision that he was allowed to consider the law to be in effect until the referendum was certified for the ballot.
The questions decided Thursday could have been resolved before candidate filing ended in March, Hatfield said.
“He had the opportunity to avoid all of this and he chose not to,” Hatfield said.
The deadline for finalizing the Nov. 3 ballot is Tuesday. One state law prohibits local election authorities from adding or removing candidates or issues after that date and another extends that prohibition to the courts.
Under Missouri law, nothing can be added or removed from general election ballots after Tuesday. Ballots must be printed and ready for delivery to overseas voters by Sept. 19. 
The law limiting the timing for court-ordered additions to the ballot was passed after the Missouri Supreme Court in 1996, less than three weeks before the election, struck the fiscal note language from a ballot question and ordered election officials to place an “opaque sticker over the previously printed ballot language…”
The state’s application to the Supreme Court asks Kavanaugh for a decision by Sept. 14. The lawsuit filed by Onder and Brattin asks for quick action without setting a goal for a decision.
The federal courts should respect the Tuesday deadline, Wolff and Smith said.
The legal doctrine of unclean hands could also play a role, Smith said.
A federal judge in December said Hoskins did not have to wait for signature verification to declare his belief that the referendum petition was unconstitutional. That could have resolved the legal questions even earlier than a random sampling.
“To the extent there is a crisis, it is a crisis of the state’s own making,” Smith said. “In asking for a stay in the judgment, there are principles that counsel against giving that extraordinary relief if the parties seeking that relief have contributed to that need for it.”
