name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Press freedom shouldn’t be a casualty in Arkansas’ data center wars
description: There’s no such thing as a slam dunk court case, but the constitutional argument against prior restraint comes close. For nearly a century, the U.S. Supreme Court has ruled against efforts to prevent news outlets from publishing material. That includes the landmark Pentagon Papers decision that showed the heavy burden the government must meet. An […]
text:
A marble plaque inscribed with the First Amendment sits on Independence Mall in Philadelphia, Pa.
(Photo by Raymond Boyd/Getty Images)There’s no such thing as a slam dunk court case, but the constitutional argument against prior restraint comes close.
For nearly a century, the U.S. Supreme Court has ruled against efforts to prevent news outlets from publishing material. That includes the landmark Pentagon Papers decision that showed the heavy burden the government must meet.
An agreement about an Arkansas data center that doesn’t include any details about national security wouldn’t meet that burden. 
So it would have been easy to shrug off Entergy Arkansas’ unsuccessful attempt to block the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette and Arkansas Times from disclosing more details about that agreement. 
But the fact that the utility even took such an extraordinary step, and the legal threat news organizations may still face, highlights the threat to a bedrock principle of a free press.
It’s also another sign of how transparency is being sacrificed during an increasingly unpopular nationwide data center boom to meet the growing demand for computing power.
Entergy argued that trade secrets were at risk if the Democrat-Gazette published further details about its agreement with a Google subsidiary for a solar facility needed for a multibillion dollar data center. 
The newspaper published a story based on confidential, non-public documents that were released to a central Arkansas woman, Jessica Kivell, through a Freedom of Information Act request. Entergy said those documents were released in error.
Entergy’s lawsuit also targeted Kivell and the Arkansas Times, even though the Times said it has never received the documents. In addition to seeking to block publication, the lawsuit also asked for an order requiring the details be removed from their online stories.



Let us know what you think...


 


There’s a reason why these kinds of prior restraint efforts are rare. A long line of cases in state and federal courts, including ones from Arkansas, spell out the high bar that must be met.
“In the First Amendment, the Founding Fathers gave the free press the protection it must have to fulfill its essential role in our democracy. The press was to serve the governed, not the governors,” Justice Hugo Black wrote in his concurring opinion in the Pentagon Papers ruling in 1971.
That reasoning is partly why U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky denied Entergy’s request for a temporary restraining order. But the risks of further action and legal threats still remain.
A day after his ruling, Rudofsky said in a court docket entry that Entergy would not be pursuing a preliminary injunction. But it’s not clear whether that closes the door on the utility seeking civil damages over the publication.
Even if Entergy doesn’t pursue any further action, the case risks creating a chilling effect on everyday citizens, journalists and news organizations trying to seek more information about data center projects around the state.
The secrecy surrounding these projects has fueled the bipartisan pushback just as much as concerns about the facilities’ energy usage.
Arkansans are being asked to trust policymakers’ decisions about data centers and companies’ assurances about them. But it’s hard to justify that trust when vital information is being kept from them. 
It’s even harder to trust those promises when data center supporters ask a court to ignore a core tenet of the First Amendment and when threats loom against citizens seeking more information about the projects.
The battle over press freedom comes at a perilous time for journalism, with reporters facing political attacks, threats of violence and legal intimidation. 
But it also comes at a politically fraught moment for data center supporters, who have seen the concerns about the facilities and artificial intelligence become a defining issue in midterm races around the country.
There should be vigorous debate about data centers and how to balance the need for them with the growing concerns that communities have. The First Amendment, however, shouldn’t fall by the wayside during that debate.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Volunteer fire departments are shrinking. For some, it’s a call to action
description: Career firefighters who also volunteer in local departments have become increasingly vital to the fire service in CT as membership shrinks.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

David Elliott stood on his front porch in sweatpants in the pre-dawn darkness in rural Northeastern Connecticut, waiting for his golden retriever to come inside for breakfast.
His alarm went off at 4:40 a.m., the start of his second 24-hour shift of the week. This is the hard one, he said.
Elliott waited for the Keurig to fill his carrot-colored mug with coffee. His duffel bag was packed.
He turned the TV to the morning news and changed into his red Fairfield Fire Department T-shirt. It takes nearly two hours to drive there, where he works as a career firefighter.

Before the sun rises, David Elliott prepares for a 24-hour shift as a Fairfield firefighter. He leaves his house in Woodstock with dogs Sweetie and Finley on Aug. 19, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Finley (Elliott’s pup) and Sweetie (Elliott’s girlfriend’s dog) piled into the back seat of his car. He drove just down the street, to the house where his parents still live, on Lake Bungee in Woodstock. They would look after the dogs while he was at work on the other side of the state.
Elliott’s next stop was the Bungay Fire Brigade, the volunteer fire station where he is chief, to drop off reports he wrote the day before. Then he started his commute southwest, through the mist and the sunrise. 
Elliott is not the only firefighter in Connecticut to work in a paid department and volunteer elsewhere. But Elliott also works as a fire marshal, he serves on committees in the Fairfield department and is a state firefighting instructor, among other things. 
He and others like him have become increasingly vital to the fire service in Connecticut as the number of certified firefighters shrinks.
David Elliott drives an emergency response vehicle along Pole Bridge Road in Woodstock on July 29, 2026. His volunteer fire department covers 31 square miles with some homes along narrow dirt roads, making access difficult or impossible for larger emergency response trucks.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Data released by Comptroller Sean Scanlon’s office in May 2025 revealed “sobering insights into the severity of Connecticut’s dwindling firefighting forces,” according to the report. Since 2017, the state has seen a 62.7% decrease in volunteer firefighters.
In 2020, the National Fire Protection Association recorded the lowest overall number of volunteer and career firefighters since 1991 and saw a drop off in the number of volunteer firefighters about 10 years ago. Almost 25% of volunteer firefighters have left since 2008, according to the NFPA.
But the shortage of volunteers indirectly points to an increase in the number of paid firefighters across the country as more departments realize the only way to keep their forces intact is to pay them.
Keith Wucik, the chief of the Preston Fire Department, said the town transitioned from an entirely volunteer to partially paid department when a 2005 consultant recommended hiring administrative and chief roles. A couple of years later, the department started hiring paid firefighters as well. 
“The town of Preston had to hire full-time firefighters and part-time firefighters to make sure we could get out the door to do our job,” Wucik said.
The fire department now has six full-time, 12 part-time and nine volunteer firefighters, and the department spends $1.2 million on firefighter salaries and benefits, excluding gear and training costs. 
“It’s a lot of money,” Wucik said. 
Fire departments across Connecticut, like Preston’s, rely on grants along with taxpayer money to fund fire departments, but budgets in small communities are generally tighter.
Woodstock’s town government budget for fire protection is $631,760 for the 2026-2027 fiscal year, which includes funding for the town’s three volunteer departments, administrative work and contracts, notably without any firefighter labor costs.
According to a 2022 report, about 64% of all Connecticut fire departments are fully volunteer.
“The volunteer service is dying. There’s no question about that,” Elliott said. Especially when called to larger emergencies, like structure fires, the three volunteer departments in Woodstock have shifted toward relying on automated and mutual aid programs that dispatch multiple stations at once just to send enough personnel. 

Places for firefighters to leave their gear at the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association remain empty on July 29, 2026. The station is one of three in Woodstock and provides emergency medical services for the town as well.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The problem with the volunteer service is the unavailability of people to drive to the station and suit up, according to Elliott. 
“It could be a Tuesday at 2 o’clock in the afternoon, and I could get 12 people ready to go right out the door and volunteer, or it could be a Friday at 6 p.m. and I got nobody,” he said.  
Jeffrey Morrissette, the state fire administrator, said he saw similar concerns about recruitment and retention through a statewide fire service survey, which concluded in late 2024. A bill passed this year was partially inspired by those survey results, he said, and aims to make public fire protection in Connecticut “more transparent.”
“There’s a lot of fear out there about the legislation that just passed this past session that the state is trying to take over,” Morrissette said. “I don’t think that was anybody’s motivation.”
The law requires fire departments to register with municipal authorities for review with the The National Emergency Response Information System, to develop local fire protection plans identifying emergency response procedures, and to create programs “to incentivize the regionalization of fire protection services and sharing fire protection resources,” among other things.
Morrissette also recognizes that departments in smaller communities have limited capacity to respond to emergencies, especially during the work week, and that people with multiple roles, like Elliott, are crucial.
“Sometimes I wonder what we would do without those people, but sometimes it’s almost to the detriment of their personal lives,” he said. 

Commitment
Elliott’s personal life seems to blend with his work, especially when he’s called on weekends and holidays. 
“We may have sat down for a meal and had a house full of people, but if there was a call, he would leave,” his mother, Barbara Elliott said, adding that it didn’t matter if it was Thanksgiving dinner or a birthday party. 
Her town “would really be hurting” without firefighters like her son to answer those calls. “These people commit a lot of time and effort to helping the community by helping people not only with fires,” she said. 




The Bungay Fire Brigade motto, “neighbors helping neighbors,” appears on engines and other vehicles that respond to calls in Woodstock on July 23, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
David Elliott displays memorabilia from his decades of volunteer and career firefighting jobs across Connecticut on his porch in Woodstock on Aug, 20, 2026. Items are arranged for the picture.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
David Elliott holds extrication equipment in Woodstock on July 23, 2026. Firefighters use the Jaws of Life to cut apart vehicles and access victims during car accidents.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror




As the volunteer fire service has atrophied, the diversity of calls fire departments respond to have expanded. 
“We are the fix-all of emergency services,” Elliott said, referring to firefighters as “professional problem solvers.” Calls often include car accidents, search and rescue, downed power lines from storms, hazmat issues, medical incidents, animals caught in trees and beeping smoke detectors. Beyond that, Elliott’s job also includes aspects of fire prevention. 
He joined the fire service in 2000 when he was just 16 at the same station in Woodstock where he volunteers today. 
“I was just hooked,” he said, remembering when he watched his older brother respond to a brush fire call. 
Firefighters from left to right, David Elliott, Josh Bottone, Adam Bottone, and Glenn Elliott in a picture on Elliott’s Facebook page, Aug. 20, 2026. Josh Bottone was the assistant chief of the Bungay Fire Brigade when the picture was taken and before he became the deputy chief for the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association, where he volunteers now. Glenn is David’s brother. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Culture
Familial ties like these are central to the fire service community and culture, along with recruitment and retention. 
Josh Bottone, the deputy chief of Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association down the road from Bungay and one of Elliott’s mentors, joined the fire service after his neighbor’s house burned down. One of the people who responded to that fire was Elliott’s aunt, a family friend and an EMT. Bottone then joined the fire service along with his two brothers and eventually became a chief in Woodstock.

Josh Bottone stands by a ladder truck in the Woodstock Volunteer Fire Association station on July 29, 2026. Bottone is the station’s deputy chief.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Both Elliott and Bottone attribute their long careers volunteering to their community connections. But Elliott sees that dedication as a rarity, since young people often leave the town for college or work after high school. If teens or young adults join, they often volunteer as a “stepping stone” to career firefighting and other emergency response jobs, he said. 
“You invest in the people as much as you can and you hope they stay,” Elliott said. After the volunteer fire department pays for basic certification classes, priced at $1,200, and one set of gear, worth $6,000, it’s costly if firefighters leave.
Richard Baron, a captain at Muddy Brook Fire Department — another volunteer department in Woodstock — sees the benefit of supporting new recruits who apply to career firefighting jobs. In that case, they also return to the volunteer departments with more experience. 
“The problem is the daytime,” he said, when they’re not available for calls.

Richard Baron stands by a tanker in the Muddy Brook Fire Department in Woodstock on July 29, 2026. Baron is a captain at the volunteer fire department and a veteran firefighter.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Like those career firefighters, Elliott brings valuable expertise to Bungay Fire Brigade. The job “helped me bring more knowledge and skills and training back to this [volunteer] department,” he said.
Establishing a presence in the community is important, but “age is legit the key,” Bottone said. Bottone, 54, says he relies on younger volunteers to go into burning buildings — a physically taxing job. In short, the fire service needs new young recruits, which is reflected in the comptroller’s 2025 report. Firefighters in Connecticut are on average older, compared to firefighters in the rest of the country.
As firefighters age out and leave the fire service, the remaining responders manage contracting departments, but a consistent call volume leads to a higher burnout rate, Elliott said.
“At some point, a system will fail,” he said.  
David Elliott boards an engine after responding to a call for his career job in Fairfield on Aug. 17, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
The next morning, after his 24-hour shift in Fairfield, during which he responded to medical calls and a fire at Sacred Heart University, Elliott began the drive home. Nearly two hours later, a quick stop at the farm stand in Woodstock transformed into a catch-up with Mrs. B. — Josh Bottone’s mother and Elliott’s neighbor — among the peaches and nectarines. He stopped for a bagel and cream cheese, washing it down with an iced coffee on the porch next to Finley. 
Elliott changed into a Bungay Fire Brigade polo and climbed into his pickup, riding to a meeting for water rescue access at a nearby lake in town.
The day had just begun.
David Elliott fills his gas tank along his route to work from Woodstock to Fairfield on Aug. 19, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

name: Kansas Reflector
title: After 9/11, this Kansas town forged an unlikely bond with the FDNY. It is honored in tumbling steel.
description: ANTHONY — Why? That’s the word that hovers over Memorial Park here, just before dusk on an evening in early September when the wind swells from the southwest and the swaying branches of the trees break the rays of the setting sun into dancing shafts of gold. text:
An American flag framed by twisted blocks of steel from the World Trade Center was seen Tuesday, Sep. 2, 2026, at Memorial Park at Anthony. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)ANTHONY — Why?
That’s the word that hovers over Memorial Park here, just before dusk on an evening in early September when the wind swells from the southwest and the swaying branches of the trees break the rays of the setting sun into dancing shafts of gold.
There is peace here, the kind of tranquility that settles over a small town at the drowsy end of the working day. This community of 2,108 in south central Kansas is like others across America, a one-stoplight town with a clock above the county courthouse that might as well have stopped decades ago.
But Anthony is different than other towns.
At Memorial Park, there are three chunks of twisted steel set above a brick and concrete base. The pieces are from the ruins of the World Trade Center and form a sculpture that seems to tumble from the blue prairie sky.
Anthony — founded in 1878 and named after the governor at the time — is the unlikely site of the state’s official 9/11 memorial. Another governor, Kathleen Sebelius, signed a bill in 2006 proclaiming the city as such, and not just because the city set a few pieces from a fallen tower of the World Trade Center on a pedestal.
In the days and weeks following the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, the residents of Anthony came together to support a ladder company in the Bronx that had lost colleagues in the twin towers. The town raised money, first for the Red Cross, then directly for the widow and children of a young fireman who died, and finally to create a memorial to the victims of 9/11 and to celebrate the friendship between the Kansas city and Engine 88, Ladder 38 of the New York department.
Donna Crowe was at work as a secretary at the Anthony Police Department that Tuesday morning, 25 years ago, when her husband called to say a plane had crashed into one of the World Trade Center towers in New York. She turned on the TV at the police department and, with the chief of police, watched on live television as a hijacked jet slammed into the other tower.
“We couldn’t believe it,” she told me. “And then it just started like a tumbling effect (with Washington and Shanksville). I can remember going outside and looking up in the sky, and it was this eerie feeling, the quietness of it. There were no planes in the sky, because they had grounded all the planes.”
Wichita is 60 miles by road to the northeast, and normally there would be commercial jets approaching or departing the national airport there.
Crowe struggled to explain what had happened to her children, an 11-year-old boy and a 10-year-old girl. They had watched the news at school and were frightened.
“For several days, we made pallets on the floor and slept together,” she said. “How do you explain it to them? I said there are some people in the world that are bad people and want to hurt others. It was hard to explain to them why, because I didn’t know. Why did it happen?”
Twenty-five years on, a library of books have been written trying to answer why. The facts give us the what but barely touch the why: Three hijacked commercial aircraft, part of a coordinated terrorist attack by al-Qaida, a Muslim militant group founded by Osama bin Laden, were flown into the World Trade Center towers in New York and the Pentagon at Washington, D.C. A fourth hijacked aircraft, United Airlines Flight 93, believed to be headed for either the White House or the U.S. Capitol, crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers who had been alerted to the previous attacks rushed the cockpit.
All told, it was the deadliest single day of terror attacks on American soil, with 2,977 dead, including the 19 hijackers who committed murder-suicide. Most of the victims died in New York, included 343 firefighters. But the numbers don’t reflect the first responders and others who died of illness related to toxin exposure at the trade center site.
Donna Crowe, a lifelong resident of Anthony, points to soil from the Flight 93 crash site, as incorporated into the town’s 9/11 memorial. Below the soil is a brick from the Pentagon. Crowe was chair of the committee that established the memorial. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)
The attacks kicked off the Global War on Terrorism and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, in which some 7,000 American troops and 8,000 contractors were killed. Indirect deaths from post-9/11 wars were estimated by a Brown University report at 4.5 million.
The day after Crowe watched the second tower fall on television at the Anthony police station, Mayor John Schott came to her at the city offices and had a task for her — they were going to adopt one of the first responders who had died.
She began researching but was soon overwhelmed by the names and photographs of the firemen who had died. She made calls to New York, but didn’t find anybody who was receptive.
“That last thing they wanted,” she said, “was to answer a call from Anthony, Kansas.”
But Schott kept trying.
Schott owned the local True Value hardware store and was serving his first year as mayor. He had relocated from Southern California, where he was a mid-level manager for Pacific Bell. Although his parents had been from Anthony, they were Baptist missionaries, and he was born and raised in the Philippines. Every few years the family would come back to the area and Schott would be re-introduced to small-town life. He had fond memories of riding his bike in Anthony, going to the local swimming pool, and visiting his grandparents in nearby Manchester, Oklahoma.
Schott wanted the same experience for his kids.
In the days after 9/11, Schott called the mayor’s office in New York and was eventually referred to Ladder Company 38, in the Belmont neighborhood of the Bronx.
“So I called them,” Schott said. “And the guy who answered the phone said ‘Hang on, let me get my lieutenant.’ And Joe Huber gets on the phone and says, ‘Yeah, what do you want?’ He was very, very skeptical, and he wouldn’t give me any information until he checked some stuff out.”
Huber called back and said one of the young men at their house, Joe Spor, had recently transferred to Rescue 3 and had been killed in the collapse of the south tower. Spor left a widow and four children, ages 6 years to 9 months.
Spor, 35, had joined the FDNY in 1994. He was a handyman who did carpentry work on the side, according to Schott, and his dream was to serve in the same rescue company his fireman father had, according to his obituary. The special operations rescue companies, of which there are only five, are the elite of the New York fire department.
Six others from Rescue 3 also died in the collapse.
Now that 25 years separates us from that Tuesday morning in September, the events have taken on the patina of history. At my elbow I have five books about the attacks, including a paperback copy of the official report of the 9/11 Commission, and all of them seem remote now, as do the histories we have here at home on the Vietnam War.
But there is one image that still conveys the terror and disorientation of the day, and that is the photo of the “Falling Man” by Associated Press photographer Richard Drew. Captured head-down in his tumble from the north tower, the unidentified man is seconds away from death. The image, at first denounced for its insensitivity, has become recognized as one of the most human images to come from the tragedy.
It not only conveys the plight of the doomed, but the sickening feeling of witnesses unable to help.
The Engine Company 88, Ladder Company 38 firehouse was built in 1908 and reamins in use today in the Belmont neighborhood of the Bronx. It has been designated a historic landmark by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission. (Photo from NYC Landmark Preservation Commission)
Both Schott and Crowe said they were driven by a motivation to do something — to do anything — . The only thing they could do was to raise money, so they organized bake sales and other community events. But Schott said it really wasn’t about the money, or the Christmas gifts that went to the Spor children. The money represented support, an effort from one tiny community in Kansas to connect in a meaningful way with the greatest of American cities that had suffered an unimaginable tragedy.
Huber, and other firefighters from Ladder 38, would eventually come to Anthony, to talk with the grade school children and attend ceremonies and make new friends. The school kids would make the firefighters Valentine’s Day cards and send them cookies.
“We just really became close to this day,” Crowe said. “I talk to (Huber) and other fireman every year on Sept. 11.”
For the memorial at the city park, Schott showed the same determination he had in finding Spor. Through Huber, he located some of the World Trade Center steel, and with the help of the national True Value cooperative managed to have it shipped to Anthony. A local artist, Sam Beam, made the design for how the pieces would be displayed, and welder Howard Hatfield put it together.
From a friend who worked at the Pentagon, Schott obtained a 250-pound limestone block from the Pentagon, and from another source received dirt and ashes from the Shanksville crash site. The block and the Shanksville material are displayed in the base of the monument.
Schott, who was mayor from 2001 to 2005 and now lives in Wichita, doesn’t remember how much money was collected for the Red Cross or Spor’s family, but he said the cost for the memorial was $80,000. All of it was raised through donations, he said, including the sale of bricks at the monument. Crowe became chair of the memorial committee, and Schott was its motor. The work, Schott said, made demands on him that at times felt uncomfortable.
“Actually, I’m an introvert,” Schott said. “It goes against everything in my body to do something public like that. But I grew up in a family that believed very strongly that you were put on this earth for a purpose. You do what you can, and what you can do is help other people.”
At an event at the Anthony memorial to commemorate the anniversary, Schott is expected to give a speech. He said he didn’t yet know what he was going to say, but that he would probably include a recitation of a Jewish prayer of remembrance. But what he really wanted to talk about was how, on 9/11, America was united.
“That’s not the case anymore,” he said. “What needs to happen is that we need to get back to understanding the golden rule, to respect and honor others, to reach out and help people when we are able.”
While the community came together to make the memorial a reality, Schott said, it wasn’t without internal soul-searching.
“In a small town this remote from New York or Pennsylvania or Washington, the question that came up a lot was, ‘Why?’ Why should we do a memorial? The simple answer is so that our children are able to feel, touch, and see actual pieces of what happened that day, so they won’t forget. There is evil in the world, but good people stand up and do something.”
Schott said the families of those who died on Sept. 11 need to know that their loved ones have not been forgotten, even 25 years later.
Crowe agreed.
“The connection, it’s terrible, it’s such a horrific ordeal that brought New York and Anthony together,” she said. “I just don’t want people to forget.”
There will be speeches at Memorial Park here, not just this month but in the years to come. There will be talk of patriotism and heroes, and candidates for public office will use the memorial as a backdrop for their own ambition. But with luck, the park will remain a place where, as the September sun dips low in the sky, one can contemplate the nature of sacrifice, compassion and the challenge of living in difficult times.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The longest commute
description: It seems only fitting on this, the 25th anniversary of the attacks that we remember those Connecticut commuters who perished.
text:
No single event in my lifetime had a greater impact than 9/11.  And for veteran commuters it is still fresh in their minds.  So I asked them to share some of those memories, excerpted below (longer remembrances can be found here).



Wrote one commuter: 
“I was just entering my office at 48th and Madison Avenue when building security told me that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. At first, I thought he must have been referring to a Cessna or some other small plane hitting a tower by accident.  It was only when I got upstairs to my office that I could see down Madison Avenue to the smoke rising from one of the towers.”  
After the attack, subway and train service was suspended, leaving commuters to get home via Grand Central Terminal on their own.
Another commuter’s recollection:
 “When we were finally able to leave the building I headed directly to Grand Central. It was still locked down and a crowd of people were waiting to get in to take a train out of the city. When they did let the crowd in I went to the front car. I remember the car had police in the front of the car and when we started to move through the tunnel to exit the terminal the police and engineer were looking at the tracks.  I didn’t understand why until later when it was explained to me that there were concerns that bombs had been placed in the tunnel. The train was so quiet and my last memory was a man in the car in a suit covered in grayish/ white dust.”  
And from another rider… 
“As the trains filled up, they left Grand Central Terminal.  I remember sitting across the aisle on the train back home from a guy who was wearing suit pants and an undershirt covered in soot, dirt, and smoke. He must have started the day with a jacket and tie, but lost them along the way. He talked a little about his experience trying to get out of the Wall Street area and said how many people were in distress and how he had stopped to help some as he made his way uptown. There were so many unsung heroes from that day who simply stopped to help others in need. I think that’s how he lost his jacket, shirt, and tie.”
And from a Stamford commuter…
“The commute back from Manhattan to Stamford that day was quite eerie. Although business had immediately shut down, it took a while for Grand Central Terminal to be secured and reopened. Once it did, the walk to the terminal was eerily quiet. When we pulled in to Stamford Station, the taxi staging area was filled with ambulances.”
Retired Captain Thom Lombard from the Stamford Police Department remembers:
“On September 11 I was the Emergency Management Director for Stamford. We were notified that remains of victims would be brought to Stamford.  I made arrangements for the use of refrigerated trucks and enlisted the assistance of local funeral directors to store remains in their facilities.  All but one agreed to assist.  No bodies were recovered (that day).”
But the pain of 9-11 didn’t end that day, as David Parent of Wallingford recounts: 
“What I remember most was what I never saw: the family and friends who had to go to the train station parking lots to retrieve the cars of loved ones who were never coming home.”
“Connecticut Explored” magazine’s Fall 2026 issue contains photos of some of the memorials to 9-11 in our state, including a discreet plaque at the Glenbrook Station honoring Sean Rooney who died in the south tower after climbing stairs to try to reach the roof hoping for rescue, which never came.  
And in Westport at Sherwood Island State Park is a more impressive, black granite memorial with 161 names, many of them commuters.
In Sherwood Island State Park is the Living Memorial for the 161 people with ties to Connecticut who los their lives in the 9/11 attacks.  Credit: Luke G. Boyd, Connecticut Explored Magazine / Connecticut Explored Magazine
It seems only fitting on this, the 25th anniversary of the attacks that we remember those Connecticut commuters who perished.  Let’s keep them and all of their loved ones in our thoughts this week.
Special thanks to Connecticut Explored magazine and photographer Luke G. Boyd.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Critics of the Legislature’s productivity ignore a key legal distinction setting Mass. apart from nearly all other states
description: It is easy to see how that storyline can spark the ire of voters and the scorn of opinion writers.  But it is a fundamentally flawed reading of legislative productivity for reasons that are virtually never acknowledged amid the easy targeting of lawmakers.
text:
EVEN-NUMBERED YEARS are always memorable on Beacon Hill, with a flurry of activity to get bills over the legislative finish line. As I write this, conference committees are working to deliver major bills to the governor’s desk before the end of the 2025-26 legislative session.  
As attention turns to the big pieces of legislation awaiting final action, an accompanying narrative invariably gets a good airing: Massachusetts has the least productive legislature in the country, with lawmakers who pass few bills across the state’s two-year legislative session.  
It is easy to see how that storyline can spark the ire of voters and the scorn of opinion writers.  But it is a fundamentally flawed reading of legislative productivity for reasons that are virtually never acknowledged amid the easy targeting of lawmakers.  
As counsel to the Massachusetts Senate, I’m constantly reminded of the flaw in those attacks by reflecting on my experience at the end of a legislative session in a very different state. More than 20 years ago, during my third year of law school at the University of Virginia, I was a legal fellow in the Virginia governor’s office. On the final days of the Virginia legislative session in Richmond, I marveled at the stacks and stacks of approved bills that were delivered to the governor’s desk. The volume of bills was rather breathtaking, but the scope of each bill was sometimes painfully narrow. 
That’s because Virginia is one of 43 states that have constitutions that limit all or most legislation to a single subject, a limitation known as the “single subject” rule. 
The situation in Massachusetts is markedly different. The Bay State is one of only seven states—along with Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Rhode Island, Connecticut, and North Carolina—that have no such limitations. Similar to Congress, which has no single-subject limitations, the Massachusetts Legislature is allowed to pass a bill touching as many topics as it wants. There are no single-subject limitations in the Commonwealth’s constitution, statutes, or legislative rules. 
It’s precisely because of that distinction between Massachusetts and most other states that I bristle at the disingenuous but persistent claim that Massachusetts has the least productive, least effective state legislature in the country.  
That bold claim has become a popular soundbite across a range of media, including The Boston Globe and CommonWealth Beacon. For support, the Legislature’s critics usually cite a 2021 report by the Washington-based information company FiscalNote, which listed the Massachusetts Legislature last among the 50 state legislatures for the percentage of bills passed relative to the number introduced. 
It’s worth noting right off the bat that claims related to “effectiveness” and “productivity” are highly subjective. By what metric can such things be measured in a legislative context? Is productivity judged by the raw number of bills passed in a legislative session, or by the breadth and potency of the policies enacted? 
On a purely factual basis, however, any discussion of legislative productivity that ignores the single-subject rule is highly unsound. Failure to consider the single-subject rule in such a discussion leaves one with an incomplete picture—even a falsity—when the quantity of bills filed and passed is the ultimate metric. 
When I hear the Legislature’s critics cling to the claim of legislative ineffectiveness while ignoring the single-subject rule, I’m reminded of the Republican congressman in 1974 who, when confronted with the mounting evidence of President Richard Nixon’s alleged misdeeds, stated unabashedly: “Don’t confuse me with the facts…I will not vote for impeachment.” 
So let’s look at that frequently cited 2021 report by FiscalNote. With respect to enacting bills, the top four states in that report—each of which enacted between 2,000 and 4,000 bills in the 2021 legislative session—are all single-subject states (Texas, Virginia, Tennessee, and New York). 
Only two of the top 30 legislatures for enacting legislation in 2021 were not single-subject jurisdictions (Rhode Island and Maine). The other five states without a single-subject rule (Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont, Connecticut, and North Carolina) were in the bottom tier. While FiscalNote updates its rankings annually, there has been little movement in the top — or bottom — states year-over-year. 
Those who understand the single-subject rule do not find FiscalNote’s data surprising. Typically, in a single-subject state, the legislature will pass a great many bills in any given legislative session, as it really has no other option but to pass lots of bills when no bill can contain more than one subject. There’s no such thing as an omnibus bill in those states. 
Compare that to Massachusetts, where a single bill in the Legislature could—and often does—contain many discrete subjects.  One need only look at one of Beacon Hill’s recently passed budget bills – with lots of policy riders — or economic development bills to see how many separate policies and topics can be effectively addressed in a single piece of legislation here. 
Now it’s fine if you don’t like omnibus bills, but facts matter. Comparing the productivity of the Massachusetts Legislature to that of any of the 43 state legislatures that are bound by the single-subject rule is neither fair nor reasonable. And when you also factor in that most states have separate legislative sessions each calendar year rather than a continuous two-year legislative session like Massachusetts—well, the annual state-to-state comparison attempted by FiscalNote starts to feel downright absurd. 
To be clear, it’s not my job as Senate counsel to defend senators from criticism of their productivity. But it is my job to know the Constitution and to advise senators accordingly. Knowing the crucial difference between states that are bound by a single-subject rule and those — like Massachusetts — that are not, I have been shocked by the absence of reporting on this key legal distinction. 
I’ve never seen even one article mention the single-subject rule in a discussion comparing the Massachusetts Legislature’s productivity and effectiveness to other state legislatures. The oversight is equivalent to saying that US presidents since Franklin Roosevelt have all failed to win third terms, but neglecting to mention that the 22nd Amendment barred them from doing so. 
Detractors are entitled to their opinions about the Massachusetts Legislature, and they are free to criticize it as they want. But it’s their responsibility to not disseminate incomplete narratives devoid of the relevant legal context. 
It’s time for the Legislature’s critics to start getting a little more confused by the facts. 
James DiTullio is counsel to the Massachusetts Senate.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota governor, challenger both slam Trump on beef imports but clash on other debate topics
description: HURON — Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers both criticized President Donald Trump on Saturday during a debate at the South Dakota State Fair, with Rhoden saying he agrees with Trump on other issues but could not support the president’s decision to import more foreign beef. “I thought he was wrongheaded in […]
text:
South Dakota's candidates for governor, Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden chat with attendees at the South Dakota State Fair in Huron on Sept. 5, 2026. (Photos by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)HURON — Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers both criticized President Donald Trump on Saturday during a debate at the South Dakota State Fair, with Rhoden saying he agrees with Trump on other issues but could not support the president’s decision to import more foreign beef.
“I thought he was wrongheaded in his logic, and the things that came out of that administration trying to defend it, I think, were weak,” Rhoden said.
Trump endorsed Rhoden last month. Rhoden said he plans to press U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins to create an advisory committee so Trump has better information “before he makes decisions like that and then gets in front of a microphone.”
“He’s kind of an impulsive guy,” Rhoden said.

Trump announced last month that he would pause tariffs on imported beef, which he said would bring prices down for consumers and allow U.S. ranchers to build up their herds from historically low levels. The backlash from U.S. cattle ranchers was swift.
Ahlers said the announcement was not the first time the Trump administration suggested importing more foreign beef, and Ahlers said the state has to be “a stronger advocate for our farmers and ranchers.” He said that means working with South Dakota’s congressional delegation to apply more pressure on Trump.
The two candidates disagreed on several other issues during the debate, which was their first since each of them won their respective party’s nomination. The debate was hosted on the fair’s Freedom Stage by the South Dakota Farmers Union.
Economic development spending
Ahlers said the governor’s economic development office has favored recruiting out-of-state companies over funding homegrown ventures. He said a Wakonda hemp producer built a hemp-based concrete plant in another state after failing to secure incentives to build it in South Dakota.
“Those are companies that are in our hometowns, that make our hometowns better, that pay better, and have people that invest right back here in South Dakota,” Ahlers said.
Rhoden said roughly 85% of the office’s economic development dollars stay in South Dakota. He said the department supported the three largest economic development projects in state history during the past several years: the Smithfield pork plant being relocated from downtown to northern Sioux Falls, CJ Schwan’s breaking ground in that city on a food production plant, and a new soybean crushing plant in Mitchell.
“We do a lot to promote ag,” Rhoden said.



 The archived livestream of the Sept. 5, 2026, debate at the South Dakota State Fair between Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers. (Courtesy of South Dakota Farmers Union)
On Medicaid expansion
A state constitutional amendment placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by the Legislature would repeal the requirement to offer expanded Medicaid eligibility if federal funding for it drops below 90%.
Medicaid is a federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes. In 2022, South Dakota voters expanded Medicaid eligibility from traditional coverage groups such as children, disabled people and the elderly to adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level. About 31,000 South Dakotans are enrolled through the expansion, out of a total of about 143,000 South Dakotans enrolled in Medicaid, according to data from the state Department of Social Services.
Ahlers said that after voters approved Medicaid expansion, Republican lawmakers are trying to undo the people’s will. He warned that rolling back Medicaid eligibility would threaten the financial viability of rural hospitals, maternity units and emergency rooms. He noted a majority of Medicaid recipients are children.

“We know that when we have healthcare, and everyone has access to it, we all do better,” Ahlers said.
Rhoden said the ballot measure would only remove the requirement to continue with expanded eligibility if federal funding drops below 90%. He opposed expansion, he said, over concerns about the federal government one day pulling funding.
“When we have $40 trillion in debt in our nation, you can bet the feds are going to be kicking that down to the states,” Rhoden said.
Separating ag and environment departments
Former Gov. Kristi Noem merged the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources by executive order, creating the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources.
Ahlers said he would restore a standalone Department of Agriculture with its own secretary.
“These two departments have different missions, although they do work together on projects,” Ahlers said. “It is important that each has their own voice and a seat at the table.”
Rhoden defended the merger, saying criticisms that it supported agriculture at the expense of environmental protection were unfair.
“Nobody on the planet has a more vested interest in protecting our environment and our natural resources, and the sustainability of our ag land, than the people that are producing on that ag land,” Rhoden said.
Rhoden, of rural Union Center, has been governor since early 2025, when he was elevated from lieutenant governor after then-Gov. Noem resigned to take a job in the Trump administration. Ahlers is a businessman and former legislator from Dell Rapids.
The two candidates will face each other in the general election Nov. 3. Advance voting begins Sept. 18, and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Patagonia, environmental groups revive old legal fights against new cuts to national monuments
description: Opponents of President Donald Trump’s decision to sharply downsize two Utah national monuments in July are re-upping their argument that he didn’t have the authority to do so. Retailer Patagonia, environmental groups and tribal organizations waged legal battles against Trump in 2017 after he ordered prior reductions of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalant[...]
text:
The Bears Ears buttes, namesake of the Bears Ears National Monument, are pictured on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Opponents of President Donald Trump’s decision to sharply downsize two Utah national monuments in July are re-upping their argument that he didn’t have the authority to do so.
Retailer Patagonia, environmental groups and tribal organizations waged legal battles against Trump in 2017 after he ordered prior reductions of Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments. The cases went dormant when former President Joe Biden restored the boundaries in 2021.
Now that the president has redrawn the boundaries even smaller than he did almost a decade ago, the environmental groups said Wednesday they requested permission to file two updated lawsuits in federal court in Washington, D.C. Retailer Patagonia also filed a new suit over the Bears Ears reductions.
The new court filings say Trump’s orders leave the landscapes open to hard rock mining and oil, gas and coal leases. And they note mining claims have been filed in recent weeks on lands cut out of the new boundaries.
Steve Bloch, legal director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, called the reductions unlawful and said in a prepared statement that “we intend to make sure Trump doesn’t have the final word over the fate of these treasured landscapes.”
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rodgers did not directly respond to the allegations in a statement to Utah News Dispatch, but focused on actions by Trump’s Democratic predecessors.
“The Obama and Biden administrations abused the Antiquities Act to lock up millions of acres of Utah’s public lands,” Rodgers said in a prepared statement. She went on to say that Trump “rightsized the Bears Ears National Monument to allow for common sense land use in these areas.”
In his first term in the White House, Trump slashed Bears Ears from roughly 1.35 million acres to roughly 228,000 acres, and Grand Staircase-Escalante from about 1.87 million acres to roughly 1 million acres. In the more dramatic cuts in July, he cut Bears Ears to about 121,000 acres and Grand Staircase-Escalante to about 182,000 acres.
Other presidents have whittled down boundaries. In the biggest change prior to 2017, President Woodrow Wilson shrunk Mount Olympus National Monument in Washington state by about half in 1915, cutting out more than 313,000 acres.
Conservationists say when Congress approved the Federal Land Policy and Management Act in 1976, it required congressional review for cuts of more than 5,000 acres. The law didn’t change the Antiquities Act of 1906, which allows presidents to proclaim national monuments but doesn’t say anything about canceling or shrinking them.
The U.S. Department of Justice sees it differently. In a legal opinion last year, the department concluded a president who finds sites “never were or no longer are deserving of the Act’s protections” can in fact eliminate the land from a national monument.
State leaders have long condemned the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante as unnecessarily big and restrictive. Utah’s Republican governor, House speaker and congressional delegation joined Trump in the Oval Office as signed the orders.
Former President Bill Clinton designated Grand Staircase-Escalante in 1996. Bears Ears, established by then President Barack Obama in 2016, was the first monument in the nation created at the urging of Native American tribes to whom the land is sacred.
It’s been managed jointly by the U.S. government and the Bears Ears Commission made up of five tribal nations: the Hopi Tribe, Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Zuni Tribe and Ute Indian Tribe. But Trump’s order on Bears Ears is ending that partnership, terminating the federal agencies’ agreement with the commission.
The environmental groups want the courts to order the monuments restored to full size and void any mining claims or mineral leases that were based on Trump’s proclamations in 2017 and 2021.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee man wrongly accused of threatening the president still facing deportation
description: Months after Ramón Morales Reyes was falsely accused by the Department of Homeland Security of penning letters threatening to assassinate President Donald Trump, his children Ana and Antonio say that their family continues to live in fear while awaiting the outcome of their father’s deportation case.  “My dad was framed for something that he did […]
text:
Antonio Morales (center left) and his sister Ana (center right) share their experiences since their father was wrongly accused of threatening President Donald Trump. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Months after Ramón Morales Reyes was falsely accused by the Department of Homeland Security of penning letters threatening to assassinate President Donald Trump, his children Ana and Antonio say that their family continues to live in fear while awaiting the outcome of their father’s deportation case. 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
“My dad was framed for something that he did not do, and DHS knew exactly what they posted beforehand,” Ana Morales, 25, said at a press conference Friday at the Milwaukee office of Voces de la Frontera. “As a daughter, seeing my dad being framed for something he did not do was very heartbreaking,” she added.
Attorney Mark Thomsen said the family is seeking $5 million in damages caused by the federal government’s accusations against Morales Reyes, which the agency has yet to retract. Thomsen was joined by immigration attorney Cain Oulahan, Morales Reyes’ children, Voces de la Frontera Executive Director Christine Neumann-Oritz, and Milwaukee Turners Executive Director Emilio de Torre. 
Accused of something he didn’t do
In May 2025, Morales Reyes, then 54, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, leaving his unoccupied vehicle on the roadside. Voces de la Frontera received a hotline call reporting the arrest. 
Born in Mexico, Morales Reyes has lived in the United States since 1986. His family described him as a hard worker and proud family man, who worked as a dishwasher.
His arrest came as the Trump administration ramped up arrests and deportations in 2025, the deadliest year in two decades for people being detained by ICE. Trump pledged to go after “the worst of the worst.” 
Morales Reyes had two encounters with law enforcement, both dating back to 1996, according to NPR. One was a hit-and-run incident in which he was arrested but not charged. The other was a disorderly conduct and property damage ticket relating to a dispute with his wife.
Attorney’s Mark Thomsen (far left) and Cain Oulahan (right) explain the case involving Ramon Morales-Reyes. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem posted a statement on her agency’s website calling Morales Reyes an “illegal alien who threatened to assassinate President Trump.” 
DHS also released images of a letter, handwritten in English, that said: “we are tired of this president messing with us Mexicans” and stating “I will self deport myself back to Mexico but not before I use my 30 yard 6 to shoot your precious president in is head — I will see him at one of his big ralleys .” The reference to “30 yard 6”appears to be an incorrectly written reference to the high caliber rifle round .30-06.
Morales Reyes couldn’t have written the letter, however, his family, attorneys, and advocates said, since he could not speak English and did not read or write proficiently even in Spanish. 
Morales Reyes had applied for a U-visa, granted to victims of crimes, after he was  assaulted during an armed robbery in September 2023. Detectives from the Milwaukee Police Department were actively investigating whether someone was trying to frame him when ICE agents arrested him and publicized the  accusation that he was a would-be assassin. It was later determined that a man who had been arrested for assaulting Morales Reyes had written the letter in an effort to get him deported before he could testify in court.
Lasting harm
In June 2025, Morales-Reyes was released from ICE custody on bond. Yet he continues to face deportation proceedings, with a hearing expected in December in which a judge may make a decision on whether Morales Reyes can remain in the country. The family has received online harassment and threats since Morales Reyes was accused of writing the letter, Ana Morales said.
“He’s been going through depression, anxiety,” she said during the Friday press conference. “He doesn’t like going out anymore because he feels like everyone knows him due to what he was framed as. And ever since, it has taken a lot from us.” 
Emilio de Torre, executive director of the Milwaukee Turners. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Ana’s brother Antonio Morales took over the mic when  his sister began to cry. “They really wanted to make this hurt us as much as possible, inflict as much pain, and they knew what they were doing intentionally,” he said of the Homeland Security arrest and accusations against his father.
“It was hard seeing your dad all over social media posted as some sort of, you know, some sort of assassin almost,” he added. “And that’s just not who my father is. Anyone who knows my father knows that isn’t him. It was just really scary seeing all those comments online, the fear that it caused my family seeing how everybody just…threatening us online over something that was just a false accusation. And I really think DHS knew that. I really think that they knew what they were doing. They wanted to do this to us. They want to do this to more immigrants, and they really want to keep terrorizing the community going forward.”
Thomsen asked members of the public to “imagine learning on social media that your father, or your grandfather, or your uncle, or your brother, or your sister was being accused of attempting to kill the president of the United States.” He added, “Imagine what that means, and then imagine that the person that is saying it is the strongest government in the world. … This was a lie, and they knew it was a lie. The lie is still up.”
Gesturing to Ana and Antonio Morales, he said, “Check it out folks, these are two young people with the courage to stand up to the biggest government on the planet, the most powerful government on the planet, and say, ‘Do the right thing America.’ If these two young folks can do it, everybody sitting at home safely can do it.”
Looking ahead
Although DHS has said in subsequent statements that Morales Reyes is no longer under investigation for threatening the president, the agency has continued to call for his deportation. Noem’s original press release accusing him of the assassination threat is still up on the government website. The Wisconsin Examiner reached out to DHS asking specifically whether the agency plans to remove the post and correct the record. The agency has not responded. 
Ana Morales (left) and Antonio Morales (right) (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Oulahan said that although Morales Reyes has a hearing in December, if a judge decides to deport him, he could remain in the country while his case is appealed. Thomsen said that the federal government has six months to respond to the family’s claim for compensation under the federal Tort Act, after which filing a civil lawsuit would be an option. Thomsen stressed, however, that avenues of recourse against the federal government are limited and that the second Trump administration has shown a willingness to violate or disregard court orders. 
De Torre said the federal government is “deceiving the public about everyday people.”
“They’re disrupting us emotionally, as you can see from Ana and Antonio. … It is disrupting our economy. It is disrupting our ability to attend houses of worship, go to school, and bring home food for our families. And on top of this, they then deny that they are doing this. Telling us that what we see is not real. How we feel and how we’re suffering is an illusion. And I’m sitting here today to say this is not so.”
Asked to describe some of her favorite memories of her father, Ana recalled how he would take her to the park and bike riding, one of his favorite activities. “I remember as a little kid on his days off I would always want corn, I’m obsessed with corn even to this day,” she said. Despite working second shift her father would always make time, she said. 
Antonio described his father as fond of video games. “He definitely made me a gamer,” he said. Occasionally Morales Reyes would let his son play. “I was just so amazed by these games,” he recalled, smiling. “It was really fun.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Klobuchar, Demuth pound pavement at the Minnesota State Fair in campaign for governor
description: After 20 consecutive years shaking sweaty hands and waving to babies at the Minnesota State Fair, Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her baby blue cottage-style booth is as much a fixture here as greasy cheese curds and costumed llamas. Arriving at the crowded Agriculture Horticulture building with a slew of staffers and a photographer on […]
text:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, and Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers and supporters Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 at the Minnesota State Fair. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)After 20 consecutive years shaking sweaty hands and waving to babies at the Minnesota State Fair, Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar and her baby blue cottage-style booth is as much a fixture here as greasy cheese curds and costumed llamas.
Arriving at the crowded Agriculture Horticulture building with a slew of staffers and a photographer on Friday morning, Klobuchar began another day of greeting supporters fanning themselves and sucking on frozen apple cider pops.
One of them was Andy Stoltmann of Rosemount. She asked where he lived and then told him that Rosemount is a growing city, which will be good for the local economy.
“It’s nice to see political people walking around, see them for real instead of seeing them on TV,” Stoltmann said.
The Reformer caught back up with Klobuchar in the Horticulture building’s bee and honey section.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters in the bees and honey section of the horticulture building during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
“You missed me. I found the queen bee,” Klobuchar informed the Reformer. She went back to the hive on display and found the queen bee again.
Klobuchar and her Republican opponent for governor, House Speaker Lisa Demuth, have both spent nearly every day at the fair to get in front of voters who aren’t at home to see their television ads.
Numerous polls show Klobuchar leading against Demuth for Minnesota governor. Klobuchar is serving her fourth term in the U.S. Senate and was first elected to her seat in 2006. Demuth has served as Minnesota House speaker for nearly two years and is serving her fourth term in the Minnesota House. She was first elected in 2018.
Demuth spent many hours at her booth listening to the concerns of Minnesotans, most notably the fraud in Minnesota’s social safety net programs that occurred under Gov. Tim Walz’s watch. The House speaker — and Minnesota Republicans in general — are hoping voters’ frustration with fraud will propel them to their first statewide win in 20 years.
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth talks to fairgoers at her campaign booth for Minnesota governor during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
The House speaker on Aug. 28 spoke in the fair’s Lee & Rose Warner Coliseum where students were presenting their beef heifers for awards. Klobuchar was also there and spoke first, receiving a loud cheer from the audience and name-dropping a few Minnesota beef cattle ranchers, including Haley Ammann, who wrote a children’s book about one of her calves.
“We need more domestic beef, right?” Klobuchar asked the cheering crowd. “We do not need foreign beef on an unfair playing field for our cattle ranchers. I will stand up for that.”
Klobuchar was referring to President Donald Trump’s signing of a proclamation last month that would allow 300,000 metric tons of beef to enter the U.S. at a reduced tariff rate. The move has angered many cattle ranchers who are concerned that the foreign beef would hinder domestic profits for U.S. producers.
Demuth didn’t mention Trump’s beef tariff exemption, though she has said it would not be good for Minnesota ranchers.
Demuth did offer one subtle jab at Klobuchar after she left the coliseum:
“I will agree with you all in this room that the Minnesota State Fair is the best state fair in the country.”
It’s a reference to Klobuchar’s 2020 bid for president when she refused to declare the Minnesota State Fair the best in the country while campaigning hard in Iowa. Klobuchar has since said that Minnesota has the best state fair.
Demuth grew up in central Minnesota and represents a rural, agriculture-heavy district. While students presented their heifers for awards, Demuth quipped to her staffers that she had never heard of that particular breed as the student and heifer galloped by and, in one black heifers’ case, said, “That one is particularly spicy” as it repeatedly shook its head and huffed.
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth speaks while 4H members show their cows at the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
After congratulating the 4-H students, Demuth began to trek back to her booth. Outside the coliseum, a 6-year-old stopped her and asked her to sign his “I’m a Lisa fan” fan.
Demuth later said she wondered whether she should have signed her name in cursive, as the boy probably wouldn’t be able to read it.
On Aug. 28, Demuth told the Reformer she was waiting to get a funnel cake from her favorite booth, Auntie M’s, which happens to be based in Paynesville — her district. She finally indulged on Sept. 1. 
Demuth has spent hours in front of her campaign booth — across the street from the Ball Park Cafe’s garlic fries — assuring supporters waiting in line to see her that she will bring “common sense” back to Minnesota. Her running mate, Ryan Wilson, echoed her sentiments while several times offering to take photos of Demuth with the people lined up to meet her.
Demuth greeted and took selfies with people wearing “Trump 2028” hats and nodded as people told her they were tired of Minnesota being a nationwide news bite because of fraud.
A mannequin dressed like Donald Trump stands with a Trump 2028 hat, which the booth also sells, at the Minnesota GOP booth at the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
One was Mike Oliver of Mankato, who said he’s tired of the lack of oversight in government programs.
“It’s not just the fraud. The excess spending, no accountability. There’s so many people that moved to Minnesota because of handouts,” he said.
Demuth said the state fair is different this year for her because she now has her own booth, and people are recognizing her and sharing their thoughts with her about how Minnesota is being run.
“The fair puts policy and politics into perspective if people want to have that conversation, and I think that’s a really good thing where it’s not all consuming. You can have these conversations and … go out and grab food or a ride,” Demuth said.
Klobuchar said people want to talk about her run for governor and her plans, but they also thank her for her office’s help getting a passport for a wedding or with adoption paperwork, for example.
“There are plenty of people that will bring things up that they’re worried about, and you talk to them about that. Then other people just want you to see their kid or their new baby,” Klobuchar said. “People know me, and I think trust me around here.” 
Sen. Amy Klobuchar talks to fairgoers and supporters during the Minnesota State Fair Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Lt. Gov. Dahlstrom reverses herself, puts Treg Taylor back in governor’s race
description: Late Friday night, Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said she will reverse a decision she made Monday and will certify former attorney general Treg Taylor as a final-four candidate in Alaska’s race for governor. Taylor’s reinstatement means he replaces his lieutenant governor, Candi English, who had taken Taylor’s spot as the fourth candidate in the […]
text:
Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor speaks at a news conference on Thursday, Dec. 15, 2022, at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)Late Friday night, Alaska Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said she will reverse a decision she made Monday and will certify former attorney general Treg Taylor as a final-four candidate in Alaska’s race for governor.
Taylor’s reinstatement means he replaces his lieutenant governor, Candi English, who had taken Taylor’s spot as the fourth candidate in the race. Taylor’s wife, Jodi, had taken English’s spot as the lieutenant governor candidate.
Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in the August primary, followed by Republican candidates Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Taylor.
In Alaska, the top four candidates from the primary, regardless of political party, advance to the November general election.
Dahlstrom’s decision came five days after she disqualified Taylor and a state House candidate, Jose Tagle, for failing to provide personal financial information on time, as required by state law. 
Dahlstrom also restored Tagle, the sole opponent against Rep. Ted Eischeid, D-Anchorage, to the ballot.
The Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates political candidates and campaigns, had recommended that the two be disqualified.
That recommendation was still in place on Friday night, but Dahlstrom said the Department of Law — which Taylor led until last year — had conducted an independent review of candidates’ financial disclosure statements.
That review, which Dahlstrom did not release Friday night, showed ”numerous potential discrepancies between filed statements and public records,” Dahlstrom said in a written statement.
“On the basis of that additional information, the Lieutenant Governor will certify the two candidates,” Dahlstrom’s statement said.
Starting last year, the Alaska Public Offices Commission had raised concerns about Taylor’s financial disclosure form, which did not list hundreds of tenants who rent from Taylor. Taylor and his wife bought Anchorage’s Inlet View Tower in 2023. 
Taylor registered as a candidate for office on June 1, submitting a new public officer financial disclosure form. State law allows 30 days for amendments, but Taylor’s form wasn’t amended with the partial names of renters until late July.
Because of that missed deadline, the Public Offices Commission voted 4-1 in late August to recommend that Taylor be disqualified. The commission also recommended that Tagle, who had filed a blank disclosure form, be disqualified. Dahlstrom adopted both recommendations on Aug. 31. 
Since then, concerns had been raised about possible omissions by other candidates, including Wilson, whose personal financial disclosure form did not disclose her ownership of Denali Disposal, a garbage company. 
Unlike Taylor’s case, no formal complaint had been filed before the primary.
“The Department of Law’s informal review has raised questions about the recommendations made on August 31,” said Dahlstrom in her statement. “I will not withhold certification from two candidates on recommendations that, in light of this additional information, I cannot apply with confidence across the field of candidates. Certification decisions have to rest on a process that can be defended as to every candidate.”
Taylor, who previously called on Republican candidates to consolidate their campaigns, issued a statement celebrating the decision.
The former attorney general said his campaign has “been about standing up to political insiders and special interests.”
“Candi and I are running to end these types of political games and put power back where it belongs: with Alaskans. Alaskans should decide our elections. Not political insiders. Not special interests. Not the establishment,” Taylor said.
The first ballots for Alaska’s November general election are scheduled to be mailed to voters starting Sept. 18.

name: VTDigger
title: Hartford considers a stricter car camping ban
description:
Some selectboard members worried it would create more hardship for people experiencing homelessness and criminalize them for being unhoused.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hartford considers a stricter car camping ban.
text:
Anthony Heath walks past the Upper Valley Haven’t Leahy Shelter and Resource Center on his way to charge his phone in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, June 18, 2026. The low-barrier shelter is on schedule to be completed in September, said Haven Executive Director Will Towne. “Hopefully I get a room in it if I’m still homeless,” said Heath who is living in a tent. Photo by James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Sept. 2, 2026.
HARTFORD — The town is grappling with a possible addition to its parking rules to clearly define “camping,” which is prohibited in municipal lots.
Some selectboard members worried it would create more hardship for people experiencing homelessness and criminalize them for being unhoused.
Town Manager Gail Ostrout said she receives “100 messages a week” regarding vehicles that remain parked for an extended period and create hazards. With the current ordinance, police are not able to take action, aside from writing a ticket.
Hartford Police proposed adding a definition of camping to the town’s parking ordinance, Chapter 220, which reads:
“A person shall be deemed to be camping if they occupy a tent or other temporary shelter, or if they use a motor vehicle, recreational vehicle, trailer, or other conveyance as a residence or place to keep the majority of their personal belongings or household possessions, regardless of whether the person sleeps in the vehicle overnight.”
Already, the ordinance states that camping or overnight sleeping is not permitted in municipal lots, and violators will be towed. However, without a definition of camping, there’s too much gray area to enforce, said Lt. William Furnari of the Hartford Police community outreach division.
“We are not going out of our way looking for cars to tow. We are trying to address those folks who, through a pattern of behavior like this, are living in the parking lot in a way that is unsafe to folks,” said Furnari.
Selectboard member Miranda Dupre worries the definition is too subjective and is hesitant about the idea of making it “basically illegal to be homeless and safe,” she said at the meeting.
She further expressed that those without residences may be safest sleeping in their car there and could just need somewhere to rest without bothering anyone.
“Where else do they go?” said Dupre.
Furnari argued that other community members aren’t feeling safe with the current situation of people essentially living in the public lots. Specifically, he pointed to those who disturb the peace and leave waste outside of the vehicle.
“We found some pretty bad stuff that we don’t want in our parking lot that could make people sick,” said Furnari.
Selectboard member Ashley Andreas said she worries this new definition will lead to police hassling more people and that the language could apply to people who aren’t causing problems, including those who simply keep most of their belongings in the car or are struggling to find housing.
Andreas added that if police could provide alternative suggestions to the people told to leave, such as a different piece of land where camping may be more appropriate, it could help “address this problem more structurally before bringing on more enforcement,” she said.
While there is a strong effort to coordinate resources, it’s not always successful, said Ostrout.
“Everyone in the police department has made an attempt to be sensitive to people’s struggles and tried to come up with creative solutions around that,” said Ostrout.
Dupre said she worries the stricter ordinance could drive more people onto private properties as a last resort.
With police now enforcing metered street parking and directing more people to the free South Main parking lot, Furnari said, the community has an incentive to make sure it’s safe and accessible for everyone.
Further, removal does not equate to an arrest.
“It’s a civil violation. It’s a traffic ticket or municipal ticket. I just want to clarify: It’s not an arrest,” said Chief Constance Kelley. “There’s no criminal affectation to it.”
Erik Krauss, the vice chair of the selectboard, said that although he appreciated the intent, the proposed definition, as it stands, is “not well crafted.” He suggested reaching out to the Vermont League of Cities and Towns for advice and referencing how other municipalities have defined camping before Hartford changes its ordinance.
The selectboard is passing along questions and requests regarding the new definition so Hartford Police can possibly return with a new version at the next regular meeting on Sept. 15 in Hartford Town Hall.
